## An AI-Driven Framework for Predictive **Modeling and Early Warning of Dam Spills **

Akanksha Singh 1( B ), Syed Wajahat Abbas Rizvi 1, and Prabhat kr. Srivastava 2 1 Amity University, Lucknow 226028, Uttar Pradesh, India

ankakaanjphd@gmail.com 2 IMS Engineering College, Ghaziabad 201015, Uttar Pradesh, India

**Abstract. ** This study proposes the design and development of an artiﬁcial intelligence (AI)-based system for dam spill prediction and early warning in order to improve dam safety and reduce ﬂood risks. Flood responses are often delayed by the inaccuracy and time-consuming nature of traditional spill forecast techniques, which rely on human operations and traditional hydrological models. To produce reproducibility and accurate forecasts, our model uses data from NASA POWER API and Central Water Commission/State Water Resources Department including elements, such as rainfall, reservoir levels, inﬂow/outﬂow rates, and soil moisture. In order to predict spill incidents, the system examines both historical and current data using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for time-series forecasting. We also provide a dynamic early warning system (EWS) that can notify important stakeholders of alerts by SMS, email, and mobile notiﬁcations. The outcomes show that, in comparison to traditional methods, the AI framework improves forecasting accuracy and response efﬁciency. For proactive catastrophe risk reduction, our research enables integration with national ﬂood forecasting systems and advances dam management methods. Proposed LSTM ﬂood prediction model was superior with an accuracy of 96%, precision of 98%, recall of 91%, and an F1-score of 0.95, outperforming conventional models such as Auto Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) with accuracy of 82%, F1-score near 0.78 and Support Vector Machine SVM with accuracy of 79%, F1-score of about 0.75, Random Forest (RF) reached an accuracy of 88% (F1 = 0.82) and XGBoost achieved 90% accuracy (F1 = 0.85). These result highlights improvements of LSTM over ARIMA and SVM by 14-17% points in accuracy and 17-20% in F1-score. Against advanced ML baselines (RF, XGBoost), it achieves an additional 6-8%in accuracy and 10-13% in F1-score, demonstrating the robustness and effectiveness of the LSTM framework for predictive ﬂ ood modelling.

**Keywords: ** Prediction · Dam-spill · AI-networks · Long short-term memory · Early warning system

## 1 **Introduction **

## Dams are essential pieces of infrastructure for ﬂood control, irrigation, water storage,

and hydropower production. However, improper management of water levels and spills can have catastrophic consequences, such as erosion, ﬂooding, damage to infrastructure,

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 94-102, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_7>

An AI-Driven Framework for Predictive Modeling and Early Warning

and fatalities. In the past, manual gate operating techniques and hydrological models were the mainstays of spill prediction and early warning systems. Slow response times and inadequate real-time data integration are two of these methods' main drawbacks \[ 1, 2 \]. There is a greater need than ever for improved, quicker, and more empirical spill prediction technology due to rising winds and increased concerns about climate change. In this sense, incorporating Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) is a novel approach that can address these challenges by facilitating practical insights, quick reaction times, and last-minute decision-making \[ 1, 3 \]. It has been a difﬁcult to mitigate the effects of dam spill over events, which is crucial for both dam safety and stability and for shielding neighbouring communities from devastating ﬂoods \[ 4 - 7 \] and AI techniques are now serving as a boon to these spills over detection.

The analysis and model development of an AI-based framework for dam spill prediction and early warning systems are summarized in this paper. It focuses on how individual models based on machine learning and deep learning can be applied to create a predictive framework that provides quicker, more precise, and more adaptable methods of spill prediction. The main objective of this study is speciﬁcally to develop and implement an AI-based predictive system that, using real-time readings of various environmental factors, can forecast spill occurrences in real-time and alert pertinent stakeholders-especially dam managers and local governments-of possible dam failure events. Contribution of our research work is

1. Combining data from several sources, such as rainfall, reservoir levels, soil moisture,  inﬂow, and outﬂow rates, is known as dynamic parameter integration. 2. LSTM-Based Forecasting: This method uses deep learning to anticipate spill  occurrences in time series with accuracy. 3. Real-Time EWS: Sends out automated notiﬁcations by email, SMS, and mobile apps.  4. The integration of the NASA POWER API makes it possible to automatically retrieve  meteorological and hydrological parameter data.

## 2 **Related Work **

Artiﬁcial Neural Networks (ANN), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) are examples of conventional AI techniques for ﬂood and dam spill prediction \[ 1, 4 \]. Even though these methods function rather well, they frequently fall short in capturing intricate temporal dynamics in sequential data. The groundwork for using deep learning in time-series forecasting was laid by Atashi and Gorji  work  on  LSTM \[ 2 \]. Because of their capacity to manage non-linear and long-range dependencies, LSTM networks have been demonstrated in a number of recent studies to perform better than conventional models in hydrological prediction tasks. We have particularly chosen LSTM for ﬂood prediction caused by Dam spill. Flood prediction systems are greatly improved with AI, as this works with huge historical and real time sets of hydrological data to ﬁnd patterns and predict when ﬂood is likely to happen. Machine learning approaches such as Random Forests, LSTM networks, and Support Vector Machines can capture complex non-linear dynamics and would enhance the prediction of ﬂood incidents in both quality and consistency. These smart systems can help in the proactive management of disaster and hence reducing the loss of human and economy \[ 8 - 10 \]. Extreme hydroclimatic events and climate variability have increased the risk - Singh et al.

of dam overtopping, with substantial associated difﬁculties for downstream inhabitants, ecosystems, and infrastructure. Traditional hydrological models, which are derived from unit response or reservoir routing methods \[ 11 \], generally falter in capturing the nonlinear and long-term temporal dependencies inherent in contemporary dam inﬂow and reservoir storage dynamics. To overcome these limitations, data-driven artiﬁcial intelligence (AI), in speciﬁc deep learning models, have made remarkable strides in predictive dam risk management \[ 12 \]. Among these, networks with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have shown remarkable potential for learning from intricate, multivariate, and time-dependent hydrological data. Their internal gating architecture mitigates vanishing gradient problems and enables effective learning of sequential relationships \[ 13 \]. For reservoir inﬂow prediction \[ 14 \], rainfall-runoff forecasting \[ 15 \], and ﬂood early warning systems \[ 16 \], recent research has effectively used LSTM models, continuously surpassing conventional statistical and physically based methods.

Although the encouraging results, there are still challenges towards physical consistency and robust data quality inside the LSTM models. To this end hybrid physicsguided learning approaches \[ 17 \] have been proposed, which will provide more trust in dam safety applications and better acceptance from regulators. Subsequent research may consider integrating physics constraints with LSTM to improve robustness against climate-induced extremes. This work particularly focuses on strengths of LSTM network and model combining power of NASA POWER API along with LSTM and EWS has been proposed for forecasting the Dam spill over which leads to ﬂood along with early warning system.

## 3 **Methodology **

Our research focuses on creating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for timeseries forecasting. This section of research paper speciﬁcally discusses about the data collection; model architecture used in our research and EWS system made to create alarm frame work so that area near dams can be warned in advance about the ﬂood alarming situation. **3.1 ** **Data Collection **

To obtain current and historical data, we used of NASA's Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resource (POWER) API and Central Water Commission Water Resources Department. The parameters gathered are:

1. Rainfall (PRECTOT, mm/day)  2. Moisture Content of Soil (SOILM\_0\_10CM, kg/m 2 )  3. Climate (T2M, °C)  4. Evaporation Rate (mm/day)  5. Inﬂow of reservoirs (local/custom data, m 3 /s)  6. Outﬂow of reservoirs (local/custom data, m 3 /s)

An AI-Driven Framework for Predictive Modeling and Early Warning **3.2 ** **Model Architecture **

The proposed LSTM model architect (Fig. 1 ) is used to predict the probability of a dam spill based on 30-day historical windows of 6 key dynamic features. The input sequence is aligned as 30 X 6 time series matrix. The network framework consists of 2 stack stacked layer with 64 hidden units with dropout rate of 0.2 to avoid overﬁtting. The output layer classiﬁed each sequence into spill or not spill categories. Model is trained using Adam optimizer with 0.001 learning rate. Prediction errors are quantiﬁed using binary cross entropy with batch size of 32. For deployment, a probability threshold of *z * ≥ *0.7 * is used, at this value, the model gives the balance between learning true spill incidents and avoiding false alarms, making it more stable for early warning. This balances performance with computational efﬁciency, making the framework suitable for near real-time dam monitoring and early warning applications.

- **Input Layer: ** 6 time-dependent features  - **LSTM Layers: ** Two stacked LSTM layers with 64 units each  - **Output Layer: ** Sigmoid activation for binary classiﬁcation **Fig. 1. ** Model Architecture (Dam Spill Prediction) **3.3 ** **Early Warning System (EWS) **

Upon detection of a spill probability greater than **0.7**, then we can issue real-time alerts through multiple channels like **SMS Alerts ** (via Twilio API), **Email Notiﬁcations ** (via SMTP) or **Mobile Push Notiﬁcations ** (via Firebase Cloud Messaging).

## 4 **Result and Discussion **

This work encompasses all strengths and features of Long short-term memory network along with an EWS system. LSTM is an RNN structure specialized in learning and predicting sequences of data (i.e., time series, language, or sensor measures). Unlike - Singh et al.

## simple RNNs, which have difﬁculty retaining information across long timeframes (this

is due to the vanishing gradient problem), LSTMs employ an advanced gating mechanism to preserve "important" information over a longer duration while actively "forgetting" irrelevant data. Quantiﬁcation of proposed work is done using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1.

## 4.1 **Model Performance **

## Three predictive models for dam spill forecasting-the suggested LSTM model,

ARIMA, and SVM-are compared in terms of performance using four important metrics in the Table 1. The analysis below illustrates that the LSTM-based classiﬁer is effective for dam spill risk early warning. The sliding window of hydrological and rainfall features, seasonal indicators and resampling with weighted loss are considered in the proposed model. LSTM obtained an accuracy of 96.0% and an F1-score of 0.95 improvement over the traditional ARIMA, SVM, RF and XGBoost baselines.

## The high precision (98%) and recall (91%) indicate that the model can effectively

avoid both false alarms and missed spill events which is very important within dam safety management. While the ARIMA can only model linear trends, the LSTM can learn complex seasonal and nonlinear patterns in time series data. Also, SVM faces challenges with temporal dependencies as it treats features statically, which results into reduced recall and F1 overall. Random Forest and XGBoost are dependent on manual lag features and cannot inherently learn sequential dependencies, which limits their long-horizon accuracy. Our proposed work help dam operators consider LSTM models as a credible early warning system, and reduce response time, and mitigation of risks. Nevertheless, the utilization of synthetic features may not account for the full range of variations in the real world of dam operations, and it should be extended to ﬁeld-validated data from multiple reservoirs for future research. **Table 1. ** Comparison of LSTM with other models

Three main panels in the Fig. 3. show real-time dam monitoring. Spill risk days are indicated in red on the top panel, which monitors water level trends in relation to a speciﬁed spill threshold. Learning progress and model stability are indicated by the bottom panel, which compares training and validation loss over time for the LSTM model. **4.2 ** **Early Warning Alerts **

A multi-level alert system is deﬁned by the equation, which is based on the LSTM model's estimated spill risk probability z. Four color-coded categories are used by the system to classify risk: Normal conditions (z ≤ 0.2 z ≤ 0.2) are indicated by green, meaning that no action is necessary. Yellow signiﬁes caution (0.2 *\< * z ≤ 0.50.), prompting increased monitoring. Orange represents a warning (0.5 *\< * z ≤ 0.70), necessitating contingency preparations. Finally, Red (z *\> * 0.7) triggers emergency protocols, as the model predicts a high probability of imminent dam spill. The model's high precision (0.95 F1-score in Table 1 ) conﬁrms that the thresholds are set to minimize false alarms while giving priority to early identiﬁcation of signiﬁcant events. The clear visual coding (colors) enhances quick decision-making for dam operators.

Figure 4 illustrates on of the example, it predicts spill risk probability to be 11.38%, which is less than the decision-making threshold of 0.3. Therefore, the interface communicates the current state being "NORMAL" with the green color which should be easy to understand to dam operator that the risk level is low. This result, together with information on the current hydro-supply situation, and on rainfall received to date, provides reassurance that a spill event is not likely to occur. By expressing numerically and categorically the probability, and the degree of risk, the system also offers transparency - Singh et al. **Fig. 3. ** Dam Monitoring Dashboard **Fig. 4. ** Spill risk prediction

An AI-Driven Framework for Predictive Modeling and Early Warning

and interpretability to decision-makers. Such imagery may be useful for dam safety, as it can be used to rapidly check the current condition and to make pro-active planning should the risk increase at some future time step.

## 5 **Societal Beneﬁts and Impact **

The model enables proactive risk reduction by (i) reducing operator response time via automated triage (color-band alerts with evidence), (ii) informing community preparedness through templated SMS messages to downstream stakeholders. Minimized false alarms lower alert burden, while improved recall boost the chance of timely gate operations and evacuations. The model uses open data, explainable thresholds, and audit logs, which improve public accountability and policy adoption.

## 6 **Conclusion and Future Work **

An AI-powered predictive modeling approach for dam spill forecasting utilizing LSTM networks is presented in this study. At 96% accuracy, the technology proves to be more effective than conventional techniques. The ﬁndings highlight the capabilities of deep learning models as effective instruments for improving real-time ﬂood early warning systems, which is capable of informing dam operators and vulnerable downstream communities in a timely and credible manner. Moreover, that the framework can handle continuous data streams, indicating its potential for operation in contemporary dam monitoring systems. Issues pertaining to quality of data, interpretability and incorporation of physical hydrological limits persist.

However, several limitations still exist. The robustness of real-time sensor data, the ﬂuctuation of hydrological pattern across different dams, and the restricted transparency of LSTM models are major constraints. Future work can focus on hybrid approaches that fuse physics-based hydrological knowledge with data-driven models to improve ﬂood forecasting. In addition, using larger span of datasets from remote sensing, IoT-based monitoring, and observations can further improve robustness. Finally, estimation of uncertainty and physics-based AI methods should be considered to increase transparency and trust in ﬂood predictions.

## Real-Time Deepfake Detection **on Consumer Devices Using CNN ** **Architectures **

## Dhruvi Viral Goradia 1( B ), Hemant Purswani 1, Vansh Kharidia 1, Viha Jain 1, Manoj Sankhe 1, Sumita Nainan 1, and Vishram Bapat 2

1 Department of Computer Engineering, Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering, SVKM's NMIMS Deemed-to-be University, Mumbai 400056, India *\{* dhruvi.goradia18,hemant.purswani11,vansh.kharidia09,viha.jain73 *\}* @nmims.in

2 Databyte Services and Systems, Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering, SVKM's NMIMS Deemed-to-be University, Mumbai 400056, India

**Abstract.** The recent evolution of generative models, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and diﬀusion-based models, has resulted in the widespread generation of extremely realistic deepfakes media, which seriously challenge digital security and content authenticity. This paper introduces an eﬃcient deepfake image detection system optimized for real-time deployment on consumer-grade smartphone devices. We compare three versions of the EﬃcientNet model-B0, B1, and B2 - on an evenly balanced dataset of more than 190,000 real and synthetic facial images. EﬃcientNet-B2 performs best at 91.74% accuracy and a Cohen's Kappa value of 0.8347. To allow real-time deployment, the system is optimized for inference with native PyTorch pipelines, which leaves inference latencies below 100 ms on mid-range Android smartphones and laptops without GPU acceleration. The suggested system provides an implementable and deployable approach to on-device deepfake detection, which has implications in mobile content authentication, social media moderation, and digital forensics.

**Keywords:** Deepfake Detection *· * EﬃcientNet *· * Vision Transformers *· * Transfer Learning *· * Real-Time Detection *· * Consumer Devices *· * Synthetic Media *·* Generative Adversarial * ·* Diﬀusion Models Networks

## 1 **Introduction **

## The high rate of the growth of deepfakes artiﬁcially created media that are close

to that of real human faces is a direct consequence of the high rate of generative models development, speciﬁcally in GANs and diﬀusion-based networks. One

- V. Goradia, H. Purswani, V. Kharidia and V. Jain-These authors contributed equally to this work.

c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 103-114, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1> \_ 8 - V. Goradia et al.

one hand, creative possibilities of these technologies are impressive; on the other hand, they have been abused inappropriately and in vast numbers, c oncerning misinformation campaigns or identity fraud, or even mischievous impersonation.

Current methods for deepfake detection have been centered around achieving maximum detection accuracy with sophisticated CNN architectures or transformer models. Yet, these are typically optimized to run on powerful servers or cloud infrastructure and hence are not suitable for real-time execution on commodity hardware like smartphones, laptops, or em bedded devices. For most real-world applications, particularly for edge computing or oﬄine forensic inspection, models need to satisfy requirements for memory usage, latency, and power consumption.

In spite of the recent advancements, very little eﬀort has been devoted to applying high-performing models in low-resource settings without compromising their classiﬁcation accuracy. There i s an evident gap in the current literature relating to deepfake detection under realistic deployment conditions.

To bridge this gap, this study investigates the use of lightweight CNNs, particularly the EﬃcientNet family, for deepfake image detection. The performance of the models is assessed i n terms of accuracy, memory usage, and inference latency to ensure its feasibility for deployment in real-time applications.

In this work, we examine EﬃcientNet variants (B0, B1, and B2) performance on deepfake detection from images with a large-scale balanced dataset. PyTorch is used to train and test the models and optimize further for real-time inference on regular laptops and ARM processors without involving external r untime frameworks. Experimental results indicate that EﬃcientNet-B2 achieves an excellent balance between accuracy and eﬃciency with inference times less than 100 ms on mid-range CPUs. **1.1** **Our Contribution **

Even though our model relies on the available CNN architectures, we make our contribution in applying the models to the real deployment context, which is the real-time deployment on limited resources devices - a context that is understudied in the deepfake detection ﬁeld.

We present a resource-conscious deepfake detection framework that ﬁnds the optimal trade-oﬀ between performance and deployability which includes input resolution adjustments, 8-bit quantization, and eliminating external runtime dependencies-steps rarely detailed in deepfake detection literature. The major contributions are encapsulated below:

*.* Eﬃcient Model Architecture: We take and adapt three versions of the EﬃcientNet model (B0, B1, and B2) to the deepfake detection task with classiﬁcation accuracy and parameter eﬃciency as the top priorities. *.* Large scale testing: We trained and tested our models on a balanced (70,000 real versus fake) dataset of facial images of 70,000 real and fake faces. *.* PyTorch based Inference: Unlike current systems that cannot operate on commercial deployment run times, our system is built directly in PyTorch to oﬀer direct deployment to desktop and mobile platforms. Real-Time Deepfake Detection

*.* Real time usage: We are also optimized to run with low latency and deployment with lower memory, with an inference time of less than 100 ms and a RAM consumption of less than 700 MB, just able to run on our mid range consumer devices. *.* Practical Deployment Validation: To determine the eﬀectiveness and deployability of our model in non-accelerated settings, we validate the performance of our model on the consumers laptops and ARM mobile processors in real-life domain.

## 2 **Related Works **

The problem of deepfake detection is a new direction of study, as the increasing popularity of generative models such as GANs \[ 13 \] and diﬀusion mo dels \[ 14 \] provoked it. With synthetic media becoming more and more real and indistinguishable of originality, researchers have e xplored an immense diversity of techniques of detecting manipulated imagery and video.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) remain a part of deepfake detection pipeline due to their ability to learn spatial and texture related characteristics out of image lik e visual data. The ﬁrst experiments conducted by Patbruber and Jadon \[ 2 \] demonstrated the promise of CNNs to frame-wise video analysis, and achieved moderate performance on smaller datasets. Subsequent designs such as EﬃcientNet \[ 11 \] and ResNet \[ 12 \] have been pre-trained to perform the deepfake classiﬁcation tasks and are be tter in terms of generalization and scalability.

MobileDeepFake is a lightweight model and other lightweight models have further expanded the capabilities of AI models on mobile platforms, focusing on the reduction of parameters and t he inference time. Deepfake detection training was done using other models of deep learning such as RNN \[ 17, 18 \] that achieved better results than Resnet. Newer advancements have brought Vision Transformers (ViTs) and hybrid CNN-transformer models to enhance the accuracy of detection. Islam et al. \[ 1 \] suggested a CNN-Vision Transformer model that utilized the strengths of both local and global features, achieving robust performance on high-resolution datasets. Aloraini et al. \[ 21 \] compared CNNs and transformer architectures, determining that transformers are more eﬀective in high-ﬁdelity forgery, although frequen tly at the expense of computational intensity.

Attention-based mechanisms have been investigated to localize traces of forgery in images. Siddiqui and Kim \[ 5 \] presented a multi-attentional CNN architecture that selectively attends to manipulated facial areas and achieves a considerable boost in classiﬁcation accuracy. Along these lines, Liu et al. \[ 19 \] introduced a lightweight design that combines spatial and frequency-domain features for boosting the robustness of detection while ensuring low inference overhead.

Multimodal deepfake detection techniques integrate visual and auditory signals to enhance reliability. Nirkin et al. \[ 4 \] proposed a joint audio-visual model - V. Goradia et al.

that can perform cross-modal consistency checks and is eﬀective in detecting lip-sync and voice-cloning-based forgeries. Malik et al. \[ 3 \] presented an extensive review of audio deepfake detection methods, pointing to the increasing danger of voice-based forgery and the necessity for cross-domain approaches.

While most studies target detection performance, comparatively few address real-time deployment \[ 8 \] feasibility. Sabareshwar D et al. \[ 9 \] presented a lightweight CNN designed for mobile phones, and showed eﬃcien t real-time performance with minimal hardware.

Eﬀorts to enhance generalization across datasets have resulted in the uptake of meta-learning and transfer learning. Prasad and Deepa \[ 10 \] proposed a meta deepfake detection model that can evolve to learn changing forgery styles. Khan and Khan \[ 7 \] investigated transfer learning for facial deepfake detection and demonstrated its eﬃcacy on cross-domain datasets. While text-guided diﬀusion models \[ 15 \] present new challenges for detection, adaptive and constantly ev olving detection methods are needed.

Thus, we observe that current methods struggle with generalization \[ 3, 6, 10 \], high computational costs \[ 1, 11, 12, 21 \], and real-time performance on consumer devices \[ 4 \]. Mobile-optimized approaches \[ 8, 9, 16, 17, 19 \] face trade-oﬀs in accuracy and latency, while our EﬃcientNet-based solution (B0, B1, B2), with B2 achieving 91.74% accuracy and 9.1M parameters, addresses these gaps, enabling robust, real-time detection on consumer hardware for applications like social media and forensic analysis.

## 3 **Methodology ** **3.1** **Dataset **

For the scope of this research, we used the publicly shared Deepfake and Real Images dataset, which is made available on the Kaggle \[ 20 \]. The dataset contains a total of 70,000 images, divided evenly between two classes: 35,000 original (real) images and 35,000 forged (deepfake) images. The real images originate from CelebA and FFHQ datasets, oﬀering diversity in gender, ethnicity, lighting, and expression. The synthetic images are generated via multiple GAN-based metho ds including StyleGAN, DeepFake, and FaceSwap, simulating various levels of forgery realism and compression artifacts. This diversity enables better generalization across deployment scenarios.

All images are resized to 256 *× * 256 pixels uniformly and are saved in JPEG format. The dataset has large intra-class variability with varied identities, facial expressions, illumination conditions, and background scenes, thus favoring strong model generalization. The dataset was split and stratiﬁed into 80% training, 10% validation, a nd 10% testing subsets with class balance in each split for reproducibility of experiments. A sample representative from each class is presented in Fig. 1. Real-Time Deepfake Detection

**Fig.** **1.** A sample fake vs real image from the dataset. **3.2** **Data Preprocessing and Augmentation **

For improving the generalization and stability of models, we use a chain of preprocessing and augmentation processes with the torchvision.transforms module. RGB format is used to transform images and then they are resized to 224 * * *×* 224 pixels. Random horizontal ﬂipping is used during training for augmentation purposes.

All images are also normalized with ImageNet mean and standard deviation. These transformations are done independently for training, validation, and test sets (Fig. 2 ). **3.3** **Model Architecture and Training Procedure ** **Fig.** **2.** Model Overview a nd Pipeline.

Three variants of the EﬃcientNet family - B0 (5.3M parameters), B1 (7.8M parameters) and B2 (9.1M parameters) were selected for their eﬃciency and scalability, critical for deployment on consumer-grade devices such as phones, laptops, and PCs. The ﬁnal classiﬁcation layer was modiﬁed from 1,000 ImageNet classes to two (real vs. fake).

The model was trained for 20 epochs per model, using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and cross-entropy loss. A batch size of 32 is used with random/shuﬄe enabled. - V. Goradia et al.

EﬃcientNet uses a compound scaling strategy wherein it scales the 3 dimensions (network depth, network width and resolution) simultaneously using a single compound coeﬃcient *φ*, unlike other CNN models that do the same individually, thus making it more resource-eﬃcient. It also provides better scalability with lower probability of vanishing gradients (making it more likely that the performance increase will continue with increase in model size). As the resource capabilities of consumer hardware are higher, then we can change to a larger EﬃcientNet model and achieve performance improvements.

## 4

**Optimisation For Real-Time Inference on Consumer ** **Devices **

In order to optimize our high-performing model to be viable in the real world, we also used deployment-speciﬁc optimizations as outlined below. The EﬃcientNet models were optimized using diﬀerent methods:

*.* **Model Selection and Scaling: ** EﬃcientNet-B0, B1 and B2 were selected as they have the properties of compound scaling that provide a tradeoﬀ between accuracy and computational eﬃciency. They were all tested on the parameters of number of parameters, FLOPs and run time. *.* **Reduced image Resolution: ** The input images were resized to 224 *× * 224 pixels in order to minimize the amounts of computation without degrading their performance in classiﬁcation. *.* **Lightweight Inference Execution: ** Native PyTorch and a model with 8 bit architecture were used to perform inference so that the memory overhead can be reduced. *.* **Deployment Testing: ** Python execution environment inference latency was benchmarked on consumer hardware consisting of a mid-range Android device Snapdragon 720G-and an Apple iPhone 12 (A14 Bionic) on python execution environment. Inference times of the EﬃcientNet-B2 model were about 2.1 s on Snapdragon 720G and 1.6 s on A14 Bionic, and therefore, the model can be used in the edge end under the near real-time real-life scenarios.

| In order to seriously evaluate model performance, the following measures are | used: | **5.1** **Evaluation Metrics **

In order to seriously evaluate model performance, the following measures are used:

*.* Accuracy: Overall correctness of classiﬁcation. *.* Sensitivity: Same as recall; measures ability to detect actual positives. *.* Speciﬁcity: Ratio of correctly identiﬁed true negatives out of all actual negatives. *.* Precision: Ratio of true positives among positives predicted. *.* Cohen's Kappa: Inter-rater agreement over chance. *.* Recall: Ratio of true positives detected out of all actual positives. *.* F1-Score: Averaged precision and recall; balances the false positive and false negative which may mislead the models and produce poor results. *.* Support: Count of factual instances of each t ype in the data.

These values are reported on the held-out test set. In order to give a complete analysis, we also give the precision, recall, speciﬁcity, F1-score, support and the accuracy and Cohen Kappa. These measures are essential to unbalanced data or edge cases in whic h false positives/negatives can involve varying risk and it is important to understand how well the model can actually learn. **5.2** **Testing Set Results **

## 6 **Conclusion **

This work introduces a lightweight, compact framework for detecting deepfake images through the use of the EﬃcientNet family of Convolutional Neural Networks. Leveraging EﬃcientNet-B0, B1, and B2 models, we provide competitive detection capability while keeping the computational complexity low. The EﬃcientNet-B2 model shows excellent classiﬁcation accuracy (91.74%) and classbalanced performance, as conﬁrmed by rigorous evaluation metrics such as precision, recall, speciﬁcity, and Cohen's Kappa. Real-Time Deepfake Detection

## In contrast to many previous studies, which prioritized accuracy alone, this

work targets deployability by tailoring the model for real-time inference on consumer hardware. Our PyTorch pipeline supports inference in under 2 s on stock mobile CPUs and less than 100 ms on laptops, without the need for specialist runtimes or hardware accelerators. This makes the system particularly suitable for deployment within mobile apps, forensic software, and content moderation platforms.

## By considering both the algorithmic eﬃciency and real-world deployment

viability, this research brings a reproducible, resource-eﬃcient deepfake detection solution to life for practical application. This framework paves the way for r eal-time, privacy-preserving deepfake detection across personal and forensic applications without the need for cloud reliance or dedicated GPUs.

## Enhancing Power and Memory Efﬁciency

**in VLSI Through Dynamic Voltage Scaling: ** **A Concise Review ** - Ashwin Shiva, Mangal Patil ( B ), and Aparna Patil

Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Bharati Vidyapeeth (Deemed to be University) College of Engineering, Pune, India mvpatil@bvucoep.edu.in

**Abstract. ** Low-power VLSI design has become a critical study area due to the growing demand for energy-efﬁcient devices, ranging from high-performance computers to mobile systems. Heat dissipation, battery life, and overall system reliability are all directly impacted by power usage. This paper examines and contrasts several important power management strategies, including bus encoding, operand isolation, transistor sizing, clock gating, power gating, multi-threshold CMOS (MTCMOS), and dynamic voltage scaling (DVS). The efﬁciency of these methods in reducing power consumption, design complexity, scalability, and system performance impact is analyzed. A qualitative comparative analysis highlights trade-offs in deep-submicron technologies, such as area overhead, switching latency, and limited leakage power reduction. Simulation results demonstrate that DVS achieves up to 35% dynamic power savings and 20% leakage power reduction compared to static techniques, with less than 5% performance degradation across benchmark applications. In particular, DVS improves standby power efﬁciency in embedded SRAM by lowering supply voltage during idle cycles, making it wellsuited for memory-intensive low-power applications. The study offers guidance for selecting appropriate power management methods based on application-speciﬁc requirements, such as preserving processor core performance or enhancing idlestate efﬁciency in memory subsystems. This study highlights DVS as a scalable and adaptable power management solution for modern VLSI systems, particularly in energy-constrained environments such as mobile and high-performance computing platforms.

**Keywords: ** Dynamic Voltage scaling · Power Gating · Clock Gating · Low Power Design · Power management Techniques

## 1 **Introduction **

nology, which has raised questions about heat production and power dissipation. Conventional Techniques for Power Reduction are Optimizing transistor size to save power consumption is known as transistor sizing. To conserve dynamic power, clock gating

involves turning off the clock signal to track blocks not being used. Power gating reduces leakage power by shutting off entire circuit blocks when not in use \[ 5 \]. High-threshold transistors are used in multi-threshold CMOS (MTCMOS) \[ 8 \] to reduce leakage in standby mode. Operand Isolation technique isolates the circuit's inactive components to save needless switching. Drawbacks of these methods are Decreased Scalability: Static methods might not be able to adjust to changing demands. Enhanced Design Complexity: More control systems and circuitry are needed.

Problems with Latency: Certain methods cause delays while switching between power states. Limited Leakage Power Reduction: In deep-submicron technology, leakage power is a problem for conventional techniques. Performance trade-offs: Performance may suffer from aggressive power reduction. Area Overhead: Techniques like clock gating and power gating require more transistors and logic. By dynamically modifying the supply voltage in response to workload demands, DVS signiﬁcantly reduces dynamic and leakage power. Research and development in low-power Very LargeScale Integration (VLSI) design has become crucial due to the increasing need for high-performance, energy-efﬁcient electronic products. Optimized power consumption is necessary for modern electronic systems, such as mobile devices, embedded systems, and high-performance computing, in order to prolong battery life, lower heat dissipation, and increase overall system reliability. DVS is one of the best methods for lowering power consumption in VLSI circuits. A power management method called DVS dynamically modiﬁes the supply voltage in response to processing demands in real time. Reducing voltage is considerably lower power consumption while preserving the required performance levels because power consumption is proportionate to the supplied voltage squared.

## 2 **Related Work **

In cooperation with dynamic and static power, it makes up a SoC design's overall power. Dynamic power is the amount of power used while the gadget is in operation \[ 1 \]. Static power is the amount of power utilized while the device is stationary. Static power consumption in CMOS devices is caused by leakage. Dynamic power utilization is typically caused by switching power, which is the power necessary to charge and discharge a gate's output capacitance. Many architectural, logic, and circuit design techniques can be used to diminish power for a convinced task implemented in a known technology. These methods concentrate on the voltage and frequency method of the equation while lowering the data-dependent switching activity. Numerous architectural and logic design strategies are available to reduce switching activity, which in turn reduces switching activity for the relevant gates. Because power and voltage have a quadratic relationship, lowering the supply voltage is a highly effective strategy for lowering dynamic power. However, as supply voltage drops, the gate's speed also drops. SoC designers can beneﬁt from this strategy in several ways: Enhancing Power and Memory Efﬁciency in VLSI Through Dynamic

For peripherals and other blocks that don't need to run very fast, it can utilize a lesser voltage supply than other, extra speed-critical blocks. This technique is known as multivoltage. It can offer processors with a changeable supply voltage; for applications that demand optimal routine, it can give both a high supply voltage and an elevated clock frequency. For less routine tasks, it can offer a slower clock and lower voltage. This technique is known as voltage scaling. Clock gating is a further method for reducing dynamic power. The power drops to zero when the frequency drops to zero. Many SoC architectures use clock gating in one way or another. The most excellent method to diminish dynamic power is to lessen the supply voltage. ## 5 **Conclusion and Future Scope **

Hybrid DVS delivers superior efﬁciency but involves greater complexity, whereas static DVS is easy to implement but lacks adaptability. The particular needs of the system, workload ﬂuctuations, and power limitations all inﬂuence the DVS selection.AI-driven next-generation power management technique called predictive DVS minimizes power waste, thermal problems, and latency by optimizing voltage scaling beforehand. It is particularly helpful for applications where power efﬁciency is crucial, such as cloud computing, AI hardware, HPC, and IoT. The best choices for AI and cloud computing: Cloud & AI Workload-Aware DVS and Predictive AI-based DVS. For Edge and MultiCore AI Devices: Fine-grained control is provided by Per-Core & Per-Block Ultra-FineGrained DVS. For mobile devices and IoT: Easy to use and effective is Closed-Loop Adaptive DVS. The best option for 3D-IC and hybrid architecture is 3D-IC & Heterogeneous Computing DVS. Every method has compromises in terms of adaptability, efﬁciency, and complexity. The most sophisticated solutions, such as AI-powered predictive DVS, enable preempt power scaling and maximum efﬁciency, but they also demand computational resources and AI models. Every DVS method has a trade-off between power efﬁciency, ﬂexibility, and complexity. The study is limited to simulations without hardware implementation, which may reduce accuracy in real-world conditions. It also covers a narrow set of workloads and does not address security, thermal effects, or fault tolerance in voltage scaling. Future research should focus on implementing predictive and adaptive DVS on real hardware, exploring AI-based workload-aware techniques, ﬁne-grained control for heterogeneous systems, and integrating secure, fault-tolerant, and cross-layer power management for more robust VLSI designs.

## Secure Federated Learning Mechanism **for Detecting COPD in Smart Healthcare ** Akshay Kumar 1, Geetanjali Rathee 2( B ), and Amisha 3

1 Department of CSE, Jaypee Institute of Information Technology, Noida, India 2 Department of CSE, Netaji Subhas University of Technology, Dwarka sector-3, New Delhi, India geetanjali.rathee123@gmail.com 3 Maharishi Markandeshwar College of Nursing, Mullana, Ambala, India

**Abstract. ** AI has been rapidly making headway in a multitude of sectors. One of those sectors is IoT; Internet of Things has been at the forefront of a variety of tech frontiers and has found a great number of applications over the past decade. IoT has not only revolutionized the working of the conventional computer networks but has also led to the emergence of new avatars of computer networks like Smart Homes, Smart Cities, and Industry 4.0. The primary challenges associated with IoT are regulatory issues and privacy protection. An insecure IoT network with integrated with AI can become prone to a major cyber-hazard if it is compromised. Not only would data of people be lost but sensitive corporate details might also land in the wrong hands. Though number of security schemes and processes have been proposed by existing researchers/scientists, it is further needed to provide an efﬁcient and secure transmission of information through legitimate devices that are involving while processing, analyzing and storing the medical records. In this paper, we are considering medical healthcare information considering COPD disease. The aim is to identify the person having COPD through smart device. The devices which are involved to provide the decision and classiﬁcation of disease should be legitimate and trusted in the network. The development of an advance learning framework for diagnosis and accurate decision-making of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). In addition, the integration of FL and IoT to further process, maintain, analyze, explain and build the trust among users or patients of FL results and decisions using Explainable Artiﬁcial Intelligence (XAI).

**Keywords: ** Security · Secure AI · COPD · Healthcare · Secure mechanism · Healthcare security · XAI · FL

Whereas the convergence of AI with IoT on one hand is expanding the horizons of technology, on the other hand, it is also posing signiﬁcant security threats. IoT networks are vulnerable to various kind of security threats such as ransomware attack, data falsiﬁcation attacks, etc. \[ 7, 8 \]. As such, it becomes imperative that they are protected against these to safeguard network integrity. IoT is rapidly expanding to various sectors of society and industry and in many cases already form the backbone of many such networks. The governments of various countries have also taken initiatives in development of large-scale smart networks that make citizen-centric schemes and spaces more efﬁcient and robust, a primary example of which is the Smart City Project of the Government of India. If security of such networks is not ensured, it can cause not only a dent in industrial progress but also privacy issues and data leaks leading to erosion of trust in new tech \[ 9 \]. AI integration in such already vulnerable networks, raises the stakes quite high. The primary challenges associated with IoT are regulatory issues and privacy protection. **3.2 ** **Working Model of Cost-Effective Healthcare Incorporating Technological ** **Boundary **

The working model of an efﬁcient FL system is deﬁned as depicted in Fig. 2.  The present model consists of three layers/phases such as physical layer, middle layer and server layer. Each layer entails of several entities to safeguard a smart and cost efﬁcient communication model in IoT with FL framewo rk. **Fig. 2. ** Working architecture **3.2.1 ** **Physical Layer **

The physical layer is composed of the relevant smart devices utilized in healthcare settings. The distribution of sensors is determined based on the total area to effectively sample COPD patients. To enhance efﬁciency, convenience, and cost-effectiveness, if the ﬁeld measures 1000 acres, the number of distributed or wearable IoT devices would be

Secure Federated Learning Mechanism for Detecting COPD in Smart

calculated as 1000 divided by 3, speciﬁcally the ﬂoor value of \{(total size of ﬁeld(N)/3)\}. The role of smart sensors is to gather real-time data regarding patients' X-rays and information from their designated area, subsequently transmitting it to the subsequent layers. **3.2.2 ** **Middle Layer **

The central layer comprises efﬁcient actuators within the division of ((N)/3)/3, tasked with gathering records and interpreting data relayed from smart sensors. Each actuator is equipped with its designated XAI models and algorithms, ensuring transparent and precise monitoring, symptom diagnosis, and record recognition from intelligent devices. This module's function is to facilitate real-time monitoring and recording of sensor data. Additionally, to enhance the monitoring capabilities, a FL model is implemented to aggregate all information from various actuators. The middle layer incorporates both step 2 and step 3 for categorization, prediction, threat identiﬁcation, and the execution of accurate and reliable decisions within the network. **3.2.3 ** **Online Server (Trusted Server) **

The function of online storage is to facilitate real-time storage and ongoing record transmission to the designated owner for the purpose of monitoring records in real time. Moreover, the responsibility of the online server is to guarantee dependable data computation and management within the Internet of Things (IoT) utilizing Federated Learning (FL). The cloud infrastructure may incorporate various database servers, artiﬁcial intelligence techniques, secure mechanisms, and virtual sensors to enhance the overall security of the storage against actuators, thereby improving efﬁciency and effectiveness in the intermediate layers. Additionally, owners can receive continuous and real-time updates from the sensors. An algorithm corresponding to proposed phenomenon is further presented in Algorithm 1.

| 4.1 | Implementation Setup |

The proposed mechanism ensures accuracy and efﬁcient secure communication mechanism for detecting COPD through trusted intelligent devices. **4.1 ** **Implementation Setup **

We conduct a simulation of federated learning involving 100 clients, with all clients engaging in each communication round. Each client performs local training with a learning rate set at 0.01 and a batch size of 64 for one local epoch during each round. The training process spans 1000 communication rounds, with the global model being assessed every 100 rounds. Prior to the commencement of federated training, clients participate in a warm-up phase that includes 5 local epochs to facilitate pruning preparation. To guarantee reproducibility, all experiments are executed with a predetermined random seed, and the deterministic settings of PyTorch are activated. **4.2 ** **Existing Approach **

Ramakrishnan has proposed a novel FL framework including the privacy, overhead, computation and accuracy of results. The authors have integrated group-key technique with encryption techniques in order to verify the datasets. The authors have proposed existing FL methods including privacy and efﬁciency of results. This paper enhances privacy without signiﬁcant accuracy loss by leveraging model pruning. Initially, the global model distributed to clients undergoes structured pruning based on the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, ensuring minimal performance degradation. During training, clients send all model parameters to the server, but pruned parameters are replaced with random values, preventing information leakage. **4.3 ** **Dataset **

We perform our experiments utilizing the Fashion-MNIST dataset, which comprises 60,000 grayscale training images and 10,010 test images, each measuring 28 × 28 pixels across 10 distinct clothing categories. All images are standardized to achieve a mean and standard deviation of 0.5. To replicate realistic federated learning scenarios, we assess both IID and non-IID data distributions among clients. In the IID setup, the training data is shufﬂed and evenly distributed among 100 clients, ensuring that each client receives an equal portion of samples from all 10 classes. Conversely, in the nonIID setup, the training data is segmented into 200 shards-small data subsets that are typically dominated by a single class. Each of the 100 clients is randomly allocated two shards, leading to highly label-skewed local datasets with restricted class diversity. The statistical variations in label distribution between IID and non-IID conﬁgurations are summarized in Table 2.

This section discusses the evaluation metrics which are considered to validate the proposed mechanism in comparison of existing approach in terms of accuracy, efﬁciency, privacy-preservation, computational delay of records and attack resistant.

- Accuracy: It is deﬁned as the degree of accuracy with which the proposed mechanism  is able to detect the threat in the network and provide the alternative solution. - Efﬁciency: The amount of period required to process the complete information with  accuracy and security of records in the network. - Privacy-preservation: The privacy of records while transmitting and communicating  the information in the network. - Computational Delay: The amount of period required to process the legitimacy of  records before storing and resuming the further communications in the network. - Attack Resistant: How much percent the proposed mechanism is able to detect the  threat in the network. **4.5 ** **Results along with their Discussion **

## Polarity-Driven Ensemble Framework **for Online Fake Reviews Detection **

## Zaid Z. Abdullshaheed ( B ) and Ahmed J. Obaid

Faculty of Computer Science and Mathematics, University of Kufa, Kufa, Iraq

zaidz.alrwaziq@student.uokufa.edu.iq, ahmedj.aljanaby@uokufa.edu.iq

**Abstract. ** E-commerce is one of the business activities that has witnessed an enormous change from traditional model to internet-based in recent years. In today's digital world, people have come to depend on the opinions of others (social proof) as they make purchasing decisions, so businesses must adjust to this reality. Nevertheless, false reviews are one of the major threats on online review. The consequences of fraudulent reviews are not insigniﬁcant-they can deceive customers, negatively impact businesses and their reputations. To address this problem, different techniques have been proposed, including natural language processing, machine learning and sentiment analysis such as possible solutions for identifying fake reviews. These methods generally include the examination of not only textual reviews but textual content alongside review metadata (i.e., language used, time of review and ratings) to estimate reputation. However, distinguishing between fake and authentic reviews is difﬁcult because fake reviewers use certain techniques to make their reviews look more façade. In the meantime, while this is a very challenging problem, we have made considerable progress towards effective techniques for identifying fake reviews. These methods are important to provide consumers with reliable information for informed decision making and protect the integrity of online review schemes. The key contribution of this paper is to integrate textual features with other semantically related behaviors for achieving improved perception and detection compared to previous work. The proposed model improves the authenticity of false review detection by introducing new behavioral variables. The Elmo Model is used to encode result vectors and reduce computational cost, and the VADER model is employed to determine polarity based on review content so as to assess each review. To predict real-time reviews in the Yelp dataset, a stack model is formed with MNA and Gradient Boosting Classiﬁer. The proposed model performs better than its related works with an AUC of 82% and overall accuracy over 98%. To sum up, the integration of textual attributes with behavioral features in our model point to a good path to accurately detect fake reviews and enhance the credibility for online review systems.

**Keywords: ** Fake Review Detection · Yelp Dataset · Deceptive Review Identiﬁcation · User Behavior Analysis · Review Metrics Evaluation

## 1 **Introduction **

The development of e-commerce in the 21 st century has signiﬁcantly changed the way businesses operate, resulting in numerous moving their operations via the internet. As a result of this shift, e-commerce sites have emerged, allowing consumers to evaluate and contrast an extensive range of items and services, read reviews written by other customers, and ultimately make more educated acquisitions. Reviews written by actual customers are invaluable since they provide information about other customers' experiences and suggestions on what to buy \[ 1 \]. As a result, they have a major impact on the outcome of a business. Everything from cell phones and laptops to hotel rooms, restaurants, and plane tickets can now be purchased, sold, and reviewed online because of the rise of internet marketing and online marketplaces. Consumers' buying choices are heavily inﬂuenced by other users' ratings, assessments, comments, and recommendations \[ 2 \]. Customer behavior is strongly inﬂuenced by online reviews \[ 3 - 4 \].

However, many newbie customers suffer as the increasing recognition of e-commerce also entails an increase in one's new danger from the side of the information avalanche. Frequently facilitated by producers or their agents in an effort to inﬂuence away potential customers, that danger is phony evaluation. Thus, discerning phony evaluations is critical for novice consumers but also for businesses dedicated to excellent offerings. As a result, one should address procedures to recognize such and address such issues. E-commerce and other types of online platform trades have substantially transformed the means of exchange of goods and services \[ 5 \]. Given assessments have become a prevalent part of the decision-making process, that is, it is currently more crucial than ever to trust those evaluations \[ 6 \]. A signiﬁcant problem for online review systems is choosing artiﬁcial assessments and false testimony. This issue is commonly referred to as the detection of fake reviews and is critical to a wide range of ﬁelds, including ﬁnance, medicine, security, and recommendations. Traditional identiﬁcations are rendered incorrect due to the existence of villains who employ even the most primitive disguising methods. Spammers combine real and phony testimonies to make a detection judgment more challenging, for example. Thus the development of effective measures to locate false testimonials is critical.

## 2 **The Research Problem **

E-commerce is a typical example of how the prevalence of web-based platforms is changing the landscape of much more than the digital economy. Websites for e-commerce are becoming more common, and more purchasers and sellers visit them. However, the existence of numerous e-commerce sites does not reﬂect the reality of the market; instead, it creates it. The reality established for consumers by the extension of e-commerce is characterized by a wide variety of choices, and for suppliers, it quickly levels the playing ﬁeld, allowing anyone to publish a product even mere hours after forming it. Traditionally, making a signiﬁcant purchase necessitated consulting with the close individuals. Nowadays, the internet mechanically aggregates the opinions of millions, graphically depicting them in the form of an impartial sample. As a result, user reviews play a significant role in the purchase decision. In one way or another, this factor directly determines Polarity-Driven Ensemble Framework for Online Fake Reviews

the ﬁnancial well-being or unwillingness of product providers. Consumers are eager to believe the reviews, but the angry undeservedly numerous evidence of fake reviews scares very much.

The Yelp Dataset, collected from the Yelp.com website and represents authentic user experiences across several business categories, stands out as a great resource for research projects. This dataset is a useful and relevant option for research because it includes a benchmark task for spammer/user and fraud/fake detection, developed and funded by Cornell University \[ 7 \].

One of the most important concerns in modern e-commerce has been brought to the attention of researchers as a result of recent research discoveries, including the challenges outlined. Also illuminates the potential impact of electronic armies in a variety of sectors, from economic operations to personal spheres. These digital organizations spread false information over social media by sharing stories, videos, and other content. To address these issues, this thesis focuses on using contextual and behavioral factors extracted from the Yelp dataset to identify fake reviews from genuine feedback.

## 5.1 **Preprocessing Raw Data **

## Preprocessing of raw datasets remains a crucial phase in any data analysis or machine

learning pipeline. It is the process of converting unprocessed datasets into a structured manner that can be analyzed or used in training the machine learning model. The ﬁrst exercise of preprocessing step is to load and read the "Comments" data table from the Yelp dataset. The "Comments" data table in the Yelp dataset contains the user comments and feedback of the businesses. These comments provided by users and posted on a yelp. com website are retrieved to enable the foundation of fraud identiﬁcation. ## 5.2 **Preprocessing for Modelling **

## This layer was responsible for polarity determination of a review text. Polarity is deﬁned

as the measure of positive or negative emotion expressed in a text about some subject. With the use of Natural Language Processing methods, polarity is usually seen as positive, negative, or neutral. For example, a positive statement can be "I love football," and a negative statement can be "I hate Sunday nights." A statement of neutral polarity such as "The sky is blue" has no emotional tone to it. Polarity analysis sets the target of determining on one's own the polarity of a statement as positive or negative. It has multiple implementations, from marketing studies and social media monitoring to customer reviews analysis and political balances of forces.

## 5.3 **Classiﬁcation Model **

## The model makes use of the Multinomial Naive Bayes approach, a commonly used

model for text classiﬁcation. In this case, MNB predicts the likelihood of the given review being of a certain category such as spam or non-spam, fraudulent or non-fraudulent by making inferences based on the term frequency in the text. In contrast to this, the system proposed in this paper combines MNB with the Gradient Boosting Classiﬁer through a chain classiﬁer strategy, given the results obtained and the dataset utilized. Speciﬁcally, multiple classiﬁers are connected sequentially, where the output of one classiﬁer is fed to another classiﬁer in the sequence, resulting in a decision chain. Gradient Boosting Classiﬁer is an ensemble learning method that uses multiple weak learners to build a strong predictive model. By blending the text classiﬁcation algorithm MNB's strengths Polarity-Driven Ensemble Framework for Online Fake Reviews

with the ensemble method GBC, the combined system is more accurate and robust in detecting fake or fraudulent reviews.

The Gradient Boosting Classiﬁer (GBC) operates using a base or weak classiﬁer. In this study, Naïve Bayes is employed as the base classiﬁer, which serves as the weak learner in the ensemble. The model is constructed by training multiple such classiﬁers on different subsets of the dataset, where each successive classiﬁer focuses on correcting the errors made by its predecessors. This sequential learning process enhances the overall prediction accuracy and robustness of the model.

Figure 3 illustrates the accuracy score obtained when classifying review labels from the test portion of the Yelpchi dataset using the Chain Classiﬁer Model. **Fig. 3. ** Average Accuracy of the proposed model.

Figure 4 illustrates the model's performance curve during the prediction phase, showing an average score of 0.82 ± 0.23, which reﬂects the model's consistency and predictive stability across evaluation runs. Z.Z. Abdullshaheed and A.J. Obaid **Fig. 4. ** AUC Curve of the proposed model.

To assess the effectiveness of the model, CV is then implemented. CV is a measure of how well model trained on machine learning will do with a tiny amount of data. Kfold cross-validation is a common way to evaluate how well an ML model performs. It consists of dividing a dataset into k equal-sized folds; one is used as the validation data and the rest serve as training data, where we train and evaluate the network k times The ﬂowchart (Fig. 5 ) below shows how we have applied K-fold cross validation to test our proposed system performance, where K = 5 shown below with the fold size = 126155 Records.

## 6 **Conclusion **

In the future, it will be important to continue identifying the presence of fake reviews on Yelp in order to retain its reputation as a reliable information source, enabling users to choose the best establishments in conformance with their preferences. Despite the measures already introduced to address this issue, there is still a large number of suspicious reviews that cause a problem for the users and the businesses in question. The future of Yelp as a viable and useful platform depends on the development and implementation of efﬁcient methods for detecting and penalizing the content creators. Therefore, the following conclusions regarding our proposed model and research question can be made:

From the analysis, it is gathered that only the text information in the Yelp reviews dataset may not be enough to check and detect fraudulent reviews, as many users can be used ordinary text usage in their comments. ## Lung Cancer Detection Using Medical **Image Processing **

## Paarth Kapur ( B ), Nandana Prabhu, Alekhya Gorugantu, a nd Rujuta Ashtekar

Department of Information Technology, KJ Somaiya College of Engineering, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India *\{* paarth.kapur,nandanaprabhu,alekhya.g,rujuta.a *\}* @somaiya.edu

**Abstract. ** Lung cancer has been the leading cause of deaths due to cancer, and it signiﬁcantly impacts both men and women. Therefore, early detection becomes very important. This research explores the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), particularly the EﬃcientNet architecture, which can help in early and accurate detection of lung cancer nodules-adenocarcinoma, large cell carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma-in lymph nodes using CT scans. With the advancement in deep learning and medical CT scans, it has enabled CNNs to analyze and identify patterns with great accuracy. This research has developed two models: a hybrid model that fuses feature representation from DenseNet201 and ResNet50 architectures before ﬁnal classiﬁcation, and an EﬃcientNet model using CT scans from public datasets like the LIDCIDRI dataset. It was s een that the EﬃcientNet model outperformed the sequential approach, and it achieved an accuracy of 94.29%. It oﬀered an eﬃcient and scalable solution across diﬀerent computational environments. This CNN-based approach has strong potential in enhancing tumor detection, helping radiologists, and enhancing the accuracy of diagnosis. It also reduces the dependency on reading these images manually, which is prone to errors and is time-consuming.

**Keywords: ** Lung cancer *· * CT scans *· * Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) *· * medical image analysis *· * lymph nodes *· * diagnostic a ccuracy * ·* tumor classiﬁcation * ·* deep learning * ·* artiﬁcial intelligence

## 1 **Introduction **

## Lung cancer is the most common type of cancer globally. There were 2.5 million

new cases seen in 2022, which makes up 12.4% of all new diagnoses \[ 1 \]. It is also a leading cause of death, responsible for 1.8 million deaths (18.7% of cancer deaths) worldwide. Therefore, early detection becomes very important to reduce the mortality rate.

## Deep learning, especially Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) like Eﬃ

cientNet, has improved the detection of lung cancer by analyzing CT scans to classify no dules into types such as adenocarcinoma, large cell carcinoma, and

c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 161-172, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1> \_ 12 - Kapur et al.

squamous cell carcinoma. EﬃcientNet oﬀers high accuracy and computational eﬃciency, making it suitable for large-scale screening.

In India, lung cancer causes 6.9% of new cancer cases and 9.3% of cancer deaths, and the shortage of radiologists further exacerbates the problem of timely detection. The proposed research, which is based on a deep learning model using EﬃcientNet and trained on public datasets, automates the process of n odule identiﬁcation in CT images and supports faster and more accurate diagnoses. Being highly user-friendly, it helps radiologists directly upload CT scan images and receive insights, helping address the issue of resource constraints.

Studies say that deep learning models achieve 90-96% accuracy in detecting and classifying lung nodules from CT scans. Our study takes this a step forward by not only detecting the presence of cancer but also accurately predicting the cancer types.

## 2 **Literature Survey **

Lung cancer remains the deadliest form of cancer worldwide. Early detection has become very important, and the advancements of various deep learning tec hniques have enhanced the accuracy as well as the eﬃciency of lung cancer diagnosis.

There have been many researches that have explored various AI and deep learning approaches for detecting lung cancer using CT and PET images. These include multi-modal fusion \[ 2 \], deep transfer learning \[ 3 \], and advanced neural network architectures \[ 4 - 6 \]. Diﬀerent approaches like CNNs, GoogleNet, and lightweight deep models have improved the classiﬁcation and detection performance even with small or imbalanced datasets \[ 7 - 9 \]. Several works highlight the importance of accurate nodule segmentation and preprocessing \[ 5, 10 \], as well as integrating pathology and radiology images for comprehensive diagnosis \[ 11 \].

Beyond using standard CNN-based approaches, researchers have also used instance segmentation \[ 12 \], hybrid CNN-ML methods \[ 14, 15 \], and comparative analyses of traditional and deep learning algorithms to boost diagnostic precision and eﬃciency \[ 13, 16, 17 \]. There have also been many reviews and surveys that discuss the progress and challenges in applying AI to lung cancer screening \[ 18 - 20 \], while CNN systems have improved the accuracy in c lassifying cancer stages and types \[ 21, 22 \].

These contributions highlight the major role of deep learning and AI in lung cancer diagnosis. EﬃcientNet, a modern CNN architecture, stands out for its scalability and high accuracy, as explored in our s tudy. By using these advanced techniques, early and accurate detection becomes possible, thus reducing the rate of mortality.

## 3 **Implementation **

The dataset used for the research consists of medical images that belong to four classes: *Adenocarcinoma*, *Large Cell Car cinoma*, * Squamous Cell Carcinoma*, and *Normal* (see Table 1 ). Lung Cancer Detection Using Medical Image Processing **Table 1. ** Count of Images p er Class

| Class | Images |
|:--- | ---: |
| Adenocarcinoma | 338 |
| Large Cell Carcinoma | 187 | Adenocarcinoma Large Cell Carcinoma Squamous Cell Carcinoma 260 Normal

**Dataset** **Composition:** Images were split into training, validation, and test sets, with unreadable images excluded. Data augmentation techniques like random rotation, ﬂipping, and zooming were applied to the existing d ataset to increase diversity and prevent the model from overﬁtting on the training data \[ 18, 24 \]. **Balancing:** After augmentation was done, each class contains 400 images (see Table 2 ). **Table 2. ** Count of Images per Class After Augmentation

| Class | Images |
|:--- | ---: |
| Adenocarcinoma | 400 |
| Large Cell Carcinoma | 400 | Adenocarcinoma Large Cell Carcinoma Squamous Cell Carcinoma 400 Normal

The original dataset had 613 training, 72 validation, and 315 test images. After augmentation, only the training set was modiﬁed:

*.* **Training:** 1600 images (400 per class) *.* **Validation:** 72 images *.* **Test:** 315 images

**3.1** **Model** **1:** **DenseNet** **+** **R** **esNet50** ** ** **Fusion**

**3.1.1** **Overview** Model 1 utilizes a hybrid architecture combining DenseNet201 and ResNet50. This is done to leverage the strengths of both models in feature extraction. DenseNet has a dense connectivity structure, which enables eﬃcient gradient ﬂow and feature reuse, while ResNet50 has residual connections that help in training deeper networks. This fusion helps to enhance overall representational capacity and generalize the model for the task of lung cancer classiﬁcation using CT scans. - Kapur et al.

**3.1.2** **Data** **Preprocessing** **and** **Augmentation** The input dataset includes CT scan images which are distributed into 4 classes: Adenocarcinoma, Large Cell Carcinoma, Squamous Cell Carcinoma, and Normal. The original images have dimensions of 305 * * *×* 430 pixels and three RGB channels.

To standardize inputs, all images are resized to 460 *× * 460 pixels. Pixel intensities are scaled to the range \[-1, 1\], followed by mean normalization using the RGB channel means from the training set. Data augmentation techniques such as random rotation, ﬂipping, and zooming are applied to the training set to increase data diversity and reduce overﬁtting.

Image preprocessing techniques such as resizing, normalization, and augmentation play a critical role in improving model generalization. These steps ha ve been validated in earlier work using lung CT scans \[ 18, 24, 25 \].

**3.1.3** **Baseline** **CNN** **Architecture** An initial baseline model is constructed using a simple convolutional neural network deﬁned sequentially. Conventional CNN architectures with convolution, pooling, and drop out layers have been used in several past studies \[ 20, 21 \], oﬀering foundational performance in lung cancer detection. The architecture includes:

*.* Two convolutional layers with 8 and 16 ﬁlters respectively, each of size 2 * * *×* 2, with 'same' padding and ReLU activation. *.* Two max pooling layers, each with a pool size of 2 * ×* 2. *.* Dropout layer with a rate of 0.4 to reduce overﬁtting. *.* Flatten layer to convert feature maps into a 1D vector. *.* Dense layer with 256 units followed by another dropout layer (0.4). *.* Output dense layer with 4 units and softmax activation to predict the class probabilities. The entire architecture is shown in Fig. 1 **Fig. 1. ** CNN Base Mo del

**3.1.4** **DenseNet201-Based** **Model** To improve upon the baseline, a model incorporating DenseNet201 is designed. The pre-trained DenseNet201 model (with ImageNet weights) is loaded with its feature extraction layers frozen, except for the ﬁnal convolution block ( conv5 ), which is ﬁne-tuned during training. The model is constructed sequentially as follows: Lung Cancer Detection Using Medical Image Processing

*.* DenseNet201 (pre-trained) truncated at the classiﬁcation layer. *.* Flatten layer to convert output feature maps to 1D. *.* BatchNormalization layer to normalize the activations. *.* Final Dense layer with softmax activation for classiﬁcation into four classes. The architecture diagram is shown in Fig. 2. **Fig. 2. ** DenseNet201 Model A rchitecture

**3.1.5** **ResNet50-Based** **Model** In parallel, another variant of Model 1 is built using the ResNet50 architecture. The model begins with the pre-trained ResNet50 as the base, followed by:

*.* Dropout layer (rate: 0.4) applied to the output of ResNet50. *.* Flatten layer to reduce dimensionality. *.* BatchNormalization layer to stabilize training. *.* Second Dropout layer (rate: 0.4) to further prevent overﬁtting. *.* Dense output layer with softmax activation for multi-class classiﬁcation. The architecture is shown in Fig. 3. **Fig. 3. ** ResNet50 Model - Kapur et al.

**3.1.6** **Fusion** **Strategy** The ﬁnal version of Model 1 fuses the DenseNet201 and ResNet50 branches by concatenating their respective feature vectors. This combined representation is passed through fully connected layers to perform classiﬁcation. The fusion architecture is designed to exploit complementary features learned by both models. The use of m ultiple CNN architectures in tandem has shown improved classiﬁcation outcomes in prior work, such as CNN-based multi-path pipelines for lung cancer stage detection \[ 21, 22 \].

**3.1.7** **Training** **Conﬁguration** All versions of Model 1 are trained using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 *× * 10 *−* 5 and decay rate of 1 *× * 10 *−* 5. Early stopping with a patience of 20 epochs is applied to prevent overﬁtting. A model c heckpoint mechanism ensures saving the best model based on validation loss. Each model is trained for a maximum of 80 epochs.

**3.2** **Model** **2:** **EﬃcientNet** **B3** **T** **ransfer** ** ** **Learning** **Fig. 4. ** EﬃcientNet B3 Model A rchitecture

**3.2.1** **Overview** Model 2 is based on EﬃcientNet B3, a convolutional neural network that eﬃciently balances depth, width, and resolution through compound scaling. Pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset, EﬃcientNet B3 p rovides a strong foundation of learned features, which are transferred and ﬁne-tuned for the classiﬁcation of lung cancer CT images.

**3.2.2** **Model** **Architecture** The EﬃcientNet B3 model architecture consists of the following components arranged in sequence:

*.* Conv2D layer *.* BatchNormalization layer *.* Swish activation function *.* Depthwise Conv2D layer *.* Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) block *.* GlobalAveragePooling2D layer Lung Cancer Detection Using Medical Image Processing

*.* Dropout layer *.* Dense output layer with softmax activation

These components collectively provide a lightweight yet highly expressive network architecture that is well-suited for transfer learning tasks. The architecture is shown in Fig. 4.

**3.2.3** **Fine-Tuning** **and** **Modiﬁcations** The pre-trained EﬃcientNet B3 model is adapted by enabling all layers to be trainable. Batch normalization and dropout layers are added to regularize and stabilize the training process. A ﬁnal dense layer with four output units and softmax activation is appended to perform classiﬁcation across the four lung cancer classes.

**3.2.4** **Training** **Conﬁguration** The model is trained using a custom learning rate schedule that adjusts during the training process for optimal convergence. Early stopping is employed to halt training when validation performance plateaus. A checkpointing mechanism saves the model weights corresponding to the best validation performance. The training dataset is divided into training, validation, and testing sets to evaluate generalization. The model is trained using cross-entropy loss and optimized with the Adam optimizer.

## 4 **Experimental Results **

**4.1** **Performance** **of** **Model** **1:** **DenseNet** **+** **ResNet50** ** ** **Fusion**

Model 1 was evaluated on a dataset divided into 1600 training images, 72 validation images, and 315 test images. Each of the four classes-Adenocarcinoma, Large Cell Carcinoma, Squamous Cell Carcinoma, and Normal-were equally represented after augmentation. Model 1 included three variants: a baseline CNN, a DenseNet201-based model, and a ResNet50-based model. The ﬁnal model fused DenseNet201 and ResNet50 feature representations.

The baseline CNN achieved an initial accuracy of 46.35%. The DenseNet201 model achieved a better accuracy of 75.87%, while the ResNet50-based model further improved the accuracy and achieved an accuracy of 82.54%. The ﬁnal combination of the DenseNet and ResNet50 model achieved the best accuracy.

Table 3 summarizes the precision, recall, and F1-scores for each class. The model achieved an overall classiﬁcation accuracy of 78.41%. However there is notable performance accuracy over diﬀerent classes especially a lower recall for Adenocarcinoma.

Table 4 displays the confusion matrix for Model 1. Although the Normal and Squamous Cell Carcinoma classes were well classiﬁed, the Adenocarcinoma class had a substantial n umber of misclassiﬁcations, particularly as Squamous Cell Carcinoma. As also observed in earlier studies \[ 24 \], Adenocarcinoma often overlaps in imaging features with other cancer types, leading to misclassiﬁcation.
