In the individual tests conducted, it was seen that Model 1 sometimes produces low-conﬁdence or incorrect predictions. For example, a Normal lung CT scan was correctly classiﬁed with only 68.16% conﬁdence; however, a case of Adenocarcinoma was i ncorrectly predicted as Normal with 75.96% conﬁdence. These inaccuracies emphasize the need for models that can have balanced performance across all classes in medical applications.

Despite Model 1's high F1 score of 0.99 for the Normal class, it shows reduced classiﬁcation conﬁdence and higher misclassiﬁcation rates across the other categories. This highlights the importance of performance across diﬀerent categories and not just having one dominant category that is easily diﬀerentiable.

Model 2 uses the EﬃcientNet-B3 architecture, and it signiﬁcantly outperformed all versions of Model 1. The reason behind this can be the model's compound scaling s trategy and use of pre-trained weights, which help it to generalize better to the task.

These results align with the ﬁndings from previous research, which reported an accuracy between 90-95% for lung cancer detection from CT scans \[ 19, 22, 23 \]. Lung Cancer Detection Using Medical Image Processing

To sum up, the numbers and stats show that Model 2 (EﬃcientNet B3) performs better than all versions of Model 1. It reaches high accuracy, precision, and recall for all classes. These ﬁndings highlight how useful advanced transfer learning models are for important medical image analysis tasks.

## 5 **Conclusion **

This study shows that the pre-trained EﬃcientNet B3 model achieves the highest accuracy (94.29%) in lung cancer classiﬁcation from CT images when compared to the hybrid CNN approaches. EﬃcientNet's transfer learning capabilities results in greater generalisation and faster learning.

In this research, it also shows the importance of various data augmentation techniques and the advantages of compound-scaled architectures for medical image analysis. However one drawback is that having a single dataset to train can introduce biasness a nd real-world clinical validation is still required. The further risk of false positives or negatives also highlights the need for further improvement.

To improve further, researchers need to validate the model using various external datasets and include more data sources like radiomics and genomics. Using 3D imaging additional techniques such as MRI, and developing explainable AI can boost diagnostic accuracy and increase trust in clinical applications. ## AI/ML Based, Low Cost OBUs for Intelligent

**Road Anomaly Detection and Control Through ** **V2X Communication **

## Komala Soares ( B ), Arundhati A. Shinde, and Mangal Patil

Bharati Vidyapeeth (Deemed to be University), College of Engineering, Pune, India pccegoa@gmail.com, \{aashinde,mvpatil\}@bvucoep.edu.in

**Abstract. ** This research presents real-time approach for categorising road surface conditions with RNNs embedded into low-cost On-Board Units. The system classiﬁes road segments into Good Road, Bad Road, and Humps and Speed Breaker, using data captured from many On-Board Units employed into ﬂeet of cars. Experiment was done on varied terrains; data was collected and labelled using manual method. After Pre-processing, the time-series data was fed into popular AI/ML models. Experimental results illustrates that the proposed Recurrent Neural Network, with 15 samples at a time, exhibits better performance with an accuracy of 99.3%. The data was interpolated with second-order polynomial. This RNN model found to be outperforming other models, like KNN, Decision Trees and SVM. The system's good accuracy, low weight and less cost validates OBU's potential for scalability and ease of deployment in automobile monitoring in smart cities. Also, Vehicle to Vehicle communication has been achieved through On Board Units for faster transfer of important messages.

**Keywords: ** Road Classiﬁcation · Machine Learning · On-Board Unit · Accelerometer · Speed Breaker Detection · IoT · Embedded Systems

## 1 **Introduction **

## Vehicles experience wear and tear on tires, suspension systems, and other part, sub

stantially due to damaged roads. Maintaining the good condition of the road is at most important for health of vehicles as well as the nature at large. This would also bring down the cost component involved in maintaining the ﬂeet of cars. Poor road conditions may also aggravate emission of unhealthy gases, inefﬁciency in fuel consumption, number of road accidents. Previous substantial study has revealed that timely detection of anomalies on the surface of road can reduce accidents and improve safety \[ 1 \]. In turn, Cheng et al. shown that reduced time to travel and optimization in choosing the route will bring in economic savings and environmental sustainability \[ 2 \].

## Primitive method of visual inspection totally relies on judgement of drivers' alone,

leading to potential biases and subjectivity. Human interpretation subjected to each one's capabilities and inconsistent, resulting in variation in decision-making and evaluations. This personal perspective can impede effective resource allocation and planning

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 173-192, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_13> - Soares et al.

of preventive maintenance \[ 4 \]. Besides, the conventional road inspections are laborious and time-consuming, which requires appointment of inspectors to examine the road network, physically. This inefﬁcient method may result in unnecessary delay in maintenance. Thereby aggravating risk of road dangers \[ 5 \]. This inevitable issue lead to path of research for a real-time monitoring and affordable solutions, to optimize maintenance, enhance road safety and address infrastructure hurdles, in resource-restricted environments. Mukherjee et al. in proposes using state-of-the-art AI \[Artiﬁcial Intelligence\] and computer vision techniques to automate road maintenance inspections, aiming to reduce labor costs and enhance efﬁciency \[ 6, 25\]. Also, there is research work discussing a supervised object detection approach using YOLO \[You Only Look Once\] and Faster R-CNN \[Region- based Convolutional Neural Network\] frameworks for real-time road distress detection, emphasizing beneﬁts in low-resource settings \[ 7 \]. Abdallah et al. investigates the application of low-cost sensing technologies, including GPS \[Global Positioning System\], accelerometers, and smartphones, to monitor roadway pavement conditions in real time \[ 8 \].

Researchers have identiﬁed road distress and classiﬁed based on various factors such as function, condition, structure, and surface characteristics. Federal highway administration \[FHWA\] has classiﬁed based on how the roads serve trafﬁc movement. The classiﬁcations are Highways, Collector Roads and Local Roads. The structural classiﬁcation of roads is as per type of construction of roads like Flexible Pavement, Rigid Pavement and Composite Pavement \[ 9 \]. Zhan et al. classiﬁes roads as per surface conditions like Good Road, Moderate Condition, Bad Road/Deteriorated, Potholes, Cracks, Alligator Cracking and Rutting \[ 1 \]. Also, the abnormalities of road are classiﬁed as Hump, Pothole, Speed Breaker, Rough Patch and Obstacle \[ 6 \].

On-Board Units (OBUs) exhibit an essential role in sensing road anomalies. OBUs are employed to collect and process road related real-time data. Each OBU houses various relevant sensors like GPS modules, accelerometers, gyroscopes and importantly, communication interfaces. OBUs supports the detection of irregularities like speed humps, potholes and severe degradations. Also, OBUs help in enhancing driver awareness towards the road condition and surroundings. Also, support integration of ADAS \[Advanced Driver Assistance Systems\] and enable scalable, safe, connective intelligent transportation system. Smith et al. proves the efﬁcacy of OBUs in determining road anomalies. The research also outlines how data can be collected efﬁciently from vehicle sensors and utilized to categorize irregularities on road surfaces, bringing out the potential of OBUs in preventive maintenance and of safety measures \[ 10 \]. Alemazkoor et al., in his research paper reveals that the use of cellphone-based or OBU-based usercontributed data can be utilized for real-time road monitoring, excluding the necessity of pricey infrastructure \[ 3 \]. Pivotal roles of a OBU used for detecting road abnormalities as extracted from previous researches are, as following. (1) **Data Acquisition**:  OBUs collect real-time data on vehicle movements, including orientation, acceleration, and location, which are key parameters for detecting anomalies. (2) **Internet of Things ** **\[IoT\] network**: On-board Units, with IoT technique, can sense the surrounding data and communicate it across to server via Road side unit, enabling identifying anomalies. (3) **Communication: ** OBUs can communicate the detected situations to other vehicles or system infrastructure via Wi-Fi protocol, enhancing collective understanding and safety. AI/ML Based, Low Cost OBUs for Intelligent Road Anomaly

(4) **Incorporation of Machine Learning models**: OBUs are developed by employing machine learning models to enhance the accuracy of detection of roughness of road, by learning hidden patterns in the data.

## 2 **Related Work **

Variety of On-Board Units have been developed over past years, with wide range of capabilities made to suit various conditions. Numerous publications research and explore possibility of integration of OBUs with intelligent transportation systems, under suitable applications, and their performance.

University of central Florida have built a cellphone-based On-Board Unit emulator for Vehicle to Infrastructure (V2I) and Pedestrian-to-Vehicle (P2V) communicating applications. The system developed by combining sensor data, computer vision techniques and cloud communication, exhibited effective warnings. Also, the model successfully validated by real-world experiments, offering cost-efﬁcient alternative to traditional OBUs \[ 11 \]. But cellphone-based OBUs face difﬁculty in terms of sensor inaccuracy, communication latency, non-scalability, battery drain, dependency on user participation, concerns over data privacy in complex environments. One of the research projects of University of Nottingham evaluates IEEE 802.11p-based V2V communication using custom OBUs in real-world tests. GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) correction broadcasting improved positioning accuracy, while machine learning models trained on performance data accurately predicted communication disruptions. Results demonstrate the potential of OBUs for enhancing vehicular communication reliability and supporting intelligent transportation applications \[ 12 \]. Angel Luis et al. presents an OBU architecture developed under the EMERGE project, integrating GNSS with augmentation services, inertial sensors, and advanced communication interfaces. Experimental results demonstrate centimetre-level accuracy, reliable system monitoring, and efﬁcient power usage under 5 W, supporting robust navigation for ADAS and autonomous vehicle applications \[ 13 \]. But the experimentation with GNSS data is limited by small-scale testing, dependence on GNSS signal availability, lack of large-scale real-world validation, and does not address latency under dense trafﬁc or multi-vendor interoperability challenges.

Qiong et al., in his paper presents the design and implementation of an OBU enabling V2V communication in VANETs for highways. Utilizing an ARM11-based platform with embedded Linux, GPS, and wireless modules, the system supports stable, real-time data exchange for safety assistance, validated through successful testing of all functional components \[ 14 \]. One research work developed an advanced OBU prototype based on an ARM i.MX platform operating at 1 GHz, featuring integrated support for 4G, GPS, Ethernet, HDMI, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and a 7-inch interactive display. The unit is capable of extracting driving parameters such as direction, acceleration, and speed.

One of the research showed how the all-inclusive data acquisition helps in providing priority to certain vehicles while managing the trafﬁc and also how to assist in diagnosing parking fault \[ 3 \]. Leyu Wei et al. developed the HKZL-CV model, conﬁgured at a sampling rate of 10 Hz. The model was primarily used for Electronic Toll Collection. The model acquires acceleration on x-y-z axes, along with latitude-longitude and vibration. Then the dataset was used to evaluate seven popular machine learning algorithms - Soares et al.

to detect and categorize longitudinal driving behaviours. Among ML models, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF) and Decision Tree (DT) demonstrated excellent accuracy in classiﬁcation \[ 15 \]. Jose et al. initiated development of Raspberry Pi-based OBU, with 1 GHz ARM CPU and 512 MB RAM. The Raspberry pi incorporated an IMU, (inertial measurement unit), an array of thermometer, weather monitoring device, pollution sensors, GPS and noise sensor. Also an antenna and display device. The experiment was focused on network metrics, like block error rate, signal-to-noise ratio, round-trip delay time and power consumption \[ 16 \]. Qihua Zhan et al. developed a cost-effective OBU designed for pavement status monitoring. This system incorporates an IMU and a GPS module to acquire data; however, the result of detection was not utilised for future analysis \[ 1 \]. Bhaskar et al. adopted a low-cost OBU model consisting of a MPU9250 9-DoF along with Neo 6 M GPS, IMU to collect real time data on vehicle mobility. The data set includes acceleration and orientation, enabling categorization of road status into bad road, normal road, pothole, and speed hump. Few of previous papers discuss about combination of Kalman ﬁltering and data fusion techniques to improve signal reliability \[ 17 \]. Masino et al. discusses about utilising kinematic data from OBUs for classifying of road status like light damage, good condition, potholes and speed humps. Some studies have achieved good classiﬁcation techniques with accuracy above 80% using parameters like RMS of vertical acceleration, maximum vertical jerk, peakto-peak pitch and roll acceleration \[ 18 \]. One of the research projects elaborates about collecting vehicle posture using an IMU and GPS module to sense abnormalities in pavement.

The system effectively distinguishes between normal and abnormal road conditions, including speed humps and potholes, achieving testing accuracies up to 86.48% with the Random Forest classiﬁer \[ 1 \]. Table 1 presents a consolidated summary of recent research studies, offering a comparative analysis of the processors and sensors employed in OBU designs, along with the methodologies and parameters integrated within the respective models.

Although existing research proposes various methods for detecting road anomalies and improving trafﬁc conditions under diverse scenarios, signiﬁcant challenges remain in developing solutions that are deployable, high-speed, low-cost, privacy-preserving, and scalable for real-world implementation. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Sect. 3 presents the proposed system architecture prototype design in detail. Section 4 outlines the experimental setup and algorithms incorporated. Section 5 reviews the performance parameters of suggested models. Section 6 debates and highlights potential future of research.

## 3 **System Architecture Proposed **

The proposed system, illustrates in Fig. 1, parts a network of On-Board Units (OBUs) incorporated in moving vehicles and a single-point server employed for processing realtime data. Each OBU accumulates vehicular information such as speed, location and acceleration and communicates to the server using Wi-Fi protocol. The server collects data from all OBUs and studies collectively to churn-out with context-aware warning like "Hump", "Speed-breaker", "Bad" as well as "Good". These warnings help maneuver the vehicles by taking proactive decisions, thereby enhancing trafﬁc ﬂow. ## 3.1 **On-Board Unit **

## Figure 2 demonstrates the On-Board Unit, featuring a tiny and low-cost design designed

for installation in the vehicle. The unit houses a microcontroller, Seeed Studio XIAO AI/ML Based, Low Cost OBUs for Intelligent Road Anomaly

ESP32C3, GPS module and an accelerometer. The devises are selected considering their reliable performance and energy efﬁciency. Overall dimensions of proposed design of OBU are 5.8 cm × 5.8 cm × 3 cm weighing 38 g. The OBU is suited for non-intrusive integration into automobiles. The ADXL345 accelerometer scans axial acceleration data along three axes in g units (gravitational units), for secure analysis of movement. Despite the OBU is designed mainly for deployment in vehicles, it can also be used by pedestrians and other mobile users. This was made possible due to OBUs lightweight and Wi-Fi capabilities. Other mobile entities of trafﬁc system can engage in seamless real-time data reception and transmission. **Fig. 2. ** Perspective and top view of an OBU

The On-Board Unit is modelled with ESP32C3, Seeed Studio XIAO, a RISC-Vbased, IoT device, with inbuilt features like Wi-Fi, BLE 5.0, UART, SPI, and I 2 C communication protocols. The ADXL345 provides measurement in the ± 16 g range and has capability of motion detection and operates in low power, which are best suited for automobile sensing applications \[ 19, 20 \]. The system integrated L76x GPS module, supporting GLONASS (Global Navigation Satellite System), QZSS (Quasi-Zenith Satellite System), GPS navigation systems, offering very good sensitivity and fast connection to satellite at low energy. Longitude and latitude are extracted for location mapping with road conditions. The OBU also includes visual LED displays for status of power-on, signal reception, and to display control signals and a Pulse Width Modulated brightness LED strip, to display the trafﬁc density around it. **3.2 ** **Data Processing at Cloud Server **

A high-end laptop serves as the central server, embeds a twelfth Generation Intel Core i7-12700H processor with frequency 2.30 GHz, RAM of 16 GB, and a 64-bit Windows 11 operating environment. This affordable features of server ensures efﬁciency at storage, computation and processing of the collected data. The server fetches and real -time acceleration data in along the x, y, and z axes sent from the ADXL345 accelerometers, embedded in the OBUs. The incoming data is saved in CSV format at server via Google Sheets. Data after going through pre-processing stages, will be utilized model development in Python 3.11 environment. Five ML classiﬁers like Naive Bayes (NB), Support Vector Machine (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbors (K-NN), Logistic Regression (LR) and - Soares et al.

## Decision Tree (DT) were trained separately using 80% of the labeled dataset. Perfor

mance parameters of each model were tabulated and compared. Optimal algorithm was identiﬁed. Among all, the Decision Tree classiﬁer performed well with good accuracy. The AI models RNN and CNN and are also trained and tested. The results are promising \[ 23 \].

## Comparative analysis suggests that Wi-Fi presents the most effective communication

medium for Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) applications. It delivers higher data throughput, popular infrastructure support, ease of incorporation and cost effectiveness, making it best suited for, high-rate data exchange applications and at short-range. Unlike NB-IoT or LoRa, Wi-Fi yields multi-device connectivity simultaneously, which are essential for vehicular networks data transfers. However, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) is suitable for short-range and low-power transmissions, it is limited by frequency capability and scalability \[ 21 \].

## 4 **Model and Algorithm **

## 4.1 **Algorithm **

## The trafﬁc management model is illustrated in Fig. 3, depicting the sequence of interac

tions, between the Automobile-mounted OBU and the server at every ﬁxed time intervals. The OBU acquires accelerometer data at speed of 1 Hz, along the x, y, and z axes. This AI/ML Based, Low Cost OBUs for Intelligent Road Anomaly

## data is collected onboard and transmitted to server. The data received at server is labelled

as either "Moving" or "Stopped." Subsequently, Python scripts aggregate, preprocess, and analyze the combined data to generate appropriate control signals, which are periodically communicated back to the OBUs along with GPS locations. Manual data labeling is time-consuming and prone to human error, inconsistency, and subjectivity. It can introduce biases such as class imbalance, limiting dataset, quality, scalability and model fairness. Despite shortcomings, the dataset is labelled manually to train AI/ML model as an alternative to costly and complex hardware design with sensors. A supervised machine learning model is developed for data classiﬁcation using different algorithms. The dataset is split into 80% for training and 20% for testing, with the models demonstrating promising accuracy results. For Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication, the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32C3 integrated within the OBU operates in both server and client modes via Wi-Fi. The OBU communicates with other nearby OBUs via Wi-Fi mesh. Corresponding algorithm is given in Fig. 4. When a "Moving" status is detected from peers, an internal counter increments, which proportionally increases the brightness of an LED- strip connected to a PWM output. This real-time visual indication enhances trafﬁc awareness, aligning with Industry 4.0 standards by facilitating efﬁcient inter-vehicle communication of trafﬁc conditions. **// Algorithm employed at server side// **

## 4.2 **Experimental Set-up **

## The core of the On-Board Units (OBUs) is built around the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32C3

microcontroller, which integrates a Type-C USB interface serving dual functionality: system programming and power supply. The OBU draws operational power directly from the vehicle's USB outlet, delivering a stable 5 V at 19 mA. As illustrated in Fig. 5, each module is mounted vertically on the visible area of the vehicle

## As soon as the OBU is powered on, it starts detecting pre assigned WiFi vicinity.

For simplicity, the OBUs are web connected though a smartphone in hotspot mode. Upon establishing a Wi-Fi connection, each module starts to capture sensor data from accelerometer and GPS modules, at 1 Hz. The sensed data including time and date is instantaneously recorded and transmitted to server in real-time, where it gets stored as comma-separated values (CSV). Besides, Vehicle to Infrastructure communication, each OBU is designed to communicate between peer Vehicles, within a 50-m radius. This autonomous exchange of vehicle status is in line with Industry 4.0 standard.

## OBUs with proposed design are put to an on-ﬁeld experimentation over actual road

with trafﬁc, from Panaji to Madgaon-Goa, to study the performance and analyze the potential of proposed model. The test and trial involved three automobiles embedded with On-Board Unit, travelled a distance of 36 km over 48 min. The actual route followed by the vehicles was retrieved using the Google Maps, as depicted in Fig. 6.

## Each of the three OBUs recorded the data independently and sent as CSV ﬁles

to server with module ID. Python applications were used to merge these ﬁles into a one master dataset with had eight key time parameters and features, which were used AI/ML Based, Low Cost OBUs for Intelligent Road Anomaly **Fig. 5. ** Installation of OBU on the dashboard **Fig. 6. ** Route of considered for Experiment

## to train machine learning model. This procedure validates effectiveness of OBU in

real-world intelligent transportation and vehicle monitoring system. The master dataset comprises 11 various features as detailed in Table 3. These features are applied as input variables for ML-based classiﬁcation and analysis. This experimental framework ensures the practicality and robustness of the OBU modules in a real-world environment, achieving valuable insights toward intelligent transportation system. **Table 3. ** Parameters exported by OBU.

## 5 **Results and Evaluation **

Once the On-Board Unit (OBU) powered on and detects the Wi-Fi, it starts to transmit motion data corresponding to the features described in Table 2 to a central server, where the data is saved in CSV format via Google Sheets. **5.1 ** **Preprocessing **

The magnitude plot of original dataset is plotted in Fig. 7. The deviations in Magnitude are visible owing to various condition of the road ways. Figure 8 indicates the magnitude with reference to time axis. Preprocessing of data is necessary as missing samples were observed, due to communication lags and Wi-Fi network quality. This data loss undoubtedly impacts the overall reliability and performance of the subsequent analysis. Hence several data preprocessing techniques employed. Basic method is **dropping ** **missing values**. But due to fear of losing substantial amount of data, other techniques like R **esampling ** method, linear interpolation, polynomial interpolation were employed and found to be useful. Resampling can be performed by standardizing the sampling intervals, with missing values substituted by the mean of surrounding entries. But **inter-** **polation methods**, polynomial of order 2 and 5 found to offer viable solutions for ﬁlling gaps. Figure 9 shows the plot of sample magnitude with time on x axis after performing linear interpolation on the dataset. Whereas, Fig. 10 indicates magnitude versus time after Polylinear interpolation of order 2. **Fig. 7. ** Magnitude plot of original data AI/ML Based, Low Cost OBUs for Intelligent Road Anomaly **Fig. 8. ** Magnitude plot on Date-Time Axis

# RNN \[20\] **5.3 ** **V2V Communication **

Communication among On-Board Units (OBUs) conﬁgured within a Wi-Fi mesh network demonstrated robust detection and reliable interconnectivity. Each OBU autonomously broadcasts its motion status (moving or stationary) to all other OBUs within the mesh. Upon receiving updates, each OBU calculates the number of nearby vehicles within a 50-m radius. As number of vehicles approach closer to a vehicle, the OBU increases the brightness of LED strip proportionally, indicating the density of vehicles around. This visual display is helpful in alerting the driver of the vehicle, and immediately prompt to take timely decisions in trafﬁc.

## 6 **Conclusion and Future Scope **

This paper presents an innovative approach towards enhancing drivers' trafﬁc awareness by employing light-weight, low-cost, small-sized and effective On-Board Units. But, the scope of this paper is limited to a linear route with good web- connectivity and fewer number of vehicles. These OBUs are modelled to give real-time trafﬁc updates, hence supporting safer driving. The proposed OBU consolidates prime features such as Wi-Fi connectivity, real-time data analytics and V2I communication. The OBUs are integrated with accelerometer and GPS modules, to monitor vehicular motion parameters and are capable of sending to centralized server. Unlike previous researches, this paper incorporates only eight key features to train and test ﬁve popular supervised machine learning AI/ML Based, Low Cost OBUs for Intelligent Road Anomaly

models: Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree (DT), K-Nearest Neighbors (K-NN), Logistic Regression (LR), and Naïve Bayes (NB) and three AI models, RNN, CNN and ANN (Artiﬁcial Neural Network). The models are assessed before and after interpolation. Results proves that CNN and RNN models promise very good precision, while the other models also perform reasonably good, validating the reliability of the data, the applicability of the models and the deployability of the proposed architecture. The prime contributions of this paper are as following

- The proposed design low-cost, low-weight OBUs are validated with reference to  performance - Design of OBUs shows capability in supporting trafﬁc management in resourceconstricted environments. - The use of on-chip Wi-Fi, external cost-effective basic sensors and LED indicators  provide seamless V2I communication.

Moreover, the paper illustrates simple method of Wi-Fi based Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication using mesh protocols, enabling OBUs to send and receive real-time trafﬁc status. This V2V communication improves vehicular awareness signiﬁcantly, towards safer driving experience.

Substantial iterations of trials and tests, validates the efﬁciency of the proposed system, based on various crucial performance metrics. However, future scope of the work may delve into large-scale deployments and the incorporation of advanced models, like federated learning protect data privacy. Reducing dependency on centralized server for data processing can also be given thought, as it increases single point failure. Security can be enhanced further by incorporating vehicle authentication protocols. These improvements will certainly strengthen the proposed system and make more suitable in smart intelligent trafﬁc management in smart city ecosystems.

**Abstract. ** Eﬀective and useful management of all the water resources, along with a water quality monitoring tool to address public health and environment issues. In today's world, AI (artiﬁcial intelligence) may help in providing endless opportunities to increase the measures that target to identify and classify the water quality issues. In order to create the perfect water quality index measuring system many attempts had been made by comparing the WQI data from the long term by monitoring the quality with which the quality of water changes over time using an ensemble stacking method. Some of the AI tools that were considered best in this ﬁeld of work were SVM, DT, XBG, CATBoost, RF, MLP and many more. Here we have taken a dataset consisting of 1726 samples over a 11-year(2003-2014) period. We have used multiple measures to evaluate the model's working such as accuracy, precision, Roc curve, etc. The generated output tells us that X GBoost gives the best output with an accuracy of 95.82%. In addition, using the ensemble model along with all other classiﬁers increases overall accuracy and performance. As such, the RF is one of the most competitive general purpose algorithms and all the meta-classiﬁers themselves, representing one of the quite stable approaches to WQ classiﬁcation along the way. The framework and methodology used in this paper serves as a useful tool to help various designers design AI-based solutions to solve water quality assessment problems.

In today's world, Classiﬁcation predictive modeling approach aims to generate the classiﬁer or mapping function or to map given input labels to the desired output labels by using various input variables, such as major water quality parameters, to discrete output variables that gives representations to such classiﬁcation categories. But even before analyzing or dataset using the various ML algorithms, we perform data preprocessing and EDA(Exploratory data analysis) especially data preparations which includes processes like dataset splitting to convert out dataset into training as well as testing and validation data subsets that gave their share in model's evaluation measures. Another major step involved in our research is data cleaning which was taken care of as a major part of achieving better performance, which we aim to get. The error values we get across are eliminated from the dataset, and the mean values were used by us to take care of the imputations of the dataset and to replace the empty values using these mean values. **2.1.1** **Dataset** The data set we have contains the historical dataset based on water quality measurements for 1,226 water bodies spread across various Indian states with the major objective the future PH levels. The dataset taken by us contains 11 parameters, including temperature, the dissolved oxygen and many more. The PH measurement is taken as the average value by default. The dataset we have depicts the water quality distribution over many prominent river systems of our country.

**2.1.2** **Determination** **of** **WQI** The WQI is computed by taking the average of the individual quality index values of chosen for the water quality parameters \[ 18 \]. This research includes the various WQI values that are employed to classify water samples according to their quality. The WQI is giv en as:

# WQI = *N* i=1 qi · wi *N* $$ i=1 wi $$ (1)

here qi represents the quality scale for another parameter that we called I, also wi is the major parameter representing weight of the given parameter I and another N indicates the number of parameters considered. The scale of quality qi is given by: qi = 100 \times (Vi −Videal) ( *S* *i* * −* *V* ideal ) (2)

Here, the given value of Vi represents the measured value, hence the taken Videal is the reference value.

WQCs are based on speciﬁc criteria set, and various statistics and measurements such as mean and standard deviation are used to represent data set variables such as DO, pH, and nitrate levels \[ 19 \].

# 3.1 **SVM**

SVM is a ML model that helps reduce classiﬁcation and regression errors and create hyperplanes between classes. It eﬀectiv ely optimizes the class margin when applied to classiﬁcation and regression problems \[ 20 \]. The SVM model is expressed as follows for a given set of observational data Ds= (xi, y i), where xi indicates input features and yi indicates the output labels: $$ y = \psi(x) \cdot w + b $$ (3) - Kumari et al.

where *ψ* ( *x* ) represents kernel function (such as radial basis, linear, or polynomial), w indicates weight vector, and b indicates bias term. Maximizing the class margin while minimizing the classiﬁcation and regression error is the main objective of the SVM model, controlled by a regularization parameter C. The SVM model handles outliers using an epsilon-insensitive loss function, which works best for high-dimensional data but may have trouble with large overlapping classes \[ 21 \].

# 3.2 **RF**

RF is an ensemble learning method that improves classiﬁcation problems using many decision trees. Each tree oﬀers a random selection of feature subsets to preserve some degree of variance between models. By combining the output from each tree through majority voting for classiﬁcation issues a ﬁnal result is calculated. The crucial factors that make RF suitable for any application are the number of trees, tree depth, and minimal sample splitting. The basis of the entire RF model creation in this study is formed by maximum trees = 300, maximum tree depth = 300, and minimum split size = 3 samples \[ 22 \]. The following are RF prediction steps:

1. Randomly selected subsets of data are used to generate multiple decision trees. 2. Prediction of outcome for test feature by a veraging the result across trees. 3. Calculation of the ﬁnal prediction based on majority voting \[ 23 \].

# 3.3 **MLP**

A neural network model called the MLP is used to simulate non-linear relationships frequently applied in water quality prediction tasks. The three main components of an MLP are the input layer, hidden la yers, and output layers. Here, neurons are linked using weights and biases that determine computations \[ 17 \]. The output *Y* *k * at the output laye r is computed as: Yk = f ⎛ ⎝ *m * $$ j=1 $$ *w* *j* *h* *j* + * b* ⎞ ⎠ (4)

where *h* *j * are hidden layer neurons, *w* *j * indicates the weights, *b* indicates the bias, and *f* represents the activation function. The weights and b iases are adjusted in such a manner to optimize model performance while training. **3.4** **Logistic** **Regression**

Logistic Regression is a statistical method for binary classiﬁcation of any value point. It oﬀers a probabilistic result for its categorical result (0 or 1) by attaching independent variables that are deployed in the same result as the dependent variable \[ 24 \]. The model applies the logit transformation, represented as:

where *p* denotes the probability of an event occurring and *β* 0 *,*  *β* 1 *,*  *.*  *.*  *.*  *,*  *β* *n * denotes coeﬃcients of the input features *x* 1 *, x* 2 *,..., x* *n*. For binary results like"yes/no" or "0/1," this model works remarkably well. **3.5** **XGBoost**

A very optimized and eﬃcient variant of gradient boosting machine (GBM) is called XGBoost. It builds an ensemble for the decision trees to correct for faults produced by them, each of which is trained successively to one before it \[ 25 \]. Given a dataset *D* *s * = *\{* ( *x* *i* *,*  *y* *i* ) *\}*, where *x* *i * denotes input features and *y* *i * denotes the targets. where *L* denotes the loss function and Ω denotes the regularization function. XGBoost works remark ably well for large-scale datasets and complex prediction tasks. **3.6** **Decision** **Tree** **(** **DT)**

The most commonly employed algorithm in classiﬁcation and regression applications is the DT. It has the same structure as a tree, with nodes representing features, branc hes representing decision rules, and leaves representing the results. Its construction involves:

1. Splitting the data based on feature values. 2. GContinuously growing the tree until each leaf node con tains instances of a single class. 3. Removing extra branches from the tree t o improve accuracy.

The entropy or Gini index is often used to measure the impurity of the node which helps to select the best split at each node \[ 26 \]. **3.7** **CATBoost**

Without requiring extensive preprocessing, CATBoost which is an advanced Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) works well with categorical data. Directly integrating c ategorical features during training, reduces gradient bias and prediction bias and minimizes overﬁtting \[ 27 \]. This approach is a reliable option for handling categorical features since it works well with datasets that are rich in structured data. The objective function that CATBoost uses is as follows: - Kumari et al. Objective = *n * $$ i=1 $$ L(yi, ˆyi)  +  \lambda

where *L* denotes the loss function, *λ* is a regularization parameter, and Ω( *f* *k* ) denotes the complexity of the *k* -th tree. CATBoost's handling of categorical variables improves its eﬃciency and accuracy for data-rich tasks.

## 4 **Relative Analysis of ML Models **

The main motive of this work is to compute and diﬀerentiate various ML models for the categorization of water quality based on features like pH, conductivity, dissolved oxygen, and others. The diﬀerent methods used in the current analysis include **RF**, **MLP** **Classiﬁer**, **LR**, **XGBoost** **(XGB)**, **DT**,  a  nd ** ** **Cat** ** ** **Boost** **(CB)**. Performance parameters such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, ROC AUC, and average precision will be used to compare these diﬀerent models.

# 4.1 **RF**

RF is a ML model that uses multiple decision trees to make predictions. It works well for classiﬁcation as it can handle many features and it avoids overﬁtting as well. This model was trained using bagging, where each tree was built using a random sample of data. In this case, 100 trees were used, and the Gini index was the criteria for splitting the data. The model resulted in the following values: Accuracy: 0 *.* 953 Precision: 0 *.* 954 Recall: 0 *.* 953 F1-Score: 0 *.* 953 ROC AUC: 0 *.* 995 Average Precision: 0 *.* 985 **Strengths:**

*.* **Accuracy** **and** **Precision:** High accuracy and precision indicate that there were minimal misclassiﬁcations in categories. *.* **Robust** **to** **Over** **ﬁtting:** The model is less prone to overﬁtting than i ndividual decision trees due to its ensemble nature. **Weaknesses:**

*.* **Computationally** **Intensive:** The performance of the model depends upon the number of trees(estimators), which can lead to higher computational costs and longer training times.

**4.2** **Multi-layer** **Perceptron** **(MLP)** **Classiﬁer**

MLP classiﬁer refers to an artiﬁcial neural network with multiple layers of neurons; it learns non-linear boundaries for decisions. The model updates the parameter using the Adam optimization strategy by the use of backpropagation. Scores found using MPL were: Accuracy: 0 *.* 702 Precision: 0 *.* 628 Recall: 0 *.* 702

*.* **Low** **Performance:** MPL relatively shows low accuracy and precision compared to models such as XG and RF Boost. *.* **Sensitive** **to** **Hyper** **parameters:** The choice of hyperparameters such as learning rate, activation function, or number of l ayers have a signiﬁcant impact on MLP eﬀectiveness. **4.3** **Logistic** **Regression** **(LR)**

LR is usually applied in binary classiﬁcation. Still, it can be employed for multiclass classiﬁcation problem solutions. The model relies on the sigmoid function for providing probabilities. It performs remarkably well with appropriately scaled data and when the features correlate linearly with the target. *.* **Interpret** **ability:** there is simplicity and understandability as LR can easily provide insights into how the input features are related to predictions. *.* **Eﬃciency:** works eﬃciently in case of separabilit y of classes. **Weaknesses:**

*.* **Limited** **to** **Linear** **Relationships:** limits its utility in certain real-world applications as a model may not perform well for complex and nonlinear distributions. *.* **Lower** **Performance** **in** **this** **Case:** exhibits lower accuracy and precision compared to more complex models in this case. *.* **Over** **ﬁtting:** overﬁts in case of large values of features inter-correlated feature spaces. **4.4** **XGBoost** **(X** **GB)**

XGBoost is the optimized gradient boosting algorithm which is high in terms of eﬃciency, ﬂexibility, and portability. It performs well with structured or tabular data since decision trees are built one a fter another, whereas every tree corrects the error of the previous ones. The results of this model were: Accuracy: 0 *.* 958 Precision: 0 *.* 951 Recall: 0 *.* 948 F1-Score: 0 *.* 949 ROC AUC: 0 *.* 995 Average Precision: 0 *.* 985 **Strengths:** There are the following strengths of XGBoost.

*.* **Superior** **Performance:** it had one of the highest performance matrices in terms of accuracy, precision, and f1-score. *.* **Handles** **Missing** **Values:** is robust in missing data and can handle unstructured data well. **Weakness:** There are the following weaknesses of XGBoost.

*.* **Training** **Time:** mostly accurate but is computationally expensive for suﬃciently large training datasets.

DT are non-linear models that divide data into subsets by recursive splitting based on feature values. **Weakness:** There are the following strengths of the decision tree:

*.* **Over** **ﬁtting:** it can be too speciﬁc and perform incorrectly for other datasets with the same number of samples. *.* **Prone** **to** **Over** **ﬁtting:** dt can overﬁt, if properly not p runed, especially with small or noisy datasets. **4.6** **Cat** **Boost** **(** **CB)**

The CATBoost algorithm handles categorical features eﬀectively by transforming them internally and is a gradient-boosting algorithm. Delivers great performance on various datasets and is robust to overﬁtting. *.* **Training** **Time** **for** **Large** **Datasets:** CATBoost may require more training time for large datasets compared to much simpler models such as Logistic Regression(LR) or Decision Tree (DT).

# 4.7 **SVM**

SVM commonly known as SVM are one of the widely used classiﬁcation and regression algorithms out there. The algorithm works by maximizing the margin between the closest points of two variant classes. This structure oﬀers easy interpretability and performs eﬀectively on problems with well-deﬁned decision boundaries. However, they are susceptible to ov erﬁtting, particularly when tree depth is excessive. *.* **Noise** **Sensitivity:** SVM Suﬀers with noisy datasets like ours due to multiple overlapping classes we have. ## Assessing the Deep Learning Model's **Performance in Forecasting Network Intrusions **

Prashant Kumar 1( B ), Chitra Kushwaha 2, Neeraj Srivastava 3, and Abha Kiran Rajpoot 4

1 Bennett University (The Times Group), Plot No 8-11, Techzone 2, Greater Noida 201310, Uttar Pradesh, India prashant.mnnit10@gmail.com 2 DRDO-Institute for System Studies & Analyses, Civil Lines, Delhi 110054, India

**Abstract. ** In the present scenario, cybersecurity is a major concern as technology is increasing day by day, so it has become a major threat. One of the major threats is an intrusion attack. An attacker may attempt to enter the system via this attack via unauthorized means to perform any malicious activity or to ﬁnd loopholes that become the reason for this. So, there is a need to deal with these loopholes. Hence, one of the sophisticated deep learning models has been covered in this work so that the system can be protected from intrusion attacks. In this methodology, we have used a multiclass classiﬁer, Deep Neural Network (DNN) model, to detect the intrusion attack. We have analyzed and validated the said model on the benchmark dataset named NSL-KDD and observed that the DNN model is giving the best accuracy among existing models. This dataset contains more than 40 features from which we have extracted the useful features and applied a deep learning model that has the capability for feature introspection and can easily perform feature engineering, along with that model can be trained by using a large size of dataset, which ensures a high accuracy rate. There are many approaches given regarding to detect intrusion attacks, but they have focused on different network systems. Here, we have developed a model to detect as well as classify intrusion attacks that is more generic and can be implemented in every network system. The results those are obtained here provide a decent accuracy, as can be seen in the result section, where we have calculated the accuracy to be ~99%, which is a good accuracy for any model to be implemented in real-time.

**Keywords: ** DDoS · Network Intrusion · NSL-KDD · Cloud Intrusion Detection · Neural Network · Nmap · Deep Learning · Internet Control Message Protocol

## 1 **Introduction **

## In the present scenario, Intrusion attacks are very frequent and dangerous for any organi

zation as well as for any individual. This attack allows the attacker to access the system without authorization and performs malicious activity. Intruders try to bypass computer security by the use of code. They can manipulate system ﬁles or crash the system, or can access another user's system through the victim's system.

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 211-221, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_15> - Kumar et al.

In 1972, A USAF paper, written by James P. Anderson, was published that outlined that serious issues are arising in computer security and instructed to become aware of this. This problem was considered in virtually every aspect of USAF operations and administration. So, by that time, security of the system is consequential. Asymmetric routing, common gateway interface scripts, protocol-speciﬁc assaults, and buffer overﬂow are just a few of the ways intrusion attacks can be carried out. In an Asymmetric Routing attack, the attacker utilizes multiple paths for the desired network device. In a buffer overﬂow attack, the attacker attempts to take control of a portion of computer memory inside a network by replacing regular data in those memory regions with a set of instructions that will be executed as part of the attack. In this case, the attacker's goal is to establish a channel via which he may acquire remote access to the network. The common gateway interface facilitates web-based interaction between servers and clients. Protocol-speciﬁc attacks can be performed by targeting any speciﬁc protocols like ICMP, User Datagram Protocol (UDP), Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), Internet Protocol (IP), Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), and ﬁnding openings for network intrusions. By generating trafﬁc volumes that are too high for the system to fully ﬁlter, a system that triggers an undetected "fail open" condition is called a Trojan. In this, stored data is erased, or the system becomes unable to open ﬁles. Worms may be produced with a single piece of code that copies itself without modifying sanctioned program ﬁles. These are frequently transmitted as email attachments and begin to demand network resources.

All these are some different ways to perform an intrusion attack can be undeniably noticed that only practice is different, but in all the methods, the attacker attains access to the system in an unsecured medium and performs malicious pursuit. Though there are varieties of methods available to evade such invasions. Some of them are pattern matching-based or machine learning and deep learning based. As time elapses, unique techniques of carrying out intrusion attacks are identiﬁed in that scenario; pattern matching-based technique lags. As a result, we have described a deep learning model to detect intrusion attacks in this study and demonstrated a diverse report of the achieved accuracy among the Multiclass/Binary classiﬁers. In order to prevent intrusion attempts, we are monitoring the system's network trafﬁc and evaluating the trained deep learning model to identify such attacks. We have classiﬁed the intrusion detection systems (IDSs) into the following three types: Host Speciﬁc IDS, Network Speciﬁc IDS, Cloud Speciﬁc IDS \[Network IDS using Deep Learning\]. Even though some work has been done in this ﬁeld previously, current research is still far from well-structured and complete results. In order to ﬁll the gap, the proposed method has been executed with NSL-KDD dataset along with a deep learning model. The following are the main contributions of the suggested method with this implementation:

- To choose a suitable benchmark dataset and to do the preprocessing on the dataset. - To develop and design the model based on Binary/Multiclass classiﬁer. - To select one of the trained machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models  that are better suited to the problem and deliver the best accuracy by testing on the validation dataset. - To get the training/validation report of accuracy of the proposed model. - To implement the model in the real-time dataset/environment and obtain the validated  accuracy.

## 2 **Related Work **

Different kinds of detection systems are available based on the network of systems that are implemented to detect intrusion attacks. Here we have categorized the models in three ways: - Host Speciﬁc IDS - Network Speciﬁc IDS - Cloud Speciﬁc IDS

In 2023 \[ 1 \], author has suggested an idea to utilize a deep Convolutional Neural Network model with AlexNet with additional network layers to validate the intended operation of urban rail transit and attained 96% accuracy, which concluded that the developed model can attain high accuracy. Next, in 2023 \[ 2 \], authors developed an AIbased Intrusion Detection technique for secure cyber physical system and introduced XAIID-SCPS technique using hybrid enhanced glow-worm, swarm optimization for feature selection, and exhibited the model by obtaining the accuracy rate of 98.87% for CICIDS2017 dataset. Next, in 2023 \[ 3 \], author has presented an optimized method for processing NIDS using vision based deep learning model multiclass classiﬁer with CNN and RNN and validated their approach by giving an accurate 2D image classiﬁcation NIDS on dataset named CSE-CIC-IDS2018 and passed that 2D images into 3 channel RGB color images by giving descent accuracy. Later on, authors \[ 4 \] introduce a fog computing-based framework to detect energy-level-based attacks on UAVs, which was implemented in smart farming. ## 3 **Methodology/Data Processing **

In the preprocessing of the dataset, we clean our data to avoid inconsistency and remove irrelevant information for implementing the model. In this paper ﬁrst we have examined the shape of dataset named NSL-KDD that hold 125972 rows x 43 columns (Fig. 1 ) and scanned all the missing values but there is no missing value, so no requisite to perform any method for it, then next we subsumed all the different type of labels and found that \_Normal: 067342, \_Neptune: 041214, \_Satan: 03633, \_Ipsweep: 03599, \_Portsweep: 02931, Smurf: 02646 times occurred in our output column. Moreover, all the labels along with counts can be seen in Table 1. By dropping the output column from the original dataset, to make it simpler to apply a model to the data, a label encoder is used to translate the categorical values into numerical values. The categorical variables in the NSL-KDD dataset are transformed into matching numerical values using encoding techniques. It entrusts the integer values to each label then categorical values would be converted into numerical values. Thereafter, different scaling methods are applied and checked on the dataset to deﬁne the range of values of every feature. For example, the formula of standardization is (1):

*X * *(* *standardized * *) * = *(* *X* -- *(* *Mean of X * *))/* *Std * *.* *Dev* *.* *of X* (1)

By applying this formula in every feature each value all values will be scaled in the range of 0 to 1, which will expedite to use of algorithms in the data. Now, before splitting the dataset, we club all the labels together except the normal label and form a binary class classiﬁcation problem. Consequently, the dataset has only two classes: one is Normal class that has 67342 samples, and another is IntrusionAttacks class that has 58630 samples (Fig. 2 ). The dataset is then divided into training and testing portions in an 80:20 ratio in order to use the feature selection procedure which will be applied in the training dataset. There are so many feature selection methods from which we have used multiple methods for feature selection and preferred Variance Threshold, Pearson Correlation, and Mutual Info Classif methods. Variance Threshold ejected all those features which does not have the deﬁned threshold. Here we have deﬁned a threshold value, so whichever column contains more than 80% value=0, is exceed. We have also

Assessing the Deep Learning Model's Performance in Forecasting

checked Pearson Correlation to ﬁnd the correlation between each and every feature and disclose the dependency between these features so that we can remove dependent features because it's not giving any effective information. This Correlation coefﬁcient between features is calculated by using the given formula (2):

Corr (X, Y) = *(* *X * − *(* *Mean of X * *))(* *Y * − *Mean of Y * *) *

*(* *X * − *(* *Mean of X * *))* ˆ2 *(* *Y * − *(* *Mean of Y * *))* ˆ2 (2)

The value of this correlation coefﬁcient would be between -1 to + 1. If its value is 0, then it means features are uncorrelated and there is no dependency between these features. After this, we have practiced another feature selection named Mutual\_info\_classif to select the best features by calculating the mutual info between every two features, using the following formula (3):

# MI (X, Y ) = H (X )--H (X \|Y ) (3)

The value of this mutual information is between 0 to 1, and we have selected features those are having top mutual info values to contain only useful information in our data.

## 5 **Conclusion **

In the past, network intrusions were detected using machine learning models and static techniques but these methods are not smart enough to ascertain it in today's time because everyday attackers are getting ingenious technologies to perform this attack so here in the discussed method, we have developed a system that uses deep learning models (DNN) and machine learning models (ML) to detect system intrusions. In this, we have established the DNN model by deep learning algorithms and achieved the accuracy of 98.96% by training our dataset named NSL-KDD, which is elegant in analogy to other machine learning methods. Here we have exhibited the plots of accuracies (training vs validation accuracy) and losses (training and validation loss) that demonstrate how our suggested model can identify intrusions in real time with a reduced false rate. Moreover, these plots and the results are obtained without applying any feature selection approaches. In the upcoming time, it can be extended to ﬁll in the loopholes that become a cause for the system to be a victim system. By this we are examining the data throughout all the incoming and outgoing packets of the network, we can help to make our system more secure and safe.

## Malware Detection and Analysis

**A Comprehensive Review of Static, Dynamic, ** **and Hybrid Approaches **

Chander Prabha 1( B ), Shalini Kumari 1, Mohammad Zubair Khan 2, and Ibrahim Aljubayri 3

1 Chitkara University Institute of Engineering and Technology, Chitkara University, Rajpura, Punjab, India prabhanice@gmail.com 2 Faculty of Computer and Information Systems, Islamic University of Madinah, Madinah 42351, Saudi Arabia zubair.762001@gmail.com 3 Department of Computer Science and Information, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh 11432, Saudi Arabia iaaljubayri@imamu.edu.sa

**Abstract. ** Malware programs constitute a big menace to current computer systems as they interrupt operations and spread within the network through the use of internet connections. The malicious programs are circulated among systems interfacing with networks. The scientiﬁc centres of interest are in striving to come up with high-powered antimalware systems that will effectively overcome such emerging threats. The signature-based detection is the most common form of detecting known malware in terms of matching patterns or signatures. Moreover, heuristic-based approaches use pre-established rules to identify malicious system operations in such structures. The signature-based methods, however, tend to be ineffective against the unknown variations of malware and highly advanced evasion strategies such as codes (obfuscation, packing, polymorphism, and metamorphism), which are especially difﬁcult. In this paper, the current methods of malicious code detection and analysis by use of static analysis, dynamic analysis, and bridge strategies are reviewed.

**Keywords: ** Malware · Machine Learning · Artiﬁcial Intelligence

## 1 **Introduction **

## Malware is an abbreviation of malicious software that signiﬁcantly threatens computer

systems worldwide. Such hostile, intrusive, and destructive programs fall within the framework of malware programs that enter computer systems while keeping their presence secret from the system owner. Among software threats, rootkits and spyware act as separate types that are distributed differently and intended purposes. Malware harms

people, ranging from minor nuisances to serious monetary damage to institutions. Ransomware became a major cause for concern when it began to target user ﬁles through encryption. Systems become unusable unless the perpetrator accepts payment from the victim before unlocking access. The evolution of this type of malware has become very signiﬁcant. Since its inception, with increasingly sophisticated encryption techniques and extortion tactics. Different forms of malware include ransomware, which is also presented as adware, which generates continuous advertising pop-ups, and Trojans that deliver complete system control to hackers. Malware through Trojans provides cybercriminals with unauthorized control of corrupted systems, while pop-up ads function as additional security threats. These malicious programs. Bank details, credit card numbers, and personal data become vulnerable when malware attacks sensitive information systems. Professional developers create malware systems that harm digital hardware equipment while damaging operational capabilities.

Management techniques in malware evolution follow its spreading frequency and technological impact growth. Between 2019 and 2024, malware research predicts that the malware analysis market growth will be substantial because it will reach 11.7 billion USD after starting from 3 billion USD during the 2024-2029 growth rate (CAGR) of 31 percent \[ 1 \]. The AVTest Institute reports that daily malware sample generation reaches 360,000, outlining an average release of 4.2 new malware examples every second \[ 2 \]. The number of malware incidents has steadily risen throughout the last ﬁve years. The yearly increase of 100 million new malware requires highly advanced mitigation tactics because of this drastic rise. While earlier malware often used basic tools, it could identify previous malware through its simple code structures until complex modern malware evolved. Modern complex malware bypasses traditional defensive technology tools such as ﬁrewalls and antivirus software and silently stays hidden in systems, causing severe network damage. Malware exists within different sets of distinct categories. Today's internet security faces severe threats from malware, including viruses and worms, trojan spyware, adware, ransomware, and ﬁreless malware. Two factors inﬂuenced the selection of these eight malware types: their widespread occurrence and their difﬁcult characteristics when operating in resource-limited Internet of Things (IoT) systems. Security threats within IoT and edge environments remain challenging to defend against because these speciﬁc malware categories are prevalent in both areas. The paper's contribution is as follows:

- Gives a systematic explanation of current malware detection methods, such as the  use of static, dynamic, and hybrid analysis techniques. - This list describes types of malware (e.g., viruses, worms, ransomware, ﬁleless  malware) and their emerging threats. - Describes the current limitations and tendencies in the dataset of malware and the  importance of having a wide range of up-to-date benchmarks. - A descriptive analysis of Windows, Android, and IoT-focused malware in order to  match the reality of threat surfaces. - Prabha et al.

## 2 **Types of Malware **

Any program that hackers create to damage computers, servers, clients, or computer networks falls under the malware classiﬁcation. Since its initial appearance, malware has transformed from basic viruses into modern, elaborate threats that adjust and bypass conventional security protocols. Initially, malware manifested as disruptive and damaging software that used ﬂoppy disks and network paths for distribution. The reason behind malware creation has dramatically changed since its initial development. Computing systems have grown more complex while internet access has expanded through all environments, creating conditions for malware to succeed. Current malware implementations use polymorphism and obfuscation features to evade traditional antivirus methods. Traditional antivirus applications cannot detect these techniques because they remain hidden from detection. The development of better malware through Machine Learning (ML) and Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) now takes place alongside improved malware detection systems based on these technologies. Developing complex malware requires advanced techniques, but researchers use them to establish strong defenses and detection systems \[ 3 \]. Fig. 1 shows the types of viruses. **Fig. 1. ** Types of Viruses

Computer Virus: Harmful computer software reproducing by changing authorized system software to embed its programming codes qualiﬁes as a virus. A virus is dangerous to computers because it spreads to other documents that become carriers of the infection \[ 4 \].

Trojan Horse: Malware under the Trojan Horse classiﬁcation uses deceptive methods to disguise itself as genuine items or applications for user installation deception. A cyberattack victim must be on guard since such threats can initiate unauthorized data theft functions and allow system entry without authorization \[ 5 \].

Spyware: A device with spyware installed becomes vulnerable to data theft of sensitive information. The data collection habits of spyware result in compromised sensitive information, which may be passed to businesses, third parties, or advertising entities \[ 6 \].

Worms: Malware that duplicates itself automatically while navigating across networks without requiring a ﬁle to attach. Malware Detection and Analysis: A Comprehensive Review

Adware: Improper advertising software collects user data to show unwanted advertisements to the computer user. The adware delivery of advertisements happens with irregular frequency through pop-up windows \[ 1 \].

Ransomware: Users navigate to an infected system where a demand for money appears before the victims can obtain data decryption services.

Botnets: Such computer networks under attacker control serve to execute large-scale cyberattacks, including DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service).

Fireless Malware: The virus evades standard detection mechanisms by focusing on Random Access Memory (RAM) while employing PowerShell and additional automated systems that system administrators commonly use. System administrators mainly depend on automated processes for their work. A system reboot helps eliminate the infection because the infection does not persist on the storage medium. Attacks that block network services and spam email malware lead to computer network takeover, creating botnet networks \[ 7 \].
