## 4 **Literature Review **

This section of the research study shows how classical ML techniques detect malware through different system environments. In an article \[ 8 \], cybersecurity researchers describe their new method, which uses advanced ML technologies to detect masked - Prabha et al.

malware through a cutting-edge model. The research conducted comprehensive testing on the model with the Obfuscated-MalMem2022 dataset, which revealed its veriﬁed capability to detect multiple malware types reliably. Implementing SMOTE algorithms to address class imbalance generates better performance for the model, which achieves almost perfect precision across binary and multi-class categorizations with four or sixteen classes. The model demonstrates a three-fold performance comprising accuracy above 99%. The staff at \[ 9 \] conducted malware behavior analysis through dynamic operation in controlled execution environments. A hybrid hierarchical IDS using an updated version of the KDD-99 dataset has been developed to improve intrusion detection. The experimental dataset includes 4,898,431 examples equally distributed for training and testing purposes. The system divides cases into several identiﬁcation stages to establish attack classiﬁcations alongside normal occurrences. At the initial level, the classiﬁer separates network events into attack or normal types, and after that, multiple stages identify attacks as DoS, R2L, U2R, and probing groups in a nested fashion. The system design optimization builds better detection accuracy throughout all system levels. The detection rate of the SSVM-based IDS reaches 97.91%, while the Overall Detection Accuracy (ODA) results in 98.79%, which surpasses the performances of Support Vector Machine (SVM), PNN, DT, NFC, and K-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) when used in this structured identiﬁcation framework. The authors in \[ 10 \] established data security needs in modern internet-connected networks by developing a system that identiﬁes normal and attack data packets using an intrusion detection system. The KDD-99 dataset, containing 32,640 samples (12,440 normal and 20,200 attack samples), creates equal training and testing datasets. The research employs supervised learning models, SVM and kNN, through dimensional reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on their data. The PCA-kNN model reached a maximum accuracy of 90.07% through cosine distance to detect network intrusions.

The two main parts of the paper, composed by the authors \[ 11 \], included feature extraction and ML classiﬁer integration. The authors executed sample data and extracted the results through the sandbox system's API calling feature. The research paper employed 42797 malware instances together with 1079 instances of benign ﬁles. A balance was created using under-sampling that reduced malware examples to 1079 instances, and then the dataset was differentially partitioned into training and testing portions of 60:40, 70:30, and 80:20 percent ratios. The dataset was trained by ﬁve ML techniques, which included KNN, Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB), MNB, DT, and RF classiﬁers. An RF classiﬁer test on the dataset resulted in 90.38% accuracy when normalized and a higher 98.91% with the imbalanced data throughout a 70:30 split ratio. The CNN network, utilizing Adam optimization, obtains unique malware characteristics from speciﬁc specimens. The process of image examination with this model generates distinctive properties that enable the identiﬁcation of a malware family to which it belongs. Through this method, analysts without established skills can beneﬁt from the acquired data, which proves effective for IoT security in creating malware protection strategies. Tests conducted on the model have demonstrated its ability to reach 96.64% accuracy. The authors in \[ 12 \] developed a fresh procedure to extract behavior characteristics. The system uses absolute time data encoding for sequences and a construction approach that adjusts based on covariance to support individual variance. The researchers designed the Malware Detection and Analysis: A Comprehensive Review

Behavior Rhythm Insider Threat Detection (BRITD) model using stacked bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) combined with a forward neural network. The system performs well in detecting diverse internal threat types alongside insider threats using the CMU CERT dataset with an accuracy rate of 0.8072 and an AUC score of 0.9730, which outperforms all other benchmark models. The authors in \[ 13 \] have proposed using the LSTM Network for detecting security incidents alongside an effective decision engine for ﬁnding any intrusion. Detection using this method obtains its results through multiple contextual elements. The authors demonstrate their study results through a complete analysis of the ﬁndings. The authors in \[ 14 \] worked with a Brazilian malware classiﬁcation dataset comprising 121000 instances and 57 distinctive attributes of portable executable (PE) ﬁles. The pre-processing phase involved label and one-hot encoding as categorical data conversion techniques before applying Extra Tree Classiﬁer (ETC) feature selection to ﬁnd the 15 most important features. Seven different ML models, Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boost (GB), SVM, LR, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), and AdaBoost (AB), were used to train the dataset. The highest accuracy rate, 99.7%, was for DT and RF during the experiment.

In \[ 15 \], the authors applied multiple machine-learning techniques to dynamically analyze the registry ﬁles with API functions, DLLs, and summary data. The bestperforming technique, among others, was gradient boosting, which showed an accuracy rate of 94.64%. The system obtains more than 92 static features from executable ﬁles before ML analyzes these features. Repeated experiments selected the gradient classiﬁer because it achieved 99.36% accuracy. The future authors plan to expand this work through deep learning models and expanded datasets to develop a robust identiﬁcation system. The authors of \[ 16 \] developed the ZeVigilante framework using multiple ML techniques to detect Zero-Day malware activities. The data originated from IEEE DataPort after extracting the cuckoo-based correlated dataset from ZeVigilante. For data balance, the authors implemented a ﬁlter technique. The analysis of malware ﬁles relied on Application Programming Interface (API) calls and PE imports. Three main steps were applied to process the data: separating a training portion of 70% with the remaining 30% for testing purposes and using KNN, RF, NN, DT, SVM, and NB as training and testing algorithms. Input-based cross-validation, implementing 10 folds, represented the approach used to determine the mean accuracy performance of these models. The RF model achieved the highest accuracies of 98.89% in dynamic testing and 98.17% for static testing. In their work \[ 17 \], the authors treated the number of opcode occurrences as a criterion for separating malware ﬁles from benign ﬁles. The authors executed different executable malware ﬁles obtained from websites inside the Cuckoo sandbox. A training set included 100 benign ﬁles gathered from different websites and 150 malware ﬁles obtained from speciﬁc websites. One hundred ﬁles were selected to perform testing tasks. The analysis included implementing three classiﬁcation methods: RF, NB, and DT algorithms. Precision, recall, and F1-score served as performance evaluation metrics for prediction accuracy assessment. The RF model achieved an accuracy of 97.97%, which proved to be the highest. Corresponding Android-based malware prediction models have been described in various academic publications. Several models are presented, but this research does not pursue the development of ML-based Android prediction models. The authors from \[ 18 \] studied a large dataset featuring 215 characteristics to - Prabha et al.

perform Android device malware classiﬁcation. A solution to prevent data ambiguity was achieved by performing up-sampling on the minority class from the highly imbalanced dataset. This study adopts RFE and RFECV to decrease the initial feature count from 215 and establish variations from 15 to 100 features. LR, SVM, GNB, DT, RF, GB, LGBM, and XGB constituted the eight different ML algorithms used in the study. The model with LGBM reached 99.29% training-test split accuracy and 99.50% crossvalidation accuracy using 100 features. RF achieved 99.1% accuracy by using only 55 features.

## 5 **Malware Datasets **

ML methods have become critical to malware detection, so the necessity for extensive, accurate data sets with diversity has risen signiﬁcantly. Research teams build resilient detection procedures with the help of these datasets to stay ahead of attackers in the ongoing cyber threat competition. Malware data collection creates speciﬁc challenges from malware sophistication and regulatory and moral barriers. Benchmark datasets represent essential tools for both measuring ML model performance and ensuring research reproducibility, and they increase the level of difﬁculty. Monitored malware detection beneﬁts from graph learning approaches because effective models require program execution ﬂow-based data for their performance. The current market datasets do not contain raw binary or graph-relevant properties, restricting their value in this ﬁeld. **5.1 ** **Analysis of Malware **

Numerous studies investigate malware from ﬁle-based or program-based viewpoints, which researchers divide into three primary analysis categories: static analysis, dynamic analysis, and hybrid analysis, as shown in Fig. 3. The analysis approach features multiple facets that this classiﬁcation system addresses for a deep examination of ﬁle programs. The percentage breakdown of researcher-used analysis methods appears in Fig. 4. **Fig. 3. ** Analysis of Malware

**Static Analysis: ** Background characteristics from sample materials can be extracted without running programs. Once the ﬁle has been analyzed, the extracted features are Malware Detection and Analysis: A Comprehensive Review

revealed after complete unpackage and decryption. The static analysis methodology allows researchers to assess before any sample execution occurs. The analysis occurs in three stages, from binary format to metadata information, before reaching code evaluation. All features are acquired by analyzing byte patterns at the binary level. The PE header and other ﬁle format details produce metadata features through analysis at this level. A comprehensive code assessment of the ﬁle requires converting it to assembly code. IDA Pro \[ 19 \] is one of the various tools analysts employ for performing disassembly.

***Dynamic Analysis***: During dynamic ﬁle analysis, the ﬁles run in controlled virtual environments to detect their actions. The execution-based evaluation of ﬁles reveals miscellaneous operational features and operational effects that might stay hidden from static analysis. The dynamic analysis brings ﬁles into operation within a sandbox or virtual machine environment for safety reasons that stop them from impacting the host system. Monitoring the ﬁle behavior consists of analyst evaluations of the API and system calls and ﬁle system changes, network interactions, and system process engagement. Dynamic analysis proves essential for detecting polymorphic and packed malware because techniques based on static analysis often fail to detect such threats.

***Hybrid Analysis: *** Static analysis operates effectively on cost, but its performance diminishes because of obfuscation and packing methods. The resistance of dynamic analysis to low-level obfuscation enables it to detect all malware variants along with new families. The analysis technique is expensive but provides limited scalability because of restricted monitoring capabilities. The hybrid analysis implements an integration strategy between static and dynamic approaches to resolve their individual weaknesses. The static analyzer can implement additional analysis after uncovering hidden code bodies through a combination of these two approaches to conduct more powerful malware detection. **Fig. 4. ** Malware detection from 2015 to 2024

**Target Operating Systems: ** The level of malware aimed at particular operating systems depends signiﬁcantly on each platform's user base dimension and market share numbers. All these platforms have received increased focus from attackers due to their - Prabha et al.

extensive global usage. The massive adoption of several operating systems has stimulated extensive investigation into detecting and classifying malware for these platforms. Research efforts regarding different operating systems are shown in Fig. 5

**Android Malware: ** Android operating systems face attacks because they have opensource code in addition to broad user adoption and an adaptable programming structure that enables cyber criminals to discover system weaknesses. Android continues to be the main operating system on smart devices and tablets, so attackers select it as their primary platform. The open nature of its codebase gives cybercriminals the advantage of identifying exploitation opportunities through analysis, while the capability to install applications from unknown sources creates additional security risks.

**Windows Malware: ** The dominant status of Windows in personal computers makes it a primary target for malware because most people use this system both in homes and enterprises alike. Success depends on the widespread adoption of Windows in critical sectors because it will uncover the maximum damage potential of an attack. **Fig. 5. ** Target operating systems

**IoT Malware: ** IoT devices spread rapidly across networks, which led to critical cybersecurity issues because of newly discovered malware made for these devices. The growing IoT threat has become a research focus point for scientists during the last ﬁve years because of its inherent vulnerabilities in these networks \[ 20 \]. Attacks on IoT devices remain common because these devices lack strong security features and work with minimal resource-optimized systems that need improved protection measures. Attackers exploit conﬁguration weaknesses found in traditional computer systems because IoT devices are installed with default passwords, outdated ﬁrmware, and insufﬁcient patch maintenance \[ 21 \]. The IoT malware family of Mirai and its variants portrays how extensive this danger is because they regularly perform worldwide attacks against millions of devices through DDoS attacks.

**Applications in Real-World Antimalware Tools: ** To ﬁght the changing threats, modern antimalware tools combine static, dynamic, and hybrid analysis methods. Tools Malware Detection and Analysis: A Comprehensive Review

such as VirusTotal and IDA Pro statically analyze ﬁles by examining ﬁle signatures, ﬁle headers, and code structure without actually running the program; they are therefore fast in detecting known variants of malware. Dynamic analysis tools (e.g., Cuckoo Sandbox, Joe Sandbox) run suspicious ﬁles in sandboxes, allowing their behavior during run time to be tracked (i.e., API calls, registry changes, and network trafﬁc) and detecting zero-day and obfuscated malware. Hybrid prevention adapts techniques of both static and dynamic in addition to machine learning to enhance detection with minimal false positives in next-gen solutions such as CrowdStrike Falcon and CylancePROTECT. Also, endpoint protection platforms (EPPs) such as Microsoft Defender ATP use threat intelligence and behavioral analytics deployed in the cloud to identify and prevent malware in real time across enterprise networks. These devices play a crucial role in cybersecurity because they present multipronged protection solutions that will react to advanced attack vectors, such as ransomware attacks and ﬁleless malware.

**Practical Impact and Societal Beneﬁts: ** The present research gives important knowledge about the current detection methods of malware, which moves directly to improving the protection of individuals, companies, and national infrastructure. The systematic review of static analysis techniques, dynamic analysis techniques, and hybrid analysis techniques can empower an antivirus developer and the IT security team with the knowledge to counter rapidly emerging malicious threats such as ransomware, ﬁleless malware, and IoT-speciﬁc attacks. Shortcomings of machine learning-based detection models can be used to enhance the real-world antimalware tools, like CrowdStrike and Microsoft Defender, making them better at detecting zero-day exploits and bypassing advanced techniques of obfuscation. Also, the presented debate concerning the malware data sets and vulnerabilities of operating systems will help policymakers and cybersecurity agencies to be informed concerning the arising threats, so that there can be improved sharing of intelligence on threats, thus proactive approaches to defense. Finally, the effort contributes to creating a safer environment in the digital world because the losses of money and the safety of data are minimized, and trust in the online work is retained, which helps ordinary users and will beneﬁt businesses and national security.

## 6 **Conclusion **

The digital world faces a global menace known as malware, which causes major damage to individuals, organizations, and economic structures. The rising complexity of malware attacks shows that malware continues to worsen its effects while becoming increasingly difﬁcult to stop worldwide. The initial line of malware defence utilises smart detection systems to serve as protective measures, blocking cyber-attack attempts on networks and systems. Detection devices achieve maximum effectiveness through the methods they apply. This paper conducts an in-depth evaluation of the technical environment involving malware by examining multiple malware detection procedures. The research includes a complete assessment of distinct malware detection methodologies. Researchers in the cybersecurity domain can use this study as their essential starting point due to its ability to provide foundational information to developers and stakeholders. Through its technical breakdown of malware defence mechanisms, the study aims to enable practitioners to construct effective defences against malware threats, which constantly - Prabha et al.

## evolve. This type of research serves as knowledge guidance to help defend against

malware, as cybercriminals maintain an unending arms race with defenders. Knowledge of malware detection methods enables the cybersecurity community to prevent digital security threats during continuous protection efforts.

## A Comprehensive Survey of Deep Learning

**Algorithms: Architectures, Applications, ** **and Trends **

Nagamani Molakatala 1( B ), S. Soundharya 2, P. Aruna 3, J. Shakulhameed 4, and R. Jayashree 5

1 School of Computer and Information Sciences, University of Hyderabad, Ranga Reddy district, Hyderabad, Telangana, India

nagamanics@uohyd.ac.in 2 Department of CSE, St. Josephs College of Engineering and Technology, Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, India 3 Department of AI&DS, Dhaanish Ahmed Institute of Technology, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India nitarunap@nehrucolleges.com 4 Department of CSE, Nehru Institute of Technology, Thirumalayampalayam, Coimbatore, India 5 Department of Information Technology, E.G.S. Pillay Engineering College (Autonomous), Nagapattinam, Tamil Nadu, India

**Abstract. ** Deep learning has changed artiﬁcial intelligence for the better, helping make progress in areas such as computer vision, natural language processing, healthcare, and autonomous systems. This survey explains the basic ideas behind deep learning and looks at how its main architectures like CNNs, RNNs, GANs, and transformers have developed, as well as popular hybrid models. We examine different applications to determine how well these models function and what their best and worst aspects are compared to others. Furthermore, this paper analyzes the latest achievements and looks at the obstacles related to deep learning such as data reliance, confusion about explanations, and high energy consumption. After a thorough examination and combining recent works, we discover the leading trends of self-supervised learning, federated learning, and efﬁcient neural architecture search. In the last part, we discuss future approaches, stressing that efﬁcient and generalizable deep learning frameworks are important for meeting the challenges of reality. Those working in research, practice, and policymaking will ﬁnd this survey helpful for realizing the beneﬁts of deep learning technologies.

**Keywords: ** Deep Learning Architectures · Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) · Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) · Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) · Transformer Models · Application Domains · Performance Evaluation · Emerging Trends

## 1 **Introduction **

Machine learning now centers on deep learning, which is revolutionizing the way machines gather information and respond. Using layered neural networks, deep learning helps computers learn from data, pick out meaningful patterns, and predict results with very little help from people. Deep learning models do not require extra work to choose or create features, because they learn these features on their own from raw information. Because of this, they are handy for tasks that require analyzing images, words, sounds, or self-driving vehicles.

Factors such as a tremendous increase in data (also called "big data"), better GPUs and TPUs, new neural network structures, and access to large labeled datasets have led to the growth of deep learning. Because of this, deep learning can now surpass previous AI techniques, performing at the highest level in different tests and areas of use.

One important point about deep learning is that it works with complex relationships by using deep neural networks. Such models, full of millions (or billions) of parameters, are able to represent detailed and abstract parts of data. By way of example, CNNs have improved computer vision by performing well in detecting objects, identifying faces, and analyzing medical images. RNNs, along with their altered forms such as LSTM and GRU, have helped greatly in handling sequential and time-series data, which has contributed to new achievements in both speech recognition and language modeling.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have made it possible for machines to make realistic images, videos, and audio based on latent samples. Lately, models based on transformers such as BERT, GPT, and Vision Transformers have achieved remarkable success in various domains because they can pay attention to all the details in the data. They have achieved the best results seen so far in language understanding, machine translation, and code generation.

This paper is designed to study deep learning algorithms by looking at their key features, their development, their applications in different domains, and the current research that is ongoing. Therefore, we learn from several different works, including Younesi et al. \[ 1 \], Mienye and Swart \[ 2 \], and Sarker \[ 3 \], which stress the importance of knowing both the core concepts of deep learning and how they differ in various domains.

Deep learning is being used in more and more areas all the time. The use of deep learning in healthcare is changing diagnostics, the search for new drugs, and monitoring patients \[ 4 \]. AI in transportation is currently used to make smart and accurate decisions in real-time trafﬁc control \[ 5 \]. In industries, deep learning helps with monitoring systems, measuring product quality, and using robots. Moreover, geosciences, cybersecurity, and the IIoT \[ 6 \] are now adopting deep learning to enhance their performance in terms of accuracy, efﬁciency, and scalability.

A main focus of this paper is the comparison of different deep learning models and how they work in various ﬁelds. In other words, CNNs work well with spatial data, while RNNs and transformers are better with time-based sequences. Image generation, making more data, and spotting unusual patterns are best handled with GANs and autoencoders. Making this comparison helps to recognize the positive and negative aspects of each architecture, supporting researchers and practitioners in selecting suitable models for their projects. - Molakatala et al.

Researchers here have also noted emerging hybrid models and new methods in machine learning training. The area is now focused on using less data and making models work for many different tasks by using techniques including self-supervised learning, few-shot learning, and transfer learning. To address privacy issues, techniques such as federated learning enable decentralized training of machine learning models that are commonly used in the sectors of healthcare and ﬁnance.

Its achievements notwithstanding, deep learning still deals with signiﬁcant challenges. More than anything, deep learning is dependant on the availability of lots of labeled data. Because these algorithms are not transparent, they are not able to be used in crucial decisions. Also, the high amount of energy used to train big models asks questions about the sustainability of deep learning. Authors in \[ 7, 8 \] note that improving a model design by reducing its complexity is becoming important to avoid increasing the computational workload.

There is active research on neural architecture search (NAS), power-efﬁcient models, and artiﬁcial intelligence that people can understand (XAI) to overcome these difﬁculties. The attempts are to make deep learning models easier to use, dependable, and less wasteful. The idea of \[ 9 \] is that joining optimization with deep learning can greatly increase the usefulness and efﬁciency of these models in practice.

Description of the main concepts of deep learning, such as activation functions, backpropagation, and how to optimize them, is presented in Sect. 2. Section 3 focuses on the main architectures of deep learning such as CNNs, RNNs, GANs, and transformers, and explains how new and hybrid models are now appearing. Section 4 discusses examples of deep learning in industries like healthcare, transportation, cybersecurity, and so on. This section compares how various architectures perform when put into real-time use. Key points and ﬁndings from the survey are listed in Sect. 6, and in Sect. 7, the authors predict where the ﬁeld is going next.

## 2 **Foundations of Deep Learning **

It is a part of machine learning that uses brain-similar algorithms to solve complex problems. Multiple levels of data abstraction can be modeled with the various layers used in deep neural networks. Its proﬁciency in ﬁnding complex forms in lots of information gives deep learning a leading role in today's AI systems, including speech recognition, classifying images, medical analysis, and self-driving cars.

The main idea behind deep learning is artiﬁcial neural networks (ANNs), which are made up of several layers of nodes (neurons) that only perform basic calculations. They do this by matching new input with appropriate outputs by continually adjusting weights. Deep learning works so well because we can place the different layers on top of each other to create a deep architecture for feature extraction.

Figure 1 illustrates in detail the deep learning system and how it is trained as described in the foundational concepts. Artiﬁcial neural networks are organized hierarchically, so raw inputs pass through several hidden layers using the ReLU activation function and are transformed into complex features at every level. The four-step learning cycle shown in the ﬁgure consists of producing predictions, checking their accuracy by computing the loss function, ﬁguring out how to change the predictions via backpropagation, and A Comprehensive Survey of Deep Learning Algorithms **Fig. 1. ** Deep Learning Architecture and Training Process

optimizing weights in different ways like using Stochastic Gradient Descent or Adam. Putting dropout and batch normalization techniques together with this cyclical process allows deep learning models to handle complex problems and perform well in different areas of AI.

Table 1 lists the basic ideas that give structure and function to all deep learning algorithms. The performance of a deep learning system, whether used for images or language, depends on the choices of its architecture, the functions it uses, and its method of being trained. As technology in this ﬁeld progresses, more advanced versions of the basic concepts are suggested to make models more accurate and easier to understand. Knowing about these essential parts helps you design solid and realistic models in AI. - Molakatala et al. **Table 1. ** Foundational Concepts in Deep Learning Concept Description Signiﬁcance

## 3 **Deep Learning Architectures **

## With deep learning architectures, we can build models that can pick out intricate pat

terns from very large datasets. With time, various architectures have been put forward, all created to work with different kinds of data and issues. Because of advances in convolutional and transformer models, AI is now being used in more areas and has had a bigger impact. In this section, we are going to analyze Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Autoencoders, and Transformers and describe their function and what makes them powerful \[ 10 \].

## 3.1 **Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) **

## CNNs have been built to handle data organized in a grid-like way, like images. As

pointed out by LeCun et al. in the 1990s, today CNNs are a central part of image classiﬁcation, object detection, and semantic segmentation in computer vision. The architecture includes convolutional layers to spot small details, pooling layers that reduce the data size, and ﬁnal fully connected layers for classiﬁcation. Enhancements in accuracy and efﬁciency have come from AlexandriaNet, Visual Geometry Group Networks, Residual Networks, and Efﬁcient Networks, using deep layers, skipped connections, and multi-stage scaling. A Comprehensive Survey of Deep Learning Algorithms **3.2 ** **Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) **

RNNs are built to work with sequences of data by recalling the past inputs through special states within the network. AML is mainly used for forecasting time series, processing language data, and understanding speech. Even so, traditional RNNs experience issues known as vanishing and exploding gradients, which makes it hard for them to understand long-term sequences. As a result of this issue, experts designed variants known as LSTMs and GRUs to overcome the problem \[ 11 \]. **3.3 ** **Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) **

LSTM is a kind of RNN that uses certain gates to learn relationships between events occurring far apart in time. Because of these gates, LSTM cells can remember and use valid information from a long sequence. Excellent results have been seen for LSTMs in working on language tasks, recognizing speech, and classifying videos. Even though they are effective, LSTMs use a lot of resources and have mostly been replaced by transformers in many ﬁelds. **3.4 ** **Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) **

In the case of GANs, there are two types of neural networks, or generators and discriminators, involved in a zero-sum game. The generator aims to manufacture synthetic information that matches the real thing, while the discriminator tries to separate real data from fake data. In 2014, Goodfellow et al. ﬁrst introduced GANs, which have changed image synthesis, data augmentation, style transfer, and super-resolution tasks. With DCGAN, StyleGAN, and CycleGAN, generated pictures have become more realistic and stable. **3.5 ** **Autoencoders **

Autoencoders are a kind of neural network that learn how to compress data on their own without being taught. There is ﬁrst an encoder that changes the input information to a hidden representation, and then a decoder that uses that hidden code to reproduce the original input. Many use autoencoders in anomaly detection, reducing the number of features, and removing noise from data. With Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), probabilities help the models create data samples in the same style as the data used for training. **3.6 ** **Transformer Networks **

Transformers have revolutionized deep learning, mainly in the ﬁeld of natural language processing. In 2017, Vaswani et al. proposed transformers, which get rid of recurrence and entirely use attention mechanisms to model how tokens are related in a sequence. Because of this type of architecture, many tasks can be handled at once, and larger sequences can be processed more proﬁciently. BERT, GPT, T5, and Vision Transformers are among the best models today, because they are powered by transformers, suitable for translation, summarization, code generation, and image understanding. - Molakatala et al.

Since the ﬁeld is advancing, AI models that use different systems together are gaining popularity and hint at even greater advances in the future.

## 4 **Applications of Deep Learning **

## Deep learning is now considered a groundbreaking approach in many areas, perform

ing remarkable work that people once did themselves. Thanks to learning from raw input data, it can improve its performance compared to traditional machine learning in many areas. Deep learning is leveraged across computer vision, healthcare, autonomous systems, and ﬁnance to drive changes in many sectors \[ 12 \]. A Comprehensive Survey of Deep Learning Algorithms **4.1 ** **Computer Vision **

Deep learning has a major role in computer vision. In image classiﬁcation, object detection, image segmentation, and facial recognition, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have shown impressive results. AlexNet, ResNet, and EfﬁcientNet have reached new heights on modes of testing with datasets such as ImageNet. For example, deep learning makes it possible for us to unlock our phones with a face, use surveillance systems all the time, and see augmented reality in our everyday life. Furthermore, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) help in generating images and making them sharper. As a result, they are used in artistic style transfer, image inpainting, and photo improvement. **4.2 ** **Natural Language Processing (NLP) **

In natural language processing, deep learning has played an important role in improving activities such as language translation, text summarization, sentiment analysis, speech recognition, and question answering. With models such as BERT, GPT, and T5, transformer architectures have done much better than earlier models in terms of accuracy and ﬂuency. Nowadays, these technologies are used in many tools, such as virtual assistants (Alexa, Siri), chatbots for customer service, live translation systems, and software for moderating content. Context and meaning understanding in transformer models allows for answers that are more effective and appropriate in any form of communication. **4.3 ** **Healthcare **

Deep learning applied to healthcare has signiﬁcantly affected diagnostic processes, how medicine is tailored, and medical visualization. Medical experts use CNNs to identify structures like tumors on MRIs, lung problems on X-rays, and eyesight problems in the eye. They are used in ﬁnding drugs, studying genomes, and understanding disease risks. Predicting patient outcomes or suggesting proper treatments is made possible through the analysis of EHRs with help from LSTMs. The use of deep learning in wearable health devices makes it possible to monitor health instantaneously and warn users when necessary. **4.4 ** **Autonomous Systems **

Deep learning plays an important role in designing self-driving cars, drones, and robots. Thanks to deep neural networks, these systems can ﬁnd objects, plot the best path, integrate different types of data, and make decisions in real time. Many self-driving cars use CNNs to sort out cameras and LiDAR sensors, while reinforcement learning and RNNs help them navigate and select the best route. Since sensors create data with many dimensions in space and time, models for these data must be able to handle both features, so deep learning becomes essential. - Molakatala et al. **4.5 ** **Finance and Business Intelligence **

In ﬁnance, algorithms that use deep learning are used for trading, checking for fraud, rating credit, and optimizing portfolios. Such models are suited for handling repeated patterns found in data like that of stocks, transactions, and economics. Applications dealing with customers in banking all include chatbots, as well as apps that provide custom ﬁnancial suggestions and process documents with the help of OCR and NLP. Advanced analytics and understanding customer habits are made possible by deep learning in business intelligence \[ 13 \].

## 5 **Comparison and Performance Analysis **

The performance of DL models depends strongly on their architecture, the nature of the data they receive, how much computation is needed, the way they train, and their ability to suit individual applications \[ 14 \]. At this stage, we thoroughly examine and compare top deep learning models, such as CNNs, RNNs, LSTM, GANs, Autoencoders, and Transformers, by looking at their accuracy, how efﬁciently they run, if they work at larger scales, how difﬁcult they are to train, and what problems they are designed for. **5.1 ** **Evaluation Criteria **

To ensure a structured and objective comparison, the following performance metrics and criteria are considered:

- ** ** **Accuracy and Generalization**: Ability to correctly predict or generate outputs on  unseen data. - ** ** **Computational Efﬁciency**: Time and hardware resources required for training and  inference. - ** ** **Scalability**: Capability to handle large datasets and complex tasks. - ** ** **Model Interpretability**: Ease of understanding how decisions are made. - ** ** **Robustness and Adaptability**: Resilience to noise, overﬁtting, or adversarial attacks. - ** ** **Application Suitability**: Relevance and success in domain-speciﬁc tasks such as  vision, language, and time-series analysis. **5.2 ** **Comparative Analysis **

## 5.3 **Domain-Speciﬁc Performance **

## The main reason why CNNs perform better than other architectures in computer vision

is their ability to detect features in different locations. ResNet and EfﬁcientNet take the lead in important benchmarks including ImageNet and MS COCO. They also help by more clearly representing images in large databases of images. Notably, ViTs from the Transformers group are showing they have high accuracy and are simpler to scale than CNNs. Still, they need to process large amounts of information and learn for a long time \[ 15 \].

## With the rise of BERT, GPT, and T5, Transformers have performed at a level previ

ously unachievable on problems such as GLUE, SQuAD, and SuperGLUE. In contrast to RNNs and LSTMs, transformers can handle multiple input elements together and detect long-term connections easily. Now, RNNs and LSTMs are mostly used for applications that require less computing power or fewer resources. Being sequential, these models are unable to scale as easily as large transformer-based architectures.

## In the ﬁelds of medical diagnostics and EHR analysis, CNNs and LSTMs show a lot

of potential. CT and MRI images are most effectively handled by CNNs, while LSTMs focus on handling repeated sets of health information. The performance of LSTMs and attention-based models is reliable in time-series forecasting, for instance, in ECG signals and weather data. There are little beneﬁts from using RNNs as vanishing gradients and problems in learning over long range stand in their way.

## Across multiple studies and standardized datasets, transformers consistently outperform

traditional RNNs and CNNs in NLP and multi-modal applications. However, CNNs remain unmatched in visual processing efﬁciency for moderately sized datasets. Below are some benchmark highlights: - Molakatala et al. - ** ** **ImageNet (Top-1 Accuracy)**:

## 6 **Conclusion **

The survey covers the main aspects, architecture, uses, and ways that deep learning models perform across many different domains. Structures such as CNNs, RNNs, and newer systems like transformers and GANs have transformed many parts of computer vision, speech, healthcare, and other sectors. We found no universal winner among all architectures; instead, the decision depends on how data is handled and used in various situations. Although there has been great progress, problems such as explaining models, using a lot of power, and needing data still exist. Understanding how things like data biases affect AI is very important for making AI systems stronger, more accessible, and fairer. The survey helps researchers and practitioners by analyzing the latest trends and how models are performing. Although deep learning has matured, it still requires constant advancements and cross-ﬁeld collaboration to reach its highest achievements in AI.

## 7 **Future Trends **

As deep learning develops, various emerging trends are helping to determine where it is heading. Self-supervised learning is increasing in popularity, since it can work with fewer labeled and more unlabeled data. Federated learning helps ensure data safety and privacy as it carries out model training on many edge devices, and this is important for medical and IoT ﬁelds. With ENAS and MobileNet becoming more popular, it is evident that people are focusing on lowering energy use and working on smaller devices. In addition, the need for explainable AI is growing to make sure model decisions are more transparent and trusted. The use of text, vision, and voice simultaneously allows deep learning models to achieve more. In the following years, there will be more interest in models that are sustainable, easy to interpret, and can function well in real-life situations, representing a new step for deep learning. ## Dynamic Blockchain-Cloud Integration **for Secure and Scalable Healthcare Data ** **Management ** Pranav Tank and Sushil Kumar Singh ( B )

Marwadi University, Rajkot, Gujarat, India \{pranavbhai.tank,sushilkumar.singh\}@marwadieducation.edu.in

**Abstract. ** When in unison with cloud-based healthcare infrastructure, blockchain technology is revolutionizing a solution to long-standing security and privacy issues experienced in the clinical setting. The image of integrity, as conceptualized in the given systematic literature review, challenges the ﬁeld of knowledge and exposes the idea that blockchain is used as a powerful shielding system, which sustains the weaknesses of traditional electronic health-record (EHR) management systems. Empirical evidence has also shown that EHR systems enabled by blockchains reinforce secure data governance and deﬁnes patients with better commercialization of their information through compelling acknowledgment procedures. The distributed model that blockchain inherits veriﬁes the integrity of the data and transparency of the system, thus, reducing the risks posed by centralized data stores. At the same time, the combination of the characteristics of blockchain and the capabilities of cloud computing eliminates the problem of scalability and allows unimpeded interaction of health care stakeholders with data and ensuring data conﬁdentiality. The outline dynamic blockchain system attracts adaptive consent management, which leads to enhancing patient autonomy manyfold and bringing conﬁdence to the wider care setting. On the whole, these observations support the conclusion that innovative security models could be a prerequisite of the healthcare sector, and blockchain-cloud integration can be seen as one of the processes that can address the current security challenges and pre-empt privacy issues in the future. Finally, the discussion on the safe healthcare systems is promoted by the research that establishes the shift-making capacity of blockchain to reconﬁgure data-management processes within cloud-based healthcare. **Keywords: ** Blockchain · Cloud Computing · Security Model

## 1 Introduction

## 1.1 Overview of Blockchain in Cloud-Based Healthcare System

## The blockchain technology has become a disruptive software framework in the health

care informatics domain with beneﬁts used to improve data security and the privacy of patients. Traditional ways of healthcare information management systems often become

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 246-256, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_18> Dynamic Blockchain-Cloud Integration for Secure and Scalable

involved in such phenomena as unauthorised access, data penetration, and centralisation of access to sensitive information, which undermines integrity and conﬁdentiality of important patient data. Differently, blockchain technology provides a decentralised architecture which eliminates these risks as it ensures integrity, transparency and patientbased control. In the recent years, a surge in cyberattacks on the healthcare industry targeting electronic health records (EHRs) has occurred, making the application of effective security and frameworks a pressing necessity. Immutable ledger design and consensus protocols provide Blockchain with an effective means by which to oppose unauthorised alteration of information and hacking attempts. The distributed fact that blockchain stores data eliminates the existence of single points of failure thus enhancing the general security status of modern healthcare systems. Blockchain combined with cloud computing reduces the problem of scalability which is experienced in traditional healthcare IT systems.

Cloud platforms will offer processing power and storage capacity necessary to maintain the large pools of health data, but blockchain will ensure the data is conﬁdential and secure in storage and transfer. The same integration enables safe and efﬁcient transfer of data between healthcare stakeholders, i.e., patients, clinicians, and researchers, facilitating a cooperative environment to enhance patient care and speed up medical research. Many studies have demonstrated effectiveness of blockchain in the protection of health information in cloud-based cyber-physical systems. A smart contract-based framework has been created with the use of Ethereum to perform secure transfers of electronic health records such that sensitive health data is not compromised by possible risks. The HIE of One project is the patient-controlled exchange of health information where the management of the health information is placed under the management of the patient, and where this exchange of information can be shared by authorised parties through blockchain technology (Fig. 1 ).

**Fig. 1. ** Overview of Blockchain Security Architecture in Cloud-based Healthcare System

The potential of blockchain is enormous, however, its adoption in cloud-based healthcare systems is encountered by many challenges. The interoperability issues, regulatory adherence, and the need of standardised protocols are some of the challenges that are to be addressed so as to be able to take full beneﬁt of this technology. In our paper we would like to investigate the use of blockchain technology that allows to create dynamic means - Tank and S.K. Singh

of consent in the medical ﬁnancial industry where the patient can have real-time control over his or her data with the help of smart contracts. The remaining goal is to discuss how the integration of blockchain and cloud computing can be synergistic in combatting the problems of scalability and security within the traditional healthcare IT systems to improve data transmission and communication between the health care stakeholders. In addition, the paper will analyze the current blockchain-related frameworks and initiatives directed at protecting electronic health records and patient-friendly management, e.g., Ethereum-based initiatives on smart contracts as well as the Health Information Exchange of One (HIE of One).

The discussion below will provide a detailed, dynamic architecture where healthcare data can be provisioned by means of integrated smart contracts executed on an infrastructure that is running on a blockchain-based cloud. First, we question the usefulness of the patient-controlled, real-time consent systems facilitated by smart contracts and then proceed to evaluate how blockchain is an effective solution to the centralized vulnerability in the current EHR infrastructures. Lastly, research plan intends to develop a secure regime of interoperability that is seamless, using such Ethereum-based smart contracts as well as the HIE framework of one program so as to obtain complementary advantages of blockchain and cloud technologies when it comes to conducting data exchange with scalability and security involved (Fig. 2 ).

## 2 Related Work

challenges in terms of data security, integrity and privacy. Traditional security mechanisms have failed fully to address the challenges, which leads to the requirement of novel solutions. A clear illustration of the same is the application of a dynamic blockchain as a paradigm of security in a cloud environment. Dynamic blockchain is a distributed and decentralized ledger of information that allows safe storing and transferring. Unlike the traditional blockchain that is impervious to changes, it is able to modify and update the data records which is of great value in clouding infrastructures where data is naturally dynamic. Moreover, the blockchain technology provides a stable platform to Smart Contracts hence, giving both consumers and vendors of services an assurance of contractual integrity. Such a security improvement increases the level of the system as a whole. ## 3 Proposed Methodology

## In the current discourse, we have proposed a methodological framework that can offer

an approach to strengthening the cloud security by utilizing smart contracts, which is a strategy that leverages on the inherent features of the blockchain, including security, transparency, and immutability, to curb the present weaknesses that currently deﬁne modern cloud infrastructures. The whole idea amalgamates three major components of Smart Contracts, Cloud Security Architecture, and Blockchain Technology. The Fig. 3 provides an operation plan of how to implement the smart cloud environment security.

## 1. User Interface Layer

The top level which is also termed as the presentation level is the main level at which all users of the system contact the system. It provides the portals and front-end applications that provide access to patients, care givers (doctors, nurses, administrative staff etc.), and other stakeholders (e.g., insurance companies) to access and interface with in the system. 2. **Application Layer (Cloud Computing Environment) ** This layer serves as the central processing point of the application, running the core business logic, application services and middleware to co-ordinate communications between the user interfaces, the smart contracts and data stores. Installed in cloud computing environment, the application level provides scalability, reliability and costeffectiveness. - Tank and S.K. Singh

**Fig. 3. ** Architecture of Blockchain-Integrated Cloud-Based Healthcare Systems

3. **Smart Contract Layer ** This layer acts as the immutable logic and rule enforcer of the system, residing directly on the blockchain. Ethereum-based Smart Contracts are self-executing contracts with the terms of the agreement directly written into code. They streamline essential healthcare processes, ensuring transparency, security, and permanence. 4. **Blockchain Layer (Ethereum) ** This is the foundational layer provides a decentralized, immutable, and transparent ledger for the entire system. Ethereum is selected for its strong smart contract capabilities, allowing complex programmatic logic to be executed on the blockchain. 5. **Data Storage Layer ** This layer is responsible for the actual storage of all healthcare-related data, distinguishing between sensitive patient health information and general system data. It utilizes a hybrid approach for optimal security, scalability, and privacy

## 4 Technological Innovation

As we look into the potential implementation of the blockchain in the cloud-based healthcare environment, we could come to a conclusion that this phenomenon is a signiﬁcant step forward toward addressing the traditional challenges of traditional data safety and privacy. In particular, systems currently based on centralized data stores are particularly vulnerable to intrusion, data corruption and loss, represented by the subsequent degradation of patient conﬁdentiality and data integrity. In comparison to them, blockchain platforms follow a completely different principle of operation: decentralized data warehousing along with immutability, improved transparency, ﬁne-grained access rules that focus the patient in the heart of the data community. Dynamic Blockchain-Cloud Integration for Secure and Scalable

**The Need for Innovation in Healthcare Data Security ** The recent cyberattacks against electronic health records (EHRs) indicate the dire need to introduce tighter security. The healthcare data is especially at risk because it is sensitive and reasonably valuable to harmful players. The immutable ledger feature of blockchain and consensus protocols is giving it a formidable block against unscheduled data manipulation and malicious attacks. The decentralization of blockchain unlike the traditional system will have single point of failure and by doing this the data will be shared across different nodes making risks of the data being stolen negligible.

**Blockchain's Role in Enhancing Data Privacy and Consent Management ** Dynamic consent management is one of the most effective contributions that blockchain makes to healthcare. Smart contracts are self-executing agreements (Self-executing agreements are programs that automate access control), and patients may be placed in a position to gain more control over their health data. With this technology, one can authorize, deny, or change the access levels in real-time, so that sensitive data spreads within a limited circle. This will inspire more conﬁdence in the medical service provider and complies with the high standards of data safekeeping, like GDPR and HIPAA.

**Synergy with Cloud Computing for Scalability and Efﬁciency ** Blockchain is secure, but cloud computing has enough scale and power to process large amounts of health information. The mixture of these technologies will lead to the creation of a new system where the healthcare providers will be able to store massive data in the cloud, but the integrity and conﬁdentiality of data transferring and storage are guaranteed by blockchain. This synergy is dealing with the problem of scale that is evident with the traditional healthcare systems and will make the information transfer practices safe and easy across the patients, clinicians, researchers and other stakeholders.

**Challenges to Adoption ** There are many barriers to integrating blockchain into healthcare as enticing as it is. Interoperability is another issue since different systems and standards must be harmonized in order to support cross-system exchange of data without problems. The monitoring of regulatory compliance and compliance with privacy laws and regulations must be well designed particularly in international professional environment where legal systems vary. Furthermore, there are no standardized protocols, and as such it becomes a need to carry out research and cooperate among stakeholders in order to make it widely-adopted.

## 5 Discussion

The current paper examines the combination of blockchain- and cloud-based technologies as one of the ways to ensure safe, scalable, and cost-effective data management in the ﬁeld of healthcare. With the ability to combine immutable and decentralized nature of blockchain with the elasticity and its capacious storage provided by cloud computing, the proposed framework will be able to help to ensure data integrity and to preserve patient privacy, as well as its real-time accessibility across the entire healthcare data ecosystem. Importantly, the conﬁguration allows optimization of performance, scalability, and data security on the one hand without affecting quality of service on the other - Tank and S.K. Singh

since it allows off-loading non-sensitive information to the cloud and keeping sensitive records and access logs on the chain. Access control and auditing are automated through smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain that does not require administrators to control, removing high administrative overheads and the chance of human error. Based on simulations and experimental analyses, evidence shows that the structure scales well with an increase in the data volume and with user demand. Also, the delay provided by the workings of the blockchain cannot be considered signiﬁcant to the wishes of partitioning of the data and implementation of the consensus protocols that include Proof-of-Authority and delegated Proof-of-Stake. In spite of these accomplishments, a number of constraints still exist. The decentralization advantages of the blockchain are reduced, albeit to a minor degree, by the trust that is granted by cloud services. Moreover, the heterogeneous Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems and blockchain implementations cannot always interact with each other, so additional standardization is still required. Lastly, there is a need to conduct a more stringent evaluation of the performance of the system in the real-time environment during the states of emergency in healthcare.

To begin with, the creation and implementation of common application programming interfaces and information structure allowing coherent communication and the exchange between heterogeneous electronic health records platforms, blockchain hubs and cloud-based systems. Second, it will introduce machine-learning-based, dynamic, and context-adequate mechanisms of the access control capable of reconciling the issues of privacy with the needs of usability of healthcare providers. Third, the incorporation of sophisticated cryptographic primitives, i.e. homomorphic encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, and secure multi-party computation, so that it is possible to perform computation on the encrypted data without revealing any sensitive values of the inputs. Four, the utilization of edge and fog computing capabilities to perform functions like local data processing and caching to implement real-time and eliminate dependency on centralized cloud computing resources.

Lastly, there is a review of energy-efﬁcient consensus algorithms and sustainable computing approach to reduce the environmental costs of the blockchain operation. Considering the above-mentioned concerns can change current heterogeneous healthcare infrastructures by implementing the dynamic integration of blockchain and cloud infrastructures that can achieve better balance between trust, efﬁciency, and scalability (Fig. 4 ). ## 6 Conclusion and Future Work

The current study has identiﬁed the impressive potential of the integration of blockchain technology and cloud computing to enhance security, support privacy, as well as introduce scalability in the management of healthcare-related data. The proposed dynamic blockchain-cloud architecture resolves the key risks in the e-health-records (EHR) governance to enable data control by patients, increase data integrity with decentralized storage, and enable the secure data exchange between the various actors in the healthcare ecosystem. Despite the positive nature of the preliminary results, a number of dimensions should be pursued further. Number one is optimization of performance and scale of the system especially in large scale deployments. Simultaneously, an attempt to develop common procedures of blockchain-cloud interactions in healthcare environments is essential. In addition, the development of the progressive encryption measures that could enhance privacy and security of data in the holistic structure deserve consideration. Lastly, it will be important to test the effectiveness through pilot studies in actual situations in a wide variety of healthcare settings to determine any possible implementation difﬁculties. The continuous development of the blockchain and cloud technology raises the potential to reinvent healthcare data management with further research in this ﬁeld, which may lead to an improvement in patient outcomes and care.

## Secure Cloud-Based PHEV Data Using

**SVM-Based Classiﬁcation and Multi-Layer ** **Hybrid Encryption **

## Surendra Reddy Vennapusa ( B ) and P. Vasuki

Department of Information Technology, Bharath Institute of Science and Technology, Chennai, Tamilnadu, India vennapusa.1626@gmail.com, hodit@bharathuniv.ac.in

**Abstract. ** Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs) are increasingly used because they consume less fuel and produce fewer emissions. While operating, these vehicles generate different kinds of data such as battery status, charging details, energy usage, and basic vehicle information. This data is usually sent through IoT networks and stored in cloud servers so that it can be monitored and analyzed. However, when vehicle data is transferred and stored in the cloud, security becomes a major concern, especially when the data is sensitive.

In this work, a simple cloud-based security method is proposed for protecting PHEV data. Instead of treating all data in the same way, the proposed approach ﬁrst separates the data based on its importance using a Support Vector Machine (SVM). This helps in identifying which data needs stronger protection. After this step, a hybrid encryption method is applied using a combination of publickey and symmetric encryption techniques. By applying encryption based on data importance, the method avoids unnecessary processing while still maintaining good security.

The proposed method is tested using PHEV-related data in a cloud environment. The performance is evaluated by observing encryption time, energy usage, and the reliability of data protection. The results show that the approach is able to secure vehicle data effectively without causing signiﬁcant delay or power overhead. Due to its simplicity and efﬁciency, the method can be used in real-time cloud-based PHEV applications.

**Keywords: ** Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs) · Cloud Security · Internet of Things (IoT) · Support Vector Machine (SVM) · Data Classiﬁcation · Hybrid Encryption · Vehicle Data Protection · Energy Efﬁciency

SVM methods have been proven to be very effective in solving data classiﬁcation problems. The necessity of a data categorization is very important in order to create a new data point and hyperplane. SVM classiﬁes data in two categories \[ 32 \], namely, linear and non-linear data. The SVM classiﬁer sets different kernels. kernel to a linear data set. Additionally, sets two kernel's, rbf and polynomia, for the nonlinear data set \[ 31 \]. 2. **IoT/Users/Customers: **

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of interconnected devices, which connect PHEV vehicles and exchange data between electric vehicles with the cloud. Usually, IoT electric devices are embedded with technologies such as sensors and software. IoT has been used by various electric vehicles organizations to achieve efﬁcient operation, provide better customer service, and increase electric vehicle users and business growth. In the ﬁeld of IOT, electric vehicle data is transmitted from one electric vehicle user to another as well as from a human to a computer via a data electric vehicle network without any interaction \[ 26 - 29 \]. 3. **Cloud Storage: **

In this proposed method, the electric vehicle data sensed through IoT is ﬁrstly stored in the cloud. Through 3-Tier hybrid security management, the data is classiﬁed with SVM methods and after applying encryption and description security techniques, the data is stored again in the cloud. Moreover, through the public internet or private network you can easily access unlimited data securely anytime anywhere \[ 30 \]. 4. **Three-Tier Hybrid Security Management for PHEV: **

In this proposed method, the 3-Tier hybrid cryptographic encryption algorithm is used for PHEV. This algorithm consists of combination features of AES, DES and RSA algorithms. First, the proposed 3-Tier hybrid algorithm assumes that the data sensed from IoT can be not directly classiﬁed from the IoT electric vehicles data. It securely stores the sensed data from IoT in the cloud. If the perceived data is small amount of data, directly 3-Tier hybrid encryption algorithm is applied \[ 4 \]. If the same is a large data set, it is classiﬁed using SVM techniques. The AES, DES and RSA techniques are combined with a distributed security 3-Tier layer and the secure data are ﬁnally stored in the cloud \[ 21 \]. **Key Generation, Encryption and Decryption ** **Steps: **

## Accurate Hybrid Intrusion Detection Model **for IoT Networks Using MCA, DBSCAN, ** **and XGBoost **

Raed S. Naje 1( B ), Jolan Rokan Naif 2, and Ameen A. Noor 1

1 College of Education, Department of Computers, Al-Mustansiriyah University, Baghdad, Iraq

\{raedsabah971,a.ameen63\}@uomustansiriyah.edu.iq 2 Informatics Institute for Postgraduate Studies, University of Information Technology and Communications, Baghdad, Iraq Dr.jolan\_alkhazraji@iips.edu.iq

**Abstract. ** With the rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices and the increasing sophistication of cyber threats, the demand for efﬁcient and realtime intrusion detection systems (IDS) has become critical. This paper proposes a high-accuracy hybrid IDS using machine learning (ML) tailored for IoT environments, integrating Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) for dimensionality reduction, Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) for unsupervised anomaly detection, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) for powerful supervised classiﬁcation. The model was evaluated using the UNSW-NB15 benchmark dataset, with an 80:20 train-test split. Experimental results demonstrated outstanding performance, achieving 99.9% accuracy and an F1 score of 99.70%, signiﬁcantly outperforming previous state-of-theart methods. Key advantages of the proposed system include low latency, high adaptability to dynamic and imbalanced data, and the ability to detect zero-day attacks. MCA effectively enhanced data quality by removing noise and redundancy, DBSCAN successfully identiﬁed anomalous patterns without prior labels, and XGBoost provided robust classiﬁcation even under challenging conditions. This work shows that in contemporary IoT networks combining supervised and unsupervised learning approaches in a hybrid model signiﬁcantly improves intrusion detection. Future efforts are urged to investigate preserving data privacy by integrating distributed training and deep learning across IoT devices.

**Keywords: ** Intrusion Detection System (IDS) · Internet of Things (IoT) · Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) · DBSCAN · XGBoost · Hybrid Machine Learning

## 1 **Introduction **

## Rising as a transforming paradigm in modern computing, the Internet of Things (IoT)

lets billions of heterogeneous devices gather, exchange, and process data across a broadspectrum including healthcare, smart cities, industrial automation, and transportation

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 271-280, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1> \_ 20 - S. Naje et al.

\[ 1 - 3 \]. Among these low-human-intervention devices are environmental sensors, connected cars, smart appliances, and security cameras \[ 4 - 6 \]. But for many cyberattacks, the ubiquitous deployment of IoT devices-often deﬁned by limited processing power, memory, and built-in security mechanisms-has attracted appeal \[ 7 - 9 \]. Among these hazards compromising user privacy, data integrity, and system availability are denial of service (DoS) attacks, eavesdropping, packet spooﬁng, and malware infections \[ 10 - 12 \]. IoT networks' lightweight communication character and distributed architecture complicate the application of traditional security mechanisms even more \[ 13 - 15 \]. Because of their resource-intensive character and inability to dynamically adapt to changing threats in real time, conventional security solutions are sometimes inappropriate for IoT environments \[ 16 - 18 \]. Deﬁning IoT networks and identifying hostile behavior depend mostly on intrusion detection systems (IDS) \[ 19 - 21 \]. Most traditional IDS systems, however, rely just on either signature-based detection or anomaly detection, which usually results in low accuracy in dynamic, real-world IoT scenarios \[ 13 - 15 \] and limited generalizing ability. Thus, much needed are intelligent, lightweight, and adaptive IDS models that can run in real time and precisely distinguish between benign and malicious behavior with minimum false alarms \[ 16 - 18 \]. This work proposes a new hybrid intrusion detection model especially suited for IoT environments in order to handle these challenges \[ 19 - 21 \]. Integrated into the model are three basic elements of Machine Learning: Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) for dimensionality reduction and feature enhancement; Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) for unsupervised detection of aberrant patterns; and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) for accurate and efﬁcient classiﬁcation of trafﬁc instances \[ 22 - 24 \]. The proposed hybrid model increases detection accuracy and responsiveness to real-time hazards by aggregating the strengths of both unsupervised and supervised machine learning methods \[ 25 - 27 \]. Benchmark IoT intrusion datasets covering a broad spectrum of attack types, including DoS, probing, and data injection, help to assess the efﬁcacy of the model \[ 28, 29 \]. In terms of detection accuracy, recall, and processing efﬁciency, experimental results show that the suggested approach greatly beats conventional approaches, so it presents a potential solution for securing next-generation IoT networks \[ 30, 31 \].

## 2 **Related Work **

The fast spread of IoT devices and the growing complexity of network infrastructures in recent years have made advanced intrusion detection systems (IDS), especially those able to run in real-time and under imbalanced data conditions \[ 32, 33 \], necessary. Because unsupervised learning-based methods can identify unknown attacks without depending on labeled datasets \[ 34, 35 \], several studies have examined them.

Duaa et al. \[ 36 \] conducted one prominent study suggesting a hybrid intrusion detection model combining DBSCAN with Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO). This model adaptively optimizes the DBSCAN epsilon ( ε ) parameter for every incoming data stream using GWO. The detecting accuracy and clustering quality are much improved by this automated tuning. The reported accuracy of the N-BaIoT dataset was 98%. Although the model attained great accuracy and real-time capabilities, its dependence on DBSCAN may restrict generalization in noisy surroundings. Accurate Hybrid Intrusion Detection Model for IoT Networks

Gutierrez and colleagues \[2024\] \[ 37 \] carried out the investigation. Evaluating several unsupervised models on the BoT-IoT dataset-a real-world, highly imbalanced dataset with many attack types-this work uses K-means++, DBSCAN, Isolation Forest, and Local Outlier Factor (LOF). Based on the ﬁndings, DBSCAN shown up to 95% accuracy in differentiating normal from abnormal trafﬁc. The research underlines how sensitively model performance is to class imbalance, so supporting the need of hybrid or ensemble-based IDS systems. Recent research on intrusion detection systems (IDS) for network security has made increasing use of artiﬁcial intelligence and machine learning techniques to raise detection accuracy and reduce false alarm rates.

proposed in the 2024 Umair Rashid et al. \[ 38 \] hybrid model combining K-Means and DBSCAN for clustering with Sequential Minimal Optimization (SMO) for classiﬁcation. On the NSL-KDD dataset, the model showed reduced false alarm rate and improved anomaly detection accuracy with a 97.36% detection accuracy. using the CICDDoS2019 dataset, combining individualised federated learning with DBSCAN to detect DDoS attacks.

FedDB, a tailored federated learning (PFL) system for identifying Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks in distributed environments, especially in IoT and SDNbased networks, was ﬁrst presented by Lee et al. \[ 39 \]. To address the difﬁculty of non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) data across clients, the system aggregates Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models for sequential data analysis with DBSCAN clustering to group clients based on model similarity. FedDB improves model personalization and performance by exchanging and mutually training clustered models, which enhances detection accuracy while maintaining user data privacy. Using the CICDDoS2019 dataset, achieved up to 97% accuracy even under imbalanced data conditions.

In this context, Kaliyaperumal et al. \[ 40 \] presented a fresh hybrid unsupervised learning model combining Autoencoder, One-Class SVM, and DBSCAN to improve cybersecurity in IoT settings. The CIC-IDS2017 and CSECIC-IDS2018 datasets were used in evaluations of the model. Dimensionality reduction was accomplished with a basic Autoencoder (bAE), OCSVM for anomaly detection, and DBSCAN to cluster aberrant trafﬁc and examine attack characteristics. With a notable decline in false positives and negatives, the proposed system attained an accuracy surpassing 98%.

Efendi et al. \[ 41 \] presented an efﬁcient method using DBSCAN, SMote, and LSTM to solve the problem of class imbalance in network trafﬁc data by means of DDoS attack detection. Comprising a lot of records, the study drew on actual data gathered via live penetration testing. First, outlier detection was done using

DBSCAN; synthetic minority samples were created using SMote to balance the dataset; LSTM was then used to learn time-based attack patterns. With a notable decrease in validation loss, the results revealed a notable improvement in model performance, attaining 99.5% accuracy and an increase in F1-score from 93.4% to 98.3%. The model suffers from limited interpretability in industrial environments and requires great computational resources and long training times even if its great efﬁcacy.

In another study, Zhukabayeva et al. (2025) \[ 42 \] suggested an integrated framework combining clustering algorithms, including K-Means and DBSCAN to analyze network

Regarding accuracy and recall, results revealed that the Random Forest model performed the best. One major beneﬁt of this system is its support of real-time threat identiﬁcation.

## 3 **Proposed Methodology **

The proposed methodology aims to detect intrusions in IoT networks through an integrated system that leverages a combination of modern data analysis techniques. The process begins with the acquisition of raw data directly from IoT devices, which is often unstructured and may contain noise or irrelevant information. Therefore, the data ﬁrst undergoes a preprocessing phase, which includes cleaning to remove missing or incorrect values, normalization to unify data scales, and encoding to convert categorical or symbolic values into numerical representations suitable for analysis (Fig. 1 ).

**Fig. 1. ** Data processing and intruder identiﬁcation method

Once the data is properly prepared, dimensionality reduction is applied using Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA). This technique transforms qualitative data into a lower-dimensional numerical format, making it easier to process while preserving the most important variance among features. This simpliﬁed representation serves as a critical input for the next step: anomaly detection.

At this point the DBSCAN method is applied to ﬁnd aberrant data patterns. Based on density, it groups data points; it treats isolated points-that which do not ﬁt any cluster-as anomalies or possible markers of hostile activity. DBSCAN's outputs enable ﬁrst knowledge of the data distribution and assist in the identiﬁcation of odd behavior.

The XGBoost method is used during classiﬁcation. With big datasets, this strong machine learning model is well-known for performance and efﬁciency. Using the UNSWNB15 dataset, split 80% for training and 20% for testing, the model is trained. The training process balances training time with prediction accuracy using 50 estimators and a learning rate of 0.1.

At last, depending on the knowledge it has gained in the previous phases, the trained model decides whether fresh data instances show normal behavior or possible intrusions. By combining dimensionality reduction, unsupervised anomaly detection, and supervised machine learning classiﬁcation, this hybrid method thus presents a useful and efﬁcient means to improve the security of IoT networks. - S. ## 5 **Conclusion **

## Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Appli

cations with Noise (DBSCAN), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) are proposed in this work to be integrated in an optimal hybrid machine learning-based intrusion detection and routing framework for IoT networks. Designed to solve the twin problems of secure, adaptive routing inside the dynamic and resource-limited Internet of Things and real-time attack detection, the system The suggested method shown better performance in several aspects. MCA reduced dimensionality effectively to preserve signiﬁcant patterns among categorical data. DBSCAN enhanced the unsupervised capacity of the - S. Naje et al.

## model to ﬁnd anomalous behavior and early identiﬁcation of either new or zero-day

attacks. Finally, XGBoost produced strong and high-accuracy classiﬁcation exceeding traditional models in terms of precision, recall, and computational economy. Experimental evaluations conﬁrmed from the USNW-NB15 dataset that the proposed hybrid system signiﬁcantly increases detection accuracy while maintaining low false alert rates and computational overhead. Future research should enlarge the proposed architecture by combining deep learning with machine learning models to enable distributed training among IoT devices without compromising data privacy.
