## A Data-Analytics Technique for Counterfeit

**Medicine Detection Using Artiﬁcial Intelligence, ** **Blockchain, OCR, and Spectroscopy **

## Binitha S. Thomson ( B ) and W. Rose Varuna

Department of Information Technology, Bharathiar University, Coimbatore, India bini2796tha@gmail.com, rosevaruna@buc.edu.in

**Abstract. ** Fake medications usually contain inactive substances, harmful chemicals, or resemble authentic wrapping, threatening the health of society and decreasing the credibility of healthcare programs. The traditional methods of detection, manual tests, chemical analysis, are usually very expensive, slow, and impractical in under-resourced environments. In order to overcome these shortcomings, the study will offer a multi-modal approach based on a combination of Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI), Optical Character Recognition (OCR), Blockchain technology, and Spectroscopy with the data analytics technique. Image-based tablet and packaging analysis is achieved with the use of AI (Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)), whereas text on labels is checked by OCR to identify its accuracy in accordance with the ofﬁcial registries; blockchain provides transparency and traceability of the supply chain, and spectroscopy detects chemical compositions of drugs. This is the ﬁrst known approach combining all four techniques for better counterfeit medicine detection. Every sample was addressed with the help of conﬁdence score, OCR match, spectroscopy match, similarity of the surface, and blockchain veriﬁcation status. The evaluation metrics are used to calculate the accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC to validate the counterfeit medicine. Using a simulated two-group data set of OTC analgesics and prescription antibiotics, the proposed data analytics technique achieved better accuracy. This paper shows that the effectiveness of the model was proved by statistical analysis, which supported the fact of the existence of signiﬁcant differences between groups, showing model robustness.

**Keywords: ** Counterfeit Medicines · Artiﬁcial Intelligence · Blockchain · Data Analytics · Pharmaceutical Supply Chain · OCR, Spectroscopy

## 1 **Introduction **

## One of the most pressing and convoluted of the global public health challenges is

the prevalence of counterfeit medicines. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), about 1 in every 10 medical products circulating in low- and middle-income countries is either substandard or falsiﬁed with very serious consequences for health and undermining of domestic health systems \[ 1 \]. Such counterfeit drugs are usually devoid of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), contain incorrect ingredients which may be harmful or are packaged to mislead the customer thinking of authentic medications \[ 2 \].

Counterfeit medicines beyond patient harm however have a dreadful economic impact, ﬁnancial loss to the suitable pharmaceutical companies and additional taxation on the regulatory execution organizations governing the pharmaceutical sector \[ 3 \]. The detection of counterfeit relied in the past on physical inspection, visual checks for packaging and laboratory based analytical techniques such as chromatography and spectroscopy. These methods work well although they are often time consuming, costly and inaccessible in low resource settings \[ 4 \].

In recent years, these limitations have witnessed the renewed interest in using datadriven and technological approaches for pharmaceutical authentication. In the view of Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI), particularly, it has the advanced great strides in automating visual and textual analysis of medical packaging. The research highlights by utilizing the CNN in detecting abnormalities in tablets that are imprint patterns and packaging features, in achieving to achieve high accuracy in differentiating authentic products from counterfeit products \[ 5 \]. To observe the further upgraded technique through the Optical Character Recognition (OCR), which extracts and cross-veriﬁes the label text against trusted databases, facilitating the subtle changes in discrepancies in fonts, spelling or batch codes to specify the counterfeiting which is to be detected \[ 6 \].

Counterfeit medicines persist to be the most harmful threat to global public health in account for about 10% of the entire pharmaceutical market \[ 7 \]. Often, these fake pharmaceutical products provide inaccurate dosages of the drugs, that may contain harmful ingredients or substance that are toxic and have no active effects which are hazardous in risk for public health that trust in the healthcare systems. Conventional approaches used for detecting counterfeit drugs, such as manual inspection that are time-consuming, labor-intensive, and inefﬁcient, while chemical analysis methods are often expensive \[ 3 \]. This signiﬁcant method for the dreadful need for modern scalable solutions and emerging technologies like AI, blockchain technology, and spectroscopic analysis are using a new path for authentic pharmaceutical veriﬁcation \[ 8, 9 \].

To improve the transparency for supply chain management and blockchain technology, modern visual and textual tools are being developed for the transformative solution in the pharmaceutical industry. The advantage of using blockchain technology, it has become a possible way to improve the product traceability, avert tampering, and verify the authenticity of the supply chain system from the origins \[ 8, 10 \]. Powered by Blockchain, mobile applications / QR-based veriﬁcation can be integrated to offer real-time consumer-level authentication and enforcement. Raman or near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy spectral signatures of suspected drugs are chemically proﬁled by comparing them to a reference database \[ 9 \].

The main value of this technique is in its ability to detect altered or substituted ingredients, even where the packaging is virtually indistinguishable to that of genuine products. Although each method has demonstrated success, there has been no integrated, multi-modal framework that combines these techniques for robust and scalable counterfeit detection. These components are mostly evaluated in isolation, which provides only partial solutions that fail against highly sophisticated counterfeits \[ 11, 12 \]. ## 2 **Literature Review **

The advanced counterfeit medicine detection approach has been implemented to improve the detection of efﬁcient counterfeit medicines, which are made from a combination of chemical and visual inspection \[ 2 \]. Besides these methods, the combination of Raman and Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIR) has also been utilized for successfully exposing chemical fakes in counterfeit medicines.

Puglia et al. \[ 5 \] demonstrated that one of the most efﬁcient methods to attain the highest accuracy of false medicine identiﬁcation by using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), as they performed an in-depth examination of the tablet surface. This is a state-of-the-art technique in the ﬁeld of Deep Learning (DL), which is an imagebased fake drug detection system. Likewise, Boesch \[ 6 \] referred to the performance for potential of OCR technology in the veriﬁcation of the text on labels of medicines.

Chen et al. \[ 8 \] reviewed the blockchain technology that has been identiﬁed as a game changer in the domain of pharmaceutical security and drug supply chain management. It initiates an unalterable, decentralized ledger that tracks each transaction and conﬁrms the pharmaceutical drug origins.

De la Fuente et al. \[ 10 \] give a detailed explanation of the blockchain-based app to improve transparency and ensure traceability in the pharmaceutical supply chain management. Zhang et al. \[ 9 \], Kumar et al. \[ 12 \] highlighted that integrating AI, spectroscopy, and blockchain technology can enable more advanced detection mechanisms, minimizing human error while improving scalability.

Mohindra et al. \[ 13 \] point out the developing concern of counterfeit medicines and direct the investigation into innovative solutions to secure the medication of the supply chain networks. The current anti-counterfeiting measures, such as RFID, magnetic strips, barcode, DNA coding, hologram, etc., provide minimal protection and can be duplicated, which do not provide traceability.

Akther et al. \[ 14 \] discuss to stress the essential need for enhancing accountability and transparency in AI approaches, particularly in high-stakes ﬁelds such as ﬁnance, healthcare, and autonomous systems. Traditional methods are addressed in AI's "black box" problems, which focus on model simpliﬁcation, interpretability tools such as SHAP and LIME, by combining with transparency during system design. These techniques are regularly insufﬁcient in assuring the auditability and consistent traceability for complex AI decisions.

A hybrid blockchain-AI solution to monitor the shipment of medication in real-time and limit counterfeit cases by 28 percent in pilot implementation has been instigated by Sharma et al. \[ 15 \]. It demonstrated the capability of embedding spectroscopy modules in a mobile edge-AI edge gadget to perform on-site counterfeit medicine tests with potential real-world implementations. Similarly, Raj et al. \[ 16 \] suggest a federated learning method

A Data-Analytics Technique for Counterfeit Medicine Detection

that enables collaborative data sharing within a speciﬁc region on detecting counterfeit drugs but preserves the privacy of data, which is extremely signiﬁcant whenever it comes to international health collaboration.

However, problems remain in developing generalizable models because of the variance in production methods of counterfeit age, regional disparities, and changes in criminal strategies. Therefore, it is vital for counterfeit medicine detection, robust for multifaceted technology.

## 3 **Research Methodology ** **3.1 ** **Framework Overview ** The four modules of the proposed system are; **3.1.1 ** **Image Analysis using AI **

Image analysis in this study is performed using Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) to detect physical and visual cues that distinguish genuine medicines from counterfeit ones. Medicines-especially tablets and capsules-have identiﬁable surface features such as shape, color, size, texture, embossing, and logo imprints that can serve as markers of authenticity. Counterfeit products often fail to replicate these details with high ﬁdelity. The goal of this module is to automate the visual inspection process and assign a Conﬁdence Score (%) that reﬂects the likelihood of a given sample being authentic based on its visual attributes.

**Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) ** The speciﬁc AI technique applied in this research is the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-a class of deep learning algorithms highly effective in analyzing visual data such as images. CNNs are particularly well-suited for this task because they can automatically learn and extract spatial hierarchies of features, from basic edges and textures to complex patterns and shapes. **Working Mechanisms of CNN **

1. **Tablet Imaging for Model Input: ** Every medicine sample (tablet or a capsule) is scanned in the form of a highresolution picture. Photos contain elements such as surface of tablets, color, shape and imprint of logo. 2. **Preprocessing: ** The images are resized, normal and augmented to make the model more robust. This gives us consistent inputs of the same dimension and is a way of avoiding overﬁtting. 3. **Feature Extraction: ** The CNN takes the image through several sets of convolutions (ﬁlters), pooling and activation functions (ReLU). Low-level features (edges, curves) of the image are captured at early layers and more abstract features (embossing, logo clarity, surface texture) at more deeper layers. B.S. Thomson and W.R. Varuna

4. **Classiﬁcation Layer: ** Once the feature extraction is done, the outputs pass through fully connected layers. o A conﬁdence score of 0 to 100 per cent is produced by a ﬁnal sigmoid or softmax function and reﬂects the prediction of the AI to be genuine. 5. **Output: ** In case the conﬁdence rating is high (e.g, *\>* 95%), the drug will be authentic. o A poor score (e.g. less than 80%) indicates possible fake nature. **3.1.2 ** **Optical Character Recognition (OCR) **

The study used OCR to check the text integrity of pharmaceutical labels since they often tampered with the labels in counterfeited products by misspelling, having the wrong batch number, or changed expiry dates \[ 6 \]. Medicine label images with high resolutions became processed via the Google Vision API. Fields extracted were name of drugs, drug manufacturers, batch numbers and their expiry/manufacture dates. They were also contrasted with a conﬁrmed database of legitimate pharmaceutical listings. String-matching algorithms, Levenshtein distance, and cosine similarity were used to measure the similarity between extracted text and reference text, leading to a calculated OCR Text Match Score ( %). **3.1.3 ** **Blockchain-Based Veriﬁcation **

Blockchain was implemented so that it ensures tamper-proof traceability of medicine batches in the supply chain, i.e., challenges historic medicine source authenticity \[ 6 \]. To log valid batches with respective metadata, a simulated smart contract enabled blockchain ledger was developed. A product sample would be scanned and its metadata (e.g. batch number, packaging date) checked up against the blockchain ledger. The match created a binary veriﬁcation output (Yes/No). Blockchain offers an open and uneditable record of transactions and thus it is optimal to determine the origin of medical products and minimize the weaknesses in supply chains \[ 4, 10 \]. **3.1.4 ** **Spectroscopy Analysis **

The chemical composition is investigated from the medicine samples where the spectroscopy approach is utilized, where the counterfeit medicines can hold no Active Pharmaceutical ingredient (APIs), or they have replaced it with something dangerous to the health of the consumers \[ 2 \].

**Procedure ** The investigation of the use of synthetic Raman spectroscopy to instead of obtaining the spectral proﬁles of each sample of medicines. According to the cosine similarity formula, these proﬁles were differentiated against a reference database of eq 1. Cosine Similarity = X ∗ Y */ * X Y (1)

XXX and YYY represents the spectral intensity vectors of the sample and reference.

A Data-Analytics Technique for Counterfeit Medicine Detection

The result was Spectroscopy Match Score (%) which represented the measure of chemical similarity. Though falsiﬁed goods can appear very similar to the real drugs in terms of appearance and text, chemical conﬁrmation can be achieved with spectroscopy, which is an essential step in detecting counterfeits \[ 9 \].

**Data Simulation: ** Two different groups of medicine were simulated. **Group A (OTC Analgesics): ** Examples include Paracetamol and Ibuprofen. **Group B (Prescription Antibiotics): ** Examples include Azithromycin and Amoxicillin.

There were 5,000 samples in each group considered as genuine or counterfeit. The following attributes were all included in each sample:

- Conﬁdence Score (%)  - Blockchain Veriﬁcation Status (Yes/No)  - OCR Text Match (%)  - Spectroscopy Match (%)  - Surface Similarity Score (%) **3.2 ** **Model Development **

For image classiﬁcation, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was made. OCR was used for the implementation of the Google Vision API. Cross-referencing a smart contract-based ledger was used to simulate blockchain veriﬁcation. Synthetic Raman spectroscopy proﬁling was performed for all medicines.

The performance of each technique was measured with the help of:

- Accuracy  - Precision  - Recall  - F1-Score  - Area Under Curve  - Confusion matrices  - One-way ANOVA for statistical signiﬁcance between groups. **3.3 ** **Dataset Overview **

A simulated dataset was constructed to assess the new method. In both medicine samples \[ 17, 18 \], half were authentic and the other half were fake, with roughly three out of four records in each medicine group being real. Overall, the technique demonstrates the brilliant potential for use in the medicine counterfeit veriﬁcation process in the pharmaceutical authentication, mainly as it is combined with the digital supply chain and regulatory management systems.

## 5 **Conclusion **

The implications from this study highlighted the convergence of the potential between AI, blockchain, OCR, and spectroscopy for the identiﬁcation of counterfeit medicines. These two groups all resulted in a mean accuracy of ≥ 94% and a mean AUC of 0.900.92 on the simulated datasets. Product traceability and OCR identiﬁcation improved from the blockchain veriﬁcation, which is used for detecting fake medicine labels. This was incorporated with the spectroscopy-based veriﬁcation stage with a very low falsenegative rate. The system is validated by expanding with the statistics in identifying the distinctions between the medicine classes that tackled these issues, which lives up to the assurances by the gaps within the multidisciplinary, data-driven method to supply chain management of the pharmaceutical industries, by governing that delivers a scalable, costeffective solution to combat the counterfeit medicine across a global scale. This model will be further developed for a real-world pharmaceutical dataset that is IoT-enabled for spot validation as per global regulatory systems like the WHO's Medical Product Alert Model for the betterment of people's health.

## An Intelligent YOLOv8 and OCR-Based System

**for Real-Time Detection of Wrong-Way Vehicles ** **and License Plate Recognition **

- A. Hamddi 1( B ), Qabas A. Hameed 1, Mohammed Basim Omar 1,  Ahmed S. Abdullah 1, Ibrahim M. Zeki 2, Israa A. Basheer 1, and A. A. Yass 1

1 Department of Computer Science, Computer Science and Mathematics College, Tikrit University, Tikrit 34001, Iraq shihab.a.hamddi@tu.edu.iq 2 Republic of Iraq, Ministry of Oil, Baghdad, Iraq

**Abstract. ** With the rapid speed of urbanization, the number of vehicles transiting among cities has increased enormously. Accordingly, many trafﬁc-related issues have occurred, such as trafﬁc jams, large numbers, and different styles of car vehicles. Road data gathering is vital for solving trafﬁc problems. Thus, in this paper, we design and develop an intelligent monitoring method that allows you to look only once (YOLO) and optical character recognition (OCR), which identiﬁes vehicles moving in the wrong-side direction of the road. In this approach, YOLO v8 is ﬁrst employed for wrong-side vehicle detection. Second, the optical character recognition (OCR) method is presented for reading and recording vehicle license plate numbers. Then the detected wrong-side vehicle data is sent to the trafﬁc center monitor for processing and issuing ﬁnes. In our methodology, the presented method demonstrated that Yolo v8 showed an exceptional performance in detecting cars driving on the wrong side and correctly identifying their license plates in most scenarios. Furthermore, OCR effectively extracted license plate text, with preprocessing playing a vital role in improving accuracy. The high precision and recall for the wrong side and right side driving detections afﬁrm the system's reliability. Moreover, the model's inference times and high precision make it viable for real-time trafﬁc monitoring applications. Future improvements are required to handle challenging plate detection scenarios.

**Keywords: ** Yolo v8 · OCR · Wrong-Way Driver Detection and Wrong-Way Driving

## 1 **Introduction **

## Road accidents are a common problem in densely populated areas. In 2023, Iraq's Min

istry of Planning reported a 0.3% rise in trafﬁc accidents, resulting in 11,552 incidents and 3,262 deaths, including many children \[ 1 \]. The road infrastructure cannot accommodate the increasing number of vehicles, leading to trafﬁc inequality. A primary cause of accidents is drivers violating trafﬁc laws, especially driving on the wrong side during

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 364-374, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_27> An Intelligent YOLOv8 and OCR-Based System for Real-Time

congestion. This behavior increases trafﬁc and seriously raises vehicle collision risk. Iraq ranks 37th globally and 5th in the Arab world for trafﬁc-related fatalities, with a death rate of 34.4 per 100,000 people \[ 2 \]. This is a familiar scenario in the majority of high-density cities. So, preventing driving on the wrong side of the road is vital. To reduce this style of prohibited driving, drivers who don't obey trafﬁc laws are required to be detected, and strict laws should be implemented. Trafﬁc monitoring is a vital research area. Analyzing vehicle directions and trafﬁc ﬂow helps identify violations like speeding, red-light running, and reckless driving. This data supports trafﬁc authorities in improving road safety. Furthermore, vehicle type and license plate numbers can help track and identify offending vehicles \[ 3, 4 \]. Many studies have focused on improving vehicle detection methods, but fewer have explored wrong-side vehicle detection. Accurate detection is the ﬁrst step in identifying a vehicle's direction. Researchers have used various YOLO versions for this purpose \[ 5 \]  \[ 6 \]. For instance, \[ 7 \], presents a realtime system using YOLO and KNN for vehicle classiﬁcation and plate recognition. In \[ 8 \] Computer vision methods were applied with Kalman ﬁltering to improve detection speed and accuracy using public datasets. The study in \[ 9 \] proposes a three-stage wrongside detection system: vehicle detection using YOLO, tracking with centroid methods, and violation identiﬁcation. Another study \[ 10 \] detects multiple trafﬁc violations using YOLO, CNN, and Mask R-CNN models, followed by OCR to extract plate numbers. After detecting the violations, violators' vehicle plates are acquired using OCR. The method in \[ 11 \] uses CNNs to identify vehicle orientation and detect wrong-way driving. Other research has emphasized license plate detection. The research \[ 12 \] uses YOLOv8, image processing, and OCR for plate recognition. While in \[ 13, 14 \] combine vehicle model detection and number plate recognition using MobileNet-V2, YOLOv4-tiny, and Paddle OCR. In current literature, the majority of the papers are attempting either vehicle and plate detection, or trafﬁc violations like speeding and wrong-side driving. But there is less research that is combining wrong-side detection along with plate recognition.

## 2 **Related Work **

Recent research on wrong-way driving (WWD) detection has explored diverse methodologies, including sensor-based systems, deep learning, and computer vision techniques \[ 15, 16 \]. Computer vision approaches, particularly those employing YOLO models combined with tracking and directional analysis, have demonstrated high accuracy, robustness, and scalability in real-world trafﬁc conditions \[ 9, 17 \]. Appearance-based models utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify vehicle orientation have also achieved signiﬁcant success, with accuracies up to 96% \[ 11, 18 \]. Enhanced YOLOv3 systems have improved detection in dense trafﬁc with accuracies of 88% (detection) and 98% (counting) \[ 19 \]. Grouping-based methods incorporating K-means clustering and IoT alerts provide robust classiﬁcation and real-time public safety notiﬁcations \[ 20 \]. Additionally, lightweight architectures such as YOLOv4-tiny combined with CFNN have achieved up to 99% mAP and real-time performance exceeding 30 FPS \[ 21 \]. The Wrong Way-LVDC framework integrates advanced detection algorithms, IoT technologies, and real-time processing (24 FPS), attaining 95.23% accuracy and supporting multi-lane monitoring \[ 22 \]. In parallel, license plate detection and recognition S.A. Hamddi et al.

systems have evolved to support WWD identiﬁcation. Multi-stage systems integrating YOLOv5, YOLOv8, and custom CNNs have achieved up to 96.1% accuracy, supported by web dashboards for real-time monitoring \[ 23 \]. Two-stage ALPR models with data augmentation have reached 92.8% accuracy under unconstrained conditions \[ 24 \]. while preprocessing-enhanced systems using YOLOv8 and OCR techniques achieved 99% detection and 98% recognition accuracy \[ 25 \]. Other CNN- and Tesseract-based systems have shown robustness across various plate formats and conditions, with accuracy ranging from 83.3% to 96.23% \[ 26, 27 \]. A hybrid model using MobileNet-V2, YOLOx, and YOLOv4-tiny demonstrated 97.5% recognition accuracy with Grad-CAM explainability \[ 28 \]. Finally, an advanced ALPR system combining YOLOv8, Faster RCNN, and SRGAN improved character recognition by reducing the Character Error Rate from 53.9% to 51.7%, illustrating the beneﬁt of integrating object detection and image enhancement techniques \[ 29 \].

## 3 **Methodology **

This section outlines the proposed system for detecting wrong-way vehicles and capturing their license plate numbers to register ﬁnes at the trafﬁc center. It begins with an overview of the system and a deﬁnition of its core components, followed by a detailed description of the dataset creation process. **3.1 ** **Proposed Framework System Overview **

In this paper, we propose a three-stage system for detecting and recognizing wrongside cars and registering their license plates, which are sent to the trafﬁc center for further processing and issuing ﬁnes. The proposed framework is presented in Fig. 1.  The framework has three main stages: wrong- side car detection, designation of wrong-side car plates, and a terminal that sends the captured data to the trafﬁc monitoring system. The system executes the following tasks:

The system for detecting wrong-way vehicles and identifying license plates has three main steps. First, it utilizes YOLOv8 to detect vehicles driving the wrong direction. Our proposed deep learning model works in real-time and is accurate, trained on a special dataset to make sure it can detect vehicles in different conditions. Next, it recognizes license plates; YOLOv8 ﬁrst ﬁnds the plate, and then EasyOCR reads the letters and numbers. EasyOCR is fast and easy to use, which is great for quick processing. Finally, the last part sends the data to a trafﬁc control system. This includes the needed hardware, like communication tools and controllers, along with software like APIs, databases, and a user interface to store and manage the violations. All these parts work together to create an efﬁcient system for tracking wrong-way drivers. Each stage will be discussed in detail including creating the dataset and training the YOLOv8 model, along with implementing Easy-OCR as shown in Fig. 2. **3.2 ** **Dataset Preparation **

The YOLOv8 model was trained for wrong-way driving detection with a custom dataset obtained by collecting 70 images from car parks at Tikrit University, with prior consent An Intelligent YOLOv8 and OCR-Based System for Real-Time **Fig. 1. ** The proposed framework **Fig. 2. ** Implementation Stages

## obtained from vehicle owners. The images contain vehicles that can be captured from

multiple angles and light variations to ensure that such diversity renders them being representative. Ethical considerations, especially privacy issues, were in force when collecting data. All images were annotated using the Roboﬂow platform which offers easy-to-use annotation and preparation tools for multiple datasets across several formats. S.A. Hamddi et al.

The dataset was annotated for three classes: Right Side, Wrong Side, and License Plate, with license plates being included for further recognition purposes. To improve model performance, data augmentation was performed on images with ﬂips, rotations, and crops; therefore, increasing the dataset from 70 to 200 images. The dataset was divided into a training set (60%), a validation set (10%), and a test set (30%) to facilitate the efﬁcient development and evaluation of the model.

# 3.3 **YOLO8 **

You Only Look Once (YOLO) comprises a real-time, single-shot deep-learning model for object detection, which processes whole images in one forward pass through a convolutional neural network (CNN), making the detection very rapid and allowing the identiﬁcation of several entities per frame \[ 30, 31 \]. It is founded on a single Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The CNN splits an image into parts and predicts the boundary boxes and possibilities for each part. However, YOLO is a single-shot detector, YOLO bypasses the part proposal stage and makes one "look" at the image to detect the objects that exist in the image, hence, speeding up the method in contrast to other models based on two-shot architectures \[ 21 \]. By reframing detection into a regression problem, YOLO predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from image pixels. The input image is partitioned into an M × M grid layout, and each grid cell is accountable for objects wired to it all the way through centers \[ 32 \]. But such an approach does have drawbacks, such as multiple objects with centers in the same cell or objects that cover more than one cell being hard to detect and thus leading to detection errors \[ 19 \]. Architectural changes from all the subsequent versions of YOLO aimed to improve the existing versions to overcome such deﬁciencies. The most recent distribution, YOLOv8 by Ultralytics, is cutting-edge, including modern components featuring anchor-free detection, improved convolutional blocks, and no mosaic augmentation during the training phase two. It ﬁnds application in diverse computer vision tasks encompassing detection, segmentation, tracking, pose estimation, and classiﬁcation. Due to its very high speed and decent accuracy, YOLOv8 is a perfect candidate for this study because real-time trafﬁc surveillance and wrong-way vehicle detection are just two examples of its use. Balancing precision and latency, and managing variable object sizes are qualities that allow it to generalize well \[ 33 \].

# 3.4 **OCR **

Optical Character Recognition is a known algorithm for recognizing digits and text recorded from an input image or with the service of an optical device \[ 34 \]. The algorithm functions as a human reading. The eye, the visual device of a human, detects the images in seconds, next are transmitted and processed within the brain. Similarly to humans, OCR is also inﬂuenced by factors that determine the success of identifying writing. An OCR algorithm can detect numbers, text, symbols, letters, and punctuation by using ML methods and pattern recognition techniques \[ 35 \]. Next, the recognized characters are subjected to various algorithms to change the image into text. This requires learning text structure and interaction approach with further components like columns, lines, and paragraphs. The next phase depends on the CRAFT Algorithm. The Region Proposal An Intelligent YOLOv8 and OCR-Based System for Real-Time

## Network (RPN) utilizes geometric indications and color deviations to determine adequate

text regions. The Character Proposal Network (CPN) further enhances the process by indicating box boundaries for distinct characters \[ 36 \]. This study uses OCR for character recognition only for wrong-side car license plates. This means OCR is not applied to the right-side car, which reduces the process overhead for the proposed framework. EasyOCR \[ 37 \] is used because of its ease of usage, built-in support, and high accuracy for Arabic and English text recognition. Easy-OCR includes many OCR methods such as sequence modeling, and feature extraction, and supplies an end-to-end pipeline. The images engaged in cleaning and improvement pre-processing steps then the images are transferred to the OCR algorithm.

and mAP@50-95 on three key classes, namely, wrong-side, right-side, and license plate are shown in Table 2. Results are very good in classes Wrong-side and right-side, having near-to-perfect precision and recall, as well as a mAP value; it means that the model is conﬁdent and robust to spot vehicles moving in the wrong direction or driving correctly. But for the License Plate class, it is comparatively lower at 0.567, and the mAP@50-95 stands at 0.598, reﬂecting a number of difﬁculties that license plate detection involves. Even considering these, the precision remains perfect, at 1.0, meaning that the model does not give too many false positives when trying to identify a license plate. **Table 2. ** Evaluation metrics results

primary objectives of detecting wrong-direction vehicles and recognizing license plates, with minor limitations observed in license plate recall performance. The YOLOv8 model showed very high accuracy in locating license plates in test images. Using bounding box coordinates, the detected plates were cropped and then fed into the preprocessing stage to enhance text recognition accuracy. Figure 4 gives an example of the process in a visual format **Fig. 4. ** License plate number extraction in OCR S.A. Hamddi et al.

Using YOLOv8 for license plate detection and Tesseract for reading the text worked really well when the images were good. But, sometimes, if the images were noisy or blurred, it messed up the character recognition, showing that there's room for improvement. Even with that, the system still did a great job of real-time license plate recognition, thanks to its strong detection and response skills. Overall, the results show that it works reliably when conditions are good and point out how important it is to enhance images for challenging situations.

## 5 **Conclusion, Limitation and Future Work **

Increasing urban infrastructure development necessitates improved road trafﬁc management systems. A deep learning framework is proposed in this paper to detect vehicles moving in the wrong direction and extract license plate information using Optical Character Recognition (OCR), followed by ﬁne enforcement based on this information. In this system, YOLOv8 is used for detecting objects. The system is integrated with an OCR for license plate recognition. A custom dataset was created, annotated, and categorized into three classes-wrong-side driving, right-side driving, and license plates-and formatted for YOLOv8 via a YAML conﬁguration ﬂow. To evaluate the model performance rigorously, the dataset was split into training, validation, and test sets. Experimental results reveal that YOLOv8 detects wrong-way vehicles quite well, and it is capable of license plate identiﬁcation with very high accuracy. With preprocessing, OCR performance improved drastically. The complete system shows promising results with respect to precision and recall, indicating a reliable system, yet more room for improvement is present to overcome the limitation of small dataset despite using transfer learning and data augmentation to mitigate the limitation of small dataset in addition to the difﬁculties faced during the recognition of plates under hard conditions.

## An IOT-Driven Smart Emission Detection

**and Alerting System for Vehicular and Ambient ** **Pollution Control **

## G. Manjula, M. K. Saravana, G. Ananya ( B ), K. Dhanush Shresti, Shrunga S. Patil, and Srushti Yaligar

Department of Computer Science and Design, Dayananda Sagar Academy of Technology and Management, Bengaluru 560082, Karnataka, India \{hod-csd,saravana-csd\}@dsatm.edu.in, ananyagorkal@gmail.com

**Abstract. ** IoT-based air pollution monitoring encompasses real-time logging of different gas parameters, which poses challenges including constant monitoring of vehicle emissions and prompt alerting when gases cross the safety limits.The paper proposes an IoT-supported system that evades these challenges with the help of an MQ7 gas sensor for carbon monoxide (CO) detection from exhaust emitted by vehicles. The sen- sor readings are processed by a NodeMCU (ESP8266) microcontroller, which cross-references the readings against ﬁxed thresholds. If high-level emissions are sensed, multi-level warnings are provided through an LCD display, buzzer, and SMS alerting using a GSM module to the owner of the vehicle. Where there are sustained violations, reports are also sent to regulatory bodies like the Regional Transport Ofﬁce (RTO). Emission data is recorded to cloud system, ThingSpeak for real-time visualization and historical purposes. The proposed system accurately detects CO, provides rapid alert generation, and stable data communication lead- ing to automated, real-time, and mobile emission monitoring, surpassing manual inspections and concurring with smart transportation objectives.

**Keywords: ** IoT-based monitoring · GSM communication · Gas Sensors (MQ7) · Real-time alert systems · Vehicle Emissions · Pollution Control

## 1 **Introduction **

## Air pollution caused by vehicle emissions is a serious issue in urban areas. Estab- lish

ing ﬁxed emission thresholds based on environmental standards is one of the most useful techniques for real-time monitoring \[ 1 \]. These systems detects irreg- ularities and sounds an alert when sensor readings surpasses these cutoffs (CO 100 ppm) \[ 2 \]. The method works well for embedded systems with constrained processing power and it is lightweight. Irregularity of emissions are caused due to faults like engine malfunction, poor fuel quality, or drifting sensors. For instance, persistently elevated CO levels or sudden increases in NO emissions may suggest possible inefﬁciencies of the system or faulty parts \[ 3 \]. Detection of such irregu- larities is important so that vehicles continue to be environmentally compliant and do not add to pollution \[ 4 \].

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 375-384, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1> \_ 28 - Manjula et al.

The paper proposes a system that utilizes the Internet of Things (IoT) for real-time emission measurement from automobiles. Embedded gas sensors moni- tors the harmful pollutants Carbon Monoxide (CO), Nitric Oxide (NO), and Hy- drocarbons (CH) over time. The sensors generate multivariate time-series data representing real-world automobile exhaust patterns and environmental factors. The system instantly notiﬁes vehicle owners or environmental authorities via SMS when it detects a legitimate irregularity using GSM modules. \[ 15 \] In dy- namic environments, this helps maintain air quality compliance and guarantees promptness. Besides being detected in real time, abnormal emission events are also stored in the cloud for analysis and visualization later. Trending past behav- ior helps improve calibration of the system and aids regulators in enforcement by pointing out recurring patterns of excessive emissions. Data from several gas sensors *viz., * MQ7 for CO, MQ135 for NO are cross-veriﬁed to improve accuracy. In order to minimize false alarms brought on by calibration drift or hardware noise, irregularities are veriﬁed only when multiple sensors record correlated spikes. Environmental context is used to interpret sensor readings, including lo- cation, time of day, and vehicle condition. For instance, high emissions at startup could be typical, but they could also be a sign of a problem when the vehicle is idle as in \[ 5 \]. The main objective of the paper is to:

1. Develop a system that precisely detect threshold violations of pollution and effective  delivery of real-time alerts. 2. Process the sensor data in real time and to check the concentrations of pollutants with  respect to regulatory thresholds predetermined in advance. 3. Detect emission irregularities precisely with minimal false positives due to transient  ﬂuctuations.

## 2 **Related Works **

In transportation systems, pollution monitoring is being dealt with IoT-based systems these days. These systems provide real-time time-series data from a stack of gas sensors, creating multivariate environmental datasets. Current re- search in the area is directed towards establishing real-time, cost-effective, and scalable pollution monitoring frameworks based on embedded microcontrollers, wireless modules, and cloud data analytics platforms \[ 6 \]. IoT-based air quality monitoring is commonly associated with intermittent connectivity issues, sensor calibration drift, and tamper-proof data logging needs for regulatory require- ments. This section discusses related work in the ﬁeld of IoT-based pollution monitoring.

Hassan *et al.,* \[ 7 \] performed a comprehensive study on the development of a lowcost, IoT-based air quality monitoring system incorporating embedded sen- sors, cloud computing, and blockchain technology. The system catered to real- time detection and safe storage of gas emission data and suggested a modular design, sensor readings from pollution sources are gathered with MQ-series sen- sors and relayed through a NodeMCU to a cloud platform for real-time display and alarming. The data was logged onto a blockchain to maintain immutability and tamper-resistance.

Benedict *et al.,* \[ 8 \] proposed a new architecture for air quality monitoring in smart cities with IoT and blockchain integration and attempted to overcome the challenge of An IOT-Driven Smart Emission Detection and Alerting System

conventional pollution monitoring systems, such as the absence of safe and tamper-proof data logging or undue dependence on centralized storage, which might be modiﬁed or tampered with and presented a decentralized system to automatically gather, store, and validate air quality information without the need for human involvement or manual veriﬁcation.

Han *et al.,* \[ 9 \] considered LoRa-based IoT systems for industrial air pollution monitoring, which prescribes the manner in which environmental data can be transmitted over longer distances under low-power environments, and scrutinized the system from both data integrity and communication reliability viewpoints. They developed a mechanism for data consistency while ensuring low energy usage in multivariate pollution monitoring and tested the same on actual de- ployment cases. The LoRa protocol's effectiveness in managing massive-scale, distributed air quality data is constrained and can be enhanced with the inclu- sion of real-time alerting functionality or hybrid communications strategies.

Yossy *et al.,* \[ 10 \] presented an IoT-based approach for air pollution monitoring employing cloud-connected sensors. The mechanism is to preprocess real-time environmental data and send it to the cloud for analysis and visualization. The cloud platform can properly model patterns of normal air quality behavior and added a web-based monitoring approach that is superior to manual inspection in responsiveness and consistency and prioritizes timely detection of genuine pollution events over unimportant ﬂuctuations.

Martins *et al.,* \[ 11 \] developed a way to track air pollution in real time based on a cloudbased IoT framework. A properly deﬁned reporting structure for data ac- quisition is employed for processing environmental sensor data through low-cost embedded systems instead of sophisticated data infrastructures. Their approach emphasizes cost-effective, real-time measurement of air quality from multiple points and sends it to the cloud for visualization and for tracking changes over time, which accurately detects pollution levels without the computationally com- plex models.

Garg *et al.,* \[ 13 \] proposed a holistic framework to assess air quality monitor- ing metrics from low-cost sensor networks. The system is based on recording multidimensional environmental data and modeling pollutant trends over time and space. Rather than using probabilistic thresholding approaches, the sys- tem draws on calibration methods and consistency checks for raising alarms about abnormal reading. The multidimensional sensing approach demonstrates a recognition of inter-sensor relationships and environment-based dynamics, sim- ilar to latent space representation in time-series irregular detection, such that it is possible to detect unusual pollution trends through deviation from predicted sensor behavior.

Islam *et al.,* \[ 12 \] conducted a survey of blockchain consensus algorithms appli- cable for use on IoT devices, with a focus on lightweight mechanisms in resource- constrained embedded systems. Their results favor the use of blockchain in air quality monitoring systems through secure and tamper-proof data transfer with- out hardware overload.

Devi *et al.,* \[ 14 \] created an Internet-of-Vehicles (IoV) driven network for real- time estimation of CO 2 emissions and their reduction. Their scheme combines vehicular IoT sensors and cloud analytics for dynamically monitoring emission data and uses reinforcement learning algorithms to optimize driving and trafﬁc parameters for efﬁcient pollution control. - Manjula et al.

Purohit *et al.,* \[ 16 \] conceptualized an air monitoring system that adapts to ensure stability in performance under varying environmental conditions. Their proposed system supports multivariate gas sensing and prioritizes system re- silience over time, which makes them ideal for outdoor applications with chang- ing sources of pollution.

| 3 | Methodology |
|:--- |:--- |
| 3.1 | System Architecture |
| The proposed IoT-enabled air pollution monitoring systems adopts a modular and layered | structure for sensing, processing data, communication, and genera- tion of alerts. | **3.1 ** **System Architecture **

The proposed IoT-enabled air pollution monitoring systems adopts a modular and layered structure for sensing, processing data, communication, and genera- tion of alerts.

The architecture of the air pollution monitoring system consists of three ma- jor elements: the sensing layer, the processing layer, and the communication layer. The sensing layer employs gas sensors, MQ7 and MQ135 to sense pol- lutants CO, NO respectively. The raw sensor readings are aggregated and fed to NodeMCU microcontroller, which computes the data locally. If the pollutant concentration exceeds set thresholds, it sends out alerts. Besides that, data is bundled for transmission to a cloud. This arrangement allows real-time detection without a high cost and complexity of hardware.

For increased scalability and historic analysis, the system uses a cloud-based platforms for data storage, visualization, and reporting. Sensor data is sent to ThingSpeak through Wi-Fi. The platforms allow for trend visualization, remote monitoring, and historic comparison to detect recurring emission irregularities. The architecture enhances accessibility and allows stakeholders to react to pol- lution events more effectively, particularly in vehicular implementations. Certain designs also complement this model using blockchain-based logging for data im- mutability. This integration enhances data security and public openness, and the system becomes appropriate for smart cities and digital governance scenarios.

Figures 1 and 3. is a schematic of the proposed IoT-based pollution monitoring and alerting system integrated into a vehicle. The steps in the imple- mentation of real-time emission monitoring and alert generation through envi- ronment sensors and cloudintegrated microcontrollers are presented as follows:

1. **Sensor Integration and Monitoring Unit: ** An MQ7 gas sensor is located close to  the vehicle exhaust to monitor levels of Carbon Monoxide (CO). The sensor provides analog signals that are proportional to gas concentration. The readings are picked up and converted into digital format by a NodeMCU ESP8266 microcontroller coded using Embedded C through the Arduino IDE. The microcontroller serves as the central processing unit, allowing for real-time processing and connectivity. 2. **Emission Analysis and Threshold Comparison: ** The microcontroller checks  whether the level of CO sensed is above the pre-programmed safety level. Threshold values are calibrated in advance according to the standards of the pollution control board (e.g., CO ≥ 50 ppm invokes alerts) and can be downloaded through the ﬁrmware. This is a logic that is implemented in embedded C code, and any transgression of threshold leads to immediate action on the part of the system. 3. **Alert Generation and Driver Notiﬁcation: ** Visual and audio alarms are activated  through a LCD display and a buzzer. These alarms enable the driver to immediately take corrective measures. An IOT-Driven Smart Emission Detection and Alerting System

4. **Remote Notiﬁcation System: ** If the condition of high emission continues, a GSM  module provides an SMS notiﬁcation to the owner of the vehicle. Ongoing breaches lead to a report being sent automatically to the Regional Transport Ofﬁce (RTO). 5. **Cloud Logging and Visualization: ** Emission data are logged periodically to a cloud  platform such as ThingSpeak or Firebase, allowing remote access, real-time visualization, and historical trend analysis.For added security, ac- countability, and traceability, the system may optionally include blockchain technology.This means that emission data are placed in a tamper-evident, immutable record book so that the information can be veriﬁed by the regu- latory bodies and defended against fraudulent alterations. 6. **Emission Mitigation Mechanism: ** The system incorporates a relay con- trolled DC  fan in conjunction with a simple air ﬁlter. The fan is automati- cally turned on to lower pollutant output as a ﬁrst step in mitigation when emissions exceed the safety threshold. **3.2 ** **Hardware Components **

The proposed system combines various low-cost and small-sized hardware pieces that together facilitate real-time monitoring, alerting, and counter measures against automotive emissions. The basic hardware pieces are enumerated be- low:

**Fig. 1. ** Sequence Diagram of the Proposed IOT-based system for Vehicle Emission Detection

1. **NodeMCU (ESP8266): ** It is a microcontroller that has Wi-Fi capabilities as the core processing unit of the system. It takes in input from gas sensors, processes emission data, and manages communication with cloud platforms and GSM modules to send alerts. 2. **MQ7 Gas Sensor: ** This sensor is used to detect the level of carbon monoxide (CO) in exhaust gases of the vehicle. It gives an analog voltage signal in proportion to CO concentration, which is utilized to check if the level of emissions is over regulatory limits. - Manjula et al.

3. **16x2 LCD Display (I2C)**:  A small liquid crystal display used to display instantaneous CO levels and warning messages to the driver. It provides an intuitive means of visualizing pollutant amounts on the vehicle. 4. **Relay Module: ** Utilized to drive external devices like a DC fan. The relay is turned ON/OFF according to pollution levels and allows the system to execute simple auto- matic alleviation actions. 5. **DC Fan and Air Filter: ** Installed close to the exhaust to lower instantaneous pollution levels when toxic gas levels are present. The fan is activated through relay control as an action against excessive emissions. 6. **GSM Module: ** Enables contact with the car owner and concerned author-ities through  the generation of SMS notiﬁcations when pollution levels cross safe limits. It enables the system to function in remote or on-the-go environ- ments without access to Wi-Fi. 7. **Power Supply Unit (with Voltage Regulator): ** Provides steady 5V to the system through a 7805 voltage regulator, which prevents unstable operation of sensors and microcontroller due to ﬂuctuation or overvoltage destruction. **3.3 ** **Software Components **

The proposed system uses a range of software tools for embedded development, mobile connectivity, and cloud communication. These software platforms allow smooth interaction between the hardware and outside systems like mobile ap- plications or cloud servers. The following tools were employed:

1. **Arduino IDE: ** An open-source development platform is employed for cod- ing and  uploading embedded C code to the NodeMCU microcontroller. It allows real-time debugging and serial monitoring for smooth communication between hardware and ﬁrmware units. 2. **Embedded C: ** Embedded C is employed to put into practice the logical sequence  of sensor data acquisition, threshold-based decision-making, and actuation control. Embedded C allows low-level access of hardware to operate sensors, relays, and communication modules. 3. **Blynk App: ** Blynk is an IoT platform based on a mobile phone for real-time monitoring and control of the pollution sensing module. It gives a graphical interface on  the smartphone of the user for visualization of emission data and alerting. 4. **ThingSpeak Cloud Platform: ** ThingSpeak is employed for logging data in the cloud  and visualization. Sensor values are sent to the cloud at regular intervals where they are logged and graphically displayed. This is helpful for long-term monitoring and historic tracking. 5. **XAMPP and MySQL: ** Local server deployment in certain conﬁgurations utilizes  XAMPP and MySQL to store and access records of emissions inde- pendent of the internet. This facilitates local network-based operation and off-line analysis of vehicle data. An IOT-Driven Smart Emission Detection and Alerting System

6. **Java SDK and Android Studio (Optional): ** These are utilized to create and test  proprietary Android apps to communicate with the microcontroller unit. The apps are programmed to send notiﬁcations and show sensor read- ings on a dashboard in real time for the convenience of the user (Fig. 2 ). **Fig. 2. ** The System Design

## 4 **Results and Discussion **

The proposed IoT-based air quality monitoring and alert system is deployed and tested under real-world vehicle conditions to ensure its functionality, responsive- ness, and reliability. The performance indicators, sensor precision, responsiveness of thresholdbased alerts, efﬁcacy of the alert delivery processes, and reliability of cloud-based data transport were used.

As shown in Fig 4. the MQ7 sensor showed accurate detection of CO concen- tration ﬂuctuations in vehicle exhaust, which corresponds well with engine con- dition and exhaust ﬂow variations. The NodeMCU (ESP8266) microcontroller processed the analog inputs efﬁciently, compared them with the set thresholds, and took corresponding actions. When the safety thresholds exceeds, the system produced instantaneous multi-level alerts, visual notiﬁcations on the LCD, audi- ble ones through the buzzer, and remote SMS notiﬁcations to the vehicle owner using GSM as shown in Fig 5. For continuous offenses, escalation notices were ready for regulatory bodies.

Furthermore, the relay-controlled DC fan effectively kicked in closer to the exhaust outlet, which served as a rudimentary yet effective emission mitigation system. All emissions data sent to cloud platforms ThingSpeak for real-time visualization and timestamped historical analysis. Graphs created from logged data veriﬁed good and error-free cloud communication.

The system always had low detection-to-alert latency ( *average * *\> * 3 *seconds* ) and had a high system uptime (98%) in trials. These outcomes justify the sys- tem's costeffectiveness, efﬁciency, and scalability to be applied across private vehicles and public transport ﬂeets of larger scales. - Manjula et al. **Fig. 3. ** Flowchart of the Data and Process Flow

## 5 **Conclusions **

## The paper introduced an IoT-based real-time air quality monitoring and alerting system

for CO emission detection from automobiles. Utilizing an MQ7 gas sensor interfaced with a NodeMCU microcontroller, the system effectively monitored and processed emission values, initiated multi-level alerts (LCD, buzzer, GSM), and stored data to cloud platforms for remote viewing. The integration of a relay- driven DC fan showcased the viability of initial onboard emission reduction. Experimental trials veriﬁed the accuracy of the system, fast response time, and its smooth integration into actual vehicular scenarios.

## The solution is affordable, scalable, and applicable to personal as well as pub- lic

transport systems. In the future, blockchain-based secure logging, predictive maintenance based on sensor data patterns, and integration with databases of transport authorities can enhance its capability in encouraging environmental compliance and facilitating smart transport ecosystems.

## Personalized Risk-Aware Intelligent Stock **Recommendation System **

Nusrat Rouf 1, Saima Saleem 2( B ), Rohit Bondugulu 3, and Majid Bashir Malik 4

1 University of Kashmir, Hazratbal, Srinagar 190006, Jammu and Kashmir, India 2 Institute of Information Technology and Management, New Delhi 110058, India

saima.saleem@iitmipu.ac.in 3 University of Hyderabad, Gachibowli 500046, Telangana, India 4 Baba Ghulam Shah Badshah University, Rajouri 185234, Jammu and Kashmir, India

**Abstract. ** This work presents an investor-centric stock recommendation framework that suggests stocks to investors based on their risk proﬁles. Unlike the traditional "one-size-ﬁts-all" approaches, this work uniquely builds on behavioral data to provide personalized recommendations. The development of the framework begins with the data collection phase, where data is collected via two modes: (1) data collection from target investors, and (2) market data collected from stock exchanges. The data collected from investors is pre-processed, and the dimensionality of data is reduced by applying Principal Component Analysis (PCA). The k-means clustering has been used to group investors into two groups: investors with high risk-taking capability and investors with low risk-taking capability. Furthermore, the market data is preprocessed and based on the beta coefﬁcient scores the companies are categorized into high risk and low risk. Finally, stocks with high risks are recommended to investors with high risk-taking capabilities, and vice versa. This work enhances the accuracy and relevancy of stock recommendations, offering a signiﬁcant advancement over traditional approaches. Furthermore, it has strong potential to increase investor participation in the stock market by reducing uncertainty and providing personalized, risk-aligned recommendations. This study introduces the ﬁrst framework that systematically aligns stock recommendations with investor risk-taking capabilities, thereby bridging a crucial gap in personalized investment advisory systems.

**Keywords: ** Risk-taking capability · Nifty50 · CAPM · Stock Recommendation

## 1 **Introduction **

## India, home to approximately 1.4 billion people, holds immense potential for stock

market participation. However, according to National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL), only 3.7% of the population holds investment accounts 1. Although over the last decade, there has been a surge in the number of dematerialized (DEMAT) accounts, the

1 " <https://www.business-standard.com/article/markets/millions-of-millennials-are-piling-into-> india-s-stock-market-shows-data-121032500065\_1.html "

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 385-398, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_29> - Rouf et al.

same trend has not been reﬂected in the number of active accounts. India ranks among the countries with the highest savings rates in Asia and across the world. Despite its profound signiﬁcance across various dimensions of economic activity, a pertinent question arises: why does investment in Indian stock markets remain limited? Empirical observations suggest that only a small fraction of investors engage regularly or intensively, while the perceived risk and volatility of equity investments continue to discourage broader participation.

Due to the availability of so many stocks in the marketplace, it is hard and challenging to choose the best ones to invest in. Investors are subject to a lot of uncertainty and randomness. Maintaining and managing a portfolio of investments is a much-puzzledover activity. When it comes to stock selection, investors normally strive for stocks with consistent risks and returns, such that the former is low and the latter is high. However, there is always a tradeoff between return and risk \[ 1 \]. Furthermore, stocks traded on the stock exchange are sometimes regarded as unpredictably volatile, which causes hesitation in the process of selecting the best stocks to invest in. Investors are primarily subjected to a great deal of unpredictability and randomness. A person with a high level of risk tolerance is typically more willing to accept greater exposure to risk by taking sole responsibility, making decisions with limited information, and exercising less need for control than someone with a low level of risk tolerance \[ 2 \]. As a result, determining an investor's risk-taking capability and suggesting the most appropriate methods of investment for them has emerged as the most challenging task for researchers. The paper makes the following contributions:

1. Collects the primary data through two modes: (i) questionnaires from investors, (ii)  market data of 29 Nifty50 companies from Yahoo Finance. 2. Develops a novel stock recommendation framework based on investors' risk-taking  capabilities. 3. Pre-processes investor data, applied PCA for dimensionality reduction, and uses kmeans clustering to group investors.  4. Annotates clusters into high-risk and low-risk investor groups using the coefﬁcient  of variance of principal components. 5. Pre-processes market data and categorizes companies into high-risk and low-risk  stocks using beta coefﬁcient scores. 6. Recommended high-risk stocks to high-risk investors and low-risk stocks to low-risk  investors.

## 2 **Literature Review **

Investor risk-taking behavior fundamentally shapes ﬁnancial decision-making, driven by the interplay of risk and return. Classical ﬁnancial models, such as Markowitz's (1952) portfolio theory, assume rational investors optimize returns with minimal risk\[ 3 \]. However, behavioral ﬁnance reveals that demographic, socioeconomic, and psychological factors like age, marital status, education, occupation, income, experience, and risk perception induce deviations from rationality, critically inﬂuencing risk tolerance and investment choices\[ 4 - 6 \].

These factors have been extensively studied for their role in tailoring investment strategies. Younger investors tend to demonstrate greater risk tolerance, which can be

Personalized Risk-Aware Intelligent Stock Recommendation System

attributed to their extended investment horizons and the potential to recover from market ﬂuctuations over time \[ 7, 8 \], while single individuals, unburdened by familial responsibilities, surpass married couples in risk-taking\[ 6 \]. Higher education enhances risk assessment, fostering riskier investments \[ 9, 10 \], and self-employed individuals, often with greater incomes, prefer volatile assets compared to salaried workers \[ 11 \]. Income correlates positively with risk tolerance, enabling wealthier investors to absorb losses \[ 12 \]. Investment experience bolsters decision-making through ﬁnancial literacy \[ 13 \], while risk perception, shaped by personal circumstances, governs asset evaluation \[ 14 \]. These insights facilitate investor segmentation, enabling personalized stock recommendations that enhance portfolio performance.

Despite these advancements, challenges persist in leveraging these factors for recommendation systems. The heterogeneity of investor proﬁles complicates model generalization, and self-reported data introduces biases. Integrating behavioral insights with quantitative risk metrics, such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), remains underexplored. Kahneman and Tversky's (1979) prospect theory marked a paradigm shift by highlighting cognitive biases in risk decisions, inspiring subsequent research \[ 15 \]. Recent research has rapidly advanced in ﬁnancial trading through recommendations \[ 16 \]. Moreover, large-scale behavioral studies and practical robo-advisor analyses demonstrate the continued signiﬁcance of questionnaire-based investor proﬁling\[ 17 \]. Portfolio design by risk assessment and reﬁnements to beta measurement further motivate our design choice to (i) use behavioral questionnaires for investor clustering and (ii) use beta-based stock stratiﬁcation while performing robustness checks on beta estimation\[ 18, 19 \].

## 3 **Methods **

Figure 1 presents work workﬂow of the design of a novel recommendation approach for stock recommendations to target investors. The steps involved in the design and development of the proposed approach are explained below: **3.1 ** **Data Preparation **

The data collection process has been discussed in this section. Initially, a structured questionnaire was developed to gather primary data aimed at analyzing the attitudes and behaviors of investors toward stock market investments. The questionnaire design process is discussed below:

**Questionnaire Designing ** The questionnaire is the most signiﬁcant tool for gathering information from respondents. According to Evans et al (2006), questionnaires are a viable option when data is needed from a large number of people \[ 20 \]. It is an effective way to capture their opinions and attitudes. The purpose of this research is to learn more about how investors behave when it comes to investing in stock markets. As a result, several studies on stock market investments undertaken by various academics were evaluated, and a well-structured, relevant questionnaire has been developed for data collection. The questionnaire has been distributed through online as well as ofﬂine modes. - Rouf et al.

While designing the questionnaire survey for this research, three main factors highlighted by Ornstein (2014) were taken into consideration\[ 21 \]:

- Assuring the participants that their information would be kept private,  - Use questions that focus on the heart of the study's work and keep the questionnaire  short, and - Capturing and sustaining the interest of responders.

Primary records were gathered by an exploratory survey method in which a questionnaire with both closed and open-ended questions was used to gather vital information about the investors, and their opinions were measured on a ﬁve-point Likert scale, which is probably the most often used score scale for inquiring respondents' critiques and views. Strongly Agree, Agree, Neutral, Disagree, and Strongly Disagree are the ﬁve variables on the scale, which range from 1 to 5.

**Fig. 1. ** The workﬂow of methodology for stock recommendation to target audience.

From the target investors, the following behavioral and demographic attributes were collected through questionnaires to assess their risk-taking capability:

- Age - to analyze the inverse relationship between age and risk tolerance.  - Marital Status - to examine how family responsibilities affect risk-taking.  - Education Level - to assess how higher/professional education inﬂuences ﬁnancial  risk tolerance.

Personalized Risk-Aware Intelligent Stock Recommendation System

- Occupation - categorized as self-employed, private, or public sector, to evaluate risk  attitudes across job types. - Income Level - to study the positive correlation between income and risk-taking  capability. - Investment Experience - to understand how prior ﬁnancial knowledge and exposure  shape investment decisions. - Risk Perception - to capture how individuals perceive and evaluate ﬁnancial risks  based on personal circumstances and experience. - Other Factors - including regularity of investment, level of ﬁnancial knowledge,  preferred investment sectors, and investment time horizon.

The ﬁrst twelve statements in the questionnaire were categorical and collected general information about the respondents for stock investment. The ﬁrst two statements collected data on stock awareness and stock investment status, respectively. The third statement gathered data on respondents' experience with investment activities. The fourth statement collected data on investors' preferred mode of investment. The ﬁfth and sixth statements collected data from respondents to determine if they were ﬁrst-generation investors or regular investors. The seventh statement was developed to determine the respondents' level of investment knowledge. The eighth statement was created to collect information on the respondents' information sources. The ninth and tenth statements collected data on stock investors' level of satisfaction and risk perceptions. The 11th statement collected information on the investors' preferred sector of investment, and it had 7 elements. The 12th statement collected information on the respondents' investment time horizon for stocks. The last ten statements of the questionnaire recorded the demographic information of stock market investors.

**Reliability & Validity of the Data ** The Cronbach alpha, often known as coefﬁcient alpha, has a range of values between 0 and 1. Cronbach's alpha is a value provided by Gliem and Gliem (2003) for determining the dependability of a questionnaire \[ 22 \]. Cronbach's alpha values were computed for various components of the questionnaire to evaluate the internal consistency and reliability of the data collection instrument. For all of the questions, the average Cronbach's alpha was found to be 0.805. Because the value found is higher than the permitted range, it can be assumed that the data acquired using this questionnaire is reliable for further study. Approximately, about 1400 questionnaires were distributed, receiving approximately 500 responses online and 300 responses ofﬂine. Only 400 people out of 800 responded that they were stock market investors. As a result, data from 400 stock market respondents was taken into consideration. **3.2 ** **Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) **

The next step involves performing EDA a concept introduced by John Tukey in the 1970s \[ 23 \]. EDA is a statistical approach used to examine and summarize the key characteristics of a dataset. As the term suggests, it represents an initial stage in which the dataset is thoroughly explored to gain insights into its structure and underlying patterns. In the context of machine learning, EDA plays a crucial role in ensuring that the data used for - Rouf et al.

model training is meaningful and reliable. The primary objective of EDA is to clean, transform, and reﬁne the data to a level where it becomes suitable for training an effective machine learning model. It is a critical step before jumping into machine learning or modelling of data. EDA is used to determine whether the selected features are good enough for model training, and if there are any correlations between variables or not.

**Handling Missing Values in Data ** In real-world scenarios, datasets are seldom clean or uniform. Data may be lost during extraction or collection due to various factors. Missing values must be handled carefully, as they can signiﬁcantly reduce the quality of performance metrics and lead to inaccurate predictions, misclassiﬁcations, or model bias. Several techniques exist for addressing missing data; however, the appropriate method largely depends on the nature of the dataset and the pattern of missingness. In this study, the averaging method was employed to impute the missing values, ensuring consistency and minimizing the impact of data loss on model performance. Figure 2. (a) depicts the presence of a few missing values in the dataset as shown by 'blue dashed lines'. Figure 2. Outliers may arise due to errors in data collection or entry, or they may genuinely reﬂect variability or volatility within the data. In this section, outliers are managed by using the Inter-Quantile Range method \[ 24 \].

**3.3 ** **Preparing the Dataset for Dimensionality Reduction **

The decision maker or analyst must choose relevant variables for clustering at the start of the clustering process. One of the most important tasks in clustering is to choose the proper variables. A useful cluster solution can be skewed by a few unnecessary or incorrect variables. Expert intuition, as well as implicit assumptions and judgments, are used to pick variables \[ 25 \]. In this section, we have used PCA to reduce the dimensionality of the data and choose the signiﬁcant features for clustering. Prior to applying PCA, feature selection was done by removing the low variance and highly correlated features to improve the efﬁciency of PCA. The categorical features like gender, investment experience, risk perception, etc, are encoded using the one-hot encoding method. Finally, the - Rouf et al.

dataset is standardized to ensure that all the features have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

**PCA ** PCA is an approach for reducing the data dimensionality, is used in a variety of ﬁelds, including statistical variables analysis \[ 26 \]. PCA converts a multivariate data set with metric variables into a new data set with uncorrelated and importance-ordered variables called principal components. The highest variability is contained in the ﬁrst variable (principal component), the second principal component contains the second highest variability, and so on. PCA identiﬁes a new feature set known as principal components which are uncorrelated combinations ofs given input features. The model performance was evaluated based on the accuracy metric before and after the application of PCA. Table 1 presents the comparison of evaluation metric before and after dimensionality reduction using PCA. **3.4 ** **Cluster Analysis (Subjective Segmentation) **

A cluster is a collection of data objects that are comparable (or connected) to one another within the same group (i.e., cluster) but not to objects in other groups (i.e., clusters). Given a set of data points, cluster analysis (or clustering, data segmentation) divides them into groups (i.e., clusters) that are as comparable as feasible. Cluster analysis assists the analyst in partitioning large amounts of data into groups depending on their characteristics. It is a method of learning that is not supervised. There is no dependent variable, preset classes, or objective function in an unsupervised analysis. To put it another way, the linkages between observations are unknown ahead of time. There is only one dataset, and the goal is to ﬁnd a pattern in it and use it to make better decisions.

Cluster analysis has primarily two applications: the ﬁrst is as a stand-alone tool. The goal of this application is to gain insight into the distribution or pattern of data. Similar items or client segmentation could be the application. It can also be beneﬁcial for grouping stream data and detecting dynamic trends or patterns. The second use is as a tool for pre-processing. It's an intermediary step for another analysis or method, this time. The clustering analysis can be used for a variety of purposes depending on the intermediate phase. For instance, creating a condensed summary of data for classiﬁcation, pattern. Finding, hypothesis creation, testing, and so on \[ 27 \]. In this work, k-means clustering has been employed on the dataset in order to group the investors into high and low risk categories.

**K-Means ** The k-means clustering algorithm divides 'n' observations into 'k' clusters, with each observation belonging to the cluster with the closest mean \[ 28 \]. The goal is to reduce the sum of squares within each cluster to a minimum. Even though this problem is NP-hard, heuristic techniques such as Lloyd's algorithm have been widely used. An iterative reﬁnement technique is used in the algorithm. It is set up by assigning each observation to a cluster at random. In the update stage, the means are computed to be the cluster centroids. Each observation is assigned to the cluster whose mean produces the smallest, within-cluster sum of squares, where the sum of squares equals the sum of the squared Euclidean distances. The new means are then updated, and the process continues until convergence to a point at which the assignment step no longer changes \[ 28 \].

Personalized Risk-Aware Intelligent Stock Recommendation System

Based on the sum of squared distances (SSE) between data points and their assigned cluster centroids, the Elbow technique estimates the number of clusters needed to produce good results. The number of clusters (k) at which the SSE begins to form an Elbow while ﬂattening out is determined. To determine the optimal number of clusters required to partition the provided dataset, the Elbow method has been used. From the results, it was observed that the difference in within-cluster dissimilarity was not signiﬁcant after 2 clusters. Therefore, the optimal value of 'k' was chosen as 2. Finally, the k-means algorithm was employed on the dataset, and two clusters were obtained.

The performance of the algorithm was evaluated using three metrics as mentioned in Table 1. The metrics are calculated before and after application of PCA and the results show that more coherent and well separated clusters are achieved after application of PCA.

**Cluster Annotation ** In order to classify the obtained clusters into two groups, we annotated the clusters based on the coefﬁcient of variance in principal components. The high variance components were assigned as the high-risk-taking group, while those with low variance were attributed as low-risk-taking groups as shown in Fig. 4.
