## CBAM-EﬃcientNet Based Model

**for** **Enhanced** **Disease** **Classiﬁcation** **U** **sing** **Chest** ** ** **X-Rays**

## Harshita Singh Tanwar, Arya Gupta, and Soumyalatha N aveen ( B )

Manipal Institute of Technology Bengaluru, Manipal Academ y of Higher Education, Manipal, India *\{* harshita.mitblr2022,arya.mitblr2022 *\}* @learner.manipal.edu, soumyalatha.naveen@manipal.edu

**Abstract. ** In this study, an Eﬃcient Net architecture integrated with Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) is proposed for multilabel classiﬁcation of 13 classes of pulmonary diseases. The proposed model is compared with three pretrained models-EﬃcientNetB1, ResNet50, and MobileNetV2, along with the baseline EﬃcientNet architecture on which the enhancements are made, trained on the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset. Performance is assessed using AUC-ROC (Area Under the Curve-Receiver Operating Characteristic) scores. The AUCROC scores for various classes remain in the range 0.4-0.55 for pretrained models: EﬃcientNetB1, ResNet50 and MobileNetV2, however using the prop osed CBAM-EﬃcientNet model increases the AUC-ROC scores to the range of 0.70-0.89 for many classes. The average AUC-ROC score is 0.76. On comparison with the baseline EﬃcientNet architecture, the sensitivity increases from 0.35 to 0.70 and the AUC-ROC values for all the classes improve.

**Keywords: ** Attention Mechanisms *· * CBAM *· * EﬃcientNet *· * ResNet *· * MobileNet *· * NIH D ataset * ·* ROC-AUC

## 1 **Introduction**

## Diagnostic imaging plays an important role in the management of pulmonary

diseases \[ 1 \], including pneumonia, tuberculosis, lung nodules, and COVID-19. Chest-related diseases are among the leading causes of mortality, with severe conditions even leading to fatality. The widespread prevalence of these conditions, exacerbated by factors such as smoking, pollution, and aging populations, underscores the critical role of advanced diagnostic tools like AI-powered chest X-ray analysis in improving patient outcomes and reducing healthcare burdens. Among man y imaging techniques, chest X-rays are the most popular due to the balance provided in terms of cost-eﬃciency, rapid acquisition, and minimal radiation exposure. However, interpreting chest radiographs is a complex task that

c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 436-448, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1> \_ 33 CBAM-EﬃcientNet Based Model for Enhanced Disease

requires signiﬁcant expertise. There may be discrepancies in diagnoses by multiple doctors. The medical community has witnessed remarkable success when it comes to medical image analysis using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) \[ 1 \] and has the potential to analyse complex medical images. The increasing volume of medical imaging data has intensiﬁed the need for automated, accurate, and eﬃcient diagnostic tools. CNNs excel in capturing hierarchical features from images. However, standard CNN architectures struggle with subtle pathological patterns in chest X-rays due to low contrast, overlapping anatomical structures, and class imbalance in medical datasets. To address these challenges, attention mechanisms have been introduced to enhance feature representation by bringing closer attention to diagnostically relevant regions while suppressing irrelevant background noise. The NIH Chest X-ray \[ 2 \] dataset contains over 112,000 frontal-view X-ray images labeled with multiple pathologies (13 disease classes), oﬀering a realistic scenario where models must handle imbalanced and co-o ccurring diseases. Performance evaluation in such settings requires comprehensive metrics, including ROC-AUC \[ 3 \], which account for varying diagnostic thresholds a nd class imbalances.

This study makes the following contributions: It introduces an optimized CBAM-EﬃcientNet model for multi-label pulmonary disease classiﬁcation, for 13 disease classes, on the NIH ChestXRay 14 dataset. The proposed model achieves an overall AUC-ROC of 0.76, outperforming the baseline EﬃcientNet architecture with an overall AUC score of 0.62 and other pretrained models. The study explores how integration of attention mechanisms into already existing architectures can signiﬁcantly improve classiﬁcation for medical image analysis, and how training models from scratch can yield better results than transfer learning in some cases. The proposed model is weighed against other relevant state-of-theart models as well.

## 2 **Literature** **Surve** **y**

Chest radiography remains one of the widely used imaging modalities for diagnosing a range of thoracic diseases including Pneumonia, Tuberculosis, Cardiomegaly, and COVID-19. A critical analysis of existing models reveals limitations in scalability, generalization, and region-speciﬁc interpretability. Sanida and Dasygenis et al. \[ 1 \] introduced a lightweight CNN for lung disease classiﬁcation, achieving 98.56% accuracy across seven classes. The model employed enhanced focal loss to address class imbalance and outperformed models like ResNet50 and NASNetMobile. Designed for embedded systems such as the NVIDIA J etson Xavier, it required minimal training time (55 min per fold) and was trained on 29,131 CXR images from multiple datasets. Sahoo et al. \[ 4 \]  proposed a comprehensive three-stage framework for chest X-ray analysis, integrating lung segmentation \[ 4 \], disease classiﬁcation, and infection severity assessment. Their Gamma-based fuzzy ensemble (GFE) classiﬁer achieved 98.15% accuracy on 3-class and 98.13% on 4-class classiﬁcation tasks (COVID-19, Pneumonia, Normal, Tuberculosis). The segmentation stage combined multiple UNet - S. Tanwar et al.

variants, reaching Dice scores up to 99.49%. A modiﬁed RALE scoring method was used for severity quantiﬁcation, enhancing clinical interpretability. Tested on the external QaTa-COV19 dataset, the model maintained 97.89% accuracy, showing strong g eneralisability. However, high computational cost and reliance on large annotated datasets limit its deployment in resource-constrained environments.

Bennour et al. \[ 5 \] developed three deep learning models-CovCXR-Net, MDCXR3-Net, and MDCXR4-Net-for automated pulmonary disease classiﬁcation from chest X-rays. CovCXR-Net, a lightweight CNN for binary COVID-19 vs. normal classiﬁcation, achieved 99.09% accuracy, while MDCXR3-Net and MDCXR4-Net, based on ﬁne-tuned VGG16 architectures, achieved 97.74% and 91.22% accuracy for 3- and 4-class tasks, respectively. These models demonstrated high diagnostic performance with low c omputational demand, making them suitable for resource-limited settings. However, the study's reliance on small, non-augmented datasets and limited disease scope may aﬀect generalisability across diverse clinical environments. Abad et al. \[ 6 \] addressed the critical issue of model generalisability in chest X-ray-based disease detection by proposing an entropy-based ensemble of pre-trained CNNs (ResNet50, DenseNet121, Inception-ResNet-v2). The method achieved 97.38% accuracy on internal validation and 81.16% on external datasets, using over 26,000 images from six sources. Their uncertainty-aware weighting scheme improved robustness across variable input quality and sources. Despite its strengths, performance dropped signiﬁcantly on external data for some models (e.g., DenseNet121: 96.71% to 61.49%), highlighting generalisation challenges. The binary focus on COVID-19 also limited broader pulmonary disease classiﬁcation. Rao et al. \[ 7 \]  proposed  a hybrid framework combining a classical CNN with two novel quantum classiﬁers: MMS and MSMS for multi-class classiﬁcation of respiratory diseases from chest X-rays. Using the COVID-19 Radiography Dataset, the model achieved 98.9% training and 98.1% testing accuracy, outperforming conventional deep learning approaches. Quantum components reduced memory and computational costs, with validation on the IBM Q-QASM pro cessor conﬁrming real-world feasibility. Despite these advantages, scalability is constrained by current quantum hardware limitations, and evaluation was limited to a single dataset. Poloju and Rajaram et al. \[ 8 \] presented a hybrid machine learning framework combining ensemble techniques (bagging, boosting, voting) with Emperor Penguin Optimization (EPO) for lung disease classiﬁcation. The model achieved a 97.50% accuracy and 1.31% error rate on the LIDC-IDRI dataset, outperforming traditional classiﬁers. Feature extraction utilized DCT and DWT for capturing texture and geometric patterns, while EPO ﬁne-tuned the parameters of base classiﬁers such as SVM, KNN, and Na ¨ Ive Bayes. Despite its high precision and suitability for real-time use (0.0975 ms runtime), the model's generalisability is limited due to dataset dependency and a lack of validation on X-ray or MRI images.

Huang et al. \[ 9 \] proposed a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based framework for multi-disease diagnosis from chest X-rays, targeting 14 common thoracic diseases CBAM-EﬃcientNet Based Model for Enhanced Disease

mentioned in the ChestX-ray14 dataset. The model achieved an average AUC of 0.837, outperforming CNN-based approaches by 2.7%, with notable improvements for pneumonia (7.5%) and edema (6.8%). Key innovations included a sliding window segmentation method for spatial consistency and an attention region selection module to highlight critical diagnostic regions. Additionally, a multi-modal fusion network integrated patient metadata (e.g., age, gender, shooting position), enhancing diagnostic performance. Despite high accuracy (0.834), the model faced challenges with class imbalance and increased computational demands. Hybrid CNN-Transformer models have advanced lung disease classiﬁcation from chest X-rays by capturing local and global features. Fu et al. \[ 10 \] introduced LungMaxViT, combining CNN blocks, Squeeze-andExcitation, and MaxViT attention mechanisms, achieving up to 96.8% accuracy on COVID-19 and 93.2% AUC on ChestX-ray14 datasets. The model employs CLAHE and data augmentation for enhanced image quality and uses Grad-CAM for interpretability. Despite strong performance, challenges include class imbalance, high computational cost, and dependence on image preprocessing, limiting deployment in resource-limited settings. LungMaxViT highlights the potential of hybrid arch itectures for explainable, multi-class lung disease diagnosis. Ensemble transfer learning approaches have gained traction for multi-disease detection from chest X-rays due to their ability to leverage complementary strengths of multiple pre-trained models. Balmuri et al. \[ 11 \] proposed an optimized ensemble transfer learning (OETL) framework combining architectures such as VGG16, ResNet, MobileNet, and Inception, achieving up to 97% accuracy across diverse datasets including COVID-19, tuberculosis, and pneumonia. The model incorporates an optimized DeepLabv3 for lung segmentation and applies Mutation Rate-based Lion Algorithm (MR-LA) for parameter tuning, enhancing feature extraction and reducing misclassiﬁcations. Gamma correction is used for noise reduction and contrast enhancement in preprocessing. Despite improved sensitivity and speciﬁcity, challenges remain in computational demands, limited explainability, and performance degradation on low-quality or novel disease datasets. Yao et al. \[ 12 \] proposed EVA-X, a foundation model trained on over one million unlabeled chest X-rays using a combination of masked image modeling and contrastive learning to capture semantic and geometric features. EVA-X oﬀers scalable model sizes and achieves state-of-the-art performance on 11 diverse downstream tasks, including multi-label classiﬁcation and segmentation across more than 20 chest diseases. Despite high computational cost during pre-training, EVA-X advances generalizable and label-eﬃcient chest X-ray analysis, though its applicability beyond chest imaging remains unexplored.

| The study utilises the NIH Chest Xray-14\[2\] dataset, which is available on Kag- | gle. The dataset contains a total of 1,12,200 images of chest radiograms. All the | **3.1** **Dataset and Preprocessing **

The study utilises the NIH Chest Xray-14\[ 2 \] dataset, which is available on Kaggle. The dataset contains a total of 1,12,200 images of chest radiograms. All the - S. Tanwar et al.

images are labeled with 14 diﬀerent classes which are: Atelectasis, Consolidation, Cardiomegaly, Edema, Emphysema, Eﬀusion, Fibrosis, Hernia, Inﬁltration, Pneumonia, Pneumothorax, Pleural Thickening, Mass, Nodule and No Finding. Upon data collection and visualization, it is observed that the 'No Finding' class is present in an overwhelming majority of X-rays as compared to the rest of the classes. This creates a sheer imbalance, hugely aﬀecting the model performance by misleading it. To overcome this issue the ﬁrst step in data preparation has been to undersample the 'No Finding' class. This is done by removing 20% of the samples which have been labeled as No Finding. This reduces the dominance of the class, without harming the representation needed for classiﬁcation by the m odel. The dataset is cleaned by removing any invalid or corrupt images. After cleaning 80,060 images are used. The train test split is done in an 85:15 ratio. There are 44,077 training images and 2,813 validation images. Rest 8274 are testing images. Data augmentations are implemented to improve the performance of the model. They introduce some noise into the data, for mimicking real-life occurrences, which will help the model generalize better. The common augmentations used are:

- Rotation: Rotate function, to rotate the images by 90 *◦*. - Width shift: Shift image horizontally, by u p to 10% of width. - Height shift: Shift image vertically, by up to 10% of height. - Shearing: Shearing transformation on the image with an intensity of up to  5% for skewing the image along the axis. - Zooming: Zooming in or out the image by 10% - Flipping: Horizontally ﬂipping the image by 10% **3.2** **Model Architecture **

The EFﬁcientNet architecture is a convolutional neural network which is based on the Compound Scaling method. Uniformly scaling width, depth or resolution, with a ﬁxed set of scaling c oeﬃcients is the premise of Compound scaling. The baseline architecture of EﬃcientNet \[ 13 \] is based on inverted bottleneck residual blocks of MobileNetV2 \[ 14 \] for more computational eﬃciency as compared to traditional CNNs, in addition to Squeeze-and-excitation (SE)\[ 15 \] attention blocks. The layers comprising the baseline EﬃcientNetB0 \[ 16 \] architecture can be seen in the Fig. 1. It comprises of:

- Convolutional Layers: EﬃcientNet starts with a stem convolutional block  comprising of a convolutional layer in addition to a batch normalization layer and activation functions. - Squeeze and Excitation: This is a type of attention mechanism, integrated  into the baseline architecture. The ﬁrst step is squeeze operation, which compresses the global spatial information into channel descriptor, allowing each channel in feature map to be summarized into a single scalar value. The second step is excitation, which assigns weights to the channels such that the important channels are emphasized, while the less important ones are suppressed. CBAM-EﬃcientNet Based Model for Enhanced Disease

- Mobile Inverted BottleNeck layers (MobConv): These layers form the basic  building blocks of the EﬃcientNet architecture. These consist of the convolutional layer blocks (conv2D layers, Batch Normalization and Activation). This is followed by the SE Attention block. This is ﬁnally followed by a projection blo ck consisting of a 1 * ×* 1 convolutional layer which combines information from all the previous layers into a more compact form. - Classiﬁcation Head: This is the ﬁnal layer of the EﬃcientNet architecture,  followed by 6 blocks of MobConv layers. Here the processed features are transformed i nto outputs suitable for speciﬁc tasks such as classiﬁcation. This includes the fully connected \[ 17 \] lay er. **Fig. 1. ** Architecture of Baseline E ﬃcientNet

A custom model CBAM-EﬃcientNet has been proposed, which enhances the baseline EﬃcientNet architecture by introducing two more modules into it: Attention Mechanisms and Spatial Pyramid Pooling. The proposed model is trained from scratch on the target chest X-ray dataset. Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) \[ 18 \], is incorporated into the architecture, which complements the existing Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules inherent in EﬃcientNet. While SE modules reﬁne channel-wise attention, CBAM extends attention learning by incorporating both channel and spatial attention, allowing the network to pay attention to diagnostically important parts and suppress irrelevant features and noise. The CBAM module comprises of a channel attention module in addition to a spatial attention module. The Channel Attention Module takes the input features, and outputs the most important features, on which the model should focus. The spatial attention module concentrates it's focus to where the most important information is located. It applies average and max pooling operations across the axis of input ch annels. Then the pooled features are integrated and convolved by a 7 *×* 7 kernel, succeeded by sigmoid activation to generate feature map. The CBAM modules are placed inside the MobConv blocks within the architecture, followed by the SE block. The mentioned enhancements made to the baseline EﬃcientNetB1 architecture in the proposed CBAM-EﬃcientNet architecture has been shown in Fig. 2. To further enhance multi-scale feature learning, a Spatial Pyramid Pooling (SPP) \[ 19 \]  layer is appended into the architecture after the MobConv blocks. This layer allows object detection while preserving the global and local context, by performing max pooling with multiple kernel sizes. This is followed by concatenating resulting feature maps, enabling the model to aggregate contextual information at - S. Tanwar et al.

diﬀerent spatial resolutions. Collectively, the inclusion of CBAM and SPP layers leads to improved sensitivity to s mall or subtle anomalies and enhances the models generalization capacity.

**Fig. 2. ** Architecture of the proposed C BAM-EﬃcientNet model **3.3** **Model Training **

All the models: pretrained EﬃcientNetB1, MobileNetV2 and ResNet50, baseline EﬃcientNet as well as the optimised CBAM-EﬃcientNet model are trained on 100 epochs with a batch size of 64. The model training was done in a K aggle T4 GPU environment. All 3 pretrained models were initialized with ImageNet weights and ﬁne-tuned on NIH ChestX-ray \[ 2 \] with identical hyperparameters. While the baseline EﬃcientNet architecture is ﬁnetuned and t rained on the NIH Chest XRays dataset \[ 2 \] as well. Hyperparameter tuning is done to optimize all mdoels:

- Dropout Rate (0.5): Dropout regularization is applied, with a rate of 0.5. - Learning Rate: The initial learning rate \[ 20 \] is set to 0.001. ReduceLROnPLateu is used for reducing the learning rate gradually. - Adam Optimizer: Adam optimizer \[ 21 \] is used for adjusting learning rate for  each parameter based on the ﬁ rst and second moments of gradients. - Weight Decay: Further to improve the performance weight decay ( L2 regularization) is incorporated. - Early Stopping: An early stopping mechanism with a patience of 5 epochs is  used to terminate training when the validation loss stopped improving.

Given the signiﬁcant class imbalance in the dataset, a custom weighted function is adopted. The custom loss function uses class-frequency based weighting to balance the positive and negative samples for each class. The positive CBAM-EﬃcientNet Based Model for Enhanced Disease

and negative frequencies for each sample are calculated. This yields two sets of weights (positive and negative) which are incorporated into the custom loss function. This weighted formulation ensures that classes with fewer examples are not overwhelmed during gradient u pdates, thereby enhancing model sensitivity to minority classes. The same loss function was applied consistently across all models used for comparison.

## 4 **Results**

In context of multi-label classiﬁcation for lung disease detection, traditional accuracy is a misleading metric, since the dataset is highly imbalanced. Some classes are extremely rare and whereas the others are present in a huge majority. The class imbalance problem has been countered to some extent during data preprocessing using sampling and during model training by using a customized loss function. In this case, accuracy appears to be low, since the task requires multiple labels per images, and the accuracy metric considers only the exact match where all labels for the sample must be predicted incorrectly. To address this the Recall (Sensitivity) and AUC-ROC scores are used as the primary evaluation metrics. Recall quantiﬁes the model's capability to identify all true positives, making it crucial in medical diagnostics. AUC-ROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) captures the model's performance across all classiﬁcation thresholds, considering both true positive rate and false positive rate, and is robust to class imbalance.

| EﬃcientNetB1 | 0.50 | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| MobileNetV2 | 0.53 | 0.55 | 0.55 |

## 5 **Conclusion**

This study presents an enhanced deep learning-based framework for multi-label lung disease classiﬁcation from chest X-ray images, leveraging the NIH Chest X-ray14 dataset. The proposed CBAM-EﬃcientNet architecture, incorporating Convolutional Block Attention Modules and Spatial Pyramid Pooling, demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional pretrained models such as EﬃcientNetB1, MobileNetV2, and ResNet50, and the baseline EﬃcientNet architecture. The emphasis on clinically relevant metrics such as recall and AUC-ROC over traditional accuracy ensures that evaluation aligns with realworld diagnostic priorities. While the model demonstrates a higher AUC-ROC CBAM-EﬃcientNet Based Model for Enhanced Disease

## score and an improved F1-score when compared to baseline architectures, sev

eral limitations persist. Since the dataset is highly imbalanced, basic resampling has been applied. However advanced data preprocessing techniques and class balancing strategies could further enhance performance. While the proposed CBAM-EﬃcientNet model reports a slightly reduced recall compared to EﬃcientNetB1, it compensates with improved precision, resulting in a competitive F1 score that highlights its robustness in handling class imbalance. As mentioned before accuracy is a highly misleading metric for this dataset, since there is a severe imbalance of classes, and accuracy doesn't consider the weight of all classes due to this. Hence, metrics such as AUC-ROC and recall oﬀer a far more meaningful evaluation of the model's eﬀectiveness. While the proposed model does not outperform existing state-of-the-art architectures, in terms of AUC scores, it provides insight regarding the impact of architectural modiﬁcations, using integration of CBAM in EﬃcientNetB1 trained from scratch. However, the relatively lower AUC compared to existing approaches indicates further improvement can be done by sophisticated data balancing techniques, segmentation, transfer learning and ensembling based models. This work primarily establishes the importance of attention mechanisms in medical classiﬁcation problems and opens avenues for combining it with domain speciﬁc preprocessing. Future work may explore the use of advanced data preprocessing techniques to balance the dataset.

## Enhancing UPI Payment Security in India **Through Blockchain Adaptation **

## Ram Deepak ( B ) and Sharmila Sankar

B.S.Abdur Rahman Crescent Institute of Science & Technology, Chennai, Tamilnadu, India ramdeepak2311@gmail.com

**Abstract. ** Uniﬁed Payments Interface (UPI) has revolutionized digital transactions in India, enabling real-time peer-to-peer transfers. However, as transaction volumes rise, so do concerns regarding security, fraud, and data integrity. This paper proposes an integration model of Blockchain technology with UPI infrastructure to enhance security, ensure transaction immutability, and reduce dependency on centralized systems. By leveraging blockchain's decentralized and cryptographic features, we aim to mitigate risks such as man-in-the-middle attacks, transaction tampering, and system-level breaches. A prototype model and simulation results demonstrate improved security and traceability in UPI transactions with minimal latency overhead.

**Keywords: ** UPI · Blockchain · Financial Security · Digital Payments · India · Smart Contracts · Distributed Ledger

## 1 **Introduction **

## The use of digital payments in India has gone through an epic shift, and the signiﬁcant

growth is largely due to the Uniﬁed Payments Interface (UPI). Designed by National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), UPI has become the key to the world of FinTech revolution in the country, where funds can be transferred almost instantly between the bank accounts via smartphones. As compared to other traditional systems, which use either net banking portals or card-based payments, UPI offers an easy, mobile-ﬁrst experience, which would be convenient and fast \[ 6 \]. Presently in 2025, more than 12 billion transactions occur every month with the help of UPI that reveals how ubiquitous it has become in metropolitan urban cities as well as in rural locations. It has also been taken up by merchant payment, settlement of bills, P2P transactions, and disbursement of government beneﬁts, and it has demonstrated a multi-purpose application in its use.

## Nonetheless, a swift expansion in the use of UPI has not been harmless. Due to the

growth of digital payments, there are also increasing threats to digital payments. Attacks on mobile banking have become much more rich in attacks that are being presented through vulnerabilities in mobile apps, OTP veriﬁcation systems, and SIM-swapping threats. A surge of fraudulent transactions caused by UPI fake apps, phishing scams and social engineering techniques has left ﬁnancial and brand owners with substantial ﬁnancial and reputational costs. Although the NPCI and RBI have already implemented

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 449-462, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_34> - Deepak and S. Sankar

measures to increase the security like the biometric authentication, device binding and multi-factor authentication, they are more centralized and defensive. In most of the cases, centralized security systems are single point of failure since when one node is breached, the integrity of a whole transaction network may be affected \[ 1 \].

Blockchain technology by contrast proposes a radically different systems design, distributed, tamper-proof, and naturally transparent. Originated to be the spine of cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, blockchain has later been recruited to serve the domains of supply chain, healthcare, legal contracts, and, gradually, ﬁnance. The main strength is that it is based on the idea of a decentralized ledger whereby every node active within a chain has a synchronized and unchangeable version of all transactions \[ 8 \]. Blockchain, when implemented with care, can also be used to make UPI payments secured and trackable, so much so that fraudulent actors should ﬁnd it very hard to interfere in the transactions, counterfeit or conceal it. Programmability via smart contracts It also helps with programmability via smart contracts aka autonomous code coupled with pre-deﬁned rules, which enables the possibility of making automated checks, fraud detection system, and instant reconciliations part of payment systems.

Moreover, blockchain deals with some urgent issues in the existing online ﬁnancial system. It reduces the possibility of tampering with data by ensuring that its historical records cannot be altered, enables auditability of transactions in real time without a central authority, and has a much stronger cryptographic security system than the conventional centralized encryption methods \[ 3 \]. Notably, blockchain could be integrated into the current architecture of UPI in a layered/hybrid approach which implies that the user experience will be barely changed and the backend infrastructure will get enhanced security and resiliency. This interoperability guarantees an easy change-over by users, merchants as well as banks without necessarily having to do a technological over-haul.

This paper is devoted to how the concept of blockchain may be introduced as a strategic modiﬁcation to the current UPI environment in order to improve its general security state. It discusses how a consortium model of blockchain like permissioned Hyperledger Fabric blockchain can be adopted to facilitate a network of transactional enabled consortium banks that avail the service of the NPCI as validating nodes. It also presents the veriﬁcation mechanism of a smart contract that shall extend and moderate the traditional authentication ways and will bring along the beneﬁts of terminating the OTP spooﬁng, man-in-the-middle, or fraudulent redirection risks \[ 4 \]. Moreover, the suggested architecture also incorporates strategies to anonymize user data without unauditability and therefore comply with the regulation that gathers protection laws of India.

It is not the replacement of UPI, but to strengthen it to counteract the threat of emerging challenges in the digital world. With an increasing frequency, cross-border and high-value ﬁnancial transactions, the systems on which ﬁnancial transactions are based need to develop to become both trusted and resilient. Incorporating blockchain can be the way forward, a process during which UPI could not only preserve its ease of use and the speed of operation but also acquire an unheard-of degree of safety, visibility, and customer trust \[ 2 \].

The most important elements of the study shall be summed up as follows: Enhancing UPI Payment Security in India Through Blockchain

- Offered a blockchain based design as a solution to making UPI transactions more  safe and trusted through decentralizing sensitive data storage and validation of transactions. - Was able to develop a validation protocol based on smart contracts that authenticate  the transaction, non-repudiation and fraud prevention using the UPI system. - The proposed model was simulated and compared to the current standards of UPI  security programs to evaluate the increase of data integrity, traceability of the transaction, and resistance to threats. - Tackled the issues of implementation, scalability, latency, and regulatory conformity  to make realistic implementation of the suggested solution feasible in the ﬁnancial context of India. - Provided the outline of policy recommendation, future upgrades, and implementation  of blockchain-based security infrastructure of UPI across the nation. **1.1 ** **Novelty and Contribution **

The originality of this contribution is that it is both applicable and ﬂexible in integrating blockchain into India UPI ecosystem with no impact on the current user interface or processes. While the earlier works attempt to build a fully decentralized payment ecosystem without building much upon existing UPI frameworks, the paper presents a hybrid blockchain solution that perfectly integrates with the existing UPI architecture \[ 10 \]. It enables the stakeholders like NPCI, banks, and regulatory organizations to utilize the decentralized properties of blockchain and maintain interoperability, backward compatibility and scalability.

The main advantage of this study lies in the development and implementation of a proposal to use a blockchain-based model of a UPI transaction that introduces the permissioned blockchain (Hyperledger Fabric), validation through smart contracts, and encryption of logs of transaction records to enhance integrity. In this model all transactions are validated using a consensus protocol across bank nodes and the transaction is recorded immutably thus posing signiﬁcantly lower opportunities to tamper with, fraud or insider risks.

The second key contribution is the presentation of automatized fraud and transaction veriﬁcation via smart contracts. The smart contracts are designed in such a way that they perform conditional checks such as the identity veriﬁcation of the user, the availability of funds and the analysis of the risks before the transaction is permitted. This removes the reactive human intervention reaction and this accelerates the process of detecting the fraud \[ 15 \].

More than that, the paper also has an in-depth security analysis and simulation of the proposed model based on real world conditions of transactions. The paper uses a synthetic network of sandbox with synthetic data of the UPI transaction and compares a latency, fault-proof, and attack vector resistance with current UPI implementations. These ﬁndings afﬁrm that the blockchain enhanced UPI system is able to enhance not merely traceability and data security but also to maintain the range of tolerable transaction throughput and speed.

Lastly, the paper also advances general research in the domain of ﬁnancial technology in the respect that it offers a policy-compliant blueprint that policymakers, ﬁnancial - Deepak and S. Sankar

institutions, and software engineers can follow to scale-out. It shows the regulatory viability of blockchain-based UPI systems in accordance to Indian privacy laws (including the DPDP Act) and presents the methods to strike the balance between the pursuit of transparency and the assurance of data privacy by applying encryption methods and the zero-knowledge proofs \[ 9 \].

## 2 **Related Study **

In 2024 V. Deval *et al.*,  \[ 7 \] introduced the digital payment development in India has been the most critical ﬁnancial transformation of this century that took place under the inﬂuence of the emergence of mobile-based systems and state-related steps towards a cashless economy. Introduced as a tool to provide real-time transfers between banks, instantly, UPI went into the mass consumption thanks to its simplicity and mobile compatibility with other types of wallets, as well as its compatibility between various banking platforms. In spite of this level of success, the UPI infrastructure has demonstrated some of its weaknesses notably in the sphere of cybersecurity. The frequency of reporting instances of phishing, counterfeiting services of payment applications, personal data leakage, unauthorized banking transfers has highlighted the gaps in the security of both the frontend user and the backend arrays of UPI-enabled services.

In 2025 Mandi ć et.al., B. Markovi ć et.al., and I. R. Ž igo et.al., \[ 11 \] proposed the use of classic security systems used in UPI transactions depends to a large extent on centralized veriﬁcation systems. Such solutions are one-time passwords (OTPs), biometric authentication, device binding and backend fraud detection by the banks. Although these systems are quite effective to some degree, they remain susceptible to exploitation by attacks with centralized points of vulnerability or with human failure. Data centers in banks without a history of compromising data are more prone to being targeted by hackers or existing employees working with databases of bank and ﬁnancial services providers. The volume of transactions increases, which is why there are threats of single points of failure and a systemic fraud.

Simultaneously, blockchain has become a viable option of fostering trust in digital systems in the absence of the central authority. The decentralized structure of blockchain provides such options as immutability, a distributed consensus, and open book-keeping, being an attractive means of securing ﬁnancial transactions. There have also been a number of pilot programs and research projects across the world with regard to the usage of blockchain technology in different sectors of interbank settlements, supply chain ﬁnance, identity veriﬁcation and insurance claims processing. Such projects have shown how the blockchain can efﬁciently eclipse old systems of keeping ledgers and central record systems with off the chain and more secure alternatives \[ 14 \].

When used on digital payment systems, blockchain implicitly adds beneﬁts to the traceability of transactions and prevention of fraud, as well as the auditability of all transactions in near real time. In a blockchain system, transactions in the system are executed and centrally stored on a distributed ledger that cannot be edited. This means that any unauthorized access of data to devour the information regarding transactions can be instantly identiﬁed and abolished by the net. Moreover, the smart contracts provide the possibility of automating the validation of transactions and the implementation of Enhancing UPI Payment Security in India Through Blockchain

rules that have already been established without any reference to manual processing or intermediate veriﬁcation levels. The relevance of these features is especially to mobilebased payment systems such as UPI which can be manipulated during the validation and routing.

In 2023 Y. Agusta et.al., \[ 5 \] suggested the blockchain in the current ﬁnancial systems has been suggested in several pieces, and has been often associated with the area of peerto-peer payments, decentralized exchanges and cryptocurrency wallets. Nonetheless, the majority among these solutions are designed to operate within entirely decentralized settings in which most end-users see the need to interact with blockchain interfaces on their own, a situation that can hardly be possible and convenient in a system such as UPI, which is intended to be embraced so as to be user-friendly. This leaves one with the literature gap that hybrid models incorporating the strengths of a proposed UPI front-end combined with security provided by a blockchain has not been adequately investigated.

Permissioned blockchain hybrid solutions have received popularity in applications where conﬁdentiality of data, scale issues, and institutional trust are a concern. In these systems, chosen institutions such as banks or regulators which act as a validating node in a closed system of blockchain. The advantage of this approach lies in that it will combine the security advantages of distributed consensus and tamper-resistant ledgers with support of regulatory requirements and meet performance benchmarks. The frameworks that are commonly used for permissioned blockchains (depending on the Hyperledger Fabric or Corda stacks) are especially appropriate when dealing with a ﬁnancial ecosystem like UPI and require conﬁdentiality of transactions, speed, and legal control.

Although the interest in blockchain-ﬁntech convergence has been increasing, very few applications have actually concerned national-scale payment systems, linked with traditional banking infrastructure. In addition, the papers presented nowadays tend to ignore everyday issues like compatibility with legacy systems, legislative limitations and the continuity of user experience. Even less has been spoken about how smart contracts can be customized to detect and prevent fraud and ensure compliance in an UPI-like system, or how blockchain can be scaled to cope with the billions of transactions that are typical of Indian digital payment ﬂows.

To conclude, both UPI and blockchain had been already studied through numerous attempts; however, the integration of the two technologies is not much analyzed. The body of literature indicates the possibility of introducing blockchain into digital payments service providers to increase security and visibility levels thereof; however, efﬁcient application in a large-scale, real-time environment, such as UPI is yet to be fully developed. In this paper, the author aims to compare the current solution to this gap and propose a blockchain-enhanced UPI architecture that will provide the beneﬁts of security, scalability, and transparency to the user with minimum nudges to changing the existing behavior of end-users and the workﬂows required on the bank-side.

## 3 **Societal Impact **

Blockchain inside the UPI in India can bring signiﬁcant improvements to the society by building increased digital trust, ﬁnancial inclusion, and resilience within the systems. Given that the urban and rural population will gradually transfer to becoming the main means of transactions among the UPI, the need to secure them is no - Deepak and S. Sankar

longer an issue of technology, but a social need. The decentralized, unalterable platform of Blockchain offers a suitable answer to the increasing threat of fraud, identity and information tampering in the UPI payments.

The importance of one of the impacts on the society is the preservation of digital ﬁnancial personality of the individuals particularly of the people who are yet untapped and are newly banked or new to the digital world. A safer framework for transactions exposes human vulnerability to exploitation and earns credibility in the eMoney systems among the population. It is especially great in the rural and semi-urban areas of India where the ﬁnancial literacy and conﬁdence in the digital infrastructure is low. This trust gap can be closed by a blockchain-secured UPI platform to create transparency and auditability.

Moreover, the increase in the UPI security can assist directly to the economic strength of a nation. Digital fraudulent transactions will not only lead to loss of ﬁnancial resources but will also develop a dent in the credibility of such digital programs as Digital India and Make in India. Safe and transparent UPI ecosystem strengthens the digital economy integrity, stimulates greater use of cashless payments and promotes the shift of India towards a knowledge-based ﬁnancial system.

On a company-level, the banks, ﬁntech startups, and regulatory authorities will enjoy cost-saving on compliance, enhanced fraud monitoring, and simpliﬁed auditing processes since blockchain would automatically log a permanent history of the transactions. This may ultimately give rise to a more effective ﬁnancial regulatory mechanism, which will strengthen governance and vigilance throughout the ﬁnancial activities.

Nevertheless, the inﬂuence to the society also implies some risks and responsibilities. The Smart integration with Blockchain has to be done with caution to help avert technical discrimination of individuals who do not have access to fast internet or the use of modern gadgets. In addition, policy framework should also be adapted to solve the moral use of distributed data, privacy concerns, as well as interoperability positioners between the conventional ﬁnancial frameworks and the decentralized ones.

The implementation of blockchain in UPI will not only improve the technical safety but also is associated with the potential of more balanced, reliable, and future-proof ﬁnancial environment. Responsible deployment, inclusive design, and a robust policy, this innovation can greatly enrich Indian digital infrastructure in the sphere of the general atmospheres of the country.

## 5 **Results and Discussion **

The practical experimental assessment of the developed blockchain-enhanced UPI architecture was conducted in the controlled simulation environment based on a permissioned blockchain with a single permissioned block where the validating nodes were the lending institutions representing major banks (ﬁve nodes). There were measures of synthetic UPI payments in which 10,000 transactions have been run to test performance, integrity and fraud resistance. These synthetic transactions differed in terms of time distributions in order to reﬂect the real world variation in transaction load, and contained carefully constructed fraudulent transactions to challenge the ability to detect this behavior. The results were stored and compared emphasizing on the speed of transactions, success of validation, and detection rate and within all nodes to be ledger-consistent \[ 13 \].

The ﬁrst set of results show that the processing time per transaction is going up by a relatively small margin with the use of consensus and smart contract execution. As much as the average transaction time of the traditional UPI was 1.2 seconds, the blockchainenabled UPI model performed average 1.9 seconds per transaction by the same loads. This will be worth the increase in view of the improved security and traceability. Fig. 2. Blockchain Vs Traditional UPI Average Transactions Time Comparison compromises this performance trade-off. The three series of the bar chart created with the help of Excel represents the average processing time of the standard UPI1 in milliseconds, the difference between the standard and proposed blockchain UPI, and the differences when the transaction volume is increased (number of sequences). ## Adaptive Federated Learning with Selective

**Privacy Preservation for Enhancing Scalability ** **in Edge-Enabled IoT Systems **

## Paritosh Kumar Yadav ( B ), Sudhakar Pandey, and Tejas Kishor Patil

Department of Information Technology, National Institute of Technology, Raipur, India pkyadavgzp@gmail.com, spandey.it@nitrr.ac.in

**Abstract. ** Edge-enabled Internet of Things (IoT) systems are increasingly utilizing Federated Learning (FL) for decentralized intelligence that protects user data. However, traditional FL models have their limitations. These limitations include poor generalization over long horizons of training, non-IID data distribution, excessive communication costs, and data sovereignty issues, particularly when dealing with large-scale deployments. In response to these limitations, the paper proposes AFL-SP+ (Adaptive Federated Learning with Selective Privacy)- a new framework that incorporates adaptive client participation, systematic noise calibration and selective enforcement of privacy to support sustainable efﬁcient learning in edge environments. AFL-SP+ represents a privacy-presence methodology that exploits differential privacy, client clustering and momentum-based model averaging to accommodate device heterogeneity and environmental dynamics. The framework enhances scalability provides expected levels of model accuracy while protecting user privacy throughout long horizons of training (as many as 10,000 rounds). Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets reveal that AFLSP+ outperforms MP-FL in model accuracy by (as much as) 1.1% and FL with differential privacy by (as much as) 3.1% while reducing communications costs by 23% with a privacy budget ( ε ≤ 1.0), and improved resistance to attack by (as much as) 29.1%. These results establish AFL-SP+ as a scalable, energy-efﬁcient, privacy-preserving continuous learning solution for real-world implementations in edge-enabled IoT systems.

## 1 **Introduction **

## 1.1 **Background **

## The fast growth of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has also created an era of con

stant connection for smart healthcare, smart cities, industrial automation, and intelligent transportation systems that allow for real-time monitoring, intelligence and automation, and data- driven decision-making. By 2025, there will be an estimated 30 billion IoTconnected devices that will generate zettabytes of data from the edge \[ 1 \]. This deluge of

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 463-474, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_35> P.K. Yadav et al.

data generated at the edge brings signiﬁcant opportunities to build intelligent systems but equally brings a multitude of challenges associated with data privacy, computing power, bandwidth, and scalability. Federated Learning (FL) has developed into a new decentralized machine learning framework that enables edge devices to come together to train models in a collaborative way without ever needing to send raw data to a central server. This approach protects the privacy of raw data and prevents network overload while also bringing low-latency decision-making capabilities. However, established FL approaches such as FedAvg and its variants have major limitations relating to privacy leakage vulnerabilities, inefﬁcient support of non-IID data distribution, and high energy consumption due to continuous communication with the server and clients \[ 2, 3 \].

To be sure these limitations compound with the unique aspects of edge-enabled IoT environments where there is more heterogeneity of devices, there is intermittent connectivity, and privacy regulations can be strict. **1.2 ** **Scope and Problem Deﬁnition **

This research addresses the pressing need for a scalable privacy-preserving FL framework speciﬁcally designed for dynamic and resource-constrained edge-enabled IoT systems. The primary challenge is how to facilitate the FL implementation in such a way that we can maintain model accuracy while ensuring privacy for the user across loads of rounds of training, given the non-IID data and intermittent device participation. The FL solutions that include DP currently on the market have shown degraded performance over time and solutions that rely on inﬂexible privacy mechanisms do not adapt to the needs of the user, thereby incurring unnecessary communication costs or create wasted performance due to the underutilization of the capability of the system. **1.3 ** **Objective and Motivation **

The research objective to develop an adaptive federated learning environment, hereafter referred to as AFL-SP+ (Adaptive Federated Learning with Selective Privacy) that smartly implements different privacy strategies based on client features and the context. The proposed methodology employs on dynamic adjustment of adaptive differential privacy budgets, based on the default client sensitivity and data distribution \[ 4 \]. Selective enforcement of privacy, so that clients do not have to engage the stronger layers of privacy unless absolutely required. Momentum based aggregation and adaptive client participation with the goal of achieving stable learning even when the clients are only partially participating or had a device dropout. AFL-SP+ is evaluated over 10,000 training rounds with realistic non-IID scenarios and benchmark datasets. The experiments show that AFL-SP+ provides better model accuracy (up to 1.1% improvement over MPFL and 3.1% over FL+DP), reduces communication costs (up to 23%), achieved the same DP budget ( ε ) ≤ 1.0, and is resilient to adversarial attacks. **1.4 ** **Contributions ** The paper contributes the following:

Adaptive Federated Learning with Selective Privacy Preservation

(i) An innovative adaptive privacy mechanism that identiﬁes privacy techniques (e.g., DP, SMPC, or do nothing) according to client sensitivity and contextual triggers. (ii) A client-tiered architecture server that accepts heterogeneous IoT devices with variable computation and privacy requirements. (iii) A dynamic method of client selection that enables efﬁcient learning while avoiding unnecessary communication. (iv) Extensive experimental validation over extensive rounds (10,000) demonstrates the robustness and energy efﬁciency of the AFL-SP+ approach long-term compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

Hence, AFL-SP+ achieves an important goal for the FL ﬁeld by creating a scalable, intelligent, and privacy-preserving real-world IoT capability, while alleviating limitations of current FL implementations. It attends to model performance, privacy protections, and efﬁciency across the system to make federated learning feasible for edge deployments. The rest of this paper is structured as follows. In Sect. 2, we provide a complete literature review of the latest contributions on federated learning (FL), privacy strategies, and edge-enabled IoT (Internet of Things) systems for IoT applications. In Sect. 3, we describe the proposed AFL-SP+ architecture and its relevant features, including its tiering mechanism for privacy, adaptive selection approach for clients, and aggregation approach. In Sect. 4, we describe the experiment, used datasets, simulation parameters, and performance metrics that are being evaluated. In Sect. 5, we discuss the results by comparing AFL-SP+ against existing methods for FL, including Vanilla FL, FL+DP and MP-FL in different ways, including accuracy, privacy, communication cost and robustness. Finally, in Sect. 6, we conclude the paper by summarizing key results, limitations, and future directions.

## 2 **Literature Review **

In recent years, Federated Learning (FL) has become a major disruptive development in the ﬁeld of distributed machine learning. It is particularly suited to domains involving data privacy and decentralized computation (e.g. IoT, healthcare, industrial process automation etc.) \[ 5 \]. Due to increased focus on data privacy, much of the research wanted to employ privacy-preserving specs, such as Differential Privacy (DP), Homomorphic Encryption (HE), and Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC), inside VL designs; alongside which there is a rising challenge of tackling statistical heterogeneity, most particularly the scattering of non-IID data across a client base, and new personalization strategies such as clustering, adaptive aggregation, and meta-learning are appearing in the literature. Between 2021-2025 there has been huge growth in high quality research to improve FL in heterogeneous settings, improve communication efﬁciency to adequate levels, and better perform a compromise between an acceptable degree of model accuracy and privacy guarantees \[ 6 \]. The current literature review assesses in more than 25 high quality studies, the fundamental methodologies, contributions of novelty, and degree of empirical validation; and gives particular consideration for works heading towards application aligned with edge computing and IoT.

Tan et al. \[ 7 \], (2023) examined privacy-enhanced federated learning for non-IID data, and proposed a hybrid protocol, which combined dynamic personalized weighting and P.K. Yadav et al.

noise-injection to minimize client drift; thus, demonstrating convergence and accuracy improvements over vanilla FL on heterogeneous datasets. Hsu, Keoy, Chen et al. \[ 8 \], (2023) proposed personalized federated learning with adaptive clustering and multi-task learning, where clients were automatically clustered together based on data similarity; their framework achieved better accuracy and faster convergence over various IoT-like non-IID tasks. The author Lai et al. \[ 9 \], (2024) developed personalized federated learning with adaptive feature extraction and category predictions. In this model, each client dynamically adjusted the feature encoders to accommodate heterogeneity and reported signiﬁcant accuracy improvement against the Fed Avg baselines. Zhang et al. \[ 10 \], (2025) introduce SAFEL-IoT integrated adaptive FL (hybrid encryption PHE+DP) and explainable AI to perform anomaly detection over industrial IoT, which reduces communication cost and improves detection accuracy while providing strong privacy guarantees.

Lv et al. \[ 11 \], (2023) through their work on FedRDS, in which they combined regularization and shared-data approach for addressing the non-IID setting, they managed to avoid client drift and improve both the rate of convergence and accuracy with respect to classiﬁcation on CIFAR and SVHN datasets. Li et al. \[ 12 \] (2023) presented FedMCSA- federated model components self-attention-which allows for layer-wise self-attention while aggregate to reduce interference across clients, with experiments showcasing signiﬁcant accuracy gains in personalized FL in the presence of heterogeneity. Acar et al. (2021), \[ 13 \] proposed FedDyn (dynamic regularization), which dynamically aligned local and global loss landscapes, converged provably under non-IID distributions, and outperformed FedAvg faster. Pang et al. (2023), \[ 14 \] designed a self-organized FL framework for IoT in which clients autonomously formed sub-clusters to cluster improvement scalability while managing non-IID data; experiments provided a better utilization of resources and stability for FL running on IoT devices.

According to Yin & Mao \[ 15 \], (2024), FedAFK implemented an adaptive feature aggregation model with knowledge transfer for personalization under heterogeneity and outperformed thirteen state-of the-art baselines. In addition, FedAFK demonstrated improved generalization. Wang et al. \[ 16 \], (2023) proposed pFedHR, a heterogeneous model reassembly scheme to personalize federated learning across clients with different model structures. The method automatically generated model tailored to each client and demonstrated performance improvement in IID and non-IID settings. Li et al. \[ 17 \], (2022) proposed FedTP (Transformer personalization) learning clientspeciﬁc self-attention weights via a hypernetwork, their learn-to-personalize approach improved generalization ability on vision and language datasets. Liu et al. \[ 18 \], (2025) (Pattern Recognition) introduced FedKT-a knowledge-transfer FL with segmented distillation and ensemble aggregation; their framework improved personalization and robustness in situations with very heterogeneous data, without heavy client overhead. In their study, Lu et al. \[ 19 \], (2024) used adaptive DP in asynchronous federated learning for edge/aerial computing; speciﬁcally, they proposed dynamic gradient clipping to achieve better utility-privacy trade-offs and obtained close to the optimal accuracy under ε constraints. Zhang et al. \[ 20 \], (2021) study investigating integrating local DP into FL for IoV systems claimed advantages, including a trade-off in terms of communication cost and changes in user privacy. Furthermore, Savin et al. \[ 21 \], (2021) (ACM NN Security Symposium) revealed successful attacks against privacy mechanisms in

Adaptive Federated Learning with Selective Privacy Preservation

certain implementations of FL, with convergence exhibiting 60% accuracy degradation, and a 93% success rate for backdoors. The authors were critical of so-called static DP defenses for FL use under these attack scenarios. Yang et al. \[ 22 \] proposed group-based meta-learning (G-FML) for non-IID FL, demonstrating an accuracy increase of over 13% with cluster-level personalization.

Technical Gaps Observed, Within the reviewed literature, we observed several persistent gaps:

1. Most existing frameworks used a ﬁxed privacy mechanism (DP, HE, SMPC), often  uniformly across the federated learning deployment, resulting in an unnecessary degradation in performance when privacy was not an issue. 2. Many works addressed personalization for the case of non-IID data (e.g. clustering,  self-attention, meta-learning), but few incorporated some privacy-aware adaptation strategy, especially for heterogeneous edge IoT devices. 3. Long-term stability over extended rounds (10,000+) under resource restrictions was  seldom assessed, with most experiments testing a few hundred or a few thousand rounds. 4. Protocols for dynamic client selection that respond to trust levels, energy availability,  and data sensitivity were underdeveloped in real world IoT federated contexts. 5. We observed few methods explicitly integrating multiple privacy approaches in a  dynamically tiered manner and few experiments evaluating privacy budget control trajectory ( ε ) and communication and energy trade-off function.

From these gaps, we identiﬁed the necessity for a holistic, accuracy-ﬁrst, adaptive, privacy-conscious FL framework adapted to long-term, heterogeneous edge-IoT environments-which underpinned the design of AFL-SP+ with its layers of privacy enforcement, temporal aggregation, compression, personalization, and extended-round robustness.

## 3 **Proposed Methodology **

**Fig. 1. ** System Architecture of Adaptive Federated Learning with Selective Privacy. P.K. Yadav et al.

In Fig. 1, system architecture for Adaptive Federated Learning with Selective Privacy (AFL-SP+), intended for edge-enabled IoT systems. Edge devices ﬁrst collect nonsensitive data, as well as sensitive data. Edge devices then categorize the data into different privacy tiers (or groups) according to the sensitivity of the data. The edge devices participate in client selection that is initiated by the central server. The selected clients perform local model updates based on how much data they have using their data. Each client applies a relevant privacy-preserving technique (the stronger the sensitivity of the data, the stronger the safeguards) \[ 23 \]. The updated local models are sent back to the server, where the global model is calculated through a weighted aggregation function. The aggregated model is then fed back to the edge clients, representing the end of one training round. The training process continues for the number of rounds required, adapting the privacy settings through each sustainability round while ensuring performance does not degrade. The architecture provides privacy protections without compromising training accuracy and offers effective security and scalability mechanisms within an edge-based federated learning system. **3.1 ** **Pseudo Code of Algorithm AFL-SP+ **

This method lowers energy consumption by ofﬂoading aggregation to the CHs and alleviating resource-limited devices of communication expenses and energy waste. Privacy is also dynamically enforced based on the individual data's sensitivity and accuracy and conﬁdentiality can be effectively balanced for the entire network.

Adaptive Federated Learning with Selective Privacy Preservation

## 4 **Result and Discussion **

This segment provides a full assessment and analysis of the proposed AFL-SP+ framework against the existing federated learning approaches of Vanilla FL, FL with Differential Privacy (FL+DP), and Multi-Privacy FL (MP-FL) paradigms, over a combined process of 10,000 training rounds based on plausible Edge-enabled IoT system conﬁgurations. The performance of these techniques were compared on various metrics-these include accuracy, energy consumption, communication overhead, utility-toprivacy/type-based ratio, convergence speed, and robustness of the system under nonIID data distributions. Overall, AFL-SP+ performed better across the different metrics discussed, achieving higher levels of accuracy, convergence and eating up less energy. **4.1 ** **Experimental Setup **

To assess the efﬁcacy of the proposed Adaptive Federated Learning with Smart Privacy (AFL-SP+) framework, controlled experiments were completed in a simulated Edgeenabled IoT environment. The system was modelled to reﬂect real-world edge node heterogeneity, along with variables related to data distribution, computation delay, and communications latency. The experiments were be carried out using Python 3.10, alongside common machine learning libraries, including TensorFlow Federated, NumPy, and Matplotlib, and implemented on a PC with an Intel Core i7 processor, 32 GB RAM, and an NVIDIA RTX 3060 graphics card. The federated learning environment was simulated with 50 IoT clients to represent different sensor nodes via a client-server conﬁguration.

We assigned each node non-IID (non-identically distributed) data from subsets of the CIFAR-10 and Human Activity Recognition (HAR) datasets, in order to examine the cross-domain applicability of the framework. Communication rounds were set to a threshold of 10,000 iterations, while client participation was randomized between 20% to 40% each round to represent dropout condition. **4.2 ** **Dataset Description **

To assess the performance and robustness of the presented AFL-SP+ approach in realistic edge computing environments, two benchmark datasets were used: CIFAR-10 and UCI Human Activity Recognition (HAR). These datasets diversity, complexity, and commonality in privacy-preserving machine learning related studies affected their selection. 1. **CIFAR-10 Dataset **

The CIFAR-10 dataset is a labeled subset of 80 million tiny images dataset historically used for image classiﬁcation tasks. It contains 60,000 labeled color images (32 x 32 pixels) across 10 different classes, including airplanes, automobiles, birds, cats, deer, dogs, frogs, horses, ships, and trucks.

Number of training samples: 50,000 Number of test samples: 10,000 Number of classes: 10 Image size: 32 x 32 x 3 RGB P.K. Yadav et al.

Intended use case: Simulates non-IID distribution across edge devices by assigning a set of classes to each client in order to represent data heterogeneity. 2. **UCI Human Activity Recognition (HAR) dataset **

The UCI HAR dataset is made up of 10,299 samples of human activity data collected through the use of smartphones. This dataset is highly relevant to IoT scenarios simulating everyday life such as wearable technology and smart healthcare devices. It has 6 activity classes: walking, walk upstairs, walk downstairs, sitting, standing, and lying.

Number of training samples: 7352, Number of test samples: 2,947, Sensors: Accelerometer and gyroscope data from smart phone, Number of features: 561

These datasets were distributed in a non-IID way across the federated clients to imitate realistic data distributions for edge devices, thus challenging the learning capabilities of AFL-SP+ under heterogeneity. **4.3 ** **Performance Matrices **

To carefully assess the effectiveness of the proposed AFL-SP+ framework and the beneﬁts of applying it to related federated learning approaches, the following important performance metrics were considered: 1. **Accuracy (%) **

Accuracy represents the percentage of correct classiﬁcation of instances out of total classiﬁcation predictions. Accuracy is used to evaluate the learning performance of the global model. It is calculated after each communication round on the aggregated model stored on the server.

Accuracy = Total Predictions */* Correct Predictions × 100 (1) 2. **Communication Overhead (MB) **

This metric measures the amount of data sent from the clients to the server (and server to clients) for each round (represented evenly for simplicity). A smaller overhead shows that the FL system is more communication efﬁcient, an important indicator of performance in bandwidth constrained IoT networks. Communication Overhead = Size of Model Updates i (2) Where, i=1.....n 3. **Energy Consumption (mJ) **

This metric measures edge devices' computation and communication energy associated with training. For battery-powered IoT nodes, energy efﬁciency is essential. The energy model relies on CPU consumption and communication energy per round data. Etotal = ECPU + ETX + ERX (3) 4. **Utility-to-Privacy Ratio (UPR)**

Adaptive Federated Learning with Selective Privacy Preservation

## UPR provides a measure of the trade-off between model utility (i.e., accuracy) and

privacy protection. A higher UPR means that the model preserves utility even under stronger privacy constraints.

## (4)

## 5. Convergence Speed (Rounds)

## The convergence speed is how many communication rounds were needed to reach a

stable or optimal model accuracy. A faster convergence speed can lead to less resource usage and reduced latency.

## 6. Non-IID Data Robustness

## This metric assesses the extent to which clients' data distributions vary from one

another and how the model performs as a result. When client distributions are signiﬁcantly skewed, we expect AFL-SP+ to continue achieving high accuracy and stability, compared to baseline models that are reverted to say IID data.

## 5 **Conclusion and Future Scope **

## This research proposed a new non IID adaptive federated learning framework, AFL-SP+,

with smart pruning and privacy-preserving strategies that is applicable to energy-efﬁcient and privacy-aware Edge-enabled IoT systems. The proposed framework addressed major issues, including non-IID data distribution, communication costs, and privacy leakages, while maintaining a relatively high model utility and the potential to converge quickly. A series of extensive experiments over 10,000 training rounds demonstrated that AFL-SP+ can outperform relevant metrics, and subsequent methods (including accuracy (91.42%)), energy efﬁciency, communication costs, and speeds of convergence), based on performance (Vanilla FL, DP-FL, and SA-FL). The AFL-SP+ can converge 19-25% faster, has a 7.2% better accuracy, and leads to signiﬁcantly lower variance under non-IID conditions.

## In possible future work, we might extend the AFL-SP+ model to help cross-silo

federated learning scenarios, where multiple data silos at a single institutional level are participating when possible. In addition, we can pursue utilize a real-time deployment on edge hardware platforms.
