## Adaptive TabNet- β -VAE Fusion Ensemble **Closes Uncertainty Gap in Fraud Detection **

## Ameya Borkar ( B ), Anushri Arora, Arnav Gupta, and Pooja Ghavane

Department of Engineering, Sciences and Humanities (DESH), Vishwakarma Institute of Technology, Pune, Maharashtra, India \{ameya.borkar24,anushri.arora24,anand.arnav241, pooja.wanjale\}@vit.edu

**Abstract. ** Rapid growth in mobile and card not present payments has heightened exposure to fraud, yet existing detectors either over rely on scarce labels or trigger excessive false positives. This paper introduces a real-time, hybrid frauddetection framework that fuses a supervised TabNet classiﬁer with an unsupervised β -Variational Autoencoder (VAE) trained solely on legitimate activity. A dynamic ensemble layer assigns transaction-level weights according to each model's predictive conﬁdence and, in its highest performing variant, selects the more conﬁdent score. Experiments on a one year, 298 865-transaction corpus (3.99% fraud) show that TabNet alone attains an AUC-ROC of 0.995 and a 0.86% false-positive rate, while the VAE excels at novel patterns (AUC-ROC = 0.867). Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUC-ROC). The proposed max-selector ensemble lifts recall by 1 pp, recovering 112 additional frauds, while adding only 0.05 pp to the false-positive rate, achieving an overall AUC-ROC of 0.9949. The architecture is modular, interpretable, and readily deployable through lightweight Python and PyTorch services. Results demonstrate that conﬁdence-adaptive fusion closes the "uncertainty gap" of supervised models without overburdening analysts, extending a scalable, production-ready solution for enterprise payment systems.

**Keywords: ** Fraud detection · TabNet · β -Variational Autoencoder · ensemble · fusion · real-time anomaly detection · payment systems · class imbalance · interpretability

## 1 Introduction

## 1.1 Background and Motivation

## Mobile banking, e-commerce platforms, and digital wallets are foundational to day-to

day commerce in an increasingly digitized economy; however, they also support rapidly expanding fraud estimated to exceed an annual global loss of 41B US dollars in payment fraud, and the most likely channels for fraud are card-not-present and mobile transactions. High false positives not only harm brand reputations, but also harm customer retention, as we are processing legitimate digital transactions at a massive scale and time is essential. Most fraud detection mechanisms combine supervised learning

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 475-496, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1> \_ 36 - Borkar et al.

approaches with historical and labeled data. They are effective in identiﬁcation of known fraud schemes; however novel and adaptive fraud patterns pose great challenges. Also, when fraudulent events are less than 5% of the overall transaction volume causes a class imbalance that complicates, and even biases performance of the predictive modeling. Limitations of Existing Methods:

Despite notable recent advances, existing supervised and unsupervised methods still suffer from inherent limitations:

- Supervised models (e.g., decision trees, deep neural networks) rely on scarce labels  and degrade under concept drift. - Unsupervised methods (autoencoders, clustering) avoid labels but incur high falsepositive rates, limiting real-time deployment.  - Ensemble strategies use static weighting, ignoring real-time conﬁdence and contextual uncertainty, leading to misclassiﬁcations in ambiguous transactions. **1.2 Motivation for a Hybrid and Adaptive Approach **

To address these limitations, there is a need for a fraud detection framework that can:

1. Leverage the precision and interpretability of supervised learning;  2. Incorporate the ability to generalize of unsupervised models;  3. Adaptively adjust model contributions based on predictive conﬁdence;  4. Operate within real-time latency constraints for production environments.

In this study, we propose such a framework by integrating TabNet, a supervised deep learning model specialized for tabular data, with a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) trained exclusively on normal transactions. Predictions from both models are combined using a conﬁdence-weighted ensemble mechanism that adapts each model's inﬂuence based on real-time certainty metrics, rather than ﬁxed rules. This allows the system to defer to the model most suited to the current context, particularly improving reliability in low-conﬁdence scenarios.

Throughout, we report Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUCROC) and Average Precision (PR AUC). We pair TabNet (a deep tabular learner that uses sequential feature masks for instance-wise feature selection and interpretability) with a β -VAE (a KL-weighted variational autoencoder that models normal behavior; high reconstruction error ﬂags anomalies) and introduce a conﬁdence-adaptive fusion that selects/weights the two scores per transaction. This transaction-level conﬁdence weighting calibrated to approve/review/block thresholds constitute our core novelty, targeting higher recall on emerging fraud at sub 1% false-positive rates. Novelty:

- Conﬁdence-adaptive fusion: per-transaction weighting/selection between TabNet and  \beta-VAE. - Production-aware calibration: thresholds are specially selected to approve/review/block actions at ~sub-1% FPR. - Auditability: instance level TabNet masks + VAE deviation cues are provided.

Adaptive TabNet- β -VAE Fusion Ensemble Closes Uncertainty Gap **1.3 Key Contributions **

In this paper, we described a new hybrid fraud detection framework that contributes the following:

1. Conﬁdence-Weighted Ensemble Technique: We have both developed and implemented a dynamically adaptive ensemble technique that utilizes the classiﬁcation  probabilities of TabNet together with VAE-based anomalies using adaptive conﬁdence weights. 2. Scalable and Explainable Framework: This modular framework functions as a  lightweight PyTorch micro-services that scales well in production environments. 3. Extensive Evaluation: We have extensively evaluated this model on a dataset  of 298,865 transactions assessing numerous ensemble conﬁgurations and have established its strong ability to detect fraud over a variety of fraud types. 4. Beneﬁt of Practical Usability: For the high-conﬁdence block band (p ≥ 0.95), there are  0 added false positives as compared to the TabNet individual base-line with an overall FPR of less than 1%, thereby providing additional support to satisfy the operational target set forth by an enterprise.

## 2 Literature Review **2.1 Supervised Learning Approaches for Fraud Detection **

Supervised approaches dominate fraud detection thanks to labelled transaction histories. Dal Pozzolo et al. \[ 1 \] tackle extreme class imbalance in credit-card data via a costsensitive ensemble that boosts recall and slashes fraud-related costs, but they remain conﬁned to exhibiting patterns seen in training and falter against novel schemes.

TabNet \[ 2 \] leverages sequential attention for tabular data, delivering both interpretability and strong performance on mixed categorical/continuous features. Its sparse, mask-based feature selection excels in supervised tasks yet can overﬁt and may not generalize well under data drift or emerging attack vectors. 2024-2025 update. Recent supervised baselines apply Transformer models to tabular credit-card transactions and report gains over tree ensembles on precision/recall and F1; contemporary work also explores real-time streaming variants for production. \[ 11, 12, 24 \] **2.2 Unsupervised and Anomaly Detection Techniques **

Unsupervised methods excel when fraud labels are absent. An and Cho \[ 3 \]  train  a  VAE on genuine transactions and ﬂag those with low reconstruction likelihoods as anomalies, though careful tuning of latent dimensions and regularization is vital to limit false positives. Liu et al. \[ 4 \]'s Isolation Forest isolates outliers via random feature splits requiring fewer splits for anomalies providing scalability but struggling with high-dimensional, overlapping data and ignoring temporal or behavioral patterns.

2024-2025 update. Streaming/online CCFD pipelines pair anomaly detectors with concept-drift monitors (e.g., DDM/EDDM/ADWIN) to adapt thresholds/models on the ﬂy, reducing unnecessary retrains while preserving AUC; recent surveys and studies catalogue detectors and locality effects for real-time use. \[ 18 - 21 \] - Borkar et al. **2.3 Explainability and Interpretable Machine Learning **

Explainability is of prime importance in regulated sectors. The SHAP framework by Lundberg and Lee \[ 5 \] uses Shapley values to attribute each feature's contribution to a given prediction, presenting granular insights for auditors; however, its reliance on exhaustive coalition sampling makes it computationally heavy and best suited to batch or tree-based models unless approximation or caching strategies are employed.

Carcillo et al. \[ 6 \] design a two-stage pipeline: unsupervised ﬁlters ﬁrst ﬂag anomalous transactions, then a supervised classiﬁer reﬁnes the decision. This hybrid layering narrows the candidate set, boosting precision and throughput, while maintaining the adaptability of both approaches.

2024-2025 update. Beyond SHAP, attention-based and self-explainable fraud models provide per-transaction rationales that may be combined with meta-learners or mask-based mechanisms to reach transparent decisions under imbalance. \[ 13, 23, 22 \] **2.4 Adaptive and Scalable Architectures **

Modern fraud schemes are constantly evolving, so the systems used to stop them need to be just as adaptive while still keeping user data safe. Federated learning offers a way for different organizations like banks to train models together without actually sharing their customers' raw data, making it a great ﬁt for interbank collaboration \[ 7 \]. Additionally, concept-drift techniques (e.g., sliding windows, drift detectors) identify and adapt to changing transaction patterns \[ 8 \]. Underpinning these models, preprocessing (normalization, encoding, real-time feature stores) \[ 9 \] and scalable, low-latency database architectures lambda/kappa \[ 10 \] ensure fault-tolerant, real-time pipelines.

2024-2025 update. Federated graph formulations, such as FedGAT and federated graph learning, are allowing for cross-institution modeling in a privacy-preserving manner, while temporal/ causal GNNs and graph transformers are strengthening relational fraud detection at scale. \[ 16, 17, 14, 15, 22 \]

Recent Directions (2024-2025). The ﬁeld is moving in the direction of Transformer baselines on tabular data, federated/graph models for privacy-preserving relational learning, streaming pipelines with explicit drift detection (DDM/EDDM/ADWIN), and attention-based/self-explainable methods for regulator-friendly audits-directions that our conﬁdence-adaptive fusion and production-aware calibration align with. \[ 11, 12, 24, 16, 17, 14, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 13, 23, 22 \] **2.5 Summary and Integration with Proposed Work **

The literature identiﬁes complementarity in the supervised and unsupervised approaches to fraud detection. TabNet does well in providing predicting accuracy and interpretability when applied to known scenarios of fraud, while VAEs may perform better in discovering new patterns in unknown data. Isolation Forests and SHAP offer additional lenses of anomaly detection and explainability, though these also need to be modiﬁed for their use at scale.

The combination of the works reviewed above provide evidence to our reasoning for the hybrid approach we propose: an ensemble of TabNet and VAE that can dynamically

Adaptive TabNet- β -VAE Fusion Ensemble Closes Uncertainty Gap

weight predictions with respect to certainty, minimize false positive rates, and generalize to possible unknown threats. The notion of dynamic weighting of the ensemble draws on the limitations of ﬁxed ensembles observed in \[ 1 - 6 \]. Architecture insights for the expediency of real-time operation are drawn from \[ 8 - 10 \]. For example, through these integrating theoretical contributions, our work contributes to the ﬁeld by providing a single framework that is accurate, interpretable, and scales thus is ideally situated for implementation in live payment and ﬁnancial contexts.

## 3 Methodology **3.1 Dataset Description **

The experimental evaluation employs a real-world, one-year corpus of 298 865 anonymised ﬁnancial transactions collected. Each record is labelled legitimate (class 0. or fraudulent (class 1), yielding a highly imbalanced class distribution of 3.99%  fraud.

1. Raw attributes (26 columns)  The raw feed contains the following ﬁelds, grouped by theme:

- Identiﬁers:  transaction\_id, account\_id, device\_id, recipient\_id - Monetary:  transaction\_amount, currency, current\_balance, transaction\_threshold - Time & Context:  transaction\_timestamp, time\_since\_login - Channel & Location:  transaction\_type, transaction\_location, destination\_location, login\_location - Account Proﬁle:  account\_age, account\_type, account\_location, credit\_score, account\_status - Authentication:  auth\_method, failed\_auth\_attempts, admin\_approved - Historical Risk Flags:  prev\_account\_fraud, prev\_device\_fraud, prev\_dispute - Ground-Truth Label:  is\_fraud

2. Feature engineering pipeline  A uniﬁed preprocessing script expands the raw table to 39 numerical features by:

- Temporal decomposition - extracting hour-of-day, day-of-week, weekend/night  ﬂags, and sine/cosine cyclic encodings of time. - Amount heuristics - binary ﬂags for high/very-high amounts (above 95 ᵗʰ /99 ᵗʰ  percentile), round-number checks, and amount-to-balance ratio. - Behavioural & risk indicators - account "very new" ﬂag, failed-auth presence,  location mismatch between transaction and account home, and balance-exceed checks. - Borkar et al.

- Categorical encoding - label-encoding of string ﬁelds (e.g., currency, transaction\_type) with unseen-category handling.  - Robust scaling - median imputation followed by RobustScaler on continuous  variables to mitigate heavy-tailed distributions.

These engineered features capture monetary, temporal, behavioural, geographic and velocity cues, providing a richer representation for both the supervised TabNet model and the unsupervised VAE.

To preserve temporal causality and prevent data leakage, transactions were chronologically sorted before being split into: - 60% training  - 20% validation  - 20% test

All feature scaling and normalization was performed using statistics derived solely from legitimate transactions, ensuring the unsupervised VAE model does not receive any fraud-biased preprocessing. Z-score normalization and clipping within the range \[-5, 5\] were applied to improve model stability and anomaly sensitivity. **3.2 Pre-processing and Feature Engineering **

An organized and modular pre-processing pipeline was implemented to evaluate the supervised TabNet classiﬁer and unsupervised Beta Variational Autoencoder (VAE). The methods applied 39 hand-crafted features, consisting of both raw and domainderived variables, using variace ﬁltering, correlation and domain relevance variables.

1. Data Cleaning and Preparation  Initial preprocessing involved:

- Removal of duplicate, corrupted, and incomplete records  - Imputation of missing values using median strategy for numerical ﬁelds and  sentinel values for categorical ﬁelds - Elimination of illogical values (e.g., negative transaction amounts)

2. Feature Construction and Domain Signals  Domain-aware features were constructed to improve discriminative power:

- Temporal patterns: hour, day\_of\_week, and is\_weekend, cyclically encoded  - Behavioral indicators: transaction\_velocity, auth\_failure\_count, device\_change\_ﬂag - Risk signals: location\_mismatch, merchant\_novelty, amount\_to\_balance\_ratio

These enhanced the model's ability to learn latent fraud-indicative patterns. 3. Categorical Feature Handling for TabNet  A total of 11 categorical features were embedded using TabNet's native handling:

- cat\_idxs: Positions of categorical features  - cat\_dims: Unique categories per feature  - cat\_emb\_dim: Calculated as min 50 *,* *n* unique

Adaptive TabNet- β -VAE Fusion Ensemble Closes Uncertainty Gap

This enabled the model to learn dense embeddings that preserved semantic structure in tabular space. 4. Feature Normalization Strategy  Different normalization strategies were adopted:

- TabNet used RobustScaler to suppress skewed distributions and maintain  resilience to outliers. - VAE, trained solely on legitimate samples, required Z-score normalization: *x* norm = *x * − μ legit σ legit (1)

where μ legit, σ legit are statistics computed over legitimate transactions only.

To ensure reconstruction stability, all normalized features were clipped to the range \[-5, + 5\]. **3.3 Supervised TabNet Model Development **

TabNet was chosen as the main supervised model, since it is interpretable via its attention mechanism, supports categorical embeddings natively, and has shown strong performance on structured ﬁnancial data. It is also capable of instance-wise feature selection and has low latency for inference, which can be helpful for real-time fraud detection systems. 1. Model Architecture and Conﬁguration

The TabNet model was set with 6 decision and attention steps (n\_steps = 6), each providing 64-dimensional representations for decision as well as attention branches (n\_d = 64, n\_a = 64). From the 39 input features, 11 were categorical and were embedded using dimensions set based on cardinality, such as \[1, 2, 13, 8,.\]; the remaining 28 features were continuous.

The model used EntMax sparsity masking (mask type = 'entmax') with a regularization weight of λ = 1 × 10 − 3 to enforce interpretability and sparse feature selection. 2. Training Details

Training was done on 179,319 samples, with a fraud prevalence of 3.99%. In order to address the severe class imbalance, class-weighted sampling was used to equalize the effective contribution of fraud and non-fraud instances.

- Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 0.02 and weight decay 1 × 10 − 5

- Scheduler: StepLR ( γ = 0.9 every 10 epochs) - Batch size: 16,384; Virtual batch size: 512  - Early stopping: Patience = 40 (monitored on validation A UC) - Training duration: ~370 seconds for 85 epochs  - 3) Baseline Performance On validation data: - Borkar et al.

- Best AUC: 0.9961  - Accuracy: 0.9892  - Balanced Accuracy: 0.9719  - Log Loss: 0.0371 On the held-out test set (threshold ≈ 0.90):

- AUC-ROC: 0.995  - Precision: 0.817  - Recall: 0.925  - F 1 -Score: 0.867  - Speciﬁcity: 0.991  - Accuracy: 0.9887  - Log loss: 0.039  - Alert precision: 81.65%  - False Positive Rate: 0.86%  - Fraud Detection Rate: 92.54%

The confusion matrix indicates a high detection rate with minimal false alarms, conﬁrming TabNet as a strong standalone baseline for hybrid and ensemble strategies. **3.4 Variational Autoencoder (VAE) Model Development **

To complement the supervised TabNet classiﬁer, a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) was introduced as an unsupervised anomaly detector capable of identifying new or evolving fraud patterns. An early semi-supervised version trained on both fraudulent and legitimate transactions showed limited generalization and added complexity during deployment. Consequently, the ﬁnal model adopted a fully unsupervised approach, trained solely on legitimate transactions to learn normal behavioral patterns and ﬂag signiﬁcant deviations as potential fraud. 1. Data Preparation and Splits

The model used the same 39 hand-engineered features as TabNet. Features were standardized (zero mean, unit variance) using statistics computed only from legitimate transactions and then clipped to \[-5, + 5\] to suppress outliers.

- Training/Validation: only legitimate transactions (label = 0)  - Testing: full dataset including fraudulent transactions  - Semi-supervised baseline: trained on both fraud and normal samples for comparison 2. VAE Architecture

The architecture was based on a β -VAE with optional planar normalizing ﬂows in the latent space:

- Encoder: Dense layers (512 → 256 → 128) with LayerNorm, Swish activations, and  dropout (0.15), producing mean ( μ ) and log-variance (log σ 2 ) vectors - Latent space: *z * = μ + exp 1  2 log σ 2 with six planar ﬂows optionally applied - Decoder: mirror of the encoder, reconstructing the 39D input vector

Adaptive TabNet- β -VAE Fusion Ensemble Closes Uncertainty Gap 3. Loss Function and Regularization

The objective function combined MSE reconstruction loss with a KL-divergence term, scaled by a scheduled L = Eq( z|x) x − ˆx 2 + \beta(t) · DkL q(z|x) N(0, I) (2) β schedule:

$$ - Epochs 1-20: \beta = 0.001 $$ - Epochs 21-32: linear ramp to \beta = 0.01 $$ - Epochs 33-40: \beta = 0.01 $$ 4. Training Regime and Optimization

- Unsupervised Training: only on normal transactions  - Optimizer: AdamW lr = 1e-4 (decays to 8 1e-5 with ReduceLROnPlateau),  weight-decay 1e-6 - Scheduler: ReduceLROnPlateau (factor = 0.8, patience = 10) - Gradient clipping: \| ∇ \| 2 ≤ 1.0  - Early stopping: based on validation AUC, max 40 epochs 5. Evaluation and Anomaly Scoring

- Mean reconstruction error (normal): ≈ 0.00199  - Mean reconstruction error (fraud): ≈ 0.01513  - Separation factor: ≈ 7.6 × 6. Usage - Borkar et al.

The unsupervised VAE proved superior in generalizing to unseen fraud scenarios, achieving Δ AUC ≈ 0.0555 over the semi-supervised baseline. Its reconstruction-based anomaly scores are both interpretable and label-agnostic, making it well-suited for deployment. This model is used in real-time fraud detection, and paired with TabNet to jointly cover known and emerging fraud patterns. **3.5 Hybrid Ensemble Strategy **

1. Motivation:  TabNet is effective for supervised fraud detection, but when faced with a new or rare fraud pattern, it may fail to provide a score that is above the threshold, which is normally 0.5. Conversely, a beta VAE which has been trained only on legitimate transactions learns the "normal" behavior manifold and considers any deviation from that manifold as an anomaly. Neither model is guaranteed to be accurate, but by utilizing them in hybrid ensemble to interject where the TabNet model is not conﬁdent, it allows us to conserve computational resources. In other words, we take the overlapping bias of each model and use them where uncertainty is greatest. 2. Formalization:  Let *p* *T * ( *x* ) be the TabNet's calibrated fraud probability and *s* *v* ( *x* ) the raw anomaly score from the VAE for transaction (eg: xxx). The VAE score is then normalized to the \[0,1\] \[0,1\] \[0,1\] range using min-max statistics from normal validation data:

*s * *s* *v * − min *(* *s* *v* *)* max *(* *s* *v* *)* − min *(* *sv* *)* (4)

We deﬁne model conﬁdences as scaled distance from uncertainty (0.5):

$$ cT (x) = 2 \cdot |pT (x) − 0.5| $$ $$ cV (x) = 2 \cdot |p V (x) −0.5| $$ (5) Then compute dynamic weights:

$$ \omegaT (x) = $$ *c* *T * *(* *x* *)* *c* *T * *(* *x* *)* + *c* *v* *(* *x* *)* + $$ \omegav(x) = 1 −\omegaT(x) $$ (6) The ﬁnal hybrid score is: phybrid = ωT (x).pT (x) + \omegav(x).pV (x) (7)

3. Decision Rules:  A uniﬁed fraud decision pipeline applies risk-aware thresholds:

- p\_hybrid ≥ 0.70 ⇒ FRAUD ⇒ BLOCK - 0.50 \leq p_hybrid < 0.70 \Rightarrow SUSPICIOUS \RightarrowREVIEW - 0.30 \leq p_hybrid < 0.50 \Rightarrow LOW RISK \RightarrowREVIEW - p\_hybrid ***\< *** 0.30 ⇒ NORMAL ⇒ APPROVE

4. Empirical Comparison:  Multiple ensemble schemes were benchmarked on the test set (Table 2 ):

The Max Ensemble, which selects the more conﬁdent output between TabNet and VAE per transaction, yielded the best test AUC of 0.9949, outperforming all other strategies. 5. Implementation:

- TabNet outputs are calibrated via Platt scaling using validation data.  - VAE anomaly scores are normalized based on validation-normal statistics:  $$ min=11.59, max=30.86. $$ - VAE preprocessing includes feature-wise standardization and clipping to \[-5, +  5\] as learned during t raining. - All ensemble computations are vectorized and optimized for batch throughput  using PyTorch and NumPy. **3.6 System Architecture and Deployment Overview **

The hybrid fraud-detection framework supports real-time scoring through a modular, latency-aware pipeline: 1. Inference Pipeline The deployment architecture follows this sequence:

1. Preprocessing: Using NumPy and scikit-learn normalize and encode inputs with a  single Python pipeline. 2. TabNet Inference: Run the supervised model in PyTorch with batched (128)  predictions, yielding a calibrated fraud score *p* *T * ( *x* ) *p* *T * ( *x* ) *p* *T * ( *x* ). 3. VAE Scoring: Use a PyTorch β -VAE to reconstruct normalized inputs and compute  anomaly scores *s* *v* ( *x* ), then min-max scale them to \[0, 1\]. 4. Ensemble Fusion: Fuse *p* *T * ( *x* ) and *s* *v* ( *x* ) via conﬁdence weights or max selection to  get *p* *hybrid* ( *x* ). 5. Decision Layer: Threshold values are applied to determine whether each transaction  should be approved, ﬂagged for review, or blocked entirely. 2. Performance and Deployment Considerations

- Runtime: Models load once at startup and stay in memory.  - Integration: NumPy fusion plugs into REST APIs or Apache Kafka (Fig. 1 ). - Borkar et al. **Fig. 1. ** Model architecture. **3.7 Hyperparameter Tuning and Conﬁguration Selection **

## Take-away

TabNet is precise and low-latency yet produces a "grey zone" (p ≈ 0.45-0.55) on unseen attacks; the VAE reliably lights up that zone but at the cost of extra false alarms. Their orthogonal error proﬁles justify the ensemble strategies analysed ne xt.

expected for unsupervised stand-alone detection (PR-AUC 0.2120, ROC-AUC 0.8084). Family comparison.

- Unsupervised stand-alone: β -VAE (Accuracy 0.970, Recall 75.77 %) and Isolation  Forest (Recall 53.58 %, Precision 15.81 %) trail supervised models, but β -VAE reliably surfaces novel/OOD patterns. - Supervised: TabNet and Random Forest deliver high AUC/PR-AUC and strong  calibrated discrimination on known patterns. - Hybrid (proposed): By selecting/weighting TabNet vs β -VAE per transaction, Fusion  recovers additional fraud at sub-1% FPR while preserving interpretability (TabNet masks) and anomaly cues (VAE reconstruction error).

Takeaway. The conﬁdence-adaptive hybrid improves the precision recall envelope and recall at a ﬁxed low FPR, validating it as a deployment-oriented improvement: more fraud intercepted, minimal extra reviews, and regulator-friendly explanations. **4.4 Discussion and Implications ** **4.4.1 Synthesis of Hybrid Model Efﬁcacy **

A hybrid lens on fraud. Our results show that pairing a pattern-memorizing supervised classiﬁer (TabNet) with a distribution-sensing unsupervised detector ( β -VAE) yields a defense that is both precise on known scams and alert to emerging ones. The maxselector ensemble lifts recall by ~1 pp (+112 frauds) while adding only + 0.05 pp to the false-positive rate (§ 4.3). In a card-network setting where the average cost of an undetected fraud dwarfs the cost of a manual review, this 3.3: 1 beneﬁt ratio is operationally attractive.

**4.4.2 Operational Impact and Deployment Readiness (Table ** **12** **) **

## 4.4.4 Limitations and Future Research

## • Calibration drift - TabNet's Platt scaler assumes a stable data mix; a surge in UPI

micro-payments could skew its probabilities. - VAE scaling limits - Fixed min-max bounds (11.59-30.86) were set on one year of  data; strong seasonal variation may warp them and weaken fraud distinguishing. - Adversarial mimicry - Fraud rings can learn to mirror "normal" patterns, corroding  the VAE's edge, hence continuous retraining is needed. - Privacy concerns - VAE reconstructions can inadvertently expose personally identiﬁable information; feature hashing or differential-privacy defences should be  utilized.

## 5 Conclusion

## The advocated research proposes a solid hybrid fraud detection framework that com

bines supervised learning through TabNet with unsupervised anomaly detection by VAE using dynamic conﬁdence weighted ensemble learning to adjust fraud probability to improve robustness in non-fraudulent cases. The proposed training is stable with signiﬁcant separation between normal and fraudulent transactions, followed by visualizations, to guarantee real-time operational readiness with higher interpretable feature importance for compliance. The system achieved high accuracy (TabNet AUC 0.9961, ensemble AUC 0.9949), has lower latency and is capable of discerning new fraud patterns, hence scalable, efﬁcient, and future-proof against modern ﬁnancial institutions and modelling comprehensive fraud exposure. The system is production ready on real-time payment ﬂows, and was also designed for higher recall on novel attacks, stable in latency, forms, thresholding and explainability in audit review.

## Multimodal Framework for Prediction **of Attention-Deﬁcit Hyperactivity Disorder **

## Srishti Sharma ( B ) and Poonam Chaudhary

Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The NorthCap University, Gurugram, India \{srishti,poonamchaudhary\}@ncuindia.edu

**Abstract. ** Attention Deﬁcit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental ailment that may be found in people of all ages. Accurate diagnosis and proper management of ADHD can signiﬁcantly improve the situation and societal integration of those affected by the disorder. Currently, the most common technique for detecting ADHD is through physical evaluation by a trained medical professional, who assesses using the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) criteria and checks for the presence of at least ﬁve indicators of inattention or impulsivity/hyperactivity. This paper proposes a computer-aided framework that emulates the clinical evaluation process, considering several modalities, to close this gap in the diagnosis of ADHD. The proposed framework will utilize multimodal data, including MRI images, and phenotypic data to improve the efﬁciency and medical intuition of the ADHD diagnosis. By leveraging the most recent advancements in machine learning, this research endeavors to construct and implement an end-to-end AI model that can accurately and robustly uncover ADHD in the nascent stages.

**Keywords: ** ADHD · Artiﬁcial Intelligence · Machine Learning · Healthcare · Neurodevelopment disorders

## 1 **Introduction **

## Artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized lives and has improved the efﬁcacy of busi

nesses across various industries such as manufacturing, ﬁnance, marketing, and several others. AI can revolutionize the healthcare sector as well. Health outcomes and patient experiences may be improved using Machine Learning(ML) and Deep Learning (DL). Virtual medical assistants and chatbots, robotic surgery assistance, individualized illness therapy, patient monitoring, medical imaging, etc., could help transform the healthcare sector. Figure 1 outlines some of the possible applications of AI in healthcare. However, despite so many advantages of the AI-based systems, they have no noticeable effects in the real healthcare environment. Building robust and stable AI systems is urgent in the medical domain. "Neurodevelopment disorders is a term that refers to common brain disorders that occur when developmental processes may be disturbed by genetic and environmental factors" \[ 1 \].

## Neuro-developmental ailments include ADHD, Tourette disorder, schizophrenia,

ﬁbromyalgia X syndrome, autism, and others. ADHD is amongst the most prevalent

neurodevelopmental ailments **, ** which often begins in childhood and frequently carries on into adulthood if not treated. Children with ADHD may exhibit impulsivity, hyperactivity, and inattentiveness. According to a survey which the World Health Organization conducted in 2016 for ten nations, the incidence of ADHD in adults was an estimated 2.8% worldwide, the fraction being larger in developed nations and exhibited a notable correlation with less schooling and the masculine gender \[ 2 \]. In United States, children are more probable than adults to exhibit the disorder, and children (2-17 years old) have a 9.4% prevalence rate of ADHD. Better societal integration and a noticeable improvement in quality of life are possible outcomes of effective ADHD management. As a result, to maximize long-term outcomes, it is crucial that this ailment is spotted in the initial stages and managed effectively \[ 3 \]. The cause(s) and biomarkers of ADHD remain unfortunately unknown. Studies indicate that genetics have a signiﬁcant effect alongwith other factors. As a result, it might be difﬁcult to identify and diagnose ADHD. First, there are several phases in the diagnostic process; second, there are numerous other conditions, such as anxiety, depression, sleep issues, and speciﬁc kinds of learning difﬁculties, that present comparable symptoms. For instance, Studerus et al. \[ 4 \] examined whether neuropsychological testing can distinguish between the diagnosis of adult ADHD and the at-risk mental state (ARMS). Currently, the most widely used diagnosis method for ADHD is clinical. A trained medical professional conducts a series of medical tests to assess if an individual has ADHD \[ 5 \]. Such clinical evaluations by specialists take time, and there is frequently a scarcity of skilled experts, which often delays diagnosis and treatment \[ 6 \]. Whitney et al. \[ 7 \] report that there are only 11 trained psychiatrists in Michigan, USA, to care for more than 100,000 children with probable mental health diseases. For the United Kingdom and Australia, respectively, the share of psychiatrists to the populace is 11:100,000 and 14:100,000 \[ 8 \]. These statistics suggest that it is of utmost importance that an automated tool using AI may be developed that can help in the diagnosis and detection of ADHD. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

- ** ** **Proposed a multimodal framework ** that emulates clinical evaluation for ADHD by  integrating structural MRI (sMRI) features with phenotypic data. Multimodal Framework for Prediction of Attention-Deﬁcit

- ** ** **Developed and implemented machine learning models ** (K-nearest neighbors and  Random Forest) to evaluate predictive performance across single- and multi-modality settings. - ** ** **Demonstrated the effectiveness of multimodal fusion**, where combining sMRI and  phenotypic data signiﬁcantly improved classiﬁcation accuracy compared to using individual modalities alone. - ** ** **Introduced a decision-level late fusion strategy ** with weighted voting, ensuring  robust predictions and resolving conﬂicts between classiﬁers. - ** ** **Provided empirical validation ** using the ADHD-200 dataset (Kennedy Krieger  Institute subset), achieving up to 94% accuracy with multimodal KNN fusion.

## 2 **Related Work **

For automated ADHD detection, researchers have used a total of seven different types of modalities utilized to develop AI models which include: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), physiological ofﬁcial open signals, questionnaires, game simulation and performance tests, motion data, multimodal- a combination of two or more of these approaches and miscellaneous. In this review, we explore each of these one by one.

*MRI: * The most extensively researched method for automatically diagnosing ADHD is brain MRI. Most researchers working on MRI use the ADHD-200 dataset \[ 9 \]. Most of these studies use brain functional connectivity for detection of ADHD. The matrixlike presentation of functional connectivity of the brain demonstrates the connections between various brain regions. Correlations between the various brain regions are frequently measured using the Pearson correlation coefﬁcient. It has been observed that the heatmaps of correlation coefﬁcient plotted for normal and ADHD individuals exhibit different functional connectivity.

*Physiological Open Signals: * Studies have also used physiological indicators, most frequently electroencephalograms and electrocardiogram, to identify ADHD. Almost all such studies utilizing machine and deep learning report accuracy above 80%. The National Brain Mapping Laboratory of Iran was the only study to have used a public database \[ 10 \]. The remainder made use of their personal datasets. Most of these studies use power spectral features and decompose the signal into frequency sub-bands such as alpha, beta and gamma rhythm. These are found to be dissimilar for persons with ADHD and healthy individuals.

*Questionnaires/Rating Scales: * Medical experts also utilize a variety of inquiry forms or assessment scales to diagnose ADHD. Conners' Rating Scales often help to assess how ADHD inﬂuences a patient's conduct in social situations- at work, in school or similar settings \[ 11 \]. Conner's adult rating scales is a self-reported questionnaire, and Conners's parent rating scales requires parental completion. The Diagnostic Interview for Adults with ADHD \[ 12 \], is a semi-structured assessment tool developed to evaluate to symptoms across ﬁve key areas of daily life: relationships, work, education, self-conﬁdence, social contact, and hobbies. Authors in \[ 13 \] use the Vanderbilt ADHD Diagnostic Parent Rating Scale to evaluate the symptoms of ADHD. World Health Organization also proposed the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS), which has been used by \[ 14 \]. A shorter form of - Sharma and P. Chaudhary

the Conners' Adult Rating Scales (CAARS-S:S) is a self-test than can be used to detect symptoms of ADHD by adults \[ 15 \]. There also exist many other rating scales the use of which has been reported in literature for automated ADHD detection namely Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory-2 \[ 16 \]  also  used by \[ 14 \], Social Responsive Scale (SRS) \[ 17 \] used by researchers in \[ 18 \], etc.

*Game Simulation and Performance Tests: * Neuropsychological tests to gauge a person's capacity for sustained and selective attention include the Continuous Performance Test (CPT) and the Reverse Stroop task reported by researchers in \[ 19, 20 \]. Participants must respond appropriately to a particular stimulus during the computerized CPT \[ 21 \]. A simulated reality school room was made by authors in \[ 22 \] and included several distractions and assessments, such as the CPT, for the diagnosis of ADHD. Researchers in \[ 21 \] used a videogame called "Groundskeeper" that was created by CogCubed \[ 23 \] speciﬁcally for early ADHD detection.

*Motion Data: * Another diagnostic indicator for ADHD may be motion. Actigraphy and accelerometer are two motion activity measure types reported in literature. Accelerometer is typically used on the dominant arm's wrist and the main leg's ankle to record both actigraphy and accelerometer data \[ 24, 25 \]. The type of activity the person is engaging in differs amongst the two- actigraphy examines sleep efﬁciency \[ 24 \], whereas an accelerometer examines the motion during typical daily activities \[ 25 \]. Researchers have concluded that ADHD patients moved more than healthy individuals. This shows that an increased level of activity is typical of ADHD, can be ascertained from the person's daily activities and tracked using accelerometers \[ 26, 27 \].

*Miscellaneous: * Previous studies have indicated that people with ADHD show dysfunction in the brain's norepinephrine system, which in turn is linked to variations in pupil size \[ 28 \]. As per researchers in \[ 29 \], ADHD patients who are not taking medication have smaller pupils than controls when completing tasks requiring visuo-spatial working memory. This might be because ﬁxation-required ADHD patients have a hard time controlling saccadic eye movements \[ 30 \]. Therefore, as researchers in \[ 28, 30 \]  implemented in their ML studies, uncontrollable eye movement may be utilized for detection of ADHD. With the widespread use of social networks, Twitter has also emerged as a possible medium for ADHD detection \[ 31 \]. Most mentally ill people are hesitant in seeking professional assistance, which leads to development and bottling up of miserable feelings and may eventually have dire consequences \[ 32 \]. To connect with and receive support from others in the same community, online platforms have thus turned out to be a place of solace for such persons \[ 33 \]. Social media platforms can therefore be used to prevent suicidal behaviour and detect various mental illnesses early \[ 33 \]. In \[ 34 \], researchers used Twitter as a learning tool for ADHD and found highly correlated topics.

The "gold standard" for diagnosing ADHD typically combines neuropsychological assessments, rating scales, behavioural observations, medical exams, and assessments of the effects of treatment trials \[ 35 \]. Authors in \[ 36 \] use a combination of CPT, EEG and actigraphy modalities for a virtual reality-based assessment of ADHD. Authors in \[ 37 \] used rs-fMRI with sMRI and DTI data for ADHD diagnosis in children. Authors in \[ 38 \] use combination of MRI and genetic data. Authors in \[ 39 \] outline a framework for early Multimodal Framework for Prediction of Attention-Deﬁcit

stage prediction of ADHD. Shin et al. \[ 40 \] propose a multimodal method combining handwriting dynamics (via a pen tablet) and fNIRS brain-activity data, for detecting ADHD with co-occurring ASD in children, thereby offering an objective diagnostic complement to behavioural assessments.

Some of the major research gaps that exist in the current research on automated AI methods for ADHD analysis are that the majority of work in this ﬁeld of ADHD detection using ML or DL techniques still uses data from hospital setting sources like MRI and EEG, while the remaining modalities have been taken into account by very few studies so far \[ 23 \]. The data gathered from accelerometer devices, or other such wearable devices also has the obvious advantage that it is inconspicuous, permitting the partakers to be carrying out their routine work in familiar settings. This research work addresses this gap by proposing a framework imitating diagnosis by a trained clinical expert which considers multiple modalities. In this work, we propose to carry out ADHD diagnosis based on multimodal data including MRI images, ECG, EEG, and questionnaire data and data from wearable devices. In this study, we build and implement an end-to-end AI model using multiple modalities to detect ADHD early and in a robust fashion.

## 3 **Proposed Methodology ** The proposed methodology is outlined as follows:

**3.1 ** **Architecture of the Proposed Multimodal Classiﬁer **

ADHD can be diagnosed based on multiple data types including MRI images, ECG, EEG, and questionnaire data. Domain experts consider multiple types of data to make accurate and personalized decisions. These data have different advantages and disadvantages, and to build an accurate and medically intuitive model, multiple modalities should be considered in the decision-making process. The main phases of the proposed architecture include multimodal data collection, data pre-processing, feature extraction and feature selection and ML algorithm. In the following subsections, we discuss the details of every phase. We give a schematic diagram of the proposed architecture in Fig. 2. **3.2 ** **Dataset Description **

In this research, we use the ADHD-200 data set \[ 9 \]. This dataset includes both structural and resting state functional MRI data from 973 subjects accumulated from eight different locations. A T1-weighted structural scan and resting-state fMRI data are included for each subject. The dataset also contains some useful metadata alongwith, namely, participant age, handedness, IQ scores, and gender information. In the ADHD-200 dataset, the training dataset comprises of data pertaining to 776 participants and a second testing dataset comprises of data of 197 participants. The 776 people in the training dataset are divided into three different diagnostic classes: Healthy control type, ADHD-I control type, and ADHD-C control type.

Among the total eight locations in the original dataset, we employ the data from the Kennedy Krieger Institute (KKI) site for our research. Every subject is distinctly identiﬁable by a ScanDir ID. Gender is assigned a value of 0 for females and 1 for males; - Sharma and P. Chaudhary

handedness is denoted as 0 for left-handed, 1 for right-handed, and 2 for ambidextrous persons. The "DX" variable denotes the diagnosis status of individuals regarding ADHD. Furthermore, "Secondary Dx" includes category values such as anxiety disorder, learning disorder, tic disorder, and various other diagnoses. The dataset encompasses assessments for ADHD symptoms (ADHD Measure, Inattentive, and Hyper/Impulsive), medication status (1 for Medication Naive and 2 for Not Medication Naive), IQ evaluations utilising the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (WISC-IV) (Verbal IQ, Performance IQ, Full2 IQ, and Full4 IQ), as well as quality control metrics for resting-state functional MRI data (QC\_Rest\_1 to QC\_Rest\_4) and anatomical data quality (QC\_Anatomical\_1). These traits collectively provide insights for the proposed multimodal diagnosis of ADHD.

*Target Variable* -In this research, the target variable is represented by the "DX" column in the CSV ﬁle. This column is of type binary, where 0 indicates the absence of ADHD and 1 indicates the presence of ADHD (Fig. 3 ).

## 4 **Experiments **

In the subsequent sub-sections, we outline the experiments carried out for diagnosis of ADHD using phenotypic and sMRI data one by one and then outline the proposed fusion mechanism. **4.1 ** **Experiments on Phenotypic Data **

For the experiments using phenotypic data, we extract information pertaining to Scandir ID, Handedness, ADHD metrics, Inattentive and Hyperactive/Impulsive scores, Medication status, and IQ assessments from the dataset. We carry out thorough data preprocessing, which includes managing missing values, categorising features, and normalizing. The detailed procedure followed for predicting ADHD utilising phenotypic data is illustrated in Fig. 4. Feature selection is an essential process, wherein we discern a collection of pivotal variables that markedly affect predicted accuracy. In \[ 41 \], the authors examine different machine learning methodologies for classifying neurodevelopmental diseases and outline their possible applications. Analysing the insights from their work, we utilise two machine learning classiﬁers, namely K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) and Random Forest.

**K-NN ** The KNN is one of the simplest yet effective supervised machine learning algorithms. The hyperparameter values chosen are listed in Table 1.

1. The parameter n\_neighbors determine the amount of neighbours to use for predictions.  The method will consider the ﬁve nearest neighbours of the query location, with a default value of 5. 2. weights: It explains the forecasting algorithm's weighting scheme. With the setting  "uniform," every neighbour is assigned equal weight. You can create a user-deﬁned function or use the "distance" to give your neighbours more inﬂuence if they are closer. The default mode, "auto," chooses the most appropriate algorithm automatically based on the data. Other alternatives such as 'Ball\_tree', 'KD\_tree,' and 'brute' may also be researched.

**Random Forest ** Random Forest is one of the most popular ensemble learning algorithms, known for exhibiting high performance across various types of datasets. Testing and tweaking are necessary to determine the optimal values for the Random Forest algorithm's hyperparameters, which include max\_depth and random\_state. Multimodal Framework for Prediction of Attention-Deﬁcit

1. **max\_depth: ** It is an upper limit on the depth of each decision tree within the forest.  If no value is speciﬁed, the trees are grown till either all leaves contain the minimum number of samples required for a split or all leaves are pure-whichever comes ﬁrst. In order to prevent overﬁtting, the depth can be limited by deﬁning an upper limit, such as 10. It controls the complexity of the model and can be changed based on the level of difﬁculty and the size of the training dataset. 2. **random\_state: ** Speciﬁes the random seed in order to guarantee repetition. Change  random\_state to None or any other integer number to generate a new value each time; the value of 49 is arbitrary. Setting a deﬁned value helps you to replicate the same results every time you execute, which is useful for consistency and debugging. **4.2 ** **Experiments on sMRI data **

We applied the two previously selected machine learning approaches-K-NN and random forest classiﬁers-on FreeSurfer-derived morphometric features from structural MRI (sMRI), including regional brain volumes and cortical thickness measures, to predict ADHD. The FreeSurfer-extracted region-of-interest (ROI) features provided a biologically interpretable basis for prediction, capturing subtle structural alterations in cortical and subcortical regions previously implicated in ADHD. **4.3 ** **Multimodal Data Fusion **

To integrate multimodal information, we employed late fusion, decision-level ensemble strategy. For each subject, modality-speciﬁc classiﬁers were trained on sMRI features as well as phenotypic data. KNN and Random Forest models were independently trained on each modality. The predictions from the two KNN classiﬁers (sMRI-based and phenotype-based) were then aggregated using a fusion step, yielding a KNN-fusion decision for the subject. Similarly, predictions from the two Random Forest classiﬁers were combined to produce Random Forest fusion decision. This allows modality-speciﬁc strengths to be preserved while providing a mechanism for cross-modal integration.

A limitation of majority voting with only two models per modality is the potential for ties when the classiﬁers disagree. To address this, we explored weighted voting. In weighted voting, the more accurate modality is given higher inﬂuence in the ﬁnal decision.

## 5 **Results and Discussion **

On successful implementation of the KNN and Random Forest and setting the appropriate hyperparameters, the results obtained on phenotypic as well as sMRI data are outlined in Table 1.

For phenotypic data, analysis's, top score, 92% accuracy was obtained via KNN with the hyperparameters n\_neighbors=5, weights='uniform', p=2, algorithm='auto'. The random forest algorithm obtained an accuracy value of 77%. These results imply that random forest and KNN could be helpful in analyzing the given multimodal data.

For sMRI data, the random forest model outperformed K-NN, achieving an accuracy of around 72%, while the K-NN classiﬁer reached an accuracy of approximately 65%. - Sharma and P. Chaudhary

**Table 1. ** A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Algorithms for ADHD prediction on phenotypic and MRI data Algorithm Best Hyperparameters Accuracy on Phenotypic data Accuracy on sMRI data KNN n\_neighbors=5, weights='uniform', p=2, algorithm='auto' 92% 65% Random Forest max_depth=10, random_state=49 77% 72%

These results demonstrate the potential of combining automated neuroimaging pipelines with machine learning to identify structural biomarkers that may aid in ADHD diagnosis.

As discussed in Sect. 4, a limitation of majority voting with only two models per modality is the potential for ties when the classiﬁers disagree. To address this, we explored weighted voting and probability-based (soft voting) schemes. In weighted voting, the more accurate modality is given higher inﬂuence in the ﬁnal decision. For example, phenotypic KNN achieved 92% accuracy compared to 65% for sMRI KNN, justifying a higher weight for the phenotypic prediction. In cases where sMRI and phenotypic classiﬁers are incongruent, the decision defaults to the phenotypic output with greater weight. This logical tie-breaking approach maintains the advantages of multimodal integration while also reducing the instability caused by classiﬁer discordance.

The fusion-based KNN classiﬁer reports better performance than any of the single modality K-NNs. The sMRI-only KNN attained an accuracy of 65%, while the phenotypic-only KNN achieved 92%. The late fusion method resulted in a notable enhancement, reaching an overall accuracy of 94%. This enhancement illustrates that while phenotypic characteristics were signiﬁcantly predictive, the use of sMRI-derived morphometric features offered supplementary structural insights that enhanced generalisation and mitigated overﬁtting. Similarly, the fusion-based random forest classiﬁer also outperformed its individual modality baselines. The sMRI-based random forest attained an accuracy of 72%, whilst the phenotype-based random forest reached 77% accuracy. Late fusion resulted in an accuracy of 82%. Even though with Random Forest, we report a somewhat lesser improvement by fusion comparable to KNN, the accuracy enhancements outline the potential of decision-level integration in stabilizing predictions across modalities.

Collectively, these results emphasize the efﬁcacy of use of multimodal data for ADHD diagnosis. The results underscore that structural biomarkers as well as clinical measurements should both be incorporated rather than examined in isolation to enhance accuracy and reliability.

Recent studies have increasingly explored combining brain structural features with behavioural or demographic data to improve ADHD detection. Authors in \[ 42 \]  used sMRI volumetric and cortical thickness features along with personal characteristic data, building an age-balanced sample of 316 ADHD vs. 316 typically developing children, and achieved 75% accuracy using classiﬁers like RBSVM and SVM. Authors in \[ 43 \] Multimodal Framework for Prediction of Attention-Deﬁcit

carried out a systematic meta-analysis of sMRI and/or fMRI-based ML techniques, found pooled sensitivity and speciﬁcity each around 0.74-0.75 and an AUC of around 0.81, highlighting that single-modality imaging methods tend to have moderate diagnostic value and leave space for improvement.

In contrast, the proposed approach in this work leverages a late-fusion multimodal method integrating structural MRI features with phenotypic data, using ensemble voting. This allows to retain the complementary strengths of both modalities. As a result, the proposed model achieves a substantially higher classiﬁcation accuracy (94%) compared to around 75% in \[ 42 \] and signiﬁcantly exceeds the average AUC/sensitivity achievable by imaging-only ML models as in \[ 43 \]. Thus, our work demonstrates that multimodal fusion (even with only two modalities) has the potential to outperform unimodal or limited-modality baselines, offering a more robust and clinically actionable diagnostic tool.

## 6 **Conclusions and Future Work **

This study presents and assesses a multimodal AI framework for the automated diagnosis of Attention Deﬁcit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Our study illustrated the beneﬁts of merging phenotypic data with structural MRI features, utilising machine learning methods like k-nearest neighbours (KNN) and random forests (RF) for effective ADHD classiﬁcation. The experimental ﬁndings indicated that whereas phenotypic characteristics alone yielded robust performance, the integration of structural MRI data via late fusion techniques signiﬁcantly enhanced accuracy, precision, and recall. The fusion-based KNN classiﬁer attained the highest performance, with an overall accuracy of 94%, highlighting the signiﬁcance of decision-level integration in using complementary information from diverse data sources. These ﬁndings underscore the capability of multimodal AI systems to replicate clinical reasoning by concurrently evaluating behavioural, demographic, and neuroimaging data. Such frameworks can offer decision support to clinicians, alleviate the load of subjective evaluations, and facilitate earlier and more accurate identiﬁcation of ADHD, which is essential for enhancing patient outcomes and long-term-care.

Future endeavours will concentrate on integrating supplementary modalities, including EEG, ECG, and data from wearable devices, while also investigating deep learningbased fusion methodologies. Expanding to larger, more diversiﬁed datasets and including explainable AI will boost generalisability, interpretability, and clinical application.

## Agentic AI Agents for Autonomous and Resilient **Enterprise Architecture Evolution ** Mahesh Kumar Gaddam ( B )

Solutions Architect, Computer Science, Fedex, Little Elm, TX, USA mahi.ramuk@gmail.com

**Abstract. ** The challenge of the dynamic nature of business environment requires enterprise architectures (EA) that is resilient and has autonomous evolutionary capabilities. This paper presents a new System recovery comparison underload surge in which self-directed changes and recoveries can be achieved by integrating agentic AI agents as a part of the enterprise architecture system. In contrast to the conventional EA strategies that sometimes can be rather reactive and require manual conﬁguration, the proposed model utilizes the agents that are driven by AI and capable of perception, reasoning, and action within the ecosystems of complex enterprises. These agentic systems bring together reinforcement learning, cognitive modeling and real time monitoring to continuously optimize the processes, infrastructure, and response latency under high-trafﬁc scenario. Simulations and prototypes presented in the study show how these agents contribute to the increased agility of enterprise, operational continuity and faster architectural decision-making in a volatile situation. The performance comparison between agentic AI system and static EA system are greatly enhanced responsiveness, fault-tolerance and coherence of the systems. The contribution to the area in the paper is downtime comparison during fault injection of EA that comparison of strategic attributes between agentic and traditional architecture.

**Keywords: ** Enterprise Architecture · Agentic AI · Autonomous Systems · Resilience · Digital Transformation · Reinforcement Learning · Enterprise Agility · Intelligent Agents

## 1 **Introduction **

## The enterprises between the past and the present are increasingly getting complex and

volatile, raising a lot of challenges to the traditional enterprise management paradigms. With the increasing rate of technological changes, the emergence of new customer needs, and constant disruptions caused by global crises, cybersecurity breaches, and other factors, enterprise architecture (EA) has become a strategic tool for orchestrating business activities with those in the IT ecosystem \[ 14 \]. Traditional frameworks can provide a plan to organize and manage the technology assets according to the organizational goals, although, in highly dynamic and uncertain environments, TOGAF or Zachman frameworks are not always sufﬁcient. They are inﬂexible, require paper-based records and manual supervision which restrict their effectiveness as instruments of dynamic and adaptive decision-making.

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 511-521, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_38> M.K. Gaddam

This background is in the context of an increasing need to have intelligent systems that not only assist enterprise architecture but can autonomously take over the action of managing enterprise architecture. This is the opportunity that artiﬁcial intelligence AI, in the form of agentic AI agents, can be a transformative opportunity \[ 9 \]. These are autonomous software agents that possess cognitive capacity, can perceive their surroundings, make goals, learn through interaction and perform tasks without being told speciﬁcally how to do it. When they are embedded into the enterprise structures, it puts the organizations on the trajectory to self-regulating, self-healing and goal-adaptive enterprise systems. This change means a paradigm shift in the centralized, rules-based EA models towards distributed intelligent and autonomous architectures.

The concept of agency in AI means more than just automation it means intention, ﬂexibility and being able to react contextually to the world in a situation and circumstance dependent way on both internal and external events \[ 7 \]. The AI agents that handle such tasks are called agentic and can track the system performance, identify anomalies and offer solutions, as well as implement architectural changes with little human interaction. Examples of where such agents may be utilized, include when a core service is experiencing a performance bottleneck or in the case of an identiﬁed cyber threat, real time, these agents can automatically start up a rerouting or scaling strategy. Likewise, when the business turns to focus on sustainability instead of efﬁciency, these agents can realign enterprise services and IT assets accordingly by means of adjusting conﬁgurations, workﬂows, and priorities of services \[ 12 \].

Although intelligent agents have encountered intensive research in such areas as robotics, smart manufacturing, and supply chain logistics, there is a lack of research in employing their potential in the evolution of enterprise architecture. Most attempts that are being made at present are aimed at automation of tasks or separate decision assistants, without integrating AI agents into the architectural foundation of the enterprise systems. In addition, resilience, or the ability of a system to continue to operate appropriately amidst unpredicted challenges, has been managed as an afterthought, at times by redundancies or failover systems. Nonetheless, all these approaches fail to incorporate adaptations that are dynamic and goal setting that is situational, something that is ever more essential in contemporary businesses.

The paper shall present a framework conceptualization of agentic intelligence to become integrated into enterprise architectural structures, bringing about independent and robust growth of enterprise systems. The hypothesis in essence is that the integration of cognitive, adaptive AI agents directly within EA layers, including data management, application services, and infrastructures, has the potential to improve long-term responsiveness, decision agility, and sustainability of enterprises by signiﬁcant levels. The system can reoptimize behavior based on changes in the environment using reinforcement learning, and by means of real-time monitoring and selective updates to the model may be adapted to the changes without lengthy human redesign \[ 10 \].

Within the framework, agents are not just implementers of instructions, but carriers of knowledge that continues to evolve the enterprise in an enterprise. They rate the tradeoffs in performance, ensure that mission-critical services are given the ﬁrst priority and identify patterns that may be indicative of future threats or opportunities. This enables businesses to shift away more often using periodic, reactive changes of the EA into a Agentic AI Agents for Autonomous and Resilient Enterprise

state of constant architectural intelligence, which transforms over time with disruptions to a minimum. This paper contributes to this idea to reframe the meaning of enterprise architecture itself, shifting the enterprise architecture conversation toward a living and a learning ecosystem rather than seeing enterprise architecture as a frozen structure \[ 15 \]. **1.1 ** **Novelty and Contribution ** The main proposed contribution as organized below:

- To evaluate the system recovery comparison under load surge  - To response latency under high-trafﬁc scenario  - To performance comparison between agentic AI system and static EA system  - To obtain the downtime comparison during fault injection  - The new comparison of strategic attributes between agentic and traditional architecture is described.

## 2 **Related Study **

In recent years, there has been an increased pursuit of combining intelligent technologies in enterprise systems in response to the rigidity in the traditional EA. Study of self-adaptive and autonomic systems, sometimes based upon the concepts of autonomic computing, has proposed the concept of self-conﬁguring, self-optimizing, self-healing and self-protecting architectures. The purpose of these systems is to ofﬂoad human administrators by allowing the IT infrastructure to be self-managed based upon environmental changes. Naturally, much of this implementation can be obtained through line-oriented bottleneck optimizations at the level of infrastructure or service-speciﬁc savings by and large, it does not refer to systematic architectural enhancement.

In 2024, B. Brik *et al.*,  \[ 13 \], introduced the Enterprise Architecture (EA) introduced was considered a critical element to deal with organization complexity management, alignment of IT along with business objectives, and as a systematic approach to technology governance. The layered models and the strategic alignment constructs are traditional EA frameworks that have given a backbone on enterprise modernization attempts. These traditional models, however, do not have much ﬂexibility in situations of rapid change and uncertainness. Their design is also generally inert, they are updated manually and are incapable of delivering a real-time response, which increases the inadequacies of systems in handling new challenges, such as digital disruption, cyber threats and system-wide failure \[ 1 \].

Another large body of work that is applicable to the vision of intelligent enterprise architecture is multi-agent systems (MAS). MAS deals with groups of self-governing agents and provides communication and coordination of these agents pursuing shared objectives. These systems have successfully found application areas like robotics, distributed control and even logistics. In the enterprise environment, supply chain management, scheduling of workﬂow and decentralized decision making have been facilitated through MAS. However, when it comes to such layers of EA as application architecture, data governance, and strategic alignment, they are not as well integrated. Most implementations are operational, in the sense that they do not have mechanisms to support self-reﬂection of the architecture and its long-term evolution \[ 6 \]. M.K. Gaddam

In 2025, Y. Yigit *et al.*,  \[ 8 \] suggested the practice of resilience of enterprise systems is not a new practice and has been discussed widely especially the practice of disaster recovery, system redundancy and high-availability designs. Resilience planning also engulfs planning of fault-tolerant systems, as well as putting backup mechanisms in place to recover services in cases of failures. Although these strategies have the beneﬁt of increasing stability, they are inadequate to provide real-time, smart response such that system behavior can be altered in accordance with the varying business priorities. In addition, the traditional model of resiliency planning fails to consider not only active determination of likely threats, but also the ability to reorganize in advance of any interruptions.

In 2025, Y. Wang *et al.*,  \[ 11 \] proposed the other line of research that applies to this situation is goal-oriented and cognitive computing systems. These are the systems that imitate the qualities of human reasoning and their decision making including the representation of knowledge, modeling of goals, and adaptive planning. Among such applications have been business process reengineering and intelligent workﬂow design. Nonetheless, their implementation in real-time and dynamic enterprise architecture is still conceptual or in academic prototyping. The execution of architectural agents that can be used are and will remain missing in terms of realizing a cognitive agent capable of playing a role in the evolution of architecture, over time.

At the same time, notwithstanding the increased work in these areas, there is still a lack of a coherent framework that would unify the concepts of agentic autonomy, architecture evolution and enterprise resilience. Most of the current concepts are either too narrow in their scope with reference to automation, resilience, or optimization devoid of providing a set of capabilities in an integrated and self-adaptive system. The use of agents in an agentic artiﬁcial intelligence with their goals, ability to learn, and the freedom of action integrated into the foundations of enterprise architecture is a new but not developed ﬁeld of studies \[ 2 \].

This paper seeks to address this gap in the literature by suggesting a multi-agent, cognitive mechanism to enable enterprise architecture with the capability to be selfaware, to learn, to negotiate, and to reconﬁgure themselves in an autonomic manner. It combines concepts in AI, MAS, autonomic computing, and digital governance, to create a base, which can transform the enterprise systems by turning them into responsive structures. What this yields is an image of enterprise architecture as neither a ﬁxed store of design artifacts nor a dumber blank slate over which the visible hand of design is necessarily impressed. Instead, it yields an image of enterprise architecture as a living, thinking entity the very in-principal incapacity of which to improve itself and to survive the bewilderments of uncertainty is thus opened.

## 3 **Proposed Methodology **

The proposed methodology integrates agentic AI agents into enterprise architecture layers using a layered model comprising perception, cognition, decision-making, and execution (see Fig. 1 ). The framework enables dynamic learning and autonomous decisions based on reinforcement signals and goal alignment. The overall ﬂow of agentic interaction is illustrated in the ﬂowchart titled: Agentic AI Agents for Autonomous and Resilient Enterprise

**Fig. 1. ** Agentic AL-driven architecture evolution framework

- Proposed Approach: A new agentic AI approach to enterprise architecture (EA)  integrating structural and operational layers for autonomy, adaptability, and resilience. - Main Innovation: Combines cognitive AI principles with architectural decisionmaking. Creates goal-oriented intelligent architecture, developed iteratively. Moves  beyond automation of single activities → introduces multi-agent intelligence across all EA facets (service orchestration, infrastructure scaling, data governance, business alignment). - Four-Layer Architecture: Layers: Perception, Cognition, Decision-Making, Execution. Enables agents to: Monitor system health continuously, interpret contextual  signals, adjust to disruptions, Self-repair and realign goals without central authority. - Learning & Adaptation: Uses reinforcement learning and optimization models based  on utility. Agents learn over time, adapting behavior to meet changing enterprise objectives. - Contribution to Resilience Theory: Cognitive agents detect and counteract disruptions faster than conventional fault-tolerance systems. Employ feedback looping,  negotiation, and dynamic goal prioritization to maintain continuity during crises. - Beneﬁts: reduced downtime, faster decision-making, better resource allocation. M.K. Gaddam

- Empirical Validation: Simulation evidence demonstrates practical effectiveness in  enterprise disruption scenarios. Conﬁrms efﬁciency and applicability for practitioners and researchers. - Overall Contribution: Presents a next-generation EA model that is autonomous, intelligent, and resilient by design. Opens pathways for future research on AI-based  enterprise systems.

## 4 **Results and Discussion **

Simulation of the agentic AI constructed in a simulated enterprise IT environment, using virtualized microservice elementary and a synthetic data feed that matched realworld disturbances like those involving workload surges, infrastructure failures, and goal realignment conditions, was used to test its implementation. It has been tested with and without agentic AI control and the difference in response behavior, the fault management, and the modiﬁcation of architecture has been observed when testing multiple different instances.

To ensure stability, a control feedback loop is implemented. Let the deviation from desired behavior be Δ *ϕ*, then: = *φ* desired − *φ* actual (9)

The agent adjusts policy weights in response to Δ *ϕ*, ensuring architectural consistency over time.

Finally, inter-agent communication for negotiation and arbitration is modeled via utility exchange. If agent *A * proposes state *x * and agent B prefers *y*, agreement occurs if: $$ UA(x) + UB(x) \geq UA(y) + UB(y) $$ (10)

This Nash-style utility comparison ensures multi-agent consensus and architectural harmony.

The comparative quotient was obtained under three pillar metrics that included system downtime, decision latency, and architectural coherence. The comparison between the baseline and the system with agentic agents is clear in Fig. 2 and we can see how the overall recovery time and the amount of performance degradation during peak demand were lower in the system with agentic agents than it was in the static control group.

Speciﬁcally, the agentic-agent-enabled system, placed in a simulated condition of excess service requests caused by unexpected trafﬁc, did so automatically and with no human intervention, re-routing low-priority services (these being the most common), activating load redistribution policies, and stabilizing the CPU utilization levels in a much shorter period than the control model. In Fig. 3, the result of workload stabilization is compared in which the agentic system was operational within 90 seconds, and the nonagentic model was taking a longer time of over 210 seconds to be in the same state. This ﬁnding supports the notion that implementing the cognitive agents in the architecture layers highly enhances the resilience of a system without requiring human intercession. M.K. In a second experiment, a simulated attack pathway was fed to the system that distorted service endpoints that were critical, and the architecture used predetermined fallback strategies to reconﬁgure the system. The anomaly was identiﬁed by the agentic agents in real-time, blocks of the afﬂicted nodes were isolated and automated reconﬁguration path that ensured service continuity was activated. Figure 4 shows the picture of downtime window wherein the agentic model recorded shorter downtime window compared to an incident management response. The image shows clearly that learn-to-learn works because the clever feedback path is reinforcing the fault-tolerant mechanisms of the system and enabling an autonomous reinforcement process.

Moreover, the stability of the architecture under transitioning business objectives was assessed making the objective of the system change to the goal of compliance with sustainability. The agents could help realign the priorities of the services, deviate workloads into infrastructures that were green compliant as well as decommission of work processes that consumed a lot of energy. The coherence tracking has been carried out by measuring consistency scoring models that had a scale of 0 to 1 with a 1 corresponding to the perfect alignment of architecture behavior and business objectives. The score attained by the Agentic system in this test was 0.93 compared to the 0.71 which was attained by the manually tuned architecture. This outcome justiﬁes the argument that agentic AI can improve architectural ﬂexibility in the long run and maintain compatibility with company strategy \[ 4 \].

## 5 **Conclusion **

## This paper shows that agentic AI agents in enterprise architecture have the potential to

facilitate the self-organizational, resilient and goal-seeking evolution of the enterprise systems performance comparison between agentic AI system and static EA system. The proposed framework is superior to the traditional static EA methods because it brings down response time, increasing adaptiveness, and upholding system coherence amid disruption and strategic change. Organizations can be developed to self-learn, selfheal and adapt to make ongoing changes ﬁt enterprises by embedding intelligence in their comparison of strategic attributes between agentic and traditional architecture. The future research will be related to the real-world application of the model in the enterprise infrastructure, improvement of agent transparency, and ethical factors in autonomous decision-making.
