## Design of an Intelligent ERP System

**for Automated Financial Compliance and Risk ** **Monitoring ** Kulasekhara Reddy Kotte ( B ) Principal Consultant, SLRI Solutions INC, Houston, TX, USA kottekula@gmail.com

**Abstract. ** Smart Enterprise Resource Planning systems have evolved in response to the rising level of complexity of ﬁnancial regulations and the ever demanding need to monitor the ﬁnancial health of corporations clustering output and anomaly detection in real time. The paper has developed a new paradigm of designing an intelligent ERP system which will automate ﬁnancial compliance and in managing risks monthly compliance violations identiﬁed. With the use of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and encompassing real-time analytics, the proposed system adds predictive compliance alerts, anomaly detection in ﬁnancial transactions, and the decision-support risk scoring to the ability of established ERP platforms. The methodology implies the use of modular architecture, the introduction of regulatory rule engines, and using the AI-based pattern recognition algorithms comparative feature assessment of traditional ERP vs intelligent ERP. Mahalanobis Distance to ﬂag transactions deviating from the normal pattern deployment shows that the system has led to better compliance with the regulations, fewer human involvement, and effective anticipatory risk control. This study indicates the way in risk values by department which intelligent automation is sought in the ERP systems to ensure sustainable ﬁnancial governance performance metrics comparison before and after intelligent ERP deployment.

**Keywords: ** Intelligent ERP · Financial Compliance · Risk Monitoring · Artiﬁcial Intelligence · Anomaly Detection · Regulatory Automation · Predictive Analytics · Enterprise Systems

## 1 **Introduction **

## Enterprises are today facing a two-pronged problem in the highly digitized and globalized

ﬁnancial world of operating with compliance bottlenecks and the issues of operational agility. Financial regulators around the globe are increasingly revising the requirements surrounding anti-money laundering (AML), tax administration, environmental social governance (ESG) and corporate reporting \[ 1 \]. Failure in adhering to such directives does not only attract ﬁnes but may also ﬁnd its way in stopping at the stage of destroying organizational image and stakeholder conﬁdence. Although the Stalwart ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) systems have been critical in the organization and execution of

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 522-533, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_39> Design of an Intelligent ERP System for Automated Financial

enterprise-wide transactions and procedures in general, they have at times failed to attribute the intelligence and real-time ability to respond to such evolving landscapes of compliance. Their use of rule-based processes and ﬁxed data as well as structures makes them reactive and labor-intensive about regulatory activities.

Meanwhile, risk management has ceased to be backward-looking audit-based activity; organizations are supposed to actively track ﬁnancial risks, rediscover anomalies, and put preventative controls in place. The wide range of activities in such an environment requires enterprise systems to do more than software that manages data. They should be able to respond to regulatory cues, recognize new risks, and respond in an automated way and avoid waiting to be acted upon by a human \[ 3 \]. The classic architecture of ERP is not by its nature capable of identifying any behavioral abnormalities to the ﬁnancial processes, nor to adapt to changes in regulations in an adaptive manner. The latter has created an interesting use case on the need to integrate artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in the core of ERP systems which have now become a new breed of intelligent ERPs.

A smart ERP employs AI/ML to enable mathematical analysis of enterprise data in large volumes in both structured and unstructured forms, learn patterns of compliance and process automated warnings or action. These systems are not just useful to store compliance checklists, but they are also useful to look out when deviations occur, their machine learning capacity to predict risks given historical data and to make the workﬂows as transparent as possible. Moreover, such systems make it possible to view and process risk indicators in real-time, so executives and ofﬁcers involved in compliance services can see necessary information in minutes. In such a way, organizations change the compliance-by-audit model towards the continuous compliance model, which becomes integrated into the day-to-day ﬁnancial functioning \[ 3 \].

Many sectors, such as the banking, healthcare, and manufacturing industries, are already testing AI-enhanced fraud detection and regulatory audit preparation and predictive ﬁnancial modeling systems \[ 4 \]. The proposed intelligent ERP in this work is, however, distinct in that it has end-to-end automated compliance and risk monitoring across a variety of modules: ﬁnance, procurement, accounts payable/receivable, reporting. Not only anomaly detection but also dynamicity of the rules, absorption of regulatory documents by using NLP and immediate decision facilitation through risk score rectiﬁcation modules. In contrast to third party compliance tools that act in silos, the proposed solution is an intrinsic aspect of the ERP architecture, and the organization-wide governance is consistent.

Besides, manual monitoring in multi-jurisdiction corporations with compliance regulation vastly diverse across the regions is not only fallible but also unsustainable. A smart ERP can learn regional ﬁnancial regulations and tax codes, and it scans its behavior accordingly, without requiring tremendous reprogramming. This ease and ﬂexibility guarantee a shorter response time when there are regulatory changes like they were in the context of tax relief programs during COVID-19 or when it comes to trade compliance in the post-Brexit environment. Moreover, AI can monitor the indirect indications of dangers, which rule-based systems could not detect, as well, such as user behavioral patterns within the record of activities, time-of-day frequencies of transactions, or anomalous relations with vendors \[ 5, 6 \]. K.R. Kotte

In this light, this paper is going to lay out architecture of an intelligent ERP system with the focus on the automation of ﬁnancial compliance activities and the real-time identiﬁcation of enterprise risks. Innovations in AI and speciﬁcally machine learning and natural language processing are incorporated into the proposed system to facilitate anomaly detection and interpretation of the regulatory documents, respectively. Its design incorporates a modular element (e.g. a regulatory rule engine, risk analytics layer and an adaptive dashboard on which compliance can be visualized). This holistic framework is focused more on companies who not only want efﬁciency, but a smart anticipation and adaptation of the ﬁnancial governance in perusing its process \[ 8 \]. **1.1 ** **Novelty and Contribution **

Its principal novelty is the fact that it is a design of end-to-end ERP that will be natively intelligent and directly optimized on automated ﬁnancial compliance and dynamic risk monitoring a space where conventional ERP systems have traditionally the following contributions to perform.

- To evaluate the clustering output and anomaly detection  - To applied monthly compliance violations identiﬁed  - The comparative feature assessment of traditional ERP vs intelligent ERP  - To obtain risk values by department  - The performance metrics comparison before and after intelligent ERP deployment

## 2 **Related Study **

Rule-based engines and policy interpretation modules have been another big trend in work to automate compliance management. The functioning of such systems underlines requirements of the law in mapping in logical terms that are executable in real time. They help in detecting non-conforming transactions, delivery of compliance reports, and escalation workﬂows. These trends carry a movement in terms of manual understanding of ﬁnancial standards to digital compliance ecosystems that may enjoy self-regulation. Nonetheless, a signiﬁcant number of these systems are operationalized as standalone compliance tools and therefore, this creates data silo and slow response dynamics.

In 2025, S.-I. Ao, M. Hurwitz, and V. Palade \[ 14 \] suggested artiﬁcial intelligence as an integrated component of enterprise systems, which has been developing fast as business contexts have grown to become complex, particularly in industry segments where compliance is high. Initial research on ERP systems put speciﬁc emphasis on efﬁciency of transactions, centralization of data stores and business process regularization. Though these systems led to signiﬁcant changes in how organizations were coordinated and how their resources were planned, these systems were not developed to respond to the dynamics of rapidly evolving regulatory environments or to complete the cognitive operations like anomaly detection or risk assessment. Consequently, the conventional ERP systems have not been efﬁcient in areas that need supreme ﬂexibility, most notably ﬁnancial control and monitoring of compliance.

In 2025, S. F. Wijaya *et al.*,  \[ 2 \] proposed the latest developments in the creation of intelligent systems heralded the arrival of AI-enhanced ERPs. Some of the capabilities Design of an Intelligent ERP System for Automated Financial

that are included in these systems are pattern recognition, natural language understanding, and real-time learning to provide contextual awareness and decision support. Enterprise application studies on AI have shown how useful machine learning algorithms can be in detecting trends in ﬁnancial transactions that tend to prove fraudulent or policy breach. Such methods involve supervised classiﬁers, clustering models and unsupervised anomaly detection frameworks that are bettered as they get exposed to new data. By incorporating such models into ERP, they can keep an eye on ﬁnancial behavior on a regular basis, and they also have the capability of providing proactive positive alerts as compared to the reactive reports provided by the current systems.

In addition, risk management practices have been incorporated in intelligent systems to forecast the danger that may arise and evaluate the weaknesses of organizational processes. Risk modeling processes have been integrated into business systems in the form of decision trees, Bayesian networks, and fuzzy logic processes that can provide a risk measurement rating taking into consideration ﬁnancial variables and past incident data \[ 11 \]. These solutions can help ﬁnancial controllers to sort the issues by the level of seriousness and possible effects. Current ERP platforms do provide oversimpliﬁed risk monitoring tools, but most of them are not smart enough to be able to anchor risks using developing internal and external factors.

In 2024, N. Salybekova *et al.*,  \[ 7 \] introduced the recent observation in the current stud studies AI, big data analytics, and cloud computing have been converging to change enterprise governance. Intelligent ERPs on the cloud can expand department-wise and geographically, merge data disparate sources and can predict breaches in compliance through predictive analytics. These solutions utilize real-time data feeds, and thus it is possible to monitor rather than audit. Nonetheless, uptake has not been greater in industries with extensive barriers to adoption, such as the data governance process, data privacy rules, and complexity in the data systems.

Even though there is a vast knowledge base founded on the effectiveness of AIpowered enterprise solutions, it is evident that there is a missing link in how compliance automation and risk management with the most extended scope should be included into the intrinsic structure of ERP systems. Many studies concentrate on singular AI tools or compliance modules augmented by third parties and not on a coherent ERP with intelligent design. In addition, there are also not many attempts to design ERP systems able to adapt to altered regulations, put ﬁnancial events into a context, and act on their own to carry on policies. The present paper will attempt to overcome these limitations by proposing a unanimously connected design of an intelligent ERP system that can combine regulatory engines, machine learning, and real-time analytics into an architectural unity of ﬁnancial compliance and risk mitigation.

## 3 **Methodology **

The proposed intelligent ERP system is designed as a multi-layered architecture to automate ﬁnancial compliance and dynamic risk monitoring in Fig. 1. The system consists of a data ingestion layer, a regulatory knowledge engine, an AI-based analytics module, a risk scoring mechanism, and an interactive dashboard. The core objective is to build a self-adaptive system that processes ﬁnancial data in real-time, compares it against dynamic compliance rules, and generates actionable outputs \[ 12 \]. K.R. Kotte

**Fig. 1. ** System Architecture of the Intelligent ERP for Compliance and Risk Monitoring

It closes the trans actionality of ERP processes to the real-time decision intelligence \[ 10 \]. The ﬁrst is the introduction of a Regulatory Knowledge Engine capable of updating its set of rules automatically about the consumption of ﬁnancial regulations around the world using NLP techniques. This makes automatic response to the variations in the policies without manual modiﬁcation of the code. The other innovation is working in a multi-model AI analytics layer that will run concurrent anomaly detection, pattern learning, behavioral scoring across multiple ﬁnancial data ﬂows. The process does not only alert concerning transactions but puts them in perspective within the scope of history and the behavior of entities.

Moreover, its study will introduce a real-time risk scoring framework that conducts consolidation of transactional understanding and classiﬁes occurrences in line with seriousness and effect- however this time, allowing compliance groups to be more efﬁcient in prioritization of measures. Another signiﬁcant technological breakthrough is the interoperability layer that enables smooth connectivity with ERP vendors that are currently in use (e.g., SAP, Oracle) via open APIs and at the same time preserving the autonomy of the AI engine. The given work has also presented a compliance automation dashboard with smart alerts and interactive heat maps besides providing traceable audit trails-which brings about control and transparency. In contrast to generic dashboards, such interface is not a passive one as AI intelligence can dynamically drive it \[ 15 \].

In a nutshell, this study does not dwell on small steps towards enhancing ERP functions. It offers a scalable, modular and adaptive system whose very nature is revolutionary about the way compliance and risk is being managed, such that it is more than a support mechanism, but an intelligent co-pilot on ﬁnancial governance. ## 4 **Results and Discussion **

Deployment of the proposed intelligent ERP was conducted in a model enterprise setting with synthetic ﬁnancial application, regulatory input, and operational processes of procurement, accounts payable and general ledger modules. After the AI-enhanced compliance engine was integrated, the level of responsiveness to ﬁnancial anomalies and regulatory non-conformities to the system became vastly enhanced. To ensure we could quantify the performance of the system, we challenged it through a series of tests in different contexts of transaction overﬂow problems, frequent changes of the rules and multi-jurisdiction compliance check scenarios. The most important metrics which were used to evaluate performance were violation detection rate, response time, alert precision, and risk score accuracy \[ 13 \].

A scoring mechanism calculates the risk level *R * for every transaction using a weighted sum of risk indicators *r* *i *:

# R = *n * $$ i=1 $$ *w* *i * · ***r*** *i* (6)

Weights *w* *i * are assigned based on domain knowledge or optimization using historical compliance incidents. To prioritize actions, we compute a compliance conﬁdence score using logistic regression: $$ P(C = 1 | x) = $$ 1 + e−(\alpha+ \beta ixi) (7)

This probability reﬂects how compliant a given transaction is. We also apply a time-series model to monitor recurring risk behaviors. Using ARIMA (Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average), the risk signal *Y* *t * is forecasted as: $$ Yt = \phi1Yt−1 + \theta1 t−1 + $$ *t* (8)

Where *ϕ* 1 is the auto-regressive coefﬁcient and *θ* 1 is the moving average coefﬁcient. The regulatory rule update engine incorporates newly published compliance regulations using NLP pipelines. The extracted conditions are formalized as Boolean logic expressions. For example, a two condition rule for a tax regulation may be: $$ R = (x1 >  \delta1) \wedge (x2 < \delta2) $$ (9)

These rules are dynamically appended to the existing policy engine. Finally, all risk metrics, predictions, and violations are visualized through a dashboard. This interface is driven by a backend that queries real-time compliance logs. The compliance violation percentage across departments is computed as: $$ V = $$ Violations Total Transactions \times 100 (10) This output is charted weekly using visual indicators. **Abstract. ** The paper establishes that comparative design metrics before and after playbook implementation metric with user task success rates by device type, and average team onboarding without interactive design playbook client feedback categories post-deployment component reuse and development time savings. The scalability factor is based on its reuse frequency and device adaptability range with visual guide compliance and hash-mapping function. It illustrates adaptive behavior of each component that is mapped to interaction states using a state transition matrix. When dealing with the digital transformation era, adaptive web portals are becoming the key to personalized and responsive user experiences regardless of devices and platforms they are used with. Nevertheless, ensuring that design stays on brand, and development is effective, though having a lot of intricacies, presents a major challenge. The paper presents the framework and guidelines of what is termed as the Interactive Design Playbook, which incorporates visual templates and block libraries to make designing and development of adaptive web portal easier. The playbook makes collaboration between cross-functional teams easier and avoids visual and functional inconsistencies through the delivery of scalable design systems and reusable modules of UI elements. Methodology involves the process of incorporating the principles of atomic design, adaptive approaches to UX, and design tokens, and the process is concluded with solid analysis of the case studies that represents the real-world practice.

**Keywords: ** Interactive Design · Component Libraries · Visual Guide · Adaptive Web Portal · Design Systems · UX/UI · Atomic Design · Responsive Interface · Design Tokens · Web Development

## 1 **Introduction **

## The need more than ever before to have seamless, responsive and user-focused online

experiences has changed the way web portals are being conceptualized and developed. The ability of users to navigate on digital platforms using a variety of devices (smartphones and tablets to desktops and wearables) has necessitated the increased need of having adaptive web portals \[ 1 \]. Not only should these platforms adapt the layout and its features that conform to different screen sizes but also take into consideration the

behavior and likes and needs of the users. Nevertheless, the scale of such adaptability does not merely involve a technological challenge; it must include all of the components of a uniﬁed design system, which would allow the efﬁciently oriented cross-functional teams to perform in a way that would be consistent in developing and implementing user interface (UI).

A typical problem that a design team is met with is fragmentation: inconsistency across visual quality and problematic reuse and a fracture between design and development. Conversely, code redundancy, unintelligible visual purpose, and multiple reworks by way of miscommunications are a problem to developers. Such incompatibility slows down the pace of development and adds to the development of a fragmented user experience across touch points \[ 4 \]. To address those problems, a lot of organizations have resorted to component libraries and design systems. Although such tools are useful to offer reusable components and a certain standardization, in most cases they do not have a real-time guide on how to construct the visuals, they are not considerate or scalable or discourse needs to be as dynamic as it is in the scenario of modern web portals.

The answer to this gap will require a more thorough, interactive experience-one that marries the visual and functional UI/UX designs and codiﬁes them to offer them into actual tools of development. Through the notion of an Interactive Design Playbook, it becomes apparent that this problem can be addressed by adopting a strategic approach. It acts as a store of UI assets and as a vibrant, living document that captures design rationale, inter-user interaction patterns, adaptive logic and responsive behaviour so that, even though they are kept tightly connected with frontend development practices, they can live on to serve as rich design documentation of UI implementations \[ 5 \].

In adaptive web portal design, such as in enterprise or multi-user portals, such a system must be not only consistent but also ﬂexible. Universal design patterns fail to succeed in a setting where individual customization, location, and device optimization matter most \[ 8 \]. There, the playbook functions as a strategy of operation of teams in situations of adaptive interface design. It makes sure all users, no matter the device or context to which they refer, get the same coherent and optimized experience.

This work investigates the architecture, modules, and effects of using Interactive Design Playbook in developing adaptive web portal design. By a fusion of theoretical underpinnings, technical implementation, and real-world testing, the paper assesses the potential success of that eco-system with regards to improving the consistency of design, speed of development, and general user satisfaction. The methodology involves modularizing components with atomic design, scalable design token introduction, and workﬂow documentation that optimizes the ﬂow between the design ﬁles and the front-end immutable development environments \[ 2 \]. **1.1 ** **Novelty and Contribution **

The main innovation of this work is the formalization and operationalization of the interactive design playbook as an ill, a kind of design system, a development guide, specially prepared to work with adaptive web portals.

- Comparative design metrics before and after playbook implementation metric and  user task success rates by device types on discussed G.C. Vegineni

## 2 **Related Study **

In 2024, Patel, V., et al. \[ 11 \] introduced the design systems and component-based architecture in contemporary web development have been a topic of increased interest among digital design and engineering communities. With organizations increasingly developing interfaces to a diverse set of devices and user target audiences, there has been a parallel rise in the need to have a coherent design systems model and ﬂexibility in its implementation. Design systems provide graphical consistency and more code reutilization in half the time by standardizing design language with logic. But in most cases, these systems have not been as useful to the extent of lacking well-formulated guidance provisions and not allowing interactive co-working methods to capitalize upon. There is an increasing appreciation that the severity of the traditionally used static design documents on their own is not sufﬁcient to guarantee a sense of real-time congruence in design perception and implementation.

In 2024, Shabur, Md.A. et.al., \[ 7 \] suggested the component libraries have become one such solution to facilitate scalable UI especially when integrated with mixed documentation software. The libraries contain re-usable UI components that can be used in other projects and on various platforms. Component libraries are particularly an avenue to standardization in the front end especially when used together with frameworks like React, Vue or Angular. However, a considerable number of component libraries are still visual-less, guidance-less, or ﬁxed to adapt to a special context. Therefore, although such tools are very effective, they tend to act independently of the rest of the design strategies and overlook overall adaptive needs.

Misalignment between designers, developers and product managers is a common issue because they use different vocabularies and have vague design intents in multidisciplinary teams. Collimation platforms and design systems have enhanced the degree of communication to an extent though they fail to eradicate the question Mark unless accompanied by a clear usage pattern and operating rules. The key to rectifying this misalignment is a centralized playbook that contains both visual and technical representations of usage instructions, design logic and implementation rules. The issue is how to create such a playbook, which is ﬂexible in terms of dynamically shifting project requirements and moreover, a playbook that is readable by all involved stakeholders \[ 14 \].

Another major aspect that has come up in the design interface of the enterprise web portal is the issue of scalability. Due to increasing size and complexity of projects, repetitive coding activities and manual documentation of design are no longer viable. Design systems and component libraries should thus be able to be extensible and theme able. Interactive Design Playbook: Visual Guides and Component

Among these characteristics is the ability to provide a theming feature that uses tokens, the capability to auto generate documentation and responsive behavior modelling. Studies have also revealed that the design of systems based on scalability is less costly in the long run in terms of maintenance and onboarding of new members of staff.

In 2024, Agulnik, M., *et al.*,  \[ 3 \] proposed the gap between design and development using real-time tools has occurred. Live opportunities to preview, internal component testing and cross platform synchronization platforms are becoming vital. However, they are disjointed and executed separately by teams that have not been strategically integrated into a centralized strategy. A playbook that integrates all these functionalities and that ﬁts into the demands of the adaptive web portals is an area that has been minimally explored, albeit being the need.

## 3 **Methodology **

Unlike the common design systems that are part of static documentation or lifeless UI kits, this playbook is dynamic and interactive as well as intensely integrated into the lifecycle of software development. It is not only about visual consistency but also the behavior design patterns, responsive thinking, addressing accessibility, and prototyping in real-time. This combination makes sure that the UI decisions can be not only visually homogeneous but technically possible under different conditions \[ 9 \].

Yet another new dimension is modularity integrated with ﬂexibility. The playbook organizes its visual and component libraries based on atomic designs so that the components could be built out of simple blocks by teams rather than constructing them at higher levels- complex templates. A set of design tokens is used to enhance these parts, allowing one to change brands, themes, contexts, and more easily in a way completely independent of the base code. Such token-driven ﬂexibility guarantees that any modiﬁcation in branding, layout norms, or tweaks handled by gadgets can be established world over and promptly.

Regarding the contribution, this study offers an entire approach towards the development, construction, and implementation of the Interactive Design Playbook, in actual software project \[ 15 \]. It also describes the architecture, the tools, the processes, and mechanisms of testing that were applied to make the playbook ﬁt in adaptive web portals of enterprise quality. The veliids is qualitatively supported by several experiments in various ﬁelds, healthcare, education, and e-commerce, with quantiﬁable increase in UI consistency, code reusability as well as the user satisfaction. It also offers open-source component models and visual guide templates that are to be adapted in the future and extended.

In addition, the study promotes a change in the way design and development teams work together. Through a common interactive backdrop, the playbook reduces the drag on handoffs and accelerates sprint performance, as well as fosters cross-functional alignment. It allows designers to think more in systems and engineers to be able to code with a proper design vision in mind with the result likely being a stronger, more uniﬁed approach to design and development of web portals that are easier to use and more pleasant to look at. This also makes the Interactive Design Playbook not only a practical abundant toolbox but also a strategic framework of development of adaptive, scalable, and

The playbook is a living framework where design decisions dynamically inﬂuence development through visual constraints and responsive logic codiﬁed in the reusable libraries \[ 6 \].

Both projects achieved better results in terms of alignment of teams, scalability of the design, and consistency of the interface when the projects are implemented. ## Optimized Breast Cancer Detection: Evaluating **Machine Learning Methods for Binary ** **Classiﬁcation **

## A. D. Aarushi, S. Sakshi,  M.  C.  Namrata, V. G. Narendra ( B ), and G. Shivaprasad ( B )

Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal Institute of Technology, Manipal, India \{narendra.vg,shiva.prasad\}@manipal.edu

**Abstract. ** This study explores a straightforward approach to determine the most suitable supervised learning method for two-class classiﬁcation in breast cancer detection, using the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset. Considering the medical signiﬁcance, both the F1 score and the recall of malignant cases are accorded the highest importance among the performance metrics. The various machine learning methods explored are K-nearest-neighbors, artiﬁcial neural networks, logistic regression with stochastic gradient descent and support vector machines (SVM). The process follows simple preprocessing. PCA and correlation coefﬁcients were used for dimensionality reduction when possible. The best performing algorithm is deemed to be SVMs with a linear kernel based on the chosen evaluation factors.

**Keywords: ** Breast Cancer Prediction · Machine Learning · Support Vector Machines · Principal Component Analysis · Gradient Descent · Logistic Regression

## 1 **Introduction **

## Cancer refers to a multifaceted group of diseases characterized by uncontrolled cell

growth in various parts of the human body. It is classiﬁed based on its site of origin and can affect individual organs, supporting tissues, the lymphatic system, or blood cells-each playing crucial roles in vital bodily functions. In 2022, cancer accounted for roughly 9.7 million fatalities worldwide, with nearly 20 million new diagnoses reported. Among these, breast cancer stands out as one of the most common and life-threatening forms of cancer worldwide \[ 1 \].

## Breast cancer is a type of carcinoma and accounted for approximately 2.26 million

deaths in 2020, making it the leading cause of cancer-related fatalities among women. The impact of cancer extends beyond physical health, often leading to severe psychological distress and signiﬁcant socioeconomic burdens for affected individuals and their families. Therefore, it is imperative to understand and address these numerous dangers, fostering advancements in prevention and early detection to mitigate the impact of cancer on both individuals and society at large.

## The main contributions of this work are as follows

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 545-560, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1> \_ 41 - D. Aarushi et al.

- Comparative Evaluation of Classical ML Algorithms: A systematic comparison of  Logistic Regression Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machines, and Artiﬁcial Neural Networks is conducted on the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset under consistent preprocessing and validation protocols. ii. Clinical Priority Metrics: Unlike many prior studies that emphasize accuracy alone, this study prioritizes recall for the malignant class and the F1 score, reﬂecting realworld medical priorities where minimizing false negatives is crucial. iii. Practical Deployment Assessment: Beyond predictive performance, the work evaluates models in terms of computational cost, training/inference time, and scalability, providing insights into their feasibility for real-world diagnostic support systems. iv. Discussion of Broader Issues: The study expands on key methodological concerns often overlooked in benchmark studies, including class imbalance handling strategies (e.g., SMOTE, cost-sensitive learning) and generalization challenges when applying models trained on a single dataset to diverse clinical populations.

This study demonstrates that lightweight machine learning models, particularly linear SVMs, can provide accurate and efﬁcient tools for breast cancer detection. By prioritizing malignant-case recall and computational feasibility, the approach supports early diagnosis, clinician trust, and deployment in resource-limited settings. While further validation on diverse populations is needed, the work contributes toward more equitable and accessible AI-driven healthcare solutions.

## 2 **Literature Review **

Currently used cutting-edge methods for breast cancer detection use machine learning and deep learning tools with a wide array of modalities as input. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as well as X-ray imaging methods such as mammography, Computed Tomography (CT) and tabular patient-speciﬁc attributional data are some commonly used modalities. \[ 2 \] Research has shown that many machine learning methods like Linear Regression, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Naïve Bayes Classiﬁer provide an acceptable accuracy with problem statements involving breast cancer detection.

\[ 3 \] reports a 95.673% accuracy using Quest Decision Trees and a 99.976% matching ratio using Radial Basis Function (RBF) SVM on the Wisconsin breast cancer dataset. This exploration showcases a comparative study of other decision tree algorithms as well, these algorithms include C&R, CHAID and C5.0. The paper also proposes different methods of data imputation for each algorithm of decision trees and evaluates the ability to handle missing values. A predictive model for assessing breast cancer risk, utilizing Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms, achieving accuracy rates of 74.73% and 73.63%, respectively is proposed in \[ 4 \]. The paper explores these algorithms on a total of 275 instances with 12 features. The author utilizes standard scaling techniques such including normalization and standardization as a preprocessing step. The performance of an enhanced version of XGBoost is also compared to standard ML algorithms on the same dataset.

In the study conducted by \[ 5 \], breast cancer data was subjected to classiﬁcation analysis. An ensemble model was systematically devised in the course of this research, leveraging Bayesian networks and Radial Basis Function. The amalgamation of these distinct

Optimized Breast Cancer Detection: Evaluating Machine Learning

classiﬁer types resulted in a notably high classiﬁcation accuracy, reaching a maximum performance level of 97.42%. \[ 6 \] employed various supervised learning methodologies when analyzing the Wisconsin dataset. Among these techniques, artiﬁcial neural networks (ANN) exhibited the highest accuracy, achieving a noteworthy precision rate of 98.57%. The paper experiments with learning rate values ranging from 0.01 to 0.5 and the number of hidden layers ranging from 5-15, all possible combinations are tested for a total of 1000 epochs. The most complex, deepest network does not have the highest accuracy, rather the best performing ANN with the highest accuracy and lowest error is the 5 hidden-layered ANN with a learning rate of 0.01.

\[ 7 \] utilizes a Deep Neural Network with inception layers alongside a linear SVM classiﬁer on thermal images obtained from Research Data Base (DMR). The paper also explores tumor area extraction using OpenCV methods such as optimal thresholding and a combinatory algorithm as a preprocessing step. The thermal images are ﬁrst preprocessed to ﬁt the DNN, passed through to obtain features and then passed through a neural network SVM model which produces and output classifying the given image as cancerous or normal. A CNN to learn the features for the classiﬁcation of a breast mass was applied in \[ 8 \]. In comparison with the hand-crafted feature extraction methods, this model showed an increment in terms of AUC from 79.9% to 84%. \[ 9 \] demonstrated a comparative study on VGG-16 and ResNet50 for benign and malignant classiﬁcation of Mammogram images, the results portrayed VGG with a higher accuracy at 94% compared to the 91% accuracy of the ResNet.

\[ 10 \] utilizes thermal imagining of breasts; these images are resized to a 228 x 228pixel size and are then passed through a conventional U-Net in order to segment out breast-speciﬁc regions. The output regions of the U-Net are passed through a deep neural network which classiﬁes them into one of two classes: abnormal and normal. The up and down convolutions in the U-Net and the concatenated versions help in feature extraction. The authors of the paper justify the use of a U-Net due to its computationally low cost and a smaller number of parameters and thus faster training speed. The accuracy obtained with the aforementioned architecture is 99.33%, other metrics include the sensitivity value which is 100%, and a speciﬁcity value of 98.67%. The use of microwave-based imaging to detect breast cancer at initial stage and its consequences for clinical practice were discussed in \[ 11 \].

\[ 13 \] compared six ML algorithms including SVM, Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), reporting that all achieved over 90% test accuracy, with MLP scoring approximately 99.04%. \[ 14 \] analyzed SVM, Bayesian Logistic Regression, and KNN, concluding that SVM delivered the best performance. In \[ 15 \], the comparison across multiple datasets and algorithms were expanded including Logistic Regression, SVM, KNN, Random Forest, Naïve Bayes, and ANN and found KNN achieved 99% accuracy in Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset, followed by ensemble methods like RF.

## 3 **Data Source **

The dataset worked on is the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset from UCI machine learning repository. This dataset was originally curated by Dr. William Wolberg, an employee of Wisconsin Hospital \[ 12 \]. Imaging was performed needle-tip-wide breast - D. Aarushi et al.

masses with biopsy. The dataset was then annotated based on identiﬁable features and outcomes. The dataset consists of over 500 entries from a series of patients. Each patient is associated with a set of attributes pertaining to the characteristics of cell nuclei found in their corresponding image. The attributes include mean radius, mean texture, mean concavity, mean area etc. with a total of 30 features as given in Table 1.

The output column of the dataset is a binary variable diagnosis which classiﬁes the entry as either benign or malignant. There is a high inter-class imbalance as only 37% of breast masses are classiﬁed as malignant, this leaves room for various machine learning methods to be prone to overﬁtting to the majority class and misprediction test cases. Additionally, the high dimensionality and large amount of data creates a concern for computation requirements, which leaves room for preprocessing and experimentation using dimensionality reduction. This dataset seemed like the best contender for this paper as the objective was to publish a comparative study of different machine learning methods. The Wisconsin breast cancer dataset is a highly reputed, credible repository of information which has been experimented on with various deep learning and machine learning methods. However, this paper explores which method is best ﬁtting on a wider scale.

## 4 **Objectives and Limitations ** **4.1 ** **Objectives **

The primary objective is to evaluate various machine learning algorithms in the premise of binary classiﬁcation, keeping in mind the characteristics of the chosen dataset. The various models experimented with are logistic regression, support vector machines, principal component analysis, decision trees and artiﬁcial neural networks. Some important measures of accuracy evaluated against are the ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve and F1 score which is a measure of both precision and recall. Recall is a variable of most importance in medical scenarios as it evaluates false negatives which can prove to be detrimental in a medical diagnosis premise, thus this parameter has been given a higher importance. ROC is a visual indicator of the true positive and false positive rate at different decision thresholds; these parameters are important parameters in cross-validating models. Secondary objectives of this endeavor include:

**Visualization of Model Performance: ** In order to provide a complex, descriptive depiction of the model's outputs. This is a complex task in a case with thirty-two input features and one output feature. Conventional graphing methods do not accommodate a large number of features.

**Performance Evaluation on Train/Test Set Divisions: ** Partitioning a limited dataset into training, testing, and cross-validation subsets poses a formidable challenge, as the endeavor consideration to ensure the attainment of robust accuracy metrics. The inherent intricacies associated with this process necessitate a proper approach to strike a balance between data scarcity and the objective to generate reliable performance assessments.

## 4.2 **Limitations **

## The study predominantly concentrates on the binary classiﬁcation of diverse method

ologies applied to a tabular dataset, with limited exploration into the assessment of - D. Aarushi et al.

alternative modalities, such as MRI scans, mammography, and other imaging methods. Consequently, this paper does not evaluate deep learning strategies, thereby constraining the exploration of additional preprocessing methodologies. The primary emphasis lies in the realm of supervised machine learning methodologies, with a deliberate exclusion of unsupervised techniques, given the dataset's inherent suitability for the former. Despite the integration of both machine learning and deep learning approaches, it is acknowledged that deep learning methodologies, characterized by implicit feature extraction processes, are acknowledged as more advanced and are consequently preferred. Conversely, tabular datasets require professional annotations and validation procedures and are, in contemporary contexts, relatively less prevalent. It is pertinent to note that the current state-of-the-art methodologies encompass the utilization of diverse Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), such as VGG and residual networks, which, regrettably, remain unexplored within the conﬁnes of this paper. This is an endeavor that is elaborated on in the future works section.

Optimized Breast Cancer Detection: Evaluating Machine Learning **5.2 ** **Preprocessing **

In order to apply machine learning methods on the dataset, the data ﬁrst had to undergo preprocessing. Upon downloading, the CSV ﬁle was analyzed to obtain a brief infographic. The values of the different attributes indicate a wide range. Normalization of quantitative attributes is imperative due to their inherent expression in diverse measurements and scales. This process becomes essential for subsequent analysis, as it ensures a standardized framework for the treatment of such attributes. Another motivation for normalization is avoiding integer overﬂow and other python-speciﬁc constraints. Thus, this was a step performed in preprocessing. Another issue was dealing with dealing with null values. The dataset contained a total of 569 entries which is a very limited number. Thus, simple removing Null values was not appropriate. One option was to replace missing values using the mean; however, this is only applicable in Gaussian distributions. The mean is not a good measure of center in skewed datasets as outliers affect the value of the mean heavily and may bias the value towards a certain class outcome. The null values were found in the 'Smoothness Mean' attribute, which followed an approximately normal distribution (see Fig. 2 ); hence, the missing values were imputed using the mean.

Non-numeric values such as the diagnosis attribute were encoded as numbers as the numeric format was suited to the computation required in future steps. Columns such as Patient ID were dropped as all customers had unique values and there was no causation between this attribute and the output. The correlation matrix was employed to assess the interrelationships among the independent variables within the input dataset and their association with the output prediction. Subsequently, variables exhibiting a correlation coefﬁcient below 0.4 were systematically excluded from the retained set of input variables intended for logistic regression using stochastic gradient descent.

**Fig. 2. ** Normal Distribution of the 'Smoothness Mean' Attribute - D. Aarushi et al. **5.3 ** **Dimensionality Reduction (Using PCA) **

Dimensionality reduction using attribute elimination is done solely for logistic regression as it depends on a linear relationship between input features. This process is described in the Logistic Regression Using Stochastic Gradient Descent subsection.

Principle component analysis is a popular dimensionality technique that uses the covariance matrix and eigen values or a large set of features to transform them into a smaller set whilst retaining the variance in the original set. Dimensionality reduction helps speed up the training and testing process of algorithms that would previously take longer, it also makes it possible to visualize datasets with a high number of features. In order to decide the number of features to retain after applying PCA, the cumulative variance was evaluated for the dataset for a range of 1 to maximum possible features retained. Precision evaluates how many correct identiﬁcations are there in a class, a higher percentage implies that majority of the identiﬁcations were correct. Recall evaluates how many identiﬁcations were missed in a class, a high recall value is desirable for the Malignant class as it implies a lack of false negatives, i.e., not many malignant tumors were misclassiﬁed into benign. Precision values would ideally be high; however, it is relatively harmless if a benign tumor is detected as malignant as compared to a malignant tumor going undetected and untreated. Therefore, this paper puts utmost importance on this criterion. It is important to note that the dataset contains signiﬁcantly more classiﬁcations of the benign class, thus making it harder to obtain high precision and recall values for malignant.

## 5.7 **K-Nearest-Neighbor (KNN) **

## This is a supervised machine learning algorithm used for binary or multi-class classiﬁca

tion. It is a non-parametric, lazy learner that evaluates class similarity based on distance between intra-class points. In order to classify a new point, the algorithm evaluates the distance between all points in the training set and the new point, retaining the k closes points and declaring the point a part of the majority class. The distance can be evaluated using various formulae such as Euclidian distance, Manhattan distance etc. In this

The only hyperparameter necessary to compute was k, thus in order to ﬁnd obtain a model which showcased the best possible accuracy, the test accuracy obtained with different k values was evaluated. Optimized Breast Cancer Detection: Evaluating Machine Learning **5.9 ** **Artiﬁcial Neural Network **

Artiﬁcial Neural Networks (ANNs) are a more complex method of implementing supervised learning, they work based on a bioinspired design based on the functionality of neurons in the human brain. Inter and intra-layer connections as well as activation functions as well was the entire process of mapping inputs to outputs is based on different parts of a neuron such as dendrites, axons etc., ANNs process information through weighted connections, enabling them to learn complex patterns and relationships from data. An artiﬁcial neural network consists of an input layer, which is connected to a series of hidden layers, followed by a ﬁnal, output layer. The process of feeding in data is termed forward propagation; all weights and biases associated with the network are optimized using back propagation which uses a function of the different of predicted output and ground truth as well as hyperparameters such as the learning rate to modify outputs for a better accuracy. Figure 8 indicates the architecture of ANN used in this work.

(a) ANN Optimal Architecture used for Breast Cancer Detection (b) Classification report for ANN **Fig. 8. ** ANN Speciﬁcations

There were multiple experiments conducted on hyperparameters, many combinations of different number of layers, neurons per layer, activation functions etc. were used but this structure provided the highest accuracy. Each hidden layer uses the sigmoid activation function whereas the output layer has a sigmoid activation which produces a one-hot encoded vector that determines the class malignant or benign. The optimizer used is Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam), this optimizer applies RMSprop and uses momentum in gradient update equations. The ANN was trained for a total of 50 epochs on the metric accuracy. After the 50th epoch, the accuracy increased to 91.7% from a low 40.6% in the ﬁrst epoch. The ﬁnal loss was 0.2503. The following table details the accuracy metrics of the ANN. The precision and recall for the malignant class is relatively lower than the same for the benign class which is not ideal. The low recall for the malignant class also suggests a high number of false negatives which implies a lot of malignant tumors are going undetected and classiﬁed as benign, which is not ideal. The overall accuracy is up to part with the other machine learning methods.

SVM's ability to conform to non-linear decision boundaries was not required for this speciﬁc dataset as the attribute patterns were not as complex, even though the accuracy for RBF SVM was comparable to the linear version. The scope of this project is unfortunately related to the complexity of the dataset, while there are preexisting issues with the dataset such as low number of samples and a relatively higher-class imbalance, the complexity would increase drastically if the same values were collected from a larger population size from diverse regions. Perhaps it would be more challenging to attain high accuracy with simple machine learning methods. Another conclusion that can be drawn is that increasing the complexity of the algorithm does not always lead to better results. The SVM outperforms the multilayer perceptron ANN which follows complex optimization algorithms.

Ensuring that the observed performance differences were not due to random variation, statistical signiﬁcance testing was conducted. Ten-fold cross-validation was used to collect fold-wise performance metrics for each algorithm. A Friedman test revealed statistically signiﬁcant differences in performance across the four algorithms (p *\< * 0.001). Post-hoc pairwise comparisons (Nemenyi test) indicated that both SVM and KNN signiﬁcantly outperformed Logistic Regression (p *\< * 0.01), while the difference between SVM and KNN was not statistically signiﬁcant (p *\> * 0.05). This supports the conclusion that SVM and KNN are the most reliable models for this dataset, while Logistic Regression is comparatively weaker.

## 7 **Future Work **

One possible follow-up for this project is to explore deep learning methods for tumor detection, localization and classiﬁcation in comparison to OpenCV methods. This would explore the different imaging modalities available through different datasets. One additional challenge that would be pursued would be to separate breast mass from other parts of the body recorded in scans. The problem statement used in this paper can be combined with other medical premise problem statements such as tumor detection in brain scans, personality disorder classiﬁers etc. to create a full-stack medical project that performs disease detection and recommends subsequent actions.

Future research could extend this study in several directions. First, models should be validated on external and diverse datasets to assess generalization across populations. Second, advanced class imbalance handling methods, such as SMOTE variants or costsensitive learning, can be explored to further reduce false negatives. Third, combining tabular features with imaging modalities through multimodal and ensemble approaches may yield improved diagnostic performance. Finally, incorporating explainable AI - D. Aarushi et al.

## techniques will enhance clinical trust and support practical deployment in healthcare settings.

## A Comprehensive Review of Text-to-Multimodal **Generation Techniques **

Nakka Venkatesh 1( B ), Deviprasad Mishra 1, and Rajkumar Patra 2

1 Department of Computer Science and Engineering, CSVTU, Bhilai, India

venkatesh.n@cmrec.ac.in, dpmishra@bitdurg.ac.in 2 Department of Computer Science and Engineering, CMRTC, Hyderabad, Telangana, India

**Abstract. ** Text-to-Multimodal generation has been one of the groundbreaking areas in Generative AI where natural language commands are employed to create a wide range of multimodal outputs ranges from images, audios, videos, 3D and even 4D visualization model assets. This feature connects with the major improvements in deep learning frameworks, especially transformer-based architectures and diffusion models. It allows a model to create prompts for text-to-multimodal tasks using Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL) and Few-Shot Learning (FSL). As a result of both zero-shot and few-shot learning on the upswing, generative frameworks now ﬁnd it convenient to create high-quality generated multimodal outputs with minimal retraining. This paper offers an in-depth review of cutting-edge methods in text-to-multimodal generation, classifying current methods that not only focus on text to multimodal and also pivots on 3D and even 4D generation models. In this work, we address the different multimodal techniques like text-audio-video-3D by using different algorithms and Diffusion models by focusing the progression of models, and analyzing challenges and future directions in multimodal generation. The paper also promotes benchmarks, datasets, and metrics, along with discussing limitations of semantic misalignment, temporal consistency in multimodal, and domain generalization. Eventually, we lay out open challenges and future directions for research in scalable, semantically-aligned, and controllable text-to-multimodal generation.

**Keywords: ** Text-to-Multimodal · Diffusion models · Prompt Engineering · Zero Shot Learning · Few Shot Learning · Generative Adversarial Networks · Deep learning Models

## 1 **Introduction **

## In the new era of generation Text-to-Multimodal generation has a signiﬁcant impact

in Generative AI. The ability to fabricate multimodal content from natural language descriptions is reshaping creative industries, education, simulation, and human-computer interaction. Multimodal learning combines different types of data, like text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-audio. In the era of Text-to-Multimodal (T2M) generation \[ 1 \], the goal is to create clear images, videos and audio sequences that capture the meaning of natural language inputs. Modern AI systems can translate natural language into diverse

modalities, encompassing text, image, audio, and video. This extends a great immerse in the ﬁeld of generative AI. Ongoing improvements, especially with diffusion models \[ 2, 3 \] and contrastive learning methods, has allowed for the creation of content that is rich in meaning and also suitable for its environment. To overcome the difﬁculty of data scarcity, zero-shot learning (ZSL) and few-shot learning (FSL) have become important strategies. These allow models to apply what they learn from the new tasks without requiring a lot of retraining or large labeled datasets. Traditionally, T2M generation relied on supervised learning methods that required large annotated datasets, like paired text-video and textaudio collections, to train generative models for creating contents based on prompts. Although these methods produce encouraging outcomes, their utility is limited by access to varied labeled datasets and the huge computational expense of training intricate models like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) \[ 4 \], Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) \[ 5 \], and Transformer- based models \[ 6 \]. Over recent years ago, zero-shot learning and few-shot learning schemes are empirically validated as extremely effective ways of overcoming data deﬁciency and enhancing model scalability. Zero-shot learning (ZSL) allows models to transfer to unseen concepts and produce corresponding modal without having seen examples, by utilizing pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP \[ 7 \] that encode textual and visual information into a shared semantic structure Few-shot learning(FSL) methods supplement this by allowing by considering fewer examples for quick adaptation to novel domains or infrequent concepts using light weight ﬁne-tuning strategies such as Low- Rank Adaptation \[ 8 \] (LoRA) and adapter layers that heavily minimize training time and computational requirements. This review paper focus on presenting an in-depth survey of techniques that maximizeT2M generation via few-shot learning and zero-shot learning with multimodal generation techniques incorporating with cutting-edge architectures, bench- marks, metrics, and signiﬁcant challenges and for large-scale and semantically consistent multimodal synthesis. Text to Multimodal can also generates by focusing on Transfer learning and large language Models (LLM) that provides rich semantic representations of textual input prompts. This paper also aims to synthesize the latest breakthroughs with the goal of promoting more generalizable, efﬁcient, and controllable on text, audio, video and 3D generation techniques for realworld applications in education, E-Commerce, Health care, entertainment and digital content creation.

Text-to-4D is a trendy topic in research, aimed at converting natural language descriptions to dynamic 3D scenes, which evolve over time. In contrast to Text-to-3D models \[ 30 \], which generate unanimous objects or environments. Text-to-4D generation \[ 33 \], a coherent model of space geometry and motion, is used to generate temporally coherent animated data: human in motion, animals, vehicles, and scene changes. Diffusion modelbased modern techniques, neural radiance ﬁelds (NeRFs), motion priors and Gaussian splatting to generate natural 4D images from the text prompt. The salient challenges are to preserve temporal coherence, i.e., objects are displayed in a consistent visual manner through time, and ﬁne-grained motion control is excellent to handle complex text instructions. The latest techniques such as Text4D, 4D-fusion and AnimateDiff-3D have also yielded positive ﬁndings, but, semantic consistency, computational expense and scalability are still issues to be addressed. Text-to-4D generation holds broad applications for AR/VR content creation, gaming, cinematic animation, robot simulation, and digital twins. For this area to be more applicable, researchers are investigating multimodal transfer learning by correlating text with 3D and video data, hence the major requirement for large-scale 4D datasets. Overall, text-to-4D \[ 33 \] generation is a big leap towards more multimodal AI, although real-time, high-quality, and controllable generation remains an open challenge \[ 33 \].

## 3 **Methodology **

The suggested methodology will seek to enhance Text-to-Multimodal generation using a combination of zero-shot and few-shot paradigms to enable scalable and semantically aligned multimodal synthesis. The method leverages large-scale pre-trained visionlanguage models like CLIP \[ 7 \], which provide a robust semantic embedding space that aligns textual and visual representations. The main idea is to use pre-trained models for zero-shot multimodal generation. This allows for the creation of outputs from new textual prompts without needing to retrain on speciﬁc datasets. To maintain time coherence and frame consistency, the method combines transformer-based temporal modeling with diffusion probabilistic models. These models produce multimodal frames sequentially with the good results. A temporal reasoning module provides the concepts of motion, frames and scene changes. Zero-shot learning technique is good at generalizing to the - Venkatesh et al.

new prompts, but tends to fail at speciﬁc or Anomalous concepts. In order to address this issue, the architecture employs few-shot learning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and adapter layers. The approach enables effective ﬁne-tuning of pre-trained models on small multimodal datasets. The sparsity-based adaptation reduces computational resources and training time as well as enhancing quality of output and coherence of meaning. Moreover, quick engineering techniques are used to regulate features of action, composition of scenes and styles by structuring the input text, as well as through conditioning systems. The last pipeline provides the compromise between broad generalization and speciﬁc accuracy by the use of zero-shot learning with rapid domain adaptation with the help of few-shot ﬁne-tuning technique. The framework also favors both general-purpose and customization functionality. Evaluation takes place on benchmark datasets using Frechet Video Distance (FVD), CLIP-based semantic similarity, and measures of temporal consistency. Moreover, transfer learning and large language models enhance the meanings of textual prompts. Overall, this approach improves existing methods by providing a scalable, efﬁcient, and meaning-consistent Text-to-Multimodal (T2M) system suitable for real-world applications like content creation, education, and entertainment.

## 5 **Future Directions **

The Text-to-Multimodal generation with zero-shot and few-shot learning has achieved signiﬁcant results, yet there are some unresolved questions which can be explored in the future research. Improving temporal consistency and realism is one of the key directions, long-length videos are a break point in Text-to-Video generation methods. Existing models are prone to ﬂickering artifacts and motion that is incoherent with long sequences. The partial or inappropriate output with the multimodal modalities (e.g. mismatched objects, inconsistent colors, or lack of spatial relations) is still produced by the current models. These issues may be overcome by the addition of deep temporal attention mechanisms to be improved and even to Text-to-3D generation methods a Centre of attention with the 3D diffusion architectures.

Multimodal transfer learning using previous knowledge of large pre-trained models on other modalities to adapt the efﬁcient cross model generation with limited new data and Multimodal transfer learning Multimodal transfer learning is another promising direction of Text-to-Multimodal generation, in addition to providing rich semantic representations of the textual input prompts. The multimodal feedback integration during the generation systems is the Text-to-Multimodal generation techniques. Fineness of style, movement and content enabling ﬁner control Multimodal generation technique: In case of Multimodal generation technique, the text prompts may be integrated with other sources like sketch, sound or reference image to give longer control of style, movement and content which can be adjusted to a more customized and detailed multimodal synthesis. In addition, Generated videos can be subject to ﬂickering, morphing objects or temporally inconsistent scene layout, and occupies massive amounts of GPU memory and takes many hours to train. The multimodal content that is generated is likely to spread bias, misinformation and copyright infringements. In order to overcome these difﬁculties the diffusion models may be applied with time attention to restore the level of consistency and as well as formulate the human-in-the-loop grading system consisting of the subjective and automotive grading to include watermarking techniques to check AI generated works.

Besides, we are able to apply the concept of dynamic prompt engineering and instruction tuning to enhance zero-shot. This method makes models comprehend abstract or - Venkatesh et al.

## complex prompts better. Nevertheless, there is still a big problem with improving eval

uation metrics of T2M. Semantic alignment, originality, and narrative coherence cannot be completely comprehended in the present measurements. Stronger, user-friendly, and work-speciﬁc assessment systems may evolve by means of the reinforcement learning based on human feedback. Lastly, it is essential to make multimodal generation to be ethically, explainable and controllable in order to deploy it responsibly. Bias, misuse of deepfake creation and privacy issues need to be tackled. It is also important to come up with systems that aid accountability, transparency, and user approval in generative applications.

It emphasizes the transformation of the ﬁeld by zero-shot and fewshot learning methods by commenting on efﬁcient, scalable and coherent text, audio, and video generation with limited supervision. Pre-trained vision-language models together with diffusion-based methods and good adaptation, like LoRA, have taken a huge stride in the creation of coherent video in reply to text. ## Generative AI as a Cyber Weapon: Synthetic **Identity Fraud and Phishing at Scale **

Praveen Kumar Maroju 1( B ) and Lakshmi Narasimha Raju Mudunuri 2

1 QA Lead Architect, Clientserver Technology Solutions, San Antonio, TX, USA

praveenkumar.maroju@gmail.com 2 Valero Energy Corporation, Senior Business systems Design Specialist-Reﬁning systems, Information Services, San Antonio, TX, USA

**Abstract. ** Due to its blistering development process, generative artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) has come out of the sphere of creativity and entered the evil ecosystem of cybercrime. In a generative AI, this paper investigates how it can be weaponized to make synthetic identity fraud and phishing factories possible on a scale. With the help of the sophisticated natural language processing (NLP) models cybercriminals may create realistic personas, create realistic-looking documents and craft texts of their phishing emails speciﬁcity, which considerably leads to the success of the attacks. This study makes a review of relevant studies and pulls out the technical details of the mechanisms, the workﬂows of operations and case studies on practical application of AI driven cyberattacks. The approach includes a comparison between textual contents of AI-generated and human-created fraudulent messages and an inquiry into the phishing data sets en masse. Output shows that the AI-ampliﬁed assaults are more linguistically genuine, scalable, and perform evasion over the conventional detection mechanisms. However, there are limitations on the data availability, on cost of computational inconveniences to the adversaries, and on dependency on training data which can provide detectable patterns. The AI-related countermeasures, real-time anomaly detection, and regulatory systems on the international front should be examined in the future to diminish the abuse and maintain useful applications of AI.

**Keywords: ** Generative AI · Cybersecurity · Synthetic Identity Fraud · Phishing · Deepfake Documents · Large Language Models · AI-Enabled Attacks · Social Engineering

## 1 **Introduction **

## The past ten years have been a breakthrough in the world of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI),

more speciﬁcally, generative models. The architecture developed with large language models (LLMs), transformer-based model, and multimodal generative systems can now be used to generate text that reads like a human wrote it by creating very realistic images and voices and even creating deepfake videos \[ 1 \]. Even though its innovations have expedited capability in education, health care, entertainment, and automation, it has also inadvertently increased the set of tools which may be employed in cyberspace by a

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026 - Virdee et al. (Eds.): ICAIN 2025, LNNS 1931, pp. 573-585, 2026.  <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-23314-1\_43> P.K. Maroju and L.N.R. Mudunuri

malicious actor. It is this dual-use characteristic of generative AI that plays into a bigger cybersecurity issue: the weaponization of AI as a tool of mass synthetic identity fraud and phishing.

Their standard ways of conducting cybercrime, e.g. phishing emails, social engineering, identity theft are traditionally based on manual input and proﬁciency in languages, as well as the availability of stolen personal information. These also restricted scalability and customization of assaults. These drawbacks are quickly fading with the introduction of generative AI into the equation. Threat actors are now able to create realistic phishing emails in variety of languages, generate relevant supporting documentation to support fraudulent accounts, and align their communications language to the targeted psychology. Such capabilities powered by AI make operations possible in speed, volume and degree of personalization hitherto unachievable \[ 5 \].

One pain point that has constantly bedeviled ﬁnancial institutions, healthcare systems, and governmental departments has been synthetic identity fraud whereby fraudsters mix and create fabricated data with driblets of genuine data. Generative AI takes this to the next level and creates convincing identity documents, deep-fake proﬁle photos and even artiﬁcial payment histories that can pass through automation-based veriﬁcation mechanisms. Likewise, phishing, which is already the leading of the most used and economically momentous cyberattacks in existence, progressively will become even more dynamic with messages customized by AI to sound and appear like the organization and prevent repetitive patterns that get it ﬂagged as spam.

This work is motivated by the fact that AI tools are becoming available to a broader range of actors which are not necessarily technical. The availability of free-access deepfake production platforms and the advent of open-source large language models, as well as cheap computing resources, have triggered a lower barrier of entry to the advanced cyberattacks orchestration process. Such democratization of powerful AI would pose immediate questions to strategies of cybersecurity defenses, legal structures and relations among countries. That risk can no longer simply be attributed to state-sponsored actors or highly skilled hackers AI has made scalable cybercrime capabilities available to a much wider group of people \[ 4 \].

This paper aims at giving a structured review of the potential of generative AI as a cyber weapon, with an emphasis on two large areas of threats: synthetic identity fraud and scale phishing. The research is aimed at:

- Technical mechanisms that allow AI-based identity fabrication and phishing campaigns to occur should be analyzed.  - Measure the effectiveness of AI-generated attacks against conventional attacks that  humans create in relation to authenticity, scalability, and evasion rates. - Outline the weaknesses of the AI-based cybercrime to know where the existing  security reigns. - Design workable and policy-oriented countermeasures able to tame the emerging  risks, and at the same time does not strangle right AI innovation.

In so doing, the paper intends to reconcile the referred stake of AI research and operational cybersecurity but also offers a threat assessment and a game plan on how to combat it \[ 3 \]. Generative AI as a Cyber Weapon: Synthetic Identity Fraud

The study is an extension of earlier work in fraud recognition, adversarial AI, and social engineering but it stands out in its experimental simulation of artiﬁcially intelligent attack method yet applying it through actual dataset of phishing attacks. The insight gained in this hybrid approach does not just quantify the effectiveness of the increased AI-generated cyberattacks but also determines which vulnerabilities of the attacks can be exploited by defenders \[ 10, 11 \]. **1.1 ** **Novelty and contribution **

Although the misuse of generative AI has been covered in recent literature, it presented rather theoretical material, covering either hypothetical cases or general ethical issues \[ 6 \]. The present work presents three important novelty aspects that make it stand out against other studies:

1. Empirical Benchmarking of AI-Generated Cyberattacks Empirical analysis of cyberattacks generated with AI This evaluation is a side-by-side comparison where the AI  generates cyberattacks and compares them to those created by humans in the context of synthetic identities and phishing messages. The testing consists of linguistic plausibility scores, spam scanner thwarting rates, and such rates of evading automatic identity detection mechanisms. 2. Integrated Threat Pipeline Simulation- The study simulates the entire theatrics of an  AI powered attack, including gathering data and creating identities, phishing message development and delivery. This type of end-to-end simulation can provide a more realistic picture as to how generative AI can be turned into operationalized malicious actors. 3. Two-pronged Technical and Policy Mitigation Response - The study proposes not  only technical mitigation responses (e.g., adversarial AI defenders, watermarking), but also to provide a two-pronged proposal response of governance (e.g. cross-border cybercrime treaties, AI provenance laws) to deeply cut an extensive system mitigation system.

The main contributions of this Work can be described as the following:

- A quantitative comparison of performance where messages synthesized via AI  demonstrated up to 32 percent more spam ﬁlters evasion compared to manuallycrafted messages and an AI-generated synthetic identity evaded automatic veriﬁcation in 38 percent of the tests performed. - Awareness of the constraints that the realization of AI-enabled cyberattacks is facing  today like the need to use stolen template data to perform high-quality forgeries of documents. - Creating a template threat modiﬁcation model that is built uniquely to match the  misuse of generative AI, and can be adopted by cybersecurity practitioners and policy makers. - Strategic actions to recommend to AI content provenance tracking and adversarial  AI countermeasures oriented to strike a balance between innovation and security.

This complement of empirical results, technical modeling, and practical mitigation measures provides a richness not only to academic discussion but also to direct
